nodes.label: Veronica Strong-Boag
nodes.date_label: The Parliament of Women (1976) · Rethinking Canada (1986) · The New Day Recalled (1988) · Contested Space (1994)
nodes.description: In The New Day Recalled (1988), Strong-Boag argues that class differences did not displace the gender hierarchy shaping girls’ and women’s lives in interwar English Canada. Its modified life-course approach connects paid work, household labour, family and ageing. Patricia Rooke praised the research but criticized its empiricism and underdeveloped theoretical explanations. Strong-Boag’s co-edited Rethinking Canada began in 1986 with Anita Clair Fellman; the fourth edition (2002) was edited with Mona Gleason and Adele Perry. In her presidential address “Contested Space” (1994), she argued that historians must confront their own privilege and connect political history with the experiences of people excluded from national narratives. Her review of J. L. Granatstein (1999) defended inclusive national history while agreeing that history teaching needed support. Later books examined adoption and disadvantaged childhoods through intersecting inequalities.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Parliament of Women (1976); Rethinking Canada: The Promise of Women’s History (1986, co-edited with Anita Clair Fellman; fourth edition 2002, with Mona Gleason and Adele Perry); The New Day Recalled (1988); “Contested Space” (1994); Paddling Her Own Canoe (2000, with Carole Gerson); Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006); Fostering Nation? (2011).
nodes.scope_note: The New Day Recalled is known through Rooke’s complete review; the monographs and Rethinking Canada editions were not read in full. Selected primary passages of the 1994 address, the complete 1999 review, selected Sangster reprint passages, institutional bibliographies and the 2023 questionnaire were read. The 1992 co-authored reply and the 1996 labour-history exchange remain unread.

nodes.label: Alexandra Walsham
nodes.date_label: Church Papists 1993 · Providence 1999 · Charitable Hatred 2006 · Disenchantment reassessed 2008 · The Reformation of the Landscape 2011
nodes.description: In “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008), Alexandra Walsham argues that cycles of desacralization and resacralization better capture religious change than a linear account of disenchantment. The Reformation of the Landscape (2011) examines how religious change and physical places shaped one another, connecting confessional identities with collective memory. Keith Thomas praised its synthesis in his 2011 review but thought Walsham sometimes too eager to overturn conventional wisdom, questioning both continuing piety at eighteenth-century spas and the extent of Protestant myth-making. With Julia Crick, she also challenged a sharp division between manuscript and print (2004). Her later work treats reused religious objects as agents of memory and investigates how early modern record-keeping shaped the archives historians inherit.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Church Papists: Catholicism, Conformity and Confessional Polemic in Early Modern England (1993); Providence in Early Modern England (1999); The Uses of Script and Print, 1300–1700 (2004), coedited with Julia Crick, including their joint introduction; Charitable Hatred: Tolerance and Intolerance in England, 1500–1700 (2006); “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008); The Reformation of the Landscape: Religion, Identity, and Memory in Early Modern Britain and Ireland (2011); “History, Memory, and the English Reformation” (2012); Catholic Reformation in Protestant Britain (2014); “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), introductory essay; “Recycling the Sacred” (2017).

The 2004 introduction, 2016 archive essay and 2017 material-culture article were read in specified excerpts. Selected monographs, cited theoretical originals, and the rest of the edited collections remain unread.

nodes.label: Bettina Bradbury
nodes.date_label: Working Families (1993) · Negotiating Identities, with Tamara Myers (2005) · Wife to Widow (2011)
nodes.description: In Working Families (1993), Bettina Bradbury argues that Montreal working-class survival depended on children's earnings and women's unpaid work as well as men's wages. She treats the household as a place of support and inequality, linking class formation to age, gender and the family life cycle. Joan Sangster credits her family-economy studies with helping recast working-class history; Cynthia Comacchio praises the integration of class and gender but questions how historians can distinguish deliberate family strategies from emergency coping. Wife to Widow (2011) follows women's transition into widowhood through law, property, religion and politics. With Tamara Myers, she also framed Negotiating Identities (2005) around the spaces between formal politics and family life.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Canadian Family History: Selected Readings (1992, editor); Working Families: Age, Gender, and Daily Survival in Industrializing Montreal (1993); Familles ouvrières à Montréal (1995, translated by Christiane Teasdale); Negotiating Identities in Nineteenth- and Twentieth-Century Montreal (2005, co-edited with Tamara Myers); Wife to Widow: Lives, Laws, and Politics in Nineteenth-Century Montreal (2011).

nodes.label: Deborah Cohen
nodes.date_label: The War Come Home (2001) · Comparison and History, co-edited (2004) · Household Gods (2006) · Family Secrets (2013)
nodes.description: Deborah Cohen argues in Household Gods: The British and their Possessions (2006) that religious values helped make domestic consumption respectable and that possessions became a means of expressing individuality. In Family Secrets (2013), she traces the changing relationship between secrecy and privacy in British families, showing how everyday negotiations could change social norms. Both books won the American Historical Association's Forkosch Prize. In the 2014 History Workshop roundtable, Matt Houlbrook praised Family Secrets' intellectual reach but questioned whether histories built from revealed secrets can capture those that never become visible. Her methodological essay ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001) examines the explanatory costs of comparison, including the difficulty of separating causes from context. With Peter Mandler, she challenged the evidence and claims about historical scale and public relevance in Jo Guldi and David Armitage's The History Manifesto in 2015.

nodes.label: Joyce Appleby
nodes.date_label: Economic Thought and Ideology (1978) · Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) · Telling the Truth about History, with Hunt and Jacob (1994) · Inheriting the Revolution (2000)
nodes.description: In Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984), Joyce Appleby argued that Jeffersonian Republicans envisioned a society of economically enterprising and politically equal individuals. Expanding commercial agriculture gave substance to that vision, making capitalism part of their challenge to inherited authority. Her Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978) had examined changing understandings of commerce and market forces. Wood’s 2000 review places her liberal Jefferson against the republican synthesis associated with Pocock, who disputed that characterization of his position. Wood praised the breadth of Inheriting the Revolution (2000) while questioning its chronology and explanation of change; Bushman, noting that its autobiographers were those with successful lives to write about, warned that readers might be drawn into the exuberance of liberal ideology and mistake it for the whole truth. With Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob, Appleby coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994). Chakrabarty’s 1997 engagement used that book to ask what kinds of past remain outside a discipline organized around shared rational standards of evidence. In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby defended evidentiary constraint while urging historians to explain interpretation and revision to the public.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978); Capitalism and a New Social Order: The Republican Vision of the 1790s (1984); Liberalism and Republicanism in the Historical Imagination (1992); Telling the Truth about History, with Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob (1994); Inheriting the Revolution: The First Generation of Americans (2000); The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism (2010).
nodes.scope_note: Selected primary web passages from “The Power of History” read, alongside publisher descriptions, Jacob’s biographical account, and selected Wood, Pocock, Chakrabarty, Cannadine and Bushman passages. Complete monographs, most cited underlying works, and the Harlan response are unread. Cannadine’s PDF text was readable; the attempted page-image check failed.

nodes.label: Maxine Berg
nodes.date_label: The Age of Manufactures (1985; second edition 1994) · A Woman in History (1996) · Luxury and Pleasure (2005)
nodes.description: Maxine Berg argues that industrialisation grew through varied forms of manufacture and the labour of women and families, rather than being adequately explained by factories and aggregate growth alone, in The Age of Manufactures (1985; revised 1994). Luxury and Pleasure in Eighteenth-Century Britain (2005) connects Asian luxury imports, demand among middling consumers and new products to industrialisation. Joyce Burnette noted its attention to consumer goods often ignored in accounts of the Industrial Revolution. With Pat Hudson, Berg also challenged aggregate measures of industrial change and later argued that slave-based Atlantic demand stimulated skills and innovation. A Woman in History (1996) recovered Eileen Power’s comparative economic history and examined its gendered remembrance. Helen Mellor praised the biography but questioned whether its medieval-history chapter adequately established Power’s historical achievement; Berg answered that collaborative work and comparative method mattered beyond major monographs.

nodes.label: Kathy Peiss
nodes.date_label: Cheap Amusements (1986) · Hope in a Jar (1998) · Zoot Suit (2011) · Information Hunters (online 2019; print 2020)
nodes.description: In Cheap Amusements (1986), Kathy Peiss argued that young working women’s leisure and sexual expressiveness helped create commercial mass culture in turn-of-the-century New York. Hope in a Jar (1998) showed how women as beauty entrepreneurs and users of cosmetics helped build American beauty culture, combining opportunities for self-definition with new constraints. Marybeth Hamilton praised Cheap Amusements as a contribution to women’s labour history but criticized its romanticizing tone and insufficient engagement with reformers’ objections to commercial leisure. In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss used gender analysis to question histories that treated business as naturally masculine and women chiefly as workers or consumers. Her later historiographical essay, Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), assessed the gains and limits of the gender turn, questioning inconsistent definitions of gender and recurring explanations based on masculine crisis.

nodes.label: Kristin L. Hoganson
nodes.date_label: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) · Consumers’ Imperium (2007) · The Heartland (2019) · Crossing Empires, with Jay Sexton (2020)
nodes.description: In Fighting for American Manhood (1998), Kristin L. Hoganson argues that ideals of masculine citizenship and political leadership helped propel the United States into the Spanish-American and Philippine-American wars. Consumers’ Imperium (2007) brings empire into the household, showing how affluent white women’s consumption of foreign goods helped form a sense of global entitlement. Christopher Endy praised the latter book’s account of women’s place in globalization, while Mary Renda asked for a more precise chronology and stronger links to political, military and economic events; Mari Yoshihara wanted more attention to the people who shaped consumer choices. In her response, Hoganson defended domestic consumption as a manifestation of empire while acknowledging that she had not established direct links between particular consumer groups and policy decisions. The Heartland (2019) challenges the presumed isolation of the rural Midwest; Crossing Empires (2020), coedited with Jay Sexton, places U.S. history within relations among empires.

nodes.label: Jean Barman
nodes.date_label: Growing Up British (1984) · The West Beyond the West (1991; third edition 2007) · “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98) · French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014)
nodes.description: Jean Barman’s The West Beyond the West (1991; third edition 2007) offered an inclusive synthesis of British Columbia’s history. Chris Arnett (2021) describes it as replacing Margaret Ormsby’s Eurocentric 1958 survey with a history in which more people could recognize their place. R. Scott Sheffield (2022) praised the survey but found its Second World War coverage brief and its conclusions about the war’s impact necessarily general. In French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women in the Making of the Pacific Northwest (2014), Barman argues that French Canadian fur-trade workers and the Indigenous women in their lives helped shape the region across the later Canada–United States border, challenging narratives written from the perspectives of those in charge. Heather Devine praised its integration of statistics and individual stories in her BC Studies review (2015/16). “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98) examines how colonial power sexualized Indigenous women’s agency, and criticizes even valued histories for treating male sources and subjects as the whole story. Her earlier educational history studied private schooling and racial inequality in education.

nodes.label: Theda Skocpol
nodes.date_label: States and Social Revolutions (1979) · Bringing the State Back In, co-edited (1985) · Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) · Diminished Democracy (2003)
nodes.description: In States and Social Revolutions (1979), Theda Skocpol argues that revolutions require an explanation combining state structures, international pressures and class relations. Comparing France, Russia and China, she places states’ administrative and coercive organizations at the centre of the account rather than treating them as expressions of class interests. William H. Sewell Jr. praised the comparison but challenged its treatment of ideology; Skocpol acknowledged that her account had been too cursory while questioning his alternative conception of culture. Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) shifted attention to American social policy, tracing veterans’ pensions and women’s organized reform. Linda Gordon disputed its handling of gender, and Skocpol challenged Gordon’s assessment of the scholarship. Marisa Chappell’s retrospective describes the book as influential for women’s and gender historians while identifying its limited treatment of race. Diminished Democracy (2003) examines the replacement of participatory associations by professionally managed civic organizations.

nodes.label: Alice Kessler-Harris
nodes.date_label: Out to Work (1982) · A Woman’s Wage (1990) · In Pursuit of Equity (2001) · Gendering Labor History (2007)
nodes.description: In In Pursuit of Equity (2001), Alice Kessler-Harris argues that gendered assumptions about breadwinning and family dependence shaped apparently fair employment and welfare policies, limiting women’s economic citizenship. Out to Work (1982) traces the transformation of women’s work into paid labour, examining how class, race, ethnicity and assumptions about wage-earning and family roles shaped that process. A Woman’s Wage (1990; updated edition 2014) examines how disputes over minimum wages, equal pay and comparable worth produce and challenge gendered social values. Gendering Labor History (2007) brings together her interventions on unions, gender, class and social policy. Reviewing that collection in 2009, Francisca de Haan praises its account of gender and class while calling its proposal to share or socialize household care perhaps utopian. The criticism qualifies that proposal rather than rejecting the collection’s historical analysis.

Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar; In Pursuit of Equity (2001); Gendering Labor History (2007); A Difficult Woman (2012).

nodes.label: Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore
nodes.date_label: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) · Jumpin’ Jim Crow (coedited, 2000) · Defying Dixie (2008) · These United States (with Thomas J. Sugrue, 2015)
nodes.description: In Gender and Jim Crow (1996), Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore argued that educated Black women sustained political activism after Black men’s disfranchisement in North Carolina, using reform work and interracial contacts to exercise influence beyond electoral politics. Defying Dixie (2008) traced the radical, interracial and international struggles of 1919–1950 that preceded the better-known civil-rights movement. Gender and Jim Crow won the Frederick Jackson Turner Award and James A. Rawley Prize. Wali Rashash Kharif praised its recovery of Black women’s organizing but argued that it needed a fuller account of slavery’s legacy. David J. Garrow praised Defying Dixie’s treatment of white moderation while criticizing its speculation about earlier court-ordered desegregation and its allocation of responsibility for the Southern left’s defeat.

nodes.label: Mary L. Dudziak
nodes.date_label: Desegregation as a Cold War Imperative (1988) · Cold War Civil Rights (2000) · Exporting American Dreams (2008) · War Time (2012)
nodes.description: In Cold War Civil Rights: Race and the Image of American Democracy (2000), Mary L. Dudziak argued that international criticism of American racism helped move the federal government toward civil rights reform. The Cold War also limited reform: anticommunism marginalized broader challenges to racial and economic inequality, while concern for national prestige could favor appearances over substantive change. Eric Arnesen’s 2002 review praised the account of federal image management but asked for stronger evidence of its effects on overseas audiences and closer analysis of the political alternatives being suppressed. Exporting American Dreams (2008) followed Thurgood Marshall between American civil rights and Kenya’s constitutional transition. War Time (2012) questioned the assumption that war is a temporary exception, arguing that this framing licenses extraordinary powers amid persistent military engagement. Eric A. Posner’s 2012 review disputed the empirical support for linking expectations of temporary war to acceptance of curtailed liberties. Dudziak’s work joins legal, African American and international history through specific connections between domestic institutions and global politics.

nodes.label: Tina Loo
nodes.date_label: Making Law, Order, and Authority (1994) · Making Good, with Carolyn Strange (1997) · States of Nature (2006) · Moved by the State (2019)
nodes.description: In States of Nature (2006), Tina Loo argues that Canadian wildlife conservation expanded state authority and marginalized customary uses, while rural people and private organizations remained major conservation actors. Conservation was also a struggle over social values and the remaking of rural Canada. The book won the Canadian Historical Association’s principal book prize in 2007 and the Harold Adams Innis Prize in 2008. Her earlier books include Making Law, Order, and Authority in British Columbia, 1821–1871 (1994). With Carolyn Strange, Making Good (1997) examined law and moral regulation; Christopher English, reviewing it for undergraduate readers, found its survey clear but said the link between the family and the reformers' goals was 'not made explicit.' Moved by the State (2019) examines forced relocation within postwar projects of welfare and development, including the disciplinary effects of participation. Fred Burrill credits its recovery of rural agency but argues that its attention to officials’ intentions misses patterns of white supremacy and gives too little weight to Inuit assessments.

nodes.label: Susan Sontag
nodes.date_label: Against Interpretation (1966) · On Photography (1977) · Illness as Metaphor (1978) · Regarding the Pain of Others (2003)
nodes.description: In On Photography (1977), Susan Sontag argues that photographs shape what people consider worth seeing and turn the world into objects of possession and apparent knowledge. In Regarding the Pain of Others (2003), she questions the assumption that images of suffering produce a shared response: captions, political commitments and viewers’ positions shape what they see. Her earlier “Against Interpretation,” collected in 1966, challenges criticism that excavates hidden meanings at the expense of art’s visible form. Illness as Metaphor (1978) examines how historically changing images of disease burden patients with fear and shame. These arguments became objects of debate. Medical historian Barbara Clow’s 2001 response argues that North American cancer experiences did not predictably produce the silence and disgrace Sontag described.

nodes.label: Susan G. Pedersen
nodes.date_label: Family, Dependence (1993) · Eleanor Rathbone (2004) · Settler Colonialism, coedited (2005) · The Guardians (2015)
nodes.description: In Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993), Susan Pedersen argues that welfare policies in Britain and France were shaped by gender relations and support for dependent family members as well as class politics, with different consequences for wages and citizenship. In The Guardians (2015), she argues that the League of Nations mandates system changed imperial sovereignty by subjecting colonial rule to international scrutiny and petitioning, helping make statehood possible without simply improving colonial government. Her work connects comparative welfare history, feminism and the history of international institutions. Eleanor Rathbone and the Politics of Conscience (2004) places feminist social reform within parliamentary and imperial politics; the collection coedited with Caroline Elkins (2005) treats settler colonialism comparatively. The Guardians won the Cundill Prize in 2015.

nodes.label: Lynn Abrams
nodes.date_label: The Orphan Country (1998) · Myth and Materiality (2005) · Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) · Feminist Lives (2023)
nodes.description: Lynn Abrams argues in Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) that oral testimony must be interpreted as a communicative encounter: historians need to ask how and why a story is told as well as what it reports. The work connects interviewing with the analysis of memory, narrative and relations between interviewer and narrator. Ronald J. Grele’s 2011 review praised its broad synthesis while noting its limited engagement with folklore. Abrams’s Feminist Lives (2023) asks how a postwar generation of British women made autonomous selves before and alongside organised women’s liberation, including through the expression of feelings. In her 2025 interview, she qualifies the reach of her own interviews: the women were white and mostly middle class by the time she spoke with them. Her work connects women’s and gender history with child welfare, Shetland society and everyday life in Scotland.

nodes.label: Patricia Nelson Limerick
nodes.date_label: Desert Passages (1985) · The Legacy of Conquest (1987) · Trails, co-editor (1991) · Something in the Soil (2000)
nodes.description: In The Legacy of Conquest (1987), Patricia Nelson Limerick argued that the American West should be understood through conquest and its continuing consequences. Economic conflict and relationships among its peoples persist beyond the supposed closing of the frontier. Her co-edited Trails: Toward a New Western History (1991) helped articulate this turn toward an ongoing regional history. Alan Taylor’s “The Old Frontiers” (2008) praised her criticism of Turner’s exclusionary historical cast; Philip J. Deloria later credited her example as a writer. Her regional approach also drew criticism: reviewing All Over the Map (1996) in 1998, Thomas D. Isern found much of her essay familiar and questioned whether treating region as a setting advanced its conceptual understanding, while acknowledging that such advancement was not her purpose. Her work with Richard White on The Frontier in American Culture (1994) connected scholarship to a public exhibition about frontier imagery.

nodes.label: Karen Dubinsky
nodes.date_label: Improper Advances (1993) · “Beyond Purity,” with Lynne Marks (1996) · The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) · Babies Without Borders (2010) · Within and Without the Nation, co-edited (2015)
nodes.description: In Improper Advances (1993), Karen Dubinsky argued that sexual violence in Ontario must be understood through unequal power and through women’s distinction between desired and coerced sex. Reading criminal case files, she treated women as sexual agents who sought pleasure and challenged coercion despite hostile courts and communities. With Lynne Marks, “Beyond Purity” (1996) defended the compatibility of women’s and gender history and the value of studying masculinity. Joan Sangster’s reply disputed their account of her position and insisted that gender history’s merits did not establish its automatic superiority. The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) extended Dubinsky’s work on sexuality to honeymooning and tourism at Niagara Falls. Babies Without Borders (2010) questioned accounts of adoption organized entirely around rescue or kidnap. Reviewing it in 2011, Ferzana Chaze praised that challenge but found its treatment of Indigenous adoption less persuasive because the socioeconomic pressures it described could themselves be seen as results of the historical oppression and marginalisation of Aboriginal communities in Canada. Dubinsky also coedited Within and Without the Nation (2015), with Adele Perry and Henry Yu.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: With Franca Iacovetta, “Murder, Womanly Virtue, and Motherhood” (1991); Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (1993); with Lynne Marks, “Beyond Purity: A Response to Sangster” (1996); The Second Greatest Disappointment: Honeymooning and Tourism at Niagara Falls (1999); Babies Without Borders: Adoption and Migration Across the Americas (2010); with Adele Perry and Henry Yu, eds., Within and Without the Nation: Canadian History as Transnational History (2015).

nodes.label: Carroll Smith-Rosenberg
nodes.date_label: The Female World of Love and Ritual (1975) · Disorderly Conduct (1985) · The Body Politic (1989) · This Violent Empire (2010)
nodes.description: In “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975), Carroll Smith-Rosenberg closely analysed the emotional, and arguably sexual, intimacy recorded in nineteenth-century American women’s letters, treating sexuality as fluid and shaped by cultural and social forces rather than settling whether these women were lesbians. Disorderly Conduct (1985) collected her essays on gender and sexuality. A 2021 OutHistory interview report calls the article pathbreaking, and Penn’s women’s studies programme credits it with establishing the legitimacy of lesbian history. The article came under intense criticism in the 1980s: by the interview report’s account, some scholars thought it essentialist for suggesting that the women might be understood as lesbian, while others thought it glorified chaste passions between women. Smith-Rosenberg also became an acknowledged resource for Spiegel’s social reading of texts. This Violent Empire (2010), in its publisher’s account, traced American national identity through exclusions that accompanied the republic’s founding.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “The Female Animal” (1973), with Charles Rosenberg; “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975); Disorderly Conduct: Visions of Gender in Victorian America (1985, Knopf); “The Body Politic” (1989); “Dis-Covering the Subject of the ‘Great Constitutional Discussion,’ 1786–1789” (1992); This Violent Empire: The Birth of an American National Identity (2010; paperback 2012).

nodes.label: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich
nodes.date_label: Good Wives (1982) · A Midwife's Tale (1990) · The Age of Homespun (2001)
nodes.description: In A Midwife's Tale (1990), Laurel Thatcher Ulrich argues that women's work and exchanges were central to the organization of an early American community. By connecting Martha Ballard's terse diary entries with other records, she reconstructs relationships that a record of public events would miss. Good Wives (1982) explains how a wife acting as a deputy husband could undertake men's work without overturning patriarchal authority. Nancy F. Cott's 1983 review praised its recovery of women's lives from contextual records. A Midwife's Tale won the 1991 Pulitzer Prize and became a collaborative PBS documentary. The Age of Homespun (2001) extends Ulrich's inquiry to textiles, social relationships and nostalgic versions of the national past. Grace Lees-Maffei's 2002 review praised that book while questioning its reception as a novel method: design historians had long treated objects as historical evidence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Good Wives: Image and Reality in the Lives of Women in Northern New England, 1650–1750 (1982); A Midwife's Tale: The Life of Martha Ballard, Based on Her Diary, 1785–1812 (1990); The Age of Homespun: Objects and Stories in the Creation of an American Myth (2001).

nodes.label: Constance Backhouse
nodes.date_label: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) · Colour-Coded (1999) · Carnal Crimes (2008)
nodes.description: In Colour-Coded (1999), Constance Backhouse argued that Canadian law created and maintained racial hierarchy, challenging the national mythology that Canada was largely free of racism. In Petticoats and Prejudice (1991), she used individual women’s encounters with courts, family law and employment law to show how legal institutions organized gender inequality. Her case histories connect legal rules to the people who administered, contested and endured them; Colour-Coded also acknowledges that her earlier work had not adequately examined race alongside gender. Petticoats won the Law and Society Association’s J. Willard Hurst Prize in 1992. Greg Marquis’s 1992 review called it “groundbreaking” and said it “opens a number of doors,” while noting that “some may quibble with the representativeness” of its cases, that class “takes a back seat to gender,” and that the Maritimes receive about eight per cent of the study. Carnal Crimes (2008) later extended her case-study approach to sexual assault law in twentieth-century Canada.

nodes.label: Nancy Leys Stepan
nodes.date_label: The Idea of Race in Science (1982) · “Race and Gender” (1986) · The Hour of Eugenics (1991) · Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) · Eradication (2011)
nodes.description: In The Hour of Eugenics (1991), Nancy Leys Stepan argued that eugenics in Brazil, Argentina and Mexico was remade through local scientific, political and cultural conditions. Race, gender, reproduction and public health therefore belong within histories of nationhood, rather than a model of Latin American science simply copying Europe. Philippa Levine credits the book with revealing the variety of eugenics, including programmes of housing and maternal care. Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) studies how images helped construct the tropics; David Arnold’s review, excerpted by the publisher, praises its advance in interpreting tropicality. Eradication (2011) places campaigns against disease alongside debates over primary health care.

nodes.label: Patricia Seed
nodes.date_label: To Love, Honor, and Obey (1988) · Ceremonies of Possession (1995) · American Pentimento (2001) · AHR transnational conversation (2006)
nodes.description: In Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995), Patricia Seed argued that European claims to the Americas drew authority from distinct cultural practices. She compared English, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Dutch ways of making possession legitimate through familiar actions, language and technical knowledge. John A. Crider welcomed its bridge between literary and historical inquiry but questioned the strength of its national patterns and the comparability of its cases. To Love, Honor, and Obey in Colonial Mexico (1988) examined changing meanings of love, free will and honor in marriage disputes. Kimberly Gauderman discussed objections to its representativeness while defending its study of competing discourses. Her “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991) prompted responses from Hernán Vidal, Rolena Adorno and Walter Mignolo in Latin American Research Review; she answered them in “More Colonial and Postcolonial Discourses” (1993). She also contributed to the six-person AHR conversation on transnational history (2006).

nodes.label: Jill Lepore
nodes.date_label: The Name of War (1998) · Historians Who Love Too Much (2001) · New York Burning (2005) · Book of Ages (2013) · These Truths (2018)
nodes.description: In The Name of War (1998), Jill Lepore argues that writing about King Philip’s War helped harden cultural boundaries and shape colonial American identity. She treats the words and later memories of war as historical forces, rather than simply records of violence. The book won the Bancroft Prize; Gordon S. Wood praised its imaginative scholarship but criticized its limited explanation of political, social and economic causes. In “Historians Who Love Too Much: Reflections on Microhistory and Biography” (2001), she reflects on the relation between the two genres. New York Burning (2005) extends her inquiry into slavery and political liberty, explicitly connected in her later account to Edmund Morgan’s American paradox. Book of Ages (2013) recovers Jane Franklin from little-studied documents, objects and portraits, while The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014) places popular culture within feminist history. These Truths (2018) expands her work to a national synthesis. Her public writing has also provoked disagreement: Wood’s 2011 review of The Whites of Their Eyes (2010) faults her treatment of popular memory.

nodes.label: Doreen Massey
nodes.date_label: Spatial Divisions of Labour (1984; second edition 1995) · Space, Place and Gender (1994) · For Space (2005)
nodes.description: Space, Place and Gender (1994) argues that space is the product of intersecting social relations and relates the conceptualization of space and place to the social construction of gender relations. For Space (2005) develops this relational account: different histories coexist in space, whose continuing construction keeps political possibilities open. This approach makes places encounters between trajectories rather than self-contained identities. In “A Global Sense of Place” (1991; collected in Space, Place and Gender, 1994) and “Power-geometry and a progressive sense of place” (1993), she develops an account of places shaped by wider connections and unequal relations of power. Its political implications remained disputed. In the 2007 review symposium, as Massey’s reply records, Matt Sparke raised questions about responsibility and the truth status of her spatial claims. She agreed that relational thinking does not guarantee a particular political response. Her own interventions include a feminist criticism of Harvey in “Flexible Sexism” (1991) and the coauthored dialogue “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), with Stuart Hall.

nodes.label: Donna Haraway
nodes.date_label: Manifesto for Cyborgs (1985) · Situated Knowledges (1988) · Primate Visions (1989) · Staying with the Trouble (2016)
nodes.description: In “Situated Knowledges” (1988), Donna Haraway argued that objectivity requires accountable, embodied perspectives. Her “Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985; collected in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women, 1991) used the human-machine figure to challenge fixed divisions between nature, culture and technology. Primate Visions (1989) made race and gender part of the historical explanation of primatology. Louise Barrett (2017) recalls gaining a new perspective from that book while recording Matt Cartmill’s hostile 1991 response to its writing. Haraway’s later companion-species work asks what humans can learn through relations with other organisms. In When Species Meet (2008), she criticizes Derrida’s response to his cat and Deleuze and Guattari’s becoming-animal, as Perry Zurn and Marie Draz respectively read her. Zurn (2018) accepts her objection to Derrida’s cat encounter but argues that deconstruction remains curious at the level of texts. “Making Kin” (2015) and Staying with the Trouble (2016) extend her account of interdependence into ecological crisis and the possibilities of living together on a damaged earth.

nodes.label: Raewyn Connell
nodes.date_label: Gender and Power (1987) · Masculinities (1995; second edition 2005) · Southern Theory (2007)
nodes.description: In Masculinities (1995), the sociologist Raewyn Connell argues that masculinities are plural, socially made and organized through unequal relations of power. Hegemonic masculinity names the dominant pattern within this hierarchy of masculinities, understood as a historically changing relation of power rather than a fixed trait of individual men. Joy Parr drew on Connell’s studies of social practice in The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), and John Tosh later acknowledged Gender and Power (1987) as a theoretical resource for Manful Assertions (1991). The framework also drew serious criticism. In their 2005 reconsideration, Connell and James W. Messerschmidt accepted the critique of trait models and rigid typologies, recognized that subordinated masculinities can influence dominant forms, and called for a more complex model of gender hierarchy that emphasizes the agency of women. Tosh subsequently defended contextual case studies against the emphasis on broad historical narratives in Connell’s “The Big Picture” (1993). Southern Theory (2007) extended Connell’s criticism of metropolitan universals to the global production of social knowledge.

nodes.label: Janet L. (Jinty) Nelson
nodes.date_label: Politics and Ritual (1986) · Charles the Bald (1992) · The Frankish World (1996) · “Gendering Courts” (2004) · King and Emperor (2019; Penguin paperback 2020)
nodes.description: In Charles the Bald (1992), Nelson explains Carolingian government through cooperation between kings, aristocrats and churchmen, challenging accounts that treat their power as necessarily competing. Politics and Ritual in Early Medieval Europe (1986) places ritual within the exercise and communication of political authority. Her work on queens, courts and masculinity makes women and gender integral to political explanation. King and Emperor (2019) follows Charlemagne chronologically, seeking the person behind the accumulated legend through close reading of fragmentary sources. Andrew J. Romig praised its source criticism but questioned its limited examination of Frankish identity and the way its biographical frame can become a general history of the period. Julia M. H. Smith praised the argument of “Gendering Courts” while judging as over-reach its inference, from the sources’ silence about Aachen’s baths after Charlemagne, that serious conversation moved from the baths to mixed-gender spaces such as the hall and the hunt.

nodes.label: Kathleen M. Brown
nodes.date_label: “Brave New Worlds” 1993 · “Changed … into the Fashion of Man” 1995 (collected 1997) · Good Wives 1996 · Foul Bodies 2009 · Undoing Slavery 2023
nodes.description: In Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996), Brown argues that gender hierarchy helped create racial categories and slavery in colonial Virginia, while racial slavery transformed gender relations. Household labor, sexuality and the differing legal treatment of English and African women help explain the consolidation of white male authority. Janet L. Coryell praised the book as “a marvelous synthesis,” noting only, as “a truly minor quibble,” that Brown does not particularly examine the intellectual underpinnings of notions about gender or race. Brown’s own retrospective on Edmund S. Morgan acknowledges his inspiration while asking how white women helped reproduce racism. Foul Bodies (2009) extends the inquiry to cleanliness and the domestic work behind public ideals of civilization; Janet Moore Lindman reads it as connecting bodily care, gender and empire.

nodes.label: Carolyn Strange
nodes.date_label: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) · Making Good, with Tina Loo (1997) · Honour, Violence and Emotions in History, coedited (2014) · Discretionary Justice (2016)
nodes.description: In Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995), Carolyn Strange argues that Toronto projected its anxieties about urban industrialization onto young wage-earning women, making their work and leisure targets of moral regulation. She shows social agencies and the city’s Morality Department meeting young working women with a mixture of paternalism and suspicion. With Tina Loo, Making Good (1997) follows law and moral regulation as contested processes of defining Canadian citizenship. Rebecca Murdock praised the first book’s research and recovery of working women’s history but questioned its periodization and wanted more explicit feminist and class analysis. Cynthia Comacchio later asked whether its account of sexual geography, considered alongside Karen Dubinsky’s work, sufficiently included sexual expression within the home. Joan Sangster credited Strange’s reinterpretation of the Bell Telephone strike’s medical testimony with explaining medical knowledge as social power. Strange’s later work includes the jointly edited Honour, Violence and Emotions in History (2014) and Discretionary Justice (2016), which treats pardon and parole as enduring, related forms of discretionary power.

Forth; Discretionary Justice: Pardon and Parole in New York from the Revolution to the Depression (2016).

nodes.label: Londa Schiebinger
nodes.date_label: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) · Nature’s Body (1993) · Plants and Empire (2004) · Secret Cures of Slaves (2017)
nodes.description: In The Mind Has No Sex? (1989), Londa Schiebinger argued that women’s exclusion from scientific institutions and scientific accounts of female incapacity reinforced one another. Nature’s Body (1993) extended this analysis to show how assumptions about gender and race shaped scientific explanations of nature. She distinguishes women’s participation, scientific institutions and the content of knowledge as connected historical problems. Plants and Empire (2004) investigates selective knowledge transfer in colonial settings; Secret Cures of Slaves (2017) examines medicine and experimentation in the Atlantic world. Nature’s Body received the Society for Social Studies of Science’s Ludwik Fleck Book Prize in 1995. Michael Stolberg’s “A Woman Down to Her Bones” (2003) argued that physicians around 1600 already emphasised and illustrated distinct features of the female skeleton, challenging the eighteenth-century chronology she shared with Laqueur. In “Skelettestreit” (2003) Schiebinger replied that such early depictions were isolated, that female-sexed skeletons became widespread only after about 1730, and that foundational shifts should not be judged by firsts.

(1999); Plants and Empire: Colonial Bioprospecting in the Atlantic World (2004); Agnotology: The Making and Unmaking of Ignorance (2008), co-edited with Robert N. nodes.label: Jane Burbank
nodes.date_label: Intelligentsia and Revolution (1986) · Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) · Empires in World History, with Frederick Cooper (2010)
nodes.description: In Empires in World History (2010), written with Frederick Cooper, Jane Burbank argues that empires governed through differences among populations and changing repertoires of power. Their comparison treats the nation-state as a contingent political arrangement rather than history’s necessary destination. Bronwen Everill praises the comparative case studies but criticizes the unclear distinction between empire and nation-state and the limited treatment of empires outside Eurasia. Burbank’s Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) challenges the image of peasants as outsiders to law, showing rural people using courts to settle disputes through formal legal procedures. Alexandra Oberländer credits this revision of peasant stereotypes while criticizing the predominance of statistical evidence and questioning the framing in terms of civil society. Burbank’s studies connect everyday legal practice with the institutions and political possibilities of empire.

nodes.label: Margaret MacMillan
nodes.date_label: Women of the Raj (1988) · Peacemakers (2001) · The Uses and Abuses of History (2008) · The War That Ended Peace (2013)
nodes.description: In Peacemakers (2001; published in the United States as Paris 1919 in 2002), Margaret MacMillan argues that the peace negotiators have been blamed too readily for later failures, restoring attention to their choices and constraints. The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; US title Dangerous Games, 2009) examines how claims about the past serve present identities and political purposes. Her international history balances individual decisions with wider social, economic and ideological pressures. Women of the Raj (1988) studies British women in colonial India, while The War That Ended Peace (2013) asks how peace gave way to war. Christopher Prior praises the latter’s clarity but questions whether its narrative gives sufficient weight to the forces favouring peace. War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020) broadens the inquiry to warfare and social organisation; Walter Scheidel criticises its accumulation of anecdotes and its failure to distinguish wartime invention from the acceleration of changes that might otherwise have occurred.

nodes.label: Amanda Vickery
nodes.date_label: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993) · The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998) · Behind Closed Doors (2009)
nodes.description: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Amanda Vickery questions recurring accounts of women’s declining power organized around capitalism and separate spheres. The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998) reconstructs genteel Georgian women’s domestic responsibilities and expanding social and intellectual horizons from letters, diaries and accounts. Anna Clark praised the archival interpretation but disputed its characterization of feminist historiography and its proposed alternative. Behind Closed Doors (2009) connects domestic objects and privacy with power, rank and gender. Helen Berry praised its range of evidence while questioning its treatment of solitary devotion and the self. Vickery’s response stresses that access to privacy was unequal and that her book does not date its invention to the Georgian period.

nodes.description: Donna R. Gabaccia argues in Foreign Relations: American Immigration in Global Perspective (2012) that U.S. immigration must be understood through the interaction of migrants’ continuing ties abroad with American diplomacy and trade. We Are What We Eat (1998) traces immigrant and ethnic eating in the United States and Americans’ long readiness to cross boundaries of taste and identity through food. Reviewing Foreign Relations in 2015, Björn A. Schmidt welcomed its transnational perspective but criticized its imprecise concept of xenophobia and insufficient engagement with research on racism. Italy’s Many Diasporas (2000) places Italian migration in a wider transnational frame. Her joint research with Franca Iacovetta and Fraser Ottanelli connects labour migration, class, ethnicity and gender, while Gender and International Migration (2015), with Katharine M. Donato, challenges the idea that substantial female migration is a recent development.

nodes.label: Emily S. Rosenberg
nodes.date_label: Spreading the American Dream (1982) · Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) · A World Connecting (2012, editor)
nodes.description: In Spreading the American Dream (1982), Emily S. Rosenberg traces how American economic and cultural expansion in the first half of the twentieth century evolved from a largely private system to an increasingly public one. Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) connects international lending and financial advising to claims of professional expertise and to ideas of gender, race and civilization; it received SHAFR’s Ferrell Senior Book award in 2000. Her later work examines contested Pearl Harbor memories and global networks. In the 2013 H-Diplo discussion of A World Connecting (2012), Erez Manela praised her synthesis but questioned its account of spatial differences and change over time; Donna R. Gabaccia asked for fuller integration of migration across the edited volume. Rosenberg defended uneven, interactive processes as an analytical framework. David A. Bell’s 2013 review likewise praised the research while criticizing weak causal explanation and the volume’s treatment of war.

nodes.label: Cecilia Morgan
nodes.date_label: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) · Gendered Pasts, co-edited (1999) · Heroines and History, with Colin M. Coates (2002) · Creating Colonial Pasts (2015) · Commemorating Canada (2016)
nodes.description: In Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996), Cecilia Morgan argues that gendered language helped constitute political and religious authority in Upper Canada. Masculine public authority and feminine domestic virtue depended on one another, but their meanings and boundaries changed with context. Patrick J. Connor praised the book’s account of class formation while asking for fuller attention to material differences between colony and Britain and to state coercion. Morgan’s “Old Ontario” (2000) proposed connecting feminist history to the workings of a white settler colony, questioning whether Careless’s “limited identities” adequately exposed domination. With Colin M. Coates, Heroines and History (2002) examines the commemoration of Madeleine de Verchères and Laura Secord. Her later work follows the making and transmission of historical memory. Reviewing Commemorating Canada (2016), Harold Kalman welcomed its accessible overview while questioning its account of the mandates of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board and Parks Canada.

nodes.label: Cynthia R. Comacchio
nodes.date_label: “Nations Are Built of Babies” (1993) · The Infinite Bonds of Family (1999) · The Dominion of Youth (2006)
nodes.description: In The Dominion of Youth (2006), Cynthia R. Comacchio argues that modern adolescence in Canada was made through changing social relations, scientific ideas and national aspirations. Institutions and adult expectations shaped this stage of life, while young people developed distinctive generational identities and cultures. “Nations Are Built of Babies” (1993) connects the medical regulation of motherhood to state intervention, class relations and national efficiency; The Infinite Bonds of Family (1999) explains family change through adaptation to economic disruption, war and depression. In a review excerpt reproduced by the publisher, Linda M. Ambrose credits Dominion with demonstrating that a distinct youth culture preceded the 1950s and 1960s. Sharon Anne Cook praises Infinite Bonds as a readable synthesis connecting family and national history, but criticizes the series’ absence of textual notes for making its historiographical positions difficult to follow. Comacchio’s own “The History of Us” (2000) evaluates the field’s demographic, feminist and labour approaches and argues for treating age as a category of historical analysis.

nodes.label: Carolyn Steedman
nodes.date_label: Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) · Dust (2001) · Labours Lost (2009)
nodes.description: Carolyn Steedman argued that working-class lives contain desires and conflicts that general accounts of class cannot adequately explain. Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) uses her own and her mother’s histories to question narratives that deny working-class people psychological individuality. Geoff Eley credited reading the book with shaping his intellectual development. Emily Cuming later questioned its occasionally rigid alignment of narrative genres with class experience and read the mother’s choice of a Lowry picture as resistance to the daughter’s interpretation. Dust (2001) examines the surviving matter of history and historians’ engagement with archives. Labours Lost (2009) restores domestic servants’ feelings and self-representations to social history while challenging Thompson’s portrayal of their resignation.

nodes.label: Luise White
nodes.date_label: The Comforts of Home (1990) · Speaking with Vampires (2000) · African Words, African Voices, coedited (2001) · The Assassination of Herbert Chitepo (2003) · Unpopular Sovereignty (2015) · Fighting and Writing (2021)
nodes.description: Luise White argues that rumour and gossip are historical sources that show how people understood and disputed colonial power. In Speaking with Vampires: Rumor and History in Colonial Africa (2000), she reads their changing details alongside written records, treating contradictions as evidence rather than simply discarding accounts as false. She seeks historical accuracy without reducing stories to a single explanation. Her earlier The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) treats prostitution as work connected to household economies and urban life. In the AHR’s 2021 reception discussion, Frederick Cooper praised its analysis of social reproduction, while Brad Weiss questioned whether its account of Haya women’s pricing sufficiently explained their migration strategies. White also coedited African Words, African Voices (2001) and later examined sovereignty and war in Rhodesia and Zimbabwe.

nodes.label: Amy Kaplan
nodes.date_label: The Social Construction of American Realism (1988) · Cultures of United States Imperialism, coedited (1993) · Manifest Domesticity (1998) · The Anarchy of Empire (2002) · Our American Israel (2018)
nodes.description: Amy Kaplan argued in The Anarchy of Empire in the Making of U.S. Culture (2002) that imperial expansion abroad, from the U.S.–Mexican War to the First World War, profoundly shaped American culture at home. Her essay Manifest Domesticity (1998) treated the home and women’s domestic role as active parts of national expansion. With Donald E. Pease she coedited Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993), calling for the study of American culture to confront empire and for postcolonial studies to include the United States. Kristin Hoganson later credited these writings with helping her develop cultural histories of masculinity, consumption and imperial power. Reception also exposed disagreements about method and scope. In 2004 Dolores Janiewski praised Kaplan’s interdisciplinary readings but criticized the limited historical contextualization of Twain’s writings on race and empire; Anders Stephanson disputed the book’s anarchy frame while admiring its individual readings. Ann Laura Stoler treated Kaplan’s account of scholarly absences as illuminating for an earlier historiography but argued that subsequent work had begun to bridge those gaps. Kaplan’s later essays on Guantánamo and Our American Israel (2018) extended her inquiry into the cultural and legal relations through which American power was made intelligible.

nodes.label: Laura F. Edwards
nodes.date_label: Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) · Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000) · The People and Their Peace (2009) · A Legal History of the Civil War and Reconstruction (2015) · Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022)
nodes.description: In The People and Their Peace (2009), Laura F. Edwards argues that local legal practice gave people without individual rights a place in maintaining the social order of the post-Revolutionary Carolinas. Centralization around individual rights could therefore reproduce and intensify racial, gender and class inequalities by excluding people who had previously participated through their subordinate status. Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) connects household gender relations to Reconstruction politics; Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000) brings Black and yeoman women into a broader synthesis of southern women’s history. Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) follows textiles as property and economic resources that people with limited rights could possess and exchange. The People and Their Peace won the Littleton-Griswold and Charles Sydnor prizes, but its interpretation remains contested. Tim Huebner praised its recovery of localized law while challenging its treatment of state appellate courts and their protection of enslaved people’s procedural rights. Jessica K. Lowe questioned the sharp division between local and state law and the account of localized law’s popular content.

nodes.label: Anna Clark
nodes.date_label: Women’s Silence, Men’s Violence (1987) · The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) · Scandal (2004) · Desire (2008; second edition 2019) · Alternative Histories of the Self (2017)
nodes.description: In The Struggle for the Breeches (1995), Anna Clark argues that British working-class formation depended on conflicts over gender, household authority and work as well as struggles between classes. Radical domestic rhetoric could promise protection and political inclusion while ultimately narrowing the movement around male breadwinners. Carole Turbin praised its integration of gender and class but criticized its repetitive structure and insufficiently explicit links between arguments. Clark’s 1992 study of Chartist domesticity explicitly draws on Gareth Stedman Jones while qualifying Joan Scott’s account of masculine citizenship. Scandal (2004) treats sexual controversy as a force in constitutional politics; William Kuhn praised its explanatory power but objected that Clark sometimes judged historical actors by modern standards. Desire (2008; revised second edition 2019) surveys European sexuality. Alternative Histories of the Self (2017), as Charles Upchurch reads it, shifts attention from finding modern sexual identities to historically specific constructions of self; her 2023 Anne Lister chapter develops queer reading as a method for connecting anatomical texts with readers’ embodied understanding.

nodes.label: Jennifer L. Morgan
nodes.date_label: “Some Could Suckle over Their Shoulder” (1997) · Laboring Women (2004) · Connexions, co-editor (2016) · “Partus sequitur ventrem” (2018) · Reckoning with Slavery (2021)
nodes.description: In Laboring Women (2004), Jennifer L. Morgan argues that enslaved women’s agricultural work and capacity to bear children jointly shaped racial slavery in the English Atlantic. Reckoning with Slavery (2021) extends that inquiry by treating race, kinship and numerical valuations as mutually constitutive: enslavers denied African kinship while exploiting maternal descent to reproduce their property. Morgan reads enslaved women as people who understood and contested these transformations, and treats the omissions in commercial and legal records as part of the history to be explained. Hartman subsequently drew on Morgan’s maternity argument in “The Belly of the World” (2016).

nodes.label: Mrinalini Sinha
nodes.date_label: Colonial Masculinity (1995) · “Giving Masculinity a History” (1999) · Specters of Mother India (2006) · Political Imaginaries, co-edited (2022)
nodes.description: In Colonial Masculinity (1995), Sinha argues that the “manly Englishman” and the “effeminate Bengali” were changing political constructions through which colonial authority and nationalist resistance were negotiated. Her imperial social formation framework studies British and Indian politics together, making masculinity part of the explanation of imperial power. Specters of Mother India (2006) follows an international controversy to show how women’s collective activism briefly opened a different route to citizenship, before subsequent political settlements curtailed it. Antoinette Burton subsequently identified its framework as an important feminist model for connecting domestic and imperial histories. Specters received the Albion Book Prize and the Joan Kelly Memorial Prize in 2007. Sinha also questions an emphasis on fragmentary histories alone in Chakrabarty’s project, proposing intersecting global histories of rights and citizenship.

nodes.label: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese
nodes.date_label: The Origins of Physiocracy (1976) · Within the Plantation Household (1988) · The Mind of the Master Class, with Eugene D. Genovese (2005)
nodes.description: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese argued that race and class shaped the lives of enslaved and slaveholding women so deeply that a shared gender did not produce a common experience. Within the Plantation Household: Black and White Women of the Old South (1988) challenges the use of models derived from New England to explain plantation households. C. Vann Woodward praised its research but disputed its treatment of Mary Chesnut’s dissent, arguing that benefiting from slavery did not automatically invalidate her criticism of it. In The Mind of the Master Class (2005), written with Eugene D. Genovese, Fox-Genovese examined the historical and religious thinking of the slaveholding elite. Steven Hahn praised its learning while questioning its claims to represent a broader ruling-class outlook and its limited analysis of gender and enslaved people’s participation.

nodes.label: Kimberlé W. Crenshaw
nodes.date_label: Race, Reform, and Retrenchment (1988) · Demarginalizing (1989) · Mapping the Margins (1991) · Critical Race Theory, co-edited (1995) · Toward a Field, coauthored (2013)
nodes.description: Kimberlé W. Crenshaw argues that treating race and sex discrimination separately obscures Black women’s subordination. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) names intersectionality as a way to expose that failure in law, feminist theory and antiracist politics. “Mapping the Margins” (1991) extends the approach to violence against women of color. Her legal framework became a resource across disciplines, including history, as she describes in a 2019 interview. It also prompted disagreement about how an analytical metaphor should travel: Jennifer C. Nash’s “On Difficulty” (2010) criticizes later scholarship that treats intersectionality as a settled truth or assumes that adding more intersections will overcome exclusion. Nash advocates retaining Crenshaw’s traffic analogy as one metaphor for investigating power. Crenshaw’s contribution belongs within an earlier and continuing Black feminist conversation, including the particular resources she takes from bell hooks and Gerda Lerner’s documentary collection.

nodes.label: Susan Reynolds
nodes.date_label: Kingdoms and Communities (1984; second edition 1997) · Fiefs and Vassals (1994) · Before Eminent Domain (2010)
nodes.description: In Fiefs and Vassals (1994), Susan Reynolds argued that historians had projected later lawyers’ categories of fiefs and vassalage onto earlier medieval relationships, making feudalism a misleading framework. Kingdoms and Communities in Western Europe, 900–1300 (1984; second edition 1997) instead foregrounded collective activity and the political ideas of lay communities, alongside hierarchy and government. Her comparisons challenged the separation of English and continental histories and insisted on distinguishing historians’ terminology from the practices it purported to describe. Reception combined admiration with disagreement: Steven G. Lane’s 1995 review welcomed the reinterpretation but questioned the sharp separation between customary and professional law and the denial of precise meanings to earlier legal vocabulary. In 2012 Reynolds acknowledged corrections by Fredric L. Cheyette and Susan Wood while maintaining her criticism of the non-Marxist feudal framework. Her contribution included studying consultation and collective judgement without equating them with equality or democracy.

nodes.label: Michelle Perrot
nodes.date_label: Les ouvriers en grève (1974; catalogued also as 1973) · L’Impossible prison (1980) · Une histoire des femmes est-elle possible ? (1984) · Histoire de la vie privée IV (1987) · Histoire des femmes en Occident, with Georges Duby (1991–1992) · Les femmes ou les silences de l’histoire (1998) · Histoire de chambres (2009)
nodes.description: Les femmes ou les silences de l’histoire (1998) investigates how women were silenced in archives and historical narratives, and how traces of their work, private lives and political action can be recovered. Its inquiry moves from recovering women’s activities to examining relations between the sexes and the making of historical evidence. Yannick Ripa praised its gathering and recontextualization of dispersed essays, while wishing Perrot had developed her observation that the field’s problematic remained hesitant. Perrot’s earlier Les ouvriers en grève combines statistical analysis with workers’ collective lives; Robert Brécy praised the study but argued that, perhaps under the influence of May 1968, it stressed the festive side of strikes when their marches and meetings answered first to the necessities of struggle. With Georges Duby she co-directed Histoire des femmes en Occident (1991–1992), a collective enterprise that made new research on women’s history in Western universities visible. Histoire de chambres (2009) connects rooms, intimacy and enclosure; Alain Corbin praised the synthesis while suggesting that changes within rural houses received overly brief treatment.

nodes.label: Jacquelyn Dowd Hall
nodes.date_label: Revolt Against Chivalry (1979) · Like a Family, coauthored (1987) · “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (2005) · Sisters and Rebels (2019)
nodes.description: In “The Long Civil Rights Movement and the Political Uses of the Past” (2005), Hall argues that the struggle extended beyond the familiar 1954–1965 southern campaign and joined racial equality to economic justice. She challenges public narratives that celebrate civil-rights victories while obscuring these wider demands. Earlier, Like a Family: The Making of a Southern Cotton Mill World (1987), written with five co-authors from Southern Oral History Program research, presented Piedmont mill workers’ culture and politics as a history of resistance and radicalism. Stephanie McCurry’s 1992 review essay judged its neglect of racial conflict the book’s greatest weakness. Sundiata Keita Cha-Jua and Clarence Lang’s “The ‘Long Movement’ as Vampire” (2007) criticized the Long Movement thesis for exaggerating continuity in African American social movements and for collapsing the concepts of Civil Rights and Black Power. Revolt Against Chivalry (1979; revised 1993) links women’s antilynching activism to struggles over racial justice and women’s authority. Hall also founded and directed UNC’s Southern Oral History Program.

nodes.label: Pat Thane
nodes.date_label: Foundations of the Welfare State (1982; second edition 1996) · Old Age in English History (2000) · Sinners? Scroungers? Saints?, with Tanya Evans (2012)
nodes.description: In Old Age in English History: Past Experiences, Present Issues (2000), Pat Thane argues that older people have long been visible, active contributors to English communities, challenging assumptions that they were uniformly dependent or supported by families alone. She treats later life as varied by resources, work, gender and personal circumstances, rather than a single experience of decline. Daniel Blackie praised the book’s account of older people’s agency but criticized its sketchier treatment of pre-industrial England and judged its modern sections stronger. Foundations of the Welfare State (1982; second edition 1996) belongs to her wider history of welfare provision. Her parliamentary Social Care memorandum (2009) traces the interdependence of state, voluntary and family support; with Tanya Evans she wrote Sinners? Scroungers? Saints? (2012), on unmarried motherhood in twentieth-century England. Her later work connects women’s unequal paid and caring work to poverty and representations in old age. With Janet Nelson and Penelope Corfield she helped establish the IHR Women’s History Seminar in 1986.

nodes.label: Paige Raibmon
nodes.date_label: Authentic Indians (2005) · Unmaking Native Space (2008) · Written as I Remember It (2014) · As I Remember It (2019)
nodes.description: Paige Raibmon argues that colonial definitions of Indigenous authenticity shaped access to land, resources and sovereignty. Authentic Indians (2005) traces how Indigenous people negotiated these imposed categories in Northwest Coast encounters, joining cultural and labour history. Brian W. Dippie’s 2006 review welcomed the book’s contribution but questioned whether its opposing categories oversimplified civilization and obscured the racial basis of exclusion. In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon connects official land policy to everyday settler practices, using a genealogical method drawn from Foucault to show how dispossession emerged from contingent interactions rather than policy alone. Her later collaborations make the research relationship and the form of publication part of historical method: Written as I Remember It (2014) credits Elsie Paul with Raibmon and Harmony Johnson; As I Remember It (2019) is a separate multimedia publication with additional collaborators. Her essay on transformational listening asks listeners to examine their assumptions rather than assume that hearing testimony automatically transforms colonial relationships.

nodes.label: Julia Kristeva
nodes.date_label: La Révolution du langage poétique (1974) · Pouvoirs de l’horreur (1980; English 1982) · Étrangers à nous-mêmes (1988; English 1991)
nodes.description: In Pouvoirs de l’horreur (1980; Powers of Horror, 1982), Julia Kristeva explains abjection as the exclusion through which a subject establishes precarious boundaries between self and other. In La Révolution du langage poétique (1974), she treats bodily drives and rhythms, the semiotic, as interacting with the symbolic organization of language. Her work connected psychoanalysis with textual interpretation and feminist debates over identity and historical time. Hayden White reviewed Desire in Language (1980) in the Journal of Modern History (1982). Reception was also critical: as Kathleen Lennon recounts, Judith Butler’s Gender Trouble (1990) questions whether Kristeva’s apparently precultural maternal drives are themselves culturally produced. Nicolás Pastor-Berdún reconstructs Spivak’s 1981 objection that Des Chinoises (1974) opposes homogeneous pictures of China and the West. In “Women’s Time” (1979; English 1981), Kristeva distinguishes three generations of feminism and favours one that neither fixes identity nor neutralizes sexual difference.

nodes.label: Gabrielle M. Spiegel
nodes.date_label: Social Logic of the Text (1990) · Romancing the Past (1993) · The Past as Text (1997) · Practicing History, editor (2005)
nodes.description: Gabrielle M. Spiegel argues that historical texts must be read both as literary forms and as interventions in particular social settings: their social logic. She developed this approach in “History, Historicism, and the Social Logic of the Text in the Middle Ages” (1990) and applied it in Romancing the Past (1993), explaining how a small group of threatened Franco-Flemish patrons used vernacular prose histories to defend aristocratic legitimacy. Robert M. Stein describes her position as a “middle ground” in which historians read documents deconstructively while still treating language as conveying information about past lives. Raymond Cormier’s 1995 review praises the book’s argument while faulting its treatment of literary commonplaces and epic distinctions, and suggesting that comparable ideological uses of antiquity appeared earlier under Henry II. The Past as Text (1997) collected her essays; Practicing History (2005), which she edited and introduced, examined historical writing after the linguistic turn. Her later work distinguishes memory from historical time and asks how historians can acknowledge mediation while attending to an absent past.

nodes.label: Penny Summerfield
nodes.date_label: Women Workers (1984; 1989 republication) · Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998) · Culture and Composure (2004) · Histories of the Self (2018 release; 2019 imprint)
nodes.description: In Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998), Penny Summerfield examines how public representations of wartime men and women shape women’s retrospective accounts of their own lives. The composure approach developed in “Culture and Composure” (2004) asks how telling a life story can produce psychic ease, and how available cultural narratives can obstruct that process. Earlier research on women’s wartime employment distinguished changes in occupation and work arrangements from the removal of gender hierarchy. “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016) argues that oral history has become an autobiographical practice in which understanding how subjectivity is constituted in an interview is more urgent; Histories of the Self (released in 2018, with a 2019 imprint) extends methodological discussion across personal narrative genres. Jon Lawrence explicitly credits Summerfield’s work on intersubjectivity in his 2022 account of reusing social-science archives. Lucy Newby and Fearghus Roulston (2026) value the analytical space opened by Summerfield’s composure model but caution that fragmented narration can be creative expression rather than evidence of an inability to tell a coherent story. Summerfield’s 2023 study of wartime correspondence applies composure to letter writing, using Foucault’s technologies of the self to investigate gendered anxiety and family separation.

nodes.scope_note: Full monographs, the 2000 chapter and original 2004 article remain unread. The 1998 book is known through publisher description and the author’s historiographical essay; the 2004 framework through the author’s selected 2023 passages and Newby/Roulston’s 2026 discussion. Only the 2016 abstract and indexed excerpts were accessible. The 2018 departmental essay was read in full; selected 2023 and 2026 passages, not complete articles, were read. Cited Foucault and Bourke originals and the underlying archival letters were not independently read.

nodes.label: Julie Cruikshank
nodes.date_label: Life Lived Like a Story, collaborative (1990) · The Social Life of Stories (1998) · Do Glaciers Listen? (2005)
nodes.description: Julie Cruikshank’s The Social Life of Stories (1998) explores the social power of storytelling and how it can mediate between social action and local knowledge. In Do Glaciers Listen? (2005), she argues that local knowledge is made through encounters and she treats environmental change, local knowledge and colonial encounters as connected themes. Life Lived Like a Story (1990) was produced through collaboration between Julie Cruikshank, Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned. Innes explicitly used her flexible account of oral history and oral tradition alongside Angela Cavender-Wilson’s in his 1999–2000 methodological article. Cole Harris praised Do Glaciers Listen? as a grounded interdisciplinary achievement but questioned its handling of scientific explanation and asked her to address communication between knowledge systems more directly (2005/06). Dorothee Schreiber challenged Harris’s framing in a published response (2008).

nodes.label: Barbara J. Fields
nodes.date_label: “Ideology and Race” (1982) · Slavery and Freedom on the Middle Ground (1985) · “Slavery, Race and Ideology” (1990) · Slaves No More, coauthor (1992) · Racecraft, with Karen E. Fields (2012)
nodes.description: In Racecraft: The Soul of Inequality in American Life (2012), Barbara J. Fields and Karen E. Fields argue that the practice of racism produces the illusion of race. They call the process that produces this illusion “racecraft.” Barbara Fields’s “Slavery, Race and Ideology in the United States of America” (1990) criticizes treating American slavery primarily as a system of race relations and rejects the biological reality of race. Her work also includes the Maryland study Slavery and Freedom on the Middle Ground (1985) and the collaborative emancipation history Slaves No More (1992). Walter Johnson’s “Brute Ideology” (2014) praised Racecraft’s analysis while questioning its narrow textual remedy and treatment of resistant political cultures.

nodes.label: Barbara Welter
nodes.date_label: “The Cult of True Womanhood” (1966) · Dimity Convictions (1976)
nodes.description: Barbara Welter argued that nineteenth-century American prescriptive literature defined ideal womanhood through piety, purity, submissiveness and domesticity. She set out this ideal, and its “four cardinal virtues”, in “The Cult of True Womanhood: 1820–1860” (1966). The framework became a widely used vocabulary for women’s history, especially for examining white middle-class domestic prescriptions. Gerda Lerner adapted it to explain class distinctions; Linda Kerber, as Isenberg reports, praised the essay’s wit and subtlety but understood Welter to regard women’s separate sphere as oppressive; Isenberg disputes that interpretation. Nancy Cott challenged the opposition between domesticity and feminism, according to Nancy Isenberg, who in turn defended the complexity of Welter’s treatment of ideology. Dimity Convictions (1976) collected her essays on nineteenth-century American women.

nodes.label: Simone de Beauvoir
nodes.date_label: The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) · Le Deuxième Sexe (1949; English 1953) · La Vieillesse (1970)
nodes.description: In Le Deuxième Sexe (The Second Sex, 1949), Beauvoir argues that women’s subordination is made through historical circumstances and social meanings rather than fixed by biology. She examines how men become the human norm while women are placed as Other, and how that unequal situation limits the exercise of freedom. The book became a major resource for feminist inquiry: Michelle Perrot recalls that it directed her first research interest toward feminism. Its reception also involves substantive disagreement. Julia Kristeva challenges its simplification of Freud while recognizing shared concerns with psychosexuality. These criticisms qualify the book’s uses as a framework for women’s and gender history.

nodes.label: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein
nodes.date_label: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) · The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983) · Divine Art, Infernal Machine (2011)
nodes.description: In The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), Elizabeth L. Eisenstein argued that the shift from manuscript to print transformed the conditions of learning in early modern Europe. Identical printed copies could circulate widely and be compared, helping reshape the Renaissance, the Reformation and the rise of modern science. It is still cited, in DeLacy’s words, as “the seminal work in the cultural history of the book.” Roger Chartier praised the synthesis while questioning the breadth of its explanatory ambition in 1981. Bruno Latour used its account of print in his work on inscriptions, while objecting that the invention of printing itself remained unexplained. The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983) abridged the larger study; Divine Art, Infernal Machine (2011) examined changing, often ambivalent attitudes toward printing.
