nodes.label: Anna Davin
nodes.date_label: Feminist History (1976) · Imperialism and Motherhood (1978) · Growing Up Poor (1996)
nodes.description: In “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978), Anna Davin argued that efforts to improve infant welfare in Britain were shaped by imperial competition and eugenic ideas about the population. She examined how maternal instruction put working-class mothers’ conduct under scrutiny while exposing tensions between their lives and reformers’ expectations. Muggeridge and Davidson describe the essay as pathbreaking and identify its influence on feminist histories of maternity care. Growing Up Poor: Home, School and Street in London, 1870–1914 (1996) reconstructs poor children’s everyday lives, especially girls’ work, schooling and family responsibilities, using institutional records, autobiography and oral testimony. Reviewer Dietrich Oberwittler praised its detailed history from below while noting that fathers, Sunday schools and cinema receive little or no attention. As Kelly Boyd recounts, Davin and Sally Alexander made feminist analysis central to History Workshop Journal in “Feminist History” (1976). In “Labouring Women: a reply to Eric Hobsbawm” (1979), Davin, Alexander and Eve Hostettler challenged Hobsbawm’s exclusion of wage-earning wives and women’s class agency, as Sonya O. Rose explains.

nodes.label: bell hooks
nodes.date_label: Ain’t I a Woman 1981 · Feminist Theory 1984 · Yearning 1990 · Black Looks 1992 · Teaching to Transgress 1994
nodes.description: In Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (1981), bell hooks argued that feminism must confront racism and sexism together to understand Black women’s historical devaluation. Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) challenged the treatment of privileged white women’s experience as universal, connecting racial hierarchy with class relations. “Postmodern Blackness” (1990) criticized postmodern theory’s exclusion of Black voices while using its critique of essentialism to affirm multiple Black identities. In Talia Bettcher’s account of the exchange, Judith Butler’s Bodies That Matter (1993) challenged hooks’s reading of Paris Is Burning by emphasizing performance’s capacity both to repeat and to unsettle dominant norms.

nodes.label: Deborah Gray White
nodes.date_label: Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985; revised 1999) · Too Heavy a Load (1998; paperback 1999) · Telling Histories, ed. (2008)
nodes.description: In Ar’n’t I a Woman? Female Slaves in the Plantation South (1985), Deborah Gray White argued that slavery must be understood through enslaved women’s work, reproduction and relationships with other women, rather than treating men’s experience as universal. She examined how racial and sexual stereotypes concealed women’s vulnerability and the networks through which they sustained family and community life. Too Heavy a Load (1998) extended White’s analysis to Black women’s organizing and the conflicts among racial solidarity, gender and class; Publishers Weekly praised its systematic focus but judged its textbook structure and tone unlikely to reach lay readers. Her edited Telling Histories (2008) examined Black women’s place in the historical profession, and the collective Scarlet and Black project, coedited with Marisa J. Fuentes (2016), brought institutional slavery research into Rutgers’s public history.

nodes.label: Gerda Lerner
nodes.date_label: “The Lady and the Mill Girl” (1969) · “Placing Women in History” (1975) · The Majority Finds Its Past (1979) · The Creation of Patriarchy (1986) · The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993)
nodes.description: In The Creation of Patriarchy (1986), Lerner argued that male dominance was made through historical changes in control over women’s sexuality and reproduction, property, law and religious symbols, rather than being biologically inevitable. As Virginia Hunter’s 1988 review observed, she reworked Engels’s historical account of the family together with Lévi-Strauss’s account of the exchange of women. Lerner later explained that she reversed Engels’s causal sequence by placing gender oppression before class oppression. Her essays include “The Lady and the Mill Girl: Changes in the Status of Women in the Age of Jackson” (1969) and “Placing Women in History: Definitions and Challenges” (1975). The Majority Finds Its Past (1979) made recovering women’s agency and rethinking historical categories a programme for women’s history, with differences of class, race, ethnicity and culture central to interpretation. Her documentary collection Black Women in White America (1972) supplied sources for researching African American women, while graduate programmes at Sarah Lawrence and Wisconsin helped train historians in the field. Her large explanatory claims also drew criticism: Virginia Hunter’s 1988 review welcomed the theoretical challenge but argued that Lerner misread the Greek sources on slavery, relied on laws to the exclusion of other evidence, and drew a developmental continuum that was “all too neat.” Linda Gordon’s memorial identified tensions between materialist explanations and Lerner’s emphasis on women’s exclusion from education and knowledge of their past. The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993) extended her inquiry to the barriers to women’s intellectual authority and the ways women challenged them.

nodes.label: Patricia Hill Collins
nodes.date_label: “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986) · Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) · Fighting Words (1998) · Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019)
nodes.description: Collins argues that Black women's ideas and actions are central to social justice, not marginal, and that Black women produce critical social theory outside elite institutions. Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) develops this argument: it sets out a Black feminist standpoint epistemology, analyses the “controlling images” through which Black women are represented, and describes intersecting oppressions as a “matrix of domination”; she later described it as examining Black feminist thought “as an example of critical social theory that did not come from elites.” Her earlier article “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986) set out the sociological significance of Black feminist thought. In “Truth-Telling and Intellectual Activism” (2013) she discusses speaking to several audiences at once. “Intersectionality’s Definitional Dilemmas” (2015) treats intersectionality as a knowledge project attentive to power relations, and Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019) asks how critical analysis and social action might inform one another.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986); Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised second edition 2000); Fighting Words (1998); Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019).
nodes.scope_note: The 1986 article, the 2000 book and Higginbotham's 1992 essay were not read on a permitted route; the 2015 and 2013 articles are known from their abstracts; selected 2024 interview responses; and parts of the publisher’s 2019 introduction were read. The original 1990 book, complete monographs, and cited originals by hooks, Kuhn, Crenshaw, Hall, Said and Du Bois were not read. Fighting Words is identified bibliographically only.

nodes.label: Ellen Ross
nodes.date_label: Sex and Society, with Rayna Rapp (1981) · “Fierce Questions and Taunts” (1982) · Survival Networks (1983) · Love and Toil (1993) · Slum Travelers, editor (2007)
nodes.description: In Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993), Ellen Ross argued that mothers’ domestic choices were essential to the survival and cultural continuity of the British working classes. The book makes poor London mothers’ distinctive experience central to working-class history. Carolyn Steedman’s 1994 review situated it within research on women’s reproduction of everyday life and highlighted its dependence on earlier women investigators’ records. Emma Griffin’s 2018 study of maternal emotions challenged Ross and other historians for finding maternal love in autobiographical accounts that also described emotional distance and violence. Ross’s Slum Travelers (2007), an edited and annotated anthology with an introduction, recovered women’s investigations of London poverty and their representations of the urban poor.

Walkowitz, “Raphael Samuel (1934–1996): An Appreciation” (1997); editor, Slum Travelers: Ladies and London Poverty, 1860–1920 (2007).

Love and Toil was assessed through its publisher abstract, Steedman’s first-page review preview and selected passages of Griffin’s accepted manuscript. nodes.label: Erika Rappaport
nodes.date_label: Shopping for Pleasure (2000) · Consuming Behaviours (coedited, 2015) · A Thirst for Empire (2017)
nodes.description: In Shopping for Pleasure (2000), Erika Rappaport argues that shops, clubs, restaurants and other commercial spaces helped make modern femininity and women’s urban public life in London’s West End. Consumer culture emerges through contested business practices, law, feminism and household power. A Thirst for Empire (2017) connects tea production, promotion and consumption across imperial markets. It won the American Historical Association’s 2018 Jerry Bentley Prize. Chris Nierstrasz praised its archival research and account of branding, but questioned whether its emphasis on the British Empire justified its claim to explain the modern world.

nodes.label: Louise Audino Tilly
nodes.date_label: The Rebellious Century, with Charles and Richard Tilly (1975) · Women, Work, and Family, with Joan W. Scott (1978) · Class Conflict and Collective Action, co-edited with Charles Tilly (1981) · Politics and Class in Milan (1992) · “Connections” (1994)
nodes.description: Louise Audino Tilly argued that women’s work long preceded industrialization and that wages did not automatically free women from family obligations. Women, Work, and Family (1978), written with Joan W. Scott, explained women’s employment through changing economic opportunities, demographic patterns and household relations in England and France. Scott later recalled that the book, written through an exchange of hundreds of letters, became a standard in the history of women, work and industrial capitalism. Patricia Hilden’s 1979 critique countered that many textile workers valued economic independence and challenged comparisons between working-class women and middle-class housewives. Tilly subsequently called for analytical women’s history that could change historians’ general questions (1989); she also disputed Scott’s deconstructionist method. She also co-edited Class Conflict and Collective Action (1981) with Charles Tilly and wrote Politics and Class in Milan, 1881–1901 (1992). Her “Connections” (1994) extended the study of workers and families across India, England and France.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Rebellious Century, 1830–1930 (1975), with Charles and Richard Tilly; Women, Work, and Family (1978), with Joan W. Scott (later Methuen edition 1987); “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985); “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989; French version 1990); The European Experience of Declining Fertility (1992), coedited with John R. Gillis and David Levine; “Connections” (1994).

Selected passages and notes of “Connections” and Cohen’s appreciation were read. Thompson’s and Passerini’s signed responses were read by OCR from an authorized scan; Tilly’s full rejoinder and the respondents’ books remain unread.

nodes.label: Laurence Fontaine
nodes.date_label: Histoire du colportage en Europe (1993; English 1996) · L’économie morale (2008; English 2014) · Le Marché (2014)
nodes.description: In L’économie morale (2008; translated as The Moral Economy, 2014), Laurence Fontaine argues that aristocratic and merchant cultures of credit coexisted, competed and changed one another in early modern Europe. Credit connected people across social ranks through obligations that could sustain survival while also producing dependence; the history of markets therefore cannot be reduced to a passage from social solidarity to impersonal calculation. Her research on peddlers, migration and women’s economic activity follows the practices through which people sought resources and room to act. Philippe Minard welcomed the inquiry into everyday economic life but argued in 2009 that its emphasis on coexistence understated the market’s growing dominance as an organizing principle between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Le Marché (2014) pursued the possibilities and dangers of access to exchange. Arnault Skornicki criticized its account of emancipation and power in 2015; Fontaine replied that her analysis also identified exclusion, short-termism and individualism as dangers within markets and that the Enlightenment thinkers she engaged placed political action and justice at the centre of moralizing the market. A CNRS economic and social historian, she formerly taught at the European University Institute.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire du colportage en Europe (1993); History of Pedlars in Europe (English edition, 1996); “Homo creditus et construction de la confiance au XVIIIe siècle” (1997), with John Brewer; “Women’s Economic Spheres and Credit in Pre-industrial Europe” (2001); L’économie morale. Pauvreté, crédit et confiance dans l’Europe préindustrielle (2008); The Moral Economy: Poverty, Credit, and Trust in Early Modern Europe (English translation, 2014); Le Marché. Histoire et usages d’une conquête sociale (2014); “Reconsidering the Moral Economy in France at the End of the Eighteenth Century” (2019).

The 2019 chapter is abstract-only. The pedlars book, Le Marché, the Brewer coauthored chapter and other listed books are not read in full. Works cited by Fontaine are not independently read here.

nodes.label: Luisa Passerini
nodes.date_label: Work Ideology and Consensus (1979) · Torino operaia e fascismo (1984; English 1987) · Autoritratto di gruppo (1988; English 1996) · Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999) · Memoria e utopia (2003; English 2007)
nodes.description: Passerini argued that workers’ memories of fascism reveal cultural identities and everyday negotiations with power, rather than offering a direct measure of consent or resistance. Torino operaia e fascismo (1984), translated as Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), combines life histories with other sources to interpret those meanings. Richard Cándida Smith praised its method but questioned how cultural resistance became political action and how clearly it separated attitudes from the fascist period from later recollection (1988). Paul Thompson later said that by the second edition of The Voice of the Past (1988) oral historians had been strongly influenced by her ideas on subjectivity, silence and memory. Joan Wallach Scott introduced the English Autobiography of a Generation (1996), which interweaves the author’s recollections with other participants’ memories of 1968. With Selma Leydesdorff and Thompson, Passerini also made gendered memory a collaborative question, warning against universal differences between men and women (1996). Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999) extended her inquiry to emotions and European belonging: Timothy Bewes criticized its lack of a unified object, consistent method and explicit thesis; her reply defended historical discontinuity and the interpretation of neglected traces (2000). Her later publications include Memoria e utopia (2003; English 2007).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Work Ideology and Consensus under Italian Fascism” (1979); Torino operaia e fascismo (1984), translated as Fascism in Popular Memory (1987); Autoritratto di gruppo (1988), translated by Lisa Erdberg as Autobiography of a Generation: Italy, 1968 (1996), foreword by Joan Wallach Scott; Memory and Totalitarianism (ed., 1992); Gender and Memory (coed. with Selma Leydesdorff and Paul Thompson, 1996; new Leydesdorff introduction, 2005); Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999); Memoria e utopia (2003), English Memory and Utopia (2007).

nodes.label: Sheila Rowbotham
nodes.date_label: Women, Resistance and Revolution (1972) · Hidden from History (1973) · Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) · Beyond the Fragments (1979) · A Century of Women (1997)
nodes.description: Hidden from History (1973) argues that women’s work and collective resistance belong at the centre of social history, with class differences preventing any simple story of universal sisterhood or steady progress. Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) connects feminist consciousness to changing material life, while asking how domestic labour, childrearing and inner experience exceed existing Marxist explanations. Gillian Scott’s 1998 review of A Century of Women valued its integration of women into wider social transformation. Intellectual debts also brought disagreement: Rowbotham recalled E. P. Thompson criticizing the assumption that experiencing oppression necessarily gives someone the best understanding of it. She accepted the need for qualifications, while rejecting the Thompsons’ suspicion that the movement was imposing ideas drawn from its members’ limited experience as young middle-class women. Her later work combines historical recovery with criticism of fixed accounts of gender domination.

nodes.label: Gertrude Himmelfarb
nodes.date_label: The Idea of Poverty (1984) · The New History and the Old (1987; revised 2004) · Poverty and Compassion (1991)
nodes.description: In The Idea of Poverty (1984), Gertrude Himmelfarb studied poverty as a changing moral and political idea, connecting social conditions with how contemporaries understood them. Poverty and Compassion (1991) argued that the material and moral dimensions of poverty were inseparable in the minds of late Victorians. The New History and the Old (1987) defended political and intellectual inquiry against the displacement she attributed to newer historical approaches. Her defense provoked disagreement: Lawrence Stone accepted some objections but disputed the claimed dominance of new history, and David Cannadine later rejected her diagnosis of disciplinary ruin. Her methodological essays criticized quantitative history as deterministic and psychohistory as lacking evidence, and later defended evidentiary method against postmodern accounts of historical knowledge.

nodes.label: Joan Kelly
nodes.date_label: The Social Relation of the Sexes (1976) · Did Women Have a Renaissance? (1977) · Women, History, and Theory (1984)
nodes.description: In “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977), Joan Kelly answered her own question in the negative, arguing that the period saw a relative contraction of the powers of secular women of the courtly and patrician elite. “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976) made relations between women and men part of explanations of historical change and challenged inherited period boundaries. In their 1994 retrospective, Alice Kessler-Harris and Amy Swerdlow quoted Catharine Stimpson’s judgement that Kelly’s investigations “altered the history of the Renaissance and shaped that of women,” and recalled the first M.A. programme in women’s history that Kelly set up with Gerda Lerner. Its claims remained contested: Brian Richardson (2020) wrote that her “partial, blunt and pessimistic assessment” needs to be nuanced considerably in view of what women achieved despite their subordination. Her essays were collected posthumously in Women, History, and Theory (1984; paperback 1986).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “The Social Relation of the Sexes: Methodological Implications of Women’s History” (1976); “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977); “The Doubled Vision of Feminist Theory” (1979); “Early Feminist Theory and the Querelle des Femmes, 1400–1789” (1982); Women, History, and Theory: The Essays of Joan Kelly (1984; paperback 1986).
nodes.scope_note: The Renaissance essay is represented through Richardson’s preface (2020); the essay itself was not read on a permitted route. The 1976 methodological essay was read in a licensed abridged reprint. Richardson’s preface p. x was read. The complete 1979 and 1982 essays, the collected volume and its introduction, Catharine R. Stimpson’s foreword, and the original works attributed to Kelly’s interlocutors remain unread.

nodes.description: Patricia Crone challenged the use of later Muslim narratives as straightforward evidence for Islam’s beginnings. In Hagarism: The Making of the Islamic World (1977), written with Michael Cook, she proposed a radical rewriting of early Islamic history. R. Stephen Humphreys credited the book with forcing historians to reconsider their sources while observing that very few accepted its reconstruction. Crone’s subsequent work examined the relations between tribal society, religious authority and imperial government. Yahya Sadowski criticized her account of enduring tribal biases in Islam as essentialist. God’s Rule, also published as Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004), traces competing political arguments across six centuries; Guillaume Dye praised its connection of texts to social practices while flagging its reliance on the disputed thesis of God’s Caliph (1986, with Martin Hinds). Peter Brown welcomed The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012) for bringing Iran into late-antique religious history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Hagarism (1977), with Michael Cook; Slaves on Horses (1980); God’s Caliph (1986), with Martin Hinds; Roman, Provincial and Islamic Law (1987); Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987); Pre-Industrial Societies (1989); Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004), published in the United States as God’s Rule; The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012).
nodes.scope_note: Selected primary passages of the revised Tribe and State chapter and the 2006 Post-Colonialism article were read. Major monographs were not read in full. Their arguments and reception are limited to the named reviews and institutional accounts. The Weber critique is mediated through Manzano; its German and English versions remain unread.

nodes.label: Leanne Betasamosake Simpson
nodes.date_label: Dancing on Our Turtle’s Back (2011) · Land as Pedagogy (2014) · As We Have Always Done (2017)
nodes.description: Simpson argues that Indigenous resurgence must build political alternatives to settler rule rather than seek inclusion within it. As We Have Always Done (2017) connects resistance to land dispossession with opposition to capitalist exploitation, white supremacy and heteropatriarchy. Dancing on Our Turtle’s Back (2011) had already argued that reconciliation requires political resurgence. “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) turns this programme toward the authority of Indigenous intellectual work. Tiffany Lethabo King’s 2023 review values the book’s significance for Black feminist and queer scholarship and Indigenous–Black alliances.

nodes.label: Gayle S. Rubin
nodes.date_label: The Traffic in Women (1975) · Thinking Sex (1984) · Sexual Traffic, with Judith Butler (1994) · Deviations (2011)
nodes.description: In “The Traffic in Women” (1975), Gayle S. Rubin argued that women’s subordination requires analysis of a sex/gender system: social arrangements that organize sexuality and produce gendered positions. In “Thinking Sex” (1984), Rubin distinguished sexual stratification from gender hierarchy and called for their separate analysis. These interventions became major resources for feminist and queer scholarship. Butler explicitly credited the first essay’s account of gender’s mobility as one reason for developing Gender Trouble (1990). The framework also attracted criticism: in her Stanford Encyclopedia entry, Mari Mikkola summarizes her own 2011 objection to the sex/gender distinction underlying accounts such as Rubin’s. Treating gender as socially constructed suggests that women and men could cease to exist if social practices changed; treating gender as a product of oppression further suggests that feminism should seek that outcome. Mikkola regards these commitments as politically unhelpful, particularly because many people value their gender. In the 1994 Butler interview, Rubin described the later essay as a correction addressing different problems and rejected an exclusive disciplinary division between feminism and sexuality studies. Deviations (2011) collected the major essays alongside further work on sexual politics, history and knowledge.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “The Traffic in Women: Notes on the ‘Political Economy’ of Sex” (1975); “Thinking Sex: Notes for a Radical Theory of the Politics of Sexuality” (1984); “Sexual Traffic,” interview with Judith Butler (1994; Portuguese journal translation 2003); Deviations: A Gayle Rubin Reader (2011, collection).
nodes.scope_note: The two major essays were not read on a permitted route; they are represented through Rubin’s 1994 interview, Mikkola’s SEP entry and the Duke description. The 1994 interview was read in selected passages of its 2003 Portuguese journal translation; English body unread. Deviations was checked through its catalogue, contents and displayed openings, not read as a whole. Mikkola’s separate 2011 article and the cited theorists’ original books remain unread.

nodes.label: Annette Gordon-Reed
nodes.date_label: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997) · The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) · “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs,” with Peter S. Onuf (2016) · On Juneteenth (2021)
nodes.description: In Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997), Annette Gordon-Reed argued that evidence of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship had been denied a fair hearing, pointing to inconsistencies in noted scholars' evaluations and their exclusion of evidence concerning the Hemings family. The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) reconstructed an enslaved family’s relationships to make its members historical subjects in their own right. Edmund S. Morgan and Marie Morgan praised its fresh perspective; Jill Lepore admired the work while questioning inferences from human nature. With Peter S. Onuf, Gordon-Reed examined Jefferson’s understanding of himself as patriarch in “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs” (2016). Gordon S. Wood praised its insights but criticized its uneven joint voice and its account of the Jefferson–Hamilton conflict. Her writing also answers criticism of biography as a form of history writing (2014) and combines Texas history with memoir in On Juneteenth (2021).

nodes.label: Silvia Federici
nodes.date_label: Wages against Housework (1975) · Caliban and the Witch (2004) · Revolution at Point Zero (2012) · “Social reproduction theory” (2019)
nodes.description: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Silvia Federici argues that capitalism developed through the coercive reorganization of reproduction, with the witch-hunts and the subordination of women central to primitive accumulation. She treats reproductive labour as a source of capitalist wealth whose unpaid status helps conceal its exploitation, a framework also developed in Revolution at Point Zero (2012). In Socialism & Democracy no. 41 (July 2006), Hester Eisenstein praises the book’s feminist reinterpretation of capitalism but criticizes its idealization of communal rural life and its one-sided assessment of capitalist development. Federici’s account connects women’s history to class relations while disputing Marx’s treatment of primitive accumulation and Foucault’s account of bodily discipline. Her 2019 intervention in social reproduction theory defends the productivity of unpaid work against competing Marxist interpretations.

nodes.label: Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing
nodes.date_label: Friction (2005) · “Unruly Edges” (2012) · The Mushroom at the End of the World (2015) · Feral Atlas, co-edited (2020)
nodes.description: An anthropologist who studies how global capitalism and environmental change are made in particular places. In Friction: An Ethnography of Global Connection (2005), set in the rainforests of Indonesia, she proposed friction instead of a “clash” of cultures as the figure for how global connections work: conflicting, awkward and sometimes productive. The Mushroom at the End of the World (2015) follows the matsutake mushroom through disturbed forests and commodity chains to ask what collaborative life remains possible in capitalist ruins. In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013) she extends Marx’s primitive accumulation, arguing that capitalism keeps depending on non-capitalist relations. A 2015 essay calls a related process “salvage accumulation”: the conversion of goods and skills made outside capitalism into capitalist value. In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), she criticises accounts that treat capitalism as a coherent whole, naming Hardt and Negri’s Empire (2000) in the main text and David Harvey in note 24. “Unruly Edges” (2012), dedicated to Donna Haraway, extends Haraway’s companion species to fungi, draws on Sidney Mintz’s histories of sugar for its account of plantations, and proposes multispecies landscapes as protagonists of world history. She co-edited Arts of Living on a Damaged Planet: Ghosts and Monsters of the Anthropocene (2017) with Nils Bubandt, Elaine Gan and Heather Anne Swanson, and Feral Atlas: The More-than-Human Anthropocene (2020) with Jennifer Deger, Alder Keleman Saxena and Feifei Zhou. The Society for Cultural Anthropology gave The Mushroom at the End of the World its 2016 Bateson Prize. In the society’s 2017 forum on the book, Katherine Sacco asked how its idea of the “latent commons” works in cities. Replying, Tsing conceded that the latent commons “is hardly a robust political program”. A 2021 talk abstract asks whether history was “denied” in an early essay by Dipesh Chakrabarty and how historians might approach the Anthropocene.

nodes.label: Nancy Fraser
nodes.date_label: Unruly Practices (1989) · “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) · Tanner Lectures on redistribution and recognition (1996) · “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014)
nodes.description: A philosopher and critical theorist who reworked Habermas’s public sphere and the theory of justice from a feminist standpoint. In “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) she criticised the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere that Habermas had described, for discounting the effects of social inequality and for its masculinist bias, and argued for a plurality of contesting publics, including what she called subaltern counterpublics. Jane Mansbridge (2017) credits the essay with moves that became established in deliberative democracy, from Habermas’s unitary public to Fraser’s plural publics. In “From Redistribution to Recognition?” (1995), expanded in her Tanner Lectures (1996) and collected in Justice Interruptus (1997), she argued that justice requires both redistribution and recognition; the lectures treat gender as a “bivalent collectivity” and propose participatory parity as the norm of justice; she rejected Charles Taylor’s and Axel Honneth’s grounding of recognition in self-realization. Judith Butler’s “Merely Cultural” (1997) prompted Fraser’s published reply, which rejected the suggestion that she treated heterosexism as merely cultural, and Redistribution or Recognition? staged a sustained debate with Honneth. With the historian Linda Gordon she co-wrote “A Genealogy of Dependency” (1994), on a keyword of the US welfare state. In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014) she looks behind Marx’s “hidden abode” of production for the conditions it depends on, reworking his account from feminist, ecological and political perspectives, and “Contradictions of Capital and Care” (2016) argues that every form of capitalist society harbours a social-reproductive contradiction.

nodes.label: Angela Y. Davis
nodes.date_label: “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) · Women, Race and Class (1981) · Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003)
nodes.description: A philosopher and activist whose writing ties the history of slavery to the politics of gender, class and punishment. In “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971), written in prison, she called the image of the Black matriarch “an open weapon of ideological warfare” and placed enslaved women at the centre of resistance to slavery. Women, Race and Class (1981) traces racism and class bias in the US women’s movement from abolition onward, and treats rape, reproductive freedom and housework through the inequalities between Black and white women. Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) argues for decarceration and prison abolition. Johnnetta Cole’s 1972 response read the essay as a refutation of the matriarchy thesis’s “falsely assumed basis in slavery”, while noting that prison confined Davis to secondary sources. Saidiya Hartman (2016) describes feminist work on gender and reproduction in slavery as following the path the essay cleared, and Jennifer L. Morgan’s Reckoning with Slavery (2021) returns to it. Ruth Thrush (2025) recounts how Women, Race and Class criticised Silvia Federici’s case for wages for housework as reformist. Discussing her memoir Backtalker (2026), Kimberlé Crenshaw named Davis as an influence on her writing in the Black memoir tradition. Davis studied with Theodor Adorno in Frankfurt and says she was drawn to philosophy through Herbert Marcuse and the critical theory of the Frankfurt School.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: If They Come in the Morning: Voices of Resistance (1971, with other political prisoners); “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971); Angela Davis: An Autobiography (1974); Women, Race and Class (1981); Blues Legacies and Black Feminism (1998); “Masked Racism: Reflections on the Prison Industrial Complex” (1998); Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003); Abolition Democracy: Beyond Empire, Prisons, and Torture (2005, interviews with Eduardo Mendieta); “Policing the Crisis Today” (2018).

Her account of Frankfurt and critical theory rests on two published interviews. Her doctoral work with Marcuse is not documented on a permitted text read here.

nodes.label: Sara Ahmed
nodes.date_label: Strange Encounters (2000) · The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004) · Queer Phenomenology (2006) · The Promise of Happiness (2010) · Living a Feminist Life (2017)
nodes.description: A feminist theorist of emotion, orientation and institutional life. The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004) asks what emotions do: Ahmed traces how they are named in speech acts and felt on the skin, and how they work in debates on terrorism, asylum, migration and reconciliation. In “Affective Economies” (2004), she argues that emotions circulate between bodies and signs, helping form the boundaries of individual and collective bodies. Queer Phenomenology (2006) reads Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Fanon with queer and critical race theory to show how bodies are oriented toward some objects and away from others. The Promise of Happiness (2010) treats happiness as a promise that directs lives toward some choices and away from others; its figures include the feminist killjoy, the unhappy queer, the angry Black woman and the melancholic migrant. A 2010 Signs article proposes that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness. Ahmed reused Judith Butler’s definition of performativity to describe the non-performativity of words such as “diversity”, which do not bring about what they name. She names Stuart Hall and Angela Davis as formative for how she takes race seriously, and she criticises Julia Kristeva’s account of French universalism and the Muslim headscarf. Reviewing Strange Encounters (2000), Julie Wuthnow called it an original contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory, but found that its chapter on global feminism underplays the power and antagonism stressed earlier in the book.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Strange Encounters: Embodied Others in Post-Coloniality (2000); The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004; second edition 2014); Queer Phenomenology: Orientations, Objects, Others (2006); The Promise of Happiness (2010); “Killing Joy: Feminism and the History of Happiness” (2010); On Being Included: Racism and Diversity in Institutional Life (2012); Living a Feminist Life (2017).

nodes.label: Wendy Brown
nodes.date_label: “Wounded Attachments” (1993) · States of Injury (1995) · Is Critique Secular?, with Asad, Butler and Mahmood (2009) · Undoing the Demos (2015) · In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019) · Nihilistic Times (2023)
nodes.description: A political theorist of power, freedom and neoliberal reason. Undoing the Demos (2015) treats neoliberalism as a governing rationality rather than a set of policies, a form of reason that extends the model of the market to every domain of life and de-democratizes the state; Brown says Foucault, among others, taught this way of thinking. Her essay “Wounded Attachments” (1993) preceded States of Injury (1995), which includes a chapter of that title and, in its publisher’s description, offers a sympathetic critique of identity politics that asks how woundedness became a basis for political identity, drawing on Nietzsche, Marx, Weber and Foucault. In her introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) she traced how Marx’s distinction between criticism and critique bound critique to secularism in Western critical theory; Judith Butler took up that distinction in the same volume. Daniel T. Rodgers (2018) used Undoing the Demos to illustrate the most enveloping use of “neoliberalism”, arguing that so stretched a term, and Brown’s language of exhaustion and collapse, may make a workable politics harder to see. In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019) reads Hayek’s joining of markets and traditional morality as a source of antidemocratic politics; Matthew McManus (2020) found its Nietzschean final chapter neglected religious questions of meaning. Nihilistic Times (2023) returns to Weber’s lectures on scholarship and politics as vocations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Wounded Attachments,” Political Theory 21, no. 3 (1993): 390–410; States of Injury: Power and Freedom in Late Modernity (1995); Is Critique Secular? Blasphemy, Injury, and Free Speech (2009, with Talal Asad, Judith Butler and Saba Mahmood; Brown’s introduction); Walled States, Waning Sovereignty (2010); Undoing the Demos: Neoliberalism’s Stealth Revolution (2015); In the Ruins of Neoliberalism: The Rise of Antidemocratic Politics in the West (2019); Nihilistic Times: Thinking with Max Weber (2023).
nodes.scope_note: Brown’s 2009 introduction and the 2022 interview were read in full; Rodgers’s 2018 essay and the reviews by McManus (2020) and Moyn (2024) were read in full. The books are unread: States of Injury is described from its publisher’s page, Undoing the Demos from Brown’s interview and Rodgers’s essay, In the Ruins of Neoliberalism and Nihilistic Times from one review each. Several pages were read in web-archive captures of permitted pages because the live pages returned 403. For “Wounded Attachments” (1993), the journal metadata and displayed notes were read; the main article text remains unread.

nodes.label: Margaret C. Jacob
nodes.date_label: The Radical Enlightenment (1981) · Living the Enlightenment (1991) · Telling the Truth about History, coauthor (1994) · The First Knowledge Economy (2014)
nodes.description: In The Radical Enlightenment (1981), Jacob located early Enlightenment radicalism in the political and religious conflicts connecting England, the Dutch Republic and French Protestant exiles. Living the Enlightenment (1991) argued that Masonic lodges helped form modern civil society by practising constitutional self-government. Her histories of science connect scientific culture to industry; The First Knowledge Economy (2014) centres mechanical knowledge and its transmission. Erik Hornung praised its evidence about British engineers but questioned whether its Continental comparison used comparable evidence. Jacob’s 2014 retrospective credits Christopher Hill and J. G. A. Pocock while opposing Jonathan Israel’s Spinoza-centred account. Her 2013 Logos essay criticizes Bruno Latour’s approach to historical motives. With Joyce Appleby and Lynn Hunt she coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), a defence of accountable historical inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Newtonians and the English Revolution, 1689–1720 (1976); The Radical Enlightenment (1981); The Cultural Meaning of the Scientific Revolution (1988); Living the Enlightenment (1991); Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Joyce Appleby and Lynn Hunt; Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West (1997); The Book That Changed Europe (2010), with Lynn Hunt and Wijnand Mijnhardt; The First Knowledge Economy (2014).

The selected monographs were not read in full; Living the Enlightenment, Scientific Culture and Telling the Truth are summarized only at publisher-description level. nodes.label: Pat Hudson
nodes.date_label: The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986) · The Industrial Revolution (1992) · History by Numbers (2000) · Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution, with Maxine Berg (2023)
nodes.description: In The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986), Pat Hudson explained industrial development in West Riding wool textiles through agrarian structures, landholding and varied routes from domestic to factory production. Her 1990 working paper with Maxine Berg, Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution, argued that regional transformation and women’s and children’s work expose changes obscured by national growth measures. With Berg, she later argued that slave-based Atlantic markets helped generate industrial skills and innovation, challenging Joel Mokyr’s supply-side explanation in 2021. Their Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023) connected slavery to production, consumption, finance and inequality. In 2025 Priya Satia criticized the book’s causal disclaimers as inconsistent with the force of its evidence and challenged its portrayal of earlier scholarship.

nodes.label: Jane Humphries
nodes.date_label: Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women (1990) · with Sara Horrell, Women’s Labour Force Participation (1995) · Childhood and Child Labour (2010) · The Lure of Aggregates (2013)
nodes.description: Jane Humphries places women’s and children’s work and fragile family economies at the centre of explanations of British industrialisation. Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution (2010) uses working men’s autobiographies to argue that industrialisation brought an upsurge in child labour, shaped by mechanization, large families and unreliable or absent breadwinners. With Sara Horrell, she studied women’s labour-force participation and the transition to the male-breadwinner family, 1790–1865 (1995). The Lure of Aggregates (2013) challenges Robert C. Allen’s high-wage interpretation for treating male earnings as a reliable measure of family wellbeing and offers cheap female and child labour as another stimulus to innovation. Reception includes a methodological dispute with Emma Griffin: Humphries questioned the causal account of breadwinner failure in Bread Winner (2020), while Griffin argued in a 2022 note that Humphries’s male-authored autobiographical sample could not sustain broad arguments about wider working-class experience.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women (1990); with Sara Horrell, Women’s Labour Force Participation and the Transition to the Male-Breadwinner Family, 1790–1865 (1995); Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution (2010); The Lure of Aggregates and the Pitfalls of the Patriarchal Perspective (2013; working paper 2011); with Benjamin Schneider, Spinning the Industrial Revolution (2019).
nodes.scope_note: The 2010 book was read only through publisher frontmatter and synopsis; main chapters remain unread. Selected 1995 article passages and selected pages of the 2011 working paper were read. The final 2013 articles and the 1990 article were read as abstracts only. The 2020 review and Griffin’s 2022 critical note supply the reception account. Referenced works by Pinchbeck, Berg, de Vries, Mokyr and Griffin were not independently read in full.

edges.relationship: Strong-Boag and Joan Sangster co-authored “Teaching Canadian History in the 1990s: Whose National History Are We Lamenting?” (1992), with Linda Kealey and Ruth Roach Pierson.

edges.relationship: In her 1999 review of Granatstein’s Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), Strong-Boag rejects its marginalization of women, workers and racialized people while agreeing that Canadian history needs stronger teaching.
edges.evidence_note: Complete review, pp. 283–285, read in the Queen’s journal PDF (1625/1713), ending at Strong-Boag’s signature on 285 before the next review. Especially 284: reforms require “faithful accounts of the past”; she supports some teaching proposals but contests the book’s hierarchy of significance. Granatstein’s book unread. The older graph source’s unread-review note is preserved, with a separate fresh-read addendum proposed.

edges.relationship: In “Contested Space” (1994), Strong-Boag criticizes Creighton’s dismissal of radical historical reinterpretations and his opposition to cultural pluralism, citing his 1969 essay and Canada’s First Century (1970).
edges.evidence_note: Selected official Érudit PDF passages, printed p. 7, nn. 15–16: she calls his position “blinkered vision”; n. 15 identifies “John A. Macdonald, Confederation and the Canadian West” in Minorities Schools and Politics (1969), p. 9, and n. 16 identifies Canada’s First Century, 106–109. This is her attributed criticism; Creighton originals unread.

edges.relationship: Strong-Boag, with Jean Barman, supervised Adele Perry’s postdoctoral fellowship in 1998–99. Strong-Boag and Perry later co-edited the fourth edition of Rethinking Canada: The Promise of Women’s History (2002), with Mona Gleason.
edges.evidence_note: Read Strong-Boag’s institutional CV, PDF leaf 34, heading “Post-doctoral supervision,” which lists Perry (York), SSHRCC, 1998–9, with Jean Barman. PDF leaf 4 lists the three editors of Rethinking Canada, fourth edition (2002). Supervision supplies the directed influence classification; the co-editing is a separate undirected collaboration retained as a second witness. No particular theoretical debt or sole supervision is claimed. Fold into the existing pair rather than adding a duplicate edge.

edges.relationship: Strong-Boag, Jean Barman and Neil Sutherland jointly compiled A Bibliography of Canadian Childhood: Articles (1987).
edges.evidence_note: Strong-Boag’s UBC embedded CV, Non-refereed publications / Other, explicitly credits the 1987 bibliography to herself with Sutherland and Barman. This is a bibliographical collaboration only; no claim of common theoretical commitments or reading of the bibliography itself. The same credit is in the UVic CV, PDF p. 15.

edges.relationship: In “Contested Space” (1994), Strong-Boag uses Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) to connect the historical disbelief of sexual-assault complainants with the exclusions of Canadian collective memory.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed p. 16, n. 64: Strong-Boag quotes Dubinsky’s conclusion about complainants leaving the “courtroom empty-handed” and extends that pattern to collective responses to abuse. Printed p. 5 n. 5 also draws on Dubinsky’s 1993 labour-history teaching essay. Only the first substantive use is proposed; Dubinsky’s book unread. No complainant’s words or narrative are reproduced.

edges.relationship: The New Day Recalled (1988) uses a modified life-course approach to show how gender hierarchy persisted across class differences in interwar English Canada.
edges.evidence_note: Mediated by Rooke’s 1989 review, pp. 165–166: outlines six life-course chapters and quotes the book’s p. 3 on class not superseding sex stratification. Book unread.

edges.relationship: Reflecting on Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006) and Fostering Nation? (2011) in her 2023 CHA questionnaire, Strong-Boag presents disadvantaged childhoods as inseparable from inequalities of gender, class, race, sexuality and disability.
edges.evidence_note: CHA questionnaire, answer to “of all your writings, which are you most proud of and why?” She describes both books in these terms; the claim is her retrospective account, not a fresh reading of either monograph. Original years checked in the CV, PDF p. 3.

edges.relationship: “Contested Space” (1994) counters laments for a single national history by arguing that historical accounts must connect political institutions with the histories of women, workers and racialized people.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed pp. 4–6 and 17: her alternative requires “many interwoven narratives” (6). This intervention precedes Who Killed Canadian History? (1998); it is not described as a reply to that book. The existing field-to-debate edge_813 is preserved; this is a person-level route supported by newly read primary passages.

edges.relationship: “Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory” (1994) argues that collective memory becomes more adequate when historians confront professional privilege and include histories of violence and exclusion.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed pp. 14–17, especially concluding p. 17: “meaningful memory for all Canadians”. Claim concerns the scholarly programme, without reproducing survivors’ accounts. Other parts of the address were sampled, not a complete fresh reading.

edges.relationship: In her historiographical essay 'By Necessity or by Right' (2002), Nancy Christie discusses Strong-Boag's 'The Girl of the New Day' (1979) as characterising women's work in the 1920s as gendered continuity rather than new job segregation.
edges.evidence_note: Body-text engagement read on pp. 121–123. Christie uses Strong-Boag’s findings in her historiographical explanation; this supports specific uptake, not supervision or a general intellectual genealogy.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Rethinking Canada (1986), co-edited by Strong-Boag and Anita Clair Fellman, in 1987, Bettina Bradbury judged that it showed Canadian women's history becoming more sophisticated, and suggested that future collections focus on specific themes.
edges.evidence_note: Complete journal review read, pp. 454–455. The closing recommendation mildly qualifies a positive appraisal; it concerns the collection’s format rather than rejecting Strong-Boag’s McClung argument. The journal credits its French translation to John A. Dickinson.

edges.relationship: Strong-Boag’s ‘The Girl of the New Day’ (1979) contributed to labour history by explaining persistent gender hierarchies within industrial modernization, as Nancy Christie discusses in 2002.
edges.evidence_note: Christie substantively credits Strong-Boag alongside Sangster and McCallum. The contribution is shared, not a claim of sole innovation; the individual uptake is separately represented by o_01.

edges.relationship: In The Last Suffragist Standing (2018), Strong-Boag contributed to biographical method through a contextual account of Laura Marshall Jamieson that analyzes gender, race, class and privilege, as Kesia Kvill’s 2019 review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Complete review read, pp. 352–354. Kvill identifies a method for writing about a woman who left few sources, while criticizing the contextual approach for sometimes displacing Jamieson and understating personal experience. This is review-based evidence; the book was not read. Kvill lacks an eligible person endpoint, so no reviewer edge is proposed.

edges.relationship: In “Killing Stones” (2011), Thomas praises Walsham’s The Reformation of the Landscape (2011) but questions its account of continuing piety at eighteenth-century spas.
edges.evidence_note: Review, paragraphs beginning “Its footnotes testify” and “Walsham, who is deeply hostile” (web lines 129, 140–142): praise accompanies “unduly optimistic”. Review passages read; monograph unread. Criticism concerns this interpretation, not the whole book.

edges.relationship: In “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008), Walsham reconsiders the Weberian disenchantment thesis and proposes cycles of desacralization and resacralization in place of a linear narrative.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final sentence, read: “cycles of desacralization and resacralization”; opening names Weber. Article body unread. This is the abstract’s stated historiographical intervention, not a fresh reading of Weber or a claim that every part of his sociology is rejected.

edges.relationship: With Julia Crick, Walsham’s “Introduction: Script, print, and history” (2004) challenges the script-to-print divide associated with Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), emphasizing the media’s continued interaction.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt pp. 3–5, especially p. 4: “lingering co-existence, interaction and symbiosis”. Joint argument, not sole authorship. Eisenstein’s original is unread here; the introduction cites its 1980 edition. Introduction beyond the excerpt unread.

edges.relationship: In their “Introduction: Script, print, and history” (2004), Walsham and Julia Crick use Chartier’s work on readers’ appropriation to question claims that printed texts impose uniform meanings.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt p. 5 and n. 9 read: Chartier “has cast doubt on the uniformity” of print. His cited works include The Cultural Uses of Print in Early Modern France (English translation, 1987). Those works unread; debt belongs to both coauthors.

edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham applies Nora’s lieux de mémoire to repurposed religious objects that sustain remembering and forgetting.
edges.evidence_note: Published article p. 1124 and n. 10 read: “lieux de mémoire”; note names Nora’s 1989 essay. Other resources share the note. Original Nora essay unread for this dossier; application is specific to remodeled objects.

edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham explicitly draws inspiration from Appadurai’s social life of things when connecting human and object histories.
edges.evidence_note: Article p. 1124 and n. 11 read: “Taking inspiration”. Appadurai’s edited The Social Life of Things (1986) is named with Kopytoff and others. No exclusive derivation; originals unread.

edges.relationship: In “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), Walsham names Stoler’s Along the Archival Grain (2009) as an inspiration for investigating the internal logic of archival records.
edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript, paragraph beginning “The Social History of the Archive responds” (body paragraph 73), n. 143: “one source of inspiration”. Passage and footnote read; Stoler’s book unread here. Attribution concerns the volume’s method, not adoption of every colonial argument.

edges.relationship: In “History, Memory, and the English Reformation” (2012), Walsham examines how personal recollection and social memory reshaped remembrance of the Reformation between 1530 and 1700.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract read: “personal recollection and social memory”. Article body unread. Limited to its stated research programme and period; no detailed conclusions inferred.

edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham treats the altered uses and afterlives of liturgical objects as a material history of religious change.
edges.evidence_note: Article pp. 1124–1125, 1154 read; combines textual, material and archaeological evidence. Middle cases unread. Contribution concerns material culture, not a claim about aggregate consumer demand.

edges.relationship: In “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), Walsham argues for examining the creation, selection and preservation of early modern records as historical practices that shape knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript opening, body paragraphs 4–12, read. Paragraph 8 makes the archive a subject of enquiry; paragraphs 10–11 state the intervention. Rest of collection unread; no claim of sole authorship of the collaborative volume.

edges.relationship: In The Reformation of the Landscape (2011), Alexandra Walsham contributes to spatial history by treating religious change and the making of landscapes as interacting processes and calling for greater historical attention to place, space and physical environment.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's introduction abstract, together with the book-level abstract and publication metadata. These explicitly describe a reciprocal account of religious change and landscape and a methodological call for attention to space. The chapter body and complete book were not accessible and are unread. This is a bounded contribution to the existing landscape-history component of spatialhistory, not a claim about GIS or the foundation of the field.

edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s chapter 1 and its notes. Carter names and quotes Bradbury in the body, then relates the argument to Western Canada. Notes 9–10 identify the 2005 chapter, pp. 150 and 136. This is substantive uptake rather than a citation-only association; no claim of supervision.

edges.relationship: Bettina Bradbury’s Working Families (1993) contributed to family history by using the household economy to connect women’s subsistence work with family survival, an approach Mary Anne Poutanen (2014) identifies as foundational and applies to residential prostitution and tavern-keeping.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete journal contribution. Poutanen explains the book’s method and describes her own applications in the body. The target includes history of the family: this edge does not claim a demographic technique or dataset. Poutanen is absent from both eligible endpoint lists, so her specific debt is evidence for the field contribution, not a proposed person edge.
edges.map_label: Household economy as a family-history method

edges.relationship: Bettina Bradbury’s “Colonial Comparisons: Rethinking Marriage, Civilization and Nation in Nineteenth-Century White Settler Societies” (2005) contributed to comparative settler-colonial history by examining how marriage regimes marked colonial difference and preserved white male authority across settler societies, as assessed by Jarett Henderson (2014).
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete journal contribution. Henderson explains the comparison across Canada, New Zealand, Australia and the Cape and explicitly assesses its methodological contribution. The edge concerns published historical analysis, without reproducing oral narratives or community knowledge. Henderson is absent from the eligible endpoint lists.
edges.map_label: Marriage regimes in comparative colonial history

edges.relationship: Thomas Laqueur was one of Deborah Cohen’s doctoral advisers (Berkeley PhD, 1996), as she acknowledges in The War Come Home (2001), alongside Gerald Feldman.
edges.evidence_note: The publisher’s indexed acknowledgments extract names Laqueur and Feldman as advisers and distinguishes the other dissertation committee members. Cohen’s Northwestern CV, p. 1, Education, confirms the Berkeley history PhD in 1996. This records supervision only, with no claim of sole supervision or doctrinal influence.

edges.relationship: In “Comparative History: Buyer Beware” (2001), Cohen uses Susan Pedersen’s Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993) as an example of comparison generating a new historical interpretation. Cohen, Guy Ortolano and Pedersen also coauthored “Peter and the special relationship” (2025).
edges.evidence_note: Read Cohen’s 2001 essay, printed p. 29, paragraph beginning “Let me offer two principal reasons to compare,” and note 11 on printed p. 32. The discussion uses Pedersen’s British/French family-allowance comparison as an example of a productive research question; Pedersen’s book remains unread. The 2025 coauthorship is confirmed by the publisher’s contents and indexed Interlude B byline. The War Come Home acknowledgments also credit Pedersen with inspiration and manuscript criticism, but those thanks do not carry or count toward this edge. Direction applies to the 2001 intellectual resource; the folded coauthorship is a separate, undirected witness.

edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen challenges the confidence in comparative method expressed in Bloch's 1928 essay.
edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, pp. 27, 30–31; notes 1, 27–28 distinguish 1928 original from 1953 English reprint. ‘technical instrument’ is the contested promise; Bloch's essay unread separately.

edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen uses Maier's Recasting Bourgeois Europe (1975) to show that comparative history can also be cross-national.
edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, p. 24, note 9: ‘maybe the best’. Maier's monograph unread; specific approving methodological example only.

edges.relationship: With Peter Mandler in ‘The History Manifesto: A Critique’ (2015), Cohen disputes Armitage and Jo Guldi's evidence for historians' retreat from long time spans and their proposed link between temporal scale and public significance.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher opening extract, paragraphs 2–4 on p. 530, especially ‘What we object to’ and ‘This is true’. Joint credit retained on both sides; quantitative and digital methods are expressly accepted. Remainder of critique, 2014 book and reply unread.

edges.relationship: In Household Gods (2006), Cohen connects British domestic consumption with religious values and the use of possessions to express individuality.
edges.evidence_note: Yale description, paragraphs 1–3: ‘religious fervor’ and ‘expressing individuality’. Publisher summary only; full book unread. Original year comes from CV, not the page's 2009 paperback date.

edges.relationship: In Family Secrets (2013), Cohen makes changing relations between privacy and secrecy part of the explanation of modern British family life, as Claire Langhamer emphasizes in her 2014 roundtable response.
edges.evidence_note: Langhamer, complete contribution, paragraphs 1–5, particularly final two: ‘driver of change’. Mediated reading supports family history, not demographic measurement or a linear progress thesis; full book unread.

edges.relationship: In ‘Comparative History: Buyer Beware’ (2001), Cohen questions whether isolating variables adequately explains national differences in comparative historical sociology.
edges.evidence_note: Complete essay, pp. 27–28, beginning ‘In its search for causes’ and ‘If similar phenomena’: ‘generalizing’ explanations are qualified, not comparison abandoned. She applies the difficulty to her own book as well.

edges.relationship: Deborah Cohen's Family Secrets (2013) supplies an analysis of secrecy and privacy that Jennifer Crane explicitly extends to the medical history of child abuse and diagnostic radiology in her 2015 article on the battered child syndrome.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's open article, including the introduction and concluding application of Cohen. Crane names Family Secrets (2013) immediately after the supporting phrase and uses its separation of secrecy from privacy to frame the recognition of child abuse. This records a documented conceptual resource for medical history, not a claim that Cohen researched diagnostic radiology. Crane has no eligible person endpoint, so no person edge is proposed. Cohen's book was not read in full.
edges.map_label: Secrecy and privacy in medical history

edges.relationship: Appleby and Hunt coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994) with Margaret Jacob.
edges.evidence_note: Norton author line names all three; AHA bibliography gives original 1994 publication. Norton’s displayed 1995 date is the paperback. Authorship only: the complete book is unread.

edges.relationship: Gordon Wood's 2000 review credits Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) with rescuing a liberal, commercially minded Jefferson from the 'republican synthesis' most associated with Pocock; Pocock replied (2000) that such a reading was compatible with his own argument.
edges.evidence_note: Wood, paragraphs beginning Several decades ago Appleby and In a series of important articles, explicitly identifies the 1984 book. Pocock’s 19 October letter rejects Wood’s dichotomy and says an entrepreneurial Jefferson could fit his argument. Mediated claim; neither monograph read.
edges.map_label: Liberal Jefferson and the republican synthesis (as framed by Wood; Pocock disputed)

edges.relationship: In “Early American Get-Up-and-Go” (2000), Wood praises the breadth of Appleby’s Inheriting the Revolution (2000) but questions its dating, account of the colonial order, and explanation of change through Jefferson’s election.
edges.evidence_note: Review paragraphs beginning Because Appleby often, Since Appleby does not describe, Moreover, Appleby never fully explains, and Still, despite these omissions. Selected review text read; Appleby’s monograph unread.

edges.relationship: In “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997), Chakrabarty uses Appleby, Hunt and Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) to question the epistemological limits of incorporating minority histories through shared rational rules of evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Official AHA text, “Rationality in the Discourse of History,” paragraphs beginning The point about historical narratives and Nevertheless, and final “Subaltern Pasts and Disciplinary Limits” section. Calls the book “important” while extending the inquiry to exclusion. All three authors retain credit; book unread. Existing group edge_392 remains.

edges.relationship: In “What is History Now?” (published 2004), Cannadine recognizes a template for disciplinary essays in Appleby, Hunt and Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) and closes by endorsing Appleby’s “The Power of History” (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 50, section IV, notes 61–62: the template was encountered when the lecture was “nearly drafted”; n61 cites the 1995 book manifestation, p. 228, and n62 the 1998 address, p. 1. Retrospective recognition, not formative influence on the already drafted sections. Joint book unread; lecture delivery 2002 distinct from publication 2004.
edges.map_label: Cannadine acknowledges joint template and Appleby address

edges.relationship: In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby identifies Said’s Orientalism (1978) as a resource for historians’ scrutiny of Western representations of other peoples.
edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning Historians’ recent self-scrutiny and note 14 name Orientalism as “Particularly resonant.” Specific uptake; no full reading of Said asserted.
edges.map_label: Said as a resource for disciplinary self-scrutiny

edges.relationship: Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) connects Jeffersonian political expectations to expanding commercial agriculture and a capitalist social vision.
edges.evidence_note: NYU description, final two argument paragraphs, explicitly links commercial agriculture, capitalism and the Jeffersonian movement. Publisher-mediated contribution; book unread.

edges.relationship: As Margaret Jacob’s AHA biography explains, Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978) reconstructs changing understandings of commerce and market forces by combining social practices with intellectual history.
edges.evidence_note: Jacob biography opening and paragraphs beginning Joyce’s first book and In her own life. Named substantive account of the method and subject; monograph unread.
edges.map_label: Economic thought as intellectual and social history (1978)

edges.relationship: In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby argues that cultural mediation and historical revision can be explained publicly while material evidence continues to constrain historical claims.
edges.evidence_note: Concluding paragraphs beginning We need to explain that historical knowledge, We could also make more salient, and History is powerful; phrase “materiality of historical evidence.” Primary web text read; print pagination uncollated. Adds a sole-authored intervention alongside the existing joint-book roster.

edges.relationship: In his response to critics (1999), Richard J. Evans disputed Joyce Appleby’s review “Does it really need defending?” (1997), arguing that she misrepresented In Defence of History (1997) as rejecting all postmodernism and defending an omniscient historian.
edges.evidence_note: Read Evans’s reply, not Appleby’s original review or his book. His introduction at https://archives.history.ac.uk/history-in-focus/Whatishistory/evans.html dates the response November 1999 and lists Appleby’s review as TLS, 31 October 1997, p. 10. This records his objection without endorsing it.
edges.map_label: Evans disputes Appleby’s reading of historical objectivity

edges.relationship: In “More Pasts Than One” (1995), Eric Foner praised Telling the Truth about History (1994), coauthored by Joyce Appleby, Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob, but argued that its account underplayed the intellectual disruption of the 1960s and left historical truth insufficiently defined.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher-hosted review. Its praise and reservations concern the joint book, not an argument attributed solely to Appleby. The book itself remains unread.
edges.map_label: Foner questions the definition of historical truth

edges.relationship: The Relentless Revolution (2010) contributed to debate over capitalism’s origins by treating capitalism as a contingent cultural formation emerging in England; William Gallois’s 2010 review identifies this distinctive intervention while criticising its limited engagement with competing scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Read the review and Appleby’s response. Gallois explicitly assesses the book’s contribution and omissions; Appleby explains her distinction between earlier capitalist practices and capitalism as a culture. The book remains unread. No claim of priority or acceptance is made.
edges.map_label: Capitalism’s contingent English origins as a cultural formation

edges.relationship: In “Who Made Luxury” (2017), Berg credits de Vries’s industrious-revolution work as an influence on her Luxury Project.
edges.evidence_note: Printed 27, introduction: “greatly influenced”; 30 discusses The Industrious Revolution (2008). This is Berg’s retrospective attribution; de Vries’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Berg’s preface to A Woman in History (1996) credits Thomas’s 1989 suggestion for her turn to biography.
edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii, paragraph 1: “I owe this change in my approach”. Specific suggestion, not supervision. Biography chapters unread.
edges.map_label: Suggestion to write the Power biography

edges.relationship: In A Woman in History (1996), Berg recalls using Clark’s books while researching women’s and family labour for The Age of Manufactures (1985).
edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii: “drawn back to books written by Alice Clark” and others. Clark’s particular title unspecified; no exclusive debt asserted.
edges.map_label: Earlier women economic historians as resources

edges.relationship: A Woman in History (1996) credits Davis’s “History’s Two Bodies” (1988) with helping Berg’s early writing.
edges.evidence_note: Preface xiv, final paragraph and note 2 continuing xv: “Two key articles helped me”. Davis’s essay unread.
edges.map_label: History’s Two Bodies as a resource

edges.relationship: In her response concerning A Woman in History (1996), Berg defends Power’s comparative programme and collaborative scholarship as achievements obscured by monograph-centred judgments.
edges.evidence_note: October 1996 response, paragraphs beginning “Major monographs” and “The Wool Trade”: “not the only measure”. Biographical interpretation, not personal contact; full book unread.

edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, Berg’s “Slavery, Atlantic trade and skills” (2021) challenges Mokyr’s supply-side explanation, locating stimuli for skill formation in slave-based Atlantic trade.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF 260–261, 275–276: “On this we agree” accepts skilled workers’ importance. Their objection concerns timing, regional concentration and stimuli; Mokyr’s original unread.
edges.map_label: Atlantic demand versus a supply-side explanation

edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, Berg’s “Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution” working paper (1990) challenges causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s national demographic series.
edges.evidence_note: Printed 30–33, Demography: “aggregative studies”. They retain local variation and Schofield’s revised interpretation. Joint critique; not rejection of reconstruction itself. 1992 journal version unread. Existing edge_1084 mediates this criticism through capitalismdebates; no direct Berg–Wrigley edge exists.
edges.map_label: Aggregate series and regional demographic causes

edges.relationship: Luxury and Pleasure in Eighteenth-Century Britain (2005) links demand for new middling-class consumer goods with product invention and industrialisation.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher book abstract, final sentence, read in the record for the 2007 manifestation; original year from Warwick and Burnette. Full book unread. Existing roster concerns the separate Clifford coedited collection.

edges.relationship: In her response about A Woman in History (1996), Berg explains how women, feminism and internationalism shaped early economic history and how gendered remembrance diminished Power’s scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: October 1996 response, paragraphs beginning “In contrast” and “She may have built”; “female scholar rather than for the history”. Full biography unread.
edges.map_label: Women and the discipline’s historical memory

edges.relationship: “Who Made Luxury” (2017) connects Asian exports and production knowledge with European imitation, manufacture and changing consumption.
edges.evidence_note: Printed 28–30, Luxury and the East: “provided models” and discussion of knowledge conveyed by traded goods. Argument read; underlying eighteenth-century accounts not independently examined.
edges.map_label: Asian production within global consumption history

edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, “Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution” (1990 working paper) contests growth accounting as a sufficient measure of industrial transformation, stressing innovation, women’s and children’s labour and regional change.
edges.evidence_note: Printed 4–5: “mis-specified”; four areas stated on 5. Joint argument, read in 1990 version; journal article (1992) unread. Existing edge_1083 is an economic-field route; this adds its named coauthor’s route.

edges.relationship: In ‘The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity’ (1992), Anna Clark applies an argument from Berg’s The Machinery Question and the Making of Political Economy 1815–1848 (1980) to explain how treating women’s and children’s work as a moral problem could shield political economy from criticism and make Chartist domestic rhetoric politically vulnerable.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF’s opening and selected substantive passages, especially printed pp. 82–85 and notes 112 and 124. Clark names Berg in the body, applies her analysis to the vulnerability of Chartist domesticity, and identifies the cited work through the two notes. This is substantive uptake, not an inference from a reference list. Clark expressly says Berg was discussing another context; the edge therefore claims application rather than attributing Clark’s account of Chartism itself to Berg. Berg’s cited p. 296 was not independently read. Original article publication is January 1992, not the publisher’s 2014 online posting. Anna Clark is a run member, distinct from Alice Clark, whose pair is already in the supplied input.
edges.map_label: Applies Berg’s analysis of labour, morality and political economy (1992)

edges.relationship: In The Machinery Question and the Making of Political Economy 1815–1848 (1980), Berg contributes to the history of technology by distinguishing contemporaries’ identification of industrialisation with machinery from the limited geographical and industrial spread of mechanisation and the continuing expansion of manual production.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publicly displayed Introduction summary and publication metadata, plus the publisher summary of chapter 2, ‘The progress of the machine’ (pp. 20–31; DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511560330.004). The Introduction contrasts the public identification of industrialisation with machines and the concentration of actual mechanisation in relatively few industries and regions. Chapter 2 states her project of charting mechanisation as the basis for examining contemporary ideas. History of technology is an editorial mapping to this documented intervention; no claim of founding the field or of later scholarly adoption follows from the summaries. The book body remains unread. This target is an existing field endpoint and is absent from the supplied Berg pair list; its prior roster mention does not constitute a direct edge.
edges.map_label: Distinguishes machinery’s public meaning from its uneven spread (1980)

edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss uses the gender-analysis framework associated with Scott’s Gender and the Politics of History (1988) to explain how business practices represent and produce economic power.
edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed pp. 221–222, especially the paragraph beginning “The framework for gender analysis pioneered by Joan Scott”; notes 4–5 identify Scott’s 1988 book alongside other feminist resources. This is a specific methodological use and recommendation, not sole derivation or a claim of supervision. Scott’s book was not independently read.

edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss uses Bederman’s Manliness and Civilization (1995) to treat masculinity as a continuing historical process rather than assume a singular crisis of manhood.
edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed p. 222, paragraph beginning “This approach is especially powerful,” calls masculinity an “always problematic category” following Bederman; note 6 identifies the 1995 book. The use concerns business organization and gender; no wholesale adoption of Bederman’s book or fresh reading of that original is claimed.

edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss questions the shifting definitions of gender in Kessler-Harris’s Do We Still Need Women’s History? (2007), using it to illustrate inconsistent applications of gender analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed p. 31, paragraph beginning “Nevertheless,” and note 34 (p. 37), referring back to the full citation in note 30: Chronicle of Higher Education, 7 December 2007, B6–7. Peiss introduces the example as “flattened and inconsistent concepts of gender.” On p. 30 she also acknowledges Kessler-Harris’s concern that women’s history remains unfinished; the critique is not a rejection of that concern. Kessler-Harris’s original was not read.

edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss includes Hoganson’s Fighting for American Manhood (1998) in a qualified criticism of histories whose recurring masculine-crisis explanations risk essentializing masculinity across different settings.
