edges.evidence_note: Peiss, printed pp. 31–32, especially the paragraph beginning “Boydston’s observations hold true,” with note 36 on p. 37 explicitly naming Hoganson alongside Summers, Dean and Gosse. The phrase “markedly similar, if not uniform” describes the cluster, not Hoganson alone. Peiss separately values Consumers’ Imperium (2007) at p. 28/note 25. The link is a bounded collective criticism, not a blanket dismissal of Hoganson; both Hoganson books remain unread.

edges.relationship: In Women’s Past and the Currents of U.S. History (2013), Peiss connects women’s history’s feminist and institutional formation with the continuing task of integrating women’s actions into wider historical explanations.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter pp. 17–20 and 30–33: the opening identifies four conceptual turns; the conclusion assesses progress “from exclusion to inclusion.” Pages 32–33 retain women’s agency as a continuing concern alongside gender analysis. Complete chapter and notes read in the authorized NYU PDF; no claim that gender history supersedes women’s history.
edges.map_label: Women’s history and its institutional formation

edges.relationship: In “Vital Industry” and Women’s Ventures (1998), Peiss asks how business helped construct gender as well as how gender shaped business, questioning the treatment of firms as naturally masculine.
edges.evidence_note: Article pp. 219–223, especially pp. 220–221 on the firm as a “masculine enterprise” and the paired questions about gender’s operation in business and business’s construction of gender. The reading includes the opening argument and named methodological resources, not the entire article.
edges.map_label: Business and gender shape one another

edges.relationship: In American Women and the Making of Modern Consumer Culture (1998), Peiss argues that women helped produce consumer culture through commercial work, political organizing and beauty businesses as well as purchasing goods.
edges.evidence_note: Journal transcription, opening paragraphs on the historical production of consumer identity and final paragraphs on African American beauty entrepreneurs and collective alternatives; conclusion beginning “Behind the compelling image.” The lecture was delivered 26 March 1998 and published in the Fall 1998 journal issue. Read as an argument, not inferred from a shared topic or a teaching appointment.
edges.map_label: Women as makers of consumer culture

edges.relationship: Cheap Amusements (1986) connects women’s wage work and leisure to cultural change, a contribution to women’s labour history identified by Marybeth Hamilton’s review.
edges.evidence_note: Hamilton’s review, pp. 283–285, opens by identifying “women’s labour history” and explains the connection between work schedules, low wages and recreation. The book itself remains unread in full; this field link is explicitly mediated by the named reviewer.
edges.map_label: Working women’s leisure and cultural change

edges.relationship: In “Bad Girls and Masked Men” (1997), Carolyn Strange draws on Kathy Peiss’s Cheap Amusements (1986), alongside Erenberg and Nasaw, to explain the shift toward mixed-sex commercial leisure, and uses Peiss’s evidence on working women’s family circumstances in her comparison of sexual opportunities and constraints.
edges.evidence_note: Journal PDF passages read. The body attributes the leisure transition to Peiss, Erenberg and Nasaw jointly; notes 9–10 connect the subsequent analysis to Cheap Amusements, pp. 34 and 52. This is documented use in Strange’s essay, not a claim of exclusive influence or supervision. Peiss’s book was not read in full.
edges.map_label: Uses leisure history to compare sexual opportunities

edges.relationship: Cheap Amusements (1986) contributes to the history of sexuality by showing how commercial leisure gave working-class women sexual autonomy alongside new vulnerabilities and dependencies, an insight Regina Kunzel uses in “The Uneven History of Modern American Sexuality” (2018) to historicize heterosexuality.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher HTML body and notes read. Kunzel explicitly uses Peiss to address the historical construction of heterosexuality. The field endpoint includes sexuality history; this does not assert that Peiss studied gay identities. Kunzel is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person edge is proposed.

edges.relationship: Hoganson’s “Edging In” (2020) credits Cott with supervising her undergraduate thesis and doctorate.
edges.evidence_note: Memoir, paragraphs beginning “These three developments” and “My senior year”; retrospective testimony; theses unread.

edges.relationship: Hoganson names Rosenberg’s Spreading the American Dream (1982) among her formative foreign-relations texts in “Edging In” (2020).
edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5: “influenced me greatly”; specific uptake unspecified.

edges.relationship: Hoganson names Rodgers’s Atlantic Crossings (1998) among her formative foreign-relations texts in “Edging In” (2020).
edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5; specific uptake unspecified; original unread.

edges.relationship: Hoganson names Kaplan and Donald Pease’s jointly edited Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as formative in “Edging In” (2020).
edges.evidence_note: Memoir, note 5; joint editorial credit; collection unread.

edges.relationship: Hoganson and Jay Sexton's introduction to Crossing Empires (2020) quotes Iriye's 2002 distinction between international and transnational history, then argues that the transnational frame does not fully capture, and can obscure, the imperial relations behind cross-border links.
edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 2–3: Iriye’s definition frames the cable example; the next paragraph says transnational “does not fully capture” its relations. Their argument is jointly authored. Iriye’s original 2002 essay and the rest of the introduction are unread.

edges.relationship: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) explains U.S. war and imperial politics through gendered citizenship, political leadership and the prestige attached to martial manhood.
edges.evidence_note: Yale publisher description, paragraphs 1–4, explicitly joins gender and international relations history and identifies politicians’ use of manhood and soldier-citizenship ideals. Illinois confirms original 1998; Yale lists later editions. Description read; full book unread.
edges.map_label: Masculinity in war and imperial politics

edges.relationship: Consumers’ Imperium (2007) makes affluent white women’s imported furnishings, dress, food and leisure practices part of the history of U.S. global power.
edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description, paragraphs 1–4, moves from exports and production to imports and household demand. Its scope is predominantly well-to-do white women; no universal consumer experience asserted. Publisher page read; full book unread.

edges.relationship: Hoganson and Jay Sexton’s Crossing Empires introduction (2020) argues that histories of cross-border connection must identify the imperial power relations that enabled them.
edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 1–3, especially cable communications as both cross-border networks and imperial routes/materials. “call out empire” states the program. Selected pages and publisher description read; contributors’ individual arguments and complete volume unread.

edges.relationship: Fighting for American Manhood (1998) contributes to military history by explaining how politicians’ anxieties about national manliness encouraged the Spanish-American and Philippine-American wars.
edges.evidence_note: Read Fraser’s substantive military-history discussion and note 83 in the journal’s open text. Fraser identifies Hoganson’s use of congressional debates as an example of historical analysis of martial masculinity. This establishes a field contribution, not personal influence on Fraser or on the historians discussed alongside her. Hoganson’s book was not read for this proposal.

edges.relationship: The Heartland: An American History (2019) recasts Midwestern history through settler colonialism and colonial dispossession, placing the United States within comparative settler-colonial historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Read Bradley’s introduction and the reviews. The claim concerns Hoganson’s historiographical framing; the book itself remains unread. No community narratives or knowledge are reproduced.

edges.relationship: The Heartland: An American History (2019) connects Midwestern agricultural and environmental history with imperial networks, including the international circulation of livestock.
edges.evidence_note: Bradley explicitly identifies environmental history; Merleaux develops the agricultural examples. This is a field contribution supported by reviews, not evidence of personal intellectual debt.

edges.relationship: In French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014), Barman invokes Greer’s warning against losing human complexity in statistics to explain her combination of counting and narrative.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 7, “Approach,” paragraph beginning “The three sections”: names Greer on the 1837 rebellion and warns against slighting “that which is not measurable.” Greer’s original and the omitted endnote 7 are unread; no particular Greer title or comprehensive methodological descent asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman praises Harris’s The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) while criticizing its male-centred sources, subjects and interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 238, main argument and note 4: Harris is among her “three best books,” each nonetheless “driven by a male perspective.” This is qualified criticism, not rejection; Harris’s book unread for this packet.

edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman uses Stoler’s account of colonial regulation of intimacy from the jointly written introduction to Tensions of Empire (1997).
edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 239–240, notes 7 and 12. Note 12 credits the introduction jointly to Ann Laura Stoler and Frederick Cooper, then explicitly assigns this insight to Stoler’s research in colonial Asia. Note 7 also recommends Race and the Education of Desire (1995). Originals unread; shared authorship is preserved rather than transferring the entire joint essay to Stoler.

edges.relationship: As coeditors of BC Studies from about 1995, Barman and Harris produced its special double issue Native Peoples and Colonialism (1997/98).
edges.evidence_note: Gavin Wilson, UBC Reports, 19 March 1998, “Special BC Studies issue devoted to First Nations”, https://archive.news.ubc.ca/ubcreports/1998/98mar19/bcstudy.html, paragraph identifying Barman as sharing editing duties with Cole Harris and final substantive paragraph dating their editorship to two and a half years earlier. Journal issue record https://bcstudies.ubc.ca/issue-single/bc-studies-no-115-116-autumn-winter-1997/ confirms no. 115–116, Autumn–Winter 1997, and the special-issue title. Accessibility language removed from the relationship because it concerns the journal’s editorial policy. Task M requires every undirected edge to use relationship_kind comparison, so the existing undirected classification is retained; relation_predicate co_edited and the sentence identify the collaboration. Do not introduce an unsupported co_editing kind or an arrow between coeditors.

edges.relationship: The West Beyond the West (1991; revised 1996; third edition 2007) offered an inclusive synthesis of British Columbia history that brought overlooked historical actors into the provincial narrative.
edges.evidence_note: UBC Green College interview/report, “A new perspective on British Columbia’s history,” identifies the 1991 synthesis and its standing; Arnett’s review (2021), opening three paragraphs, describes its inclusiveness. Edition dates checked on UBC Press’s French Canadians author biography. Existing regional roster row is preserved. Book unread.

edges.relationship: In “Taming Aboriginal Sexuality” (1997/98), Barman argues that colonial power sexualized Indigenous women’s agency, narrowing how their actions could be understood.
edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 238–241 set out the analytical shift to women; p. 264’s concluding argument explicitly makes agency, not just individual women, the object of sexualization. Opening and conclusion read; middle cases not systematically read. No community narrative or narrator quotation reproduced.
edges.map_label: Gender, race and the sexualization of agency

edges.relationship: Growing Up British in British Columbia: Boys in Private School (1984) studied the appeal of British schooling and its effects on the province’s social fabric.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher synopsis and contents read; institutional interview’s “Research and resistance” section identifies the dissertation-to-book trajectory. Publisher bibliography indexed record supplies original 1984; current ebook date 2007 is not substituted. Claim is limited to the documented research question; book unread.

edges.relationship: French Canadians, Furs, and Indigenous Women (2014) argues that French Canadian fur-trade workers, together with the Indigenous women in their lives, shaped the Pacific Northwest, and calls for moving beyond narratives written from the perspectives of those in charge.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample introduction, pp. 3–4 and 6–9, read. The relationship states Barman’s historiographical intervention; later chapters and family appendix unread. It does not endorse a racial definition of Métis identity or reproduce family histories.

edges.relationship: In her BC Studies review (2006/07) of Birthright, Adele Perry praises Jean Barman’s introduction to the published play (2005) for giving readers interpretive guidance for examining its representations of interracial intimacy.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own website (HTTP 200). Perry discusses Barman’s contextual introduction and earlier Skinner biography. Her criticism of unmarked alterations is explicitly directed at Joan Bryans’ adaptation; it is not attributed to Barman. This edge records the substantive review of Barman’s introduction, without inferring influence on Perry’s research. The 2005 publication year is confirmed in Barman’s own bibliography accompanying her Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry. The play and introduction themselves were not read. The web posting date (2013) is distinct from the review’s issue date (2006/07).
edges.map_label: Perry reviews Barman’s introduction to Birthright

edges.relationship: In her BC Studies review (2006/07), Jennifer S. H. Brown praises Jean Barman and Bruce McIntyre Watson’s Leaving Paradise: Indigenous Hawaiians in the Pacific Northwest, 1787–1898 (2006) for organizing fragmentary evidence into an insightful narrative and making the scale and dynamics of Hawaiian presence in the region comprehensible.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own website (HTTP 200). The reviewer is credited there as Jennifer Brown. She evaluates the coauthored book’s narrative, comparative treatment of the border, and biographical research. This is a favourable substantive review, represented as an undirected comparison; it does not establish that Brown adopted the book in her own subsequent research. The publisher’s hardback listing confirms May 2006; the later paperback is dated December 2021. The book itself was not read. The web posting date (2013) is distinct from the review’s issue date (2006/07).

edges.relationship: In “Mars Unshackled” (1990), Skocpol and Meyer Kestnbaum criticize Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) for separating revolutionary politics from state centralization and international warfare.
edges.evidence_note: Primary coauthored chapter, pp. 15–16, subsection An “Internalist” Interpretation: “Most problematic” identifies the separation. Joint argument; Hunt’s book unread in this inquiry.

edges.relationship: In “Mars Unshackled” (1990), Skocpol and Meyer Kestnbaum explicitly compare her States and Social Revolutions (1979) with Huntington’s Political Order in Changing Societies (1968) on state centralization and popular mobilization.
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter, pp. 14–15: “Like Samuel Huntington.” A bounded comparison, not an asserted debt; Huntington’s book unread.

edges.relationship: As Mead recounts in 1994, Gordon’s “Response to Theda Skocpol” (1993) contests the generalized treatment of women and gender in the debate over Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992).
edges.evidence_note: Mead, p. 304 and n. 15 (p. 308), quotes Gordon, Response, p. 188, distinguishing women, masculinities and variable gender systems. Original unread.

edges.relationship: As Mead recounts in 1994, Skocpol’s “Soldiers, Workers, and Mothers” (1993) challenges Gordon’s ranking of scholarship on gender and early American social policy.
edges.evidence_note: Mead, pp. 304–305 and n. 16 (p. 308), reports Skocpol’s charge of an elitist “hierarchy” and reproduces her reply. Original unread; no blanket rejection of feminist history asserted.
edges.map_label: Disputing a hierarchy of gender scholarship

edges.relationship: States and Social Revolutions (1979) combines state organization, international pressures and agrarian class relations in a comparative explanation of revolutionary transformation.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge book description, Description section; publisher summary only, not a fresh full-book reading. Existing field roster and ideology-debate strand retained.

edges.relationship: Chappell’s 2018 retrospective identifies Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) as a stimulus to women’s and gender historians’ study of state-building, while recording criticism of its maternalism and racial omissions.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences 2–5: “bring the state back in.” Reception is Chappell’s assessment; article body and Skocpol’s book unread in full.

edges.relationship: Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) contributed to political history through Skocpol’s account of American state formation, emphasizing courts, patronage-based parties, federalism and federated civic organizations, as Robert C. Lieberman’s 2024 historiographical essay explains.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s open HTML section and bibliography. Lieberman explicitly identifies the institutional argument and its extension in subsequent research. American political development is mapped to the existing political-history field, whose description includes institutions and power. The 1992 book was not independently read.
edges.map_label: American state formation and social provision

edges.relationship: In the 2019 interview, Kessler-Harris credits Gerda Lerner as a major influence in her turn toward women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: LaborOnline excerpts, paragraph beginning “I discovered the newly organized”; “a major influence in my life.” Retrospective self-report; full Jewish Social Studies interview unread. Lerner is another candidate in entries.json.
edges.map_label: Lerner and the turn to women’s history

edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris and Linda K. Kerber coedited U.S. History as Women’s History (1995), with Kathryn Kish Sklar.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). CV p. 3. The UNC Press page returned 403 to me. Extra support: the In Pursuit of Equity acknowledgments, p. xi (licensed preview), say 'Linda Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar, my coeditors of U.S. History as Women's History, helped to clarify the argument that appeared in that volume and became a part of chapter 3', and p. x thanks Kerber for 'intellectual companionship and willingness to offer acute criticism'. Apply the co-editing convention (contribution, undirected). Optionally add akh_equity_2001 to source_ids. Phrase seen: “U.S. History as Women's History, University of North Carolina Press, l995. edited with Linda K. Kerber and Kathryn Kish Sklar” Read at: https://professorsemeritus.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/content/CVs%20for%20Fellows%20Directory/Alice%20Kessler-Harris.pdf

edges.relationship: In In Pursuit of Equity (2001), Kessler-Harris relies on Cott's account of 1920s feminists' disputes over whether economic equality was an appropriate goal to set up her argument about economic citizenship.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed publisher preview (In Pursuit of Equity, 2001), introduction p. 4 and n. 12: 'And into the 1920s, historian Nancy Cott tells us, different kinds of feminists disputed bitterly over whether economic equality was an appropriate goal.' Cott is also thanked as a reader of the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xi). Read by Fable (F02-009); book body otherwise unread.

edges.relationship: As Eileen Boris reports, Kessler-Harris’s 1993 review of Skocpol’s Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) questions the paternalism/maternalism divide because both camps supported a male breadwinner family wage.
edges.evidence_note: Boris’s 4 August 1994 posting, first two substantive sentences: “the same family wage.” Chappell’s displayed notes 38/42 date the review to December 1993; Boris’s “earlier this year” is imprecise. Original review unread; mediated attribution only. Skocpol is another candidate.

edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris and Carroll Smith-Rosenberg coedited Women in Culture and Politics: A Century of Change (1986), with Judith Friedlander and Blanche Wiesen Cook.
edges.evidence_note: Author CV, printed p. 3, edited-books entry names all four. Bibliographic collaboration only; collection body unread. Smith-Rosenberg is another candidate in entries.json.

edges.relationship: As Francisca de Haan reports, Kessler-Harris invokes E. H. Carr in the introduction to Gendering Labor History (2007) to defend history prompted by present questions.
edges.evidence_note: De Haan (2009), paragraph beginning “The essays are preceded,” citing collection p. 3: “challenging events of the day.” Named-reader attribution; original introduction and Carr passage unread.

edges.relationship: In Gendering Labor History (2007), Kessler-Harris reframes women’s limited union membership as a question about exclusion by employers and male unions, as de Haan explains.
edges.evidence_note: De Haan, pp. 111–113, opening-essay discussion, citing collection pp. 23–25: “kept out.” Review read; original 1975 essay and 2007 reprint unread.

edges.relationship: Gendering Labor History (2007) makes masculinity and the interaction of gender and class part of explaining labour and social policy, as de Haan argues.
edges.evidence_note: De Haan, paragraphs on Parts 2–3: “mutual interaction.” Named-reader evidence; individual essays unread.
edges.map_label: Gender and class shape labour history

edges.relationship: Kessler-Harris coedited U.S. History as Women’s History (1995) and contributed its chapter on the construction of the 1939 Social Security amendments, “Designing Women and Old Fools.”
edges.evidence_note: UNC publisher description and contributor list name her topic. CV p. 4 identifies her chapter, “Designing Women and Old Fools.” Chapter body unread; no further chapter argument asserted.
edges.map_label: Women in Social Security policy (1995 chapter)

edges.relationship: In “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000), Joan Sangster cites Alice Kessler-Harris’s call in “A New Agenda for American Labor History” (1989) to treat gender, like class, as a historical process as symptomatic of feminist labour history’s move away from subordinating gender to class.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 140–142 and note 48 in the journal PDF. The body explicitly engages the framework; the note identifies the 1989 and 1993 essays. This is specific historiographical use. Those essays were not independently read.
edges.map_label: Gender as a historical process in Sangster’s historiography

edges.relationship: Gendering Labor History (2007) contributes to global history through its concluding essay on women’s wage labour, which Francisca de Haan’s 2009 review identifies as an attempt to examine gender within a global history of women’s paid work.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal publisher’s page. De Haan explicitly assesses the concluding essay’s global scope. The claim concerns the 2007 collection as reviewed; neither the collection nor the earlier version of that essay was independently read. This is a bounded contribution, not a founding claim.
edges.map_label: Gender in global histories of women’s paid work

edges.relationship: Gilmore credits Jacquelyn Dowd Hall, cochair of her dissertation committee for Gender and Jim Crow (dissertation 1992; book 1996), with encouraging history from below, labor analysis and attention to apparently lost causes.
edges.evidence_note: HNN interview excerpt, first question and answer (web lines 43–49): Gilmore states “Hall cochaired my dissertation committee” and describes the approach. CV p. 1 dates dissertation. Specific retrospective testimony; no sole-supervisor or sole-source claim. Original interview remainder and dissertation unread.
edges.map_label: Hall’s supervision and history from below

edges.relationship: Gilmore and Thomas J. Sugrue coauthored These United States: A Nation in the Making, 1890 to the Present (2015).
edges.evidence_note: Sugrue’s own biography, paragraph beginning The Long Year (web lines 35–36), explicitly names the coauthor; Gilmore CV p. 2 dates trade book to 2015 and distinguishes 2016 textbooks. Collaboration only; no direction of intellectual dependence and no full-book reading.

edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) recovers Black women’s club, reform and interracial organizing as political action in North Carolina.
edges.evidence_note: Kharif review, pp. 1–2, especially p. 2 paragraph beginning “Gilmore has carefully examined”: emphasizes club records and previously obscured female leadership. Complete review read; monograph unread. Regional and socially selective recovery, not a claim about all Southern women.

edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) explains how white-supremacist politics mobilized gender and how Black women developed political strategies within that racial order.
edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description of second edition, paragraphs 1–3 (web lines 72–75), especially “manipulation of concepts of gender.” Publisher summary read; 1996 original date checked in CV. Book and new preface unread; no direct derivation from Scott inferred.
edges.map_label: Gender and the making of white supremacy

edges.relationship: Defying Dixie (2008) extends the history of Black freedom struggles into interwar radical organizing and international connections.
edges.evidence_note: O’Brien review, opening paragraphs and final assessment (web lines 19–23, 40–41), singles out Soviet archival materials and struggles before 1955. Complete review read; book unread. Contribution is to historical scope and interpretation, not proof that every earlier organization directly produced later campaigns.
edges.map_label: Earlier radical roots of civil rights

edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) treats Black women's organizing after Black men's disfranchisement, including efforts to forge political ties with white women, as political activism.
edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description and quoted American Historical Review assessment (web lines 73–80), specifically “redefines what should count as” politics; Kharif pp. 1–2 corroborates organizing outside formal participation. Publisher page and complete Kharif review read, not the full AHR review or book. No general displacement of institutional political history claimed.

edges.relationship: Yale’s 2019 retirement tribute identifies the use of individual and family lives to build historical interpretation as a defining method in Gender and Jim Crow (1996) and Defying Dixie (2008).
edges.evidence_note: Yale tribute, paragraphs 2–4 (web lines 72–74): describes “biography as the building blocks of historiography” and specifies Pettey’s family and the radical activists. Institutional methodological assessment; monographs unread. No claim that Gilmore founded collective biography.

edges.relationship: In the 2019 preface to Gender and Jim Crow (originally 1996), Gilmore credits Kimberlé Crenshaw’s critical race writing, identifying “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), with teaching her to recognize race in its stated absence and white supremacy as continually remade.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-linked licensed preview in its standard browser viewer, including the preface pp. xi–xvi. The body names Crenshaw and describes what her writing taught Gilmore; note 2 identifies the 1989 article. This is Gilmore’s retrospective intellectual-debt statement, not an inference from shared topics or a footnote. The underlying article and the complete 1996 book were not read for this backfill.

edges.relationship: Gilmore states in the 2019 preface to Gender and Jim Crow (originally 1996) that Robin D. G. Kelley’s Hammer and Hoe (1990) influenced her Defying Dixie (2008).
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-linked licensed preview in its standard browser viewer, including the preface pp. xi–xvi. Gilmore directly names Kelley’s book and her own book in the influence sentence. Note 4 gives Hammer and Hoe’s original 1990 publication. Defying Dixie’s original 2008 year is retained from the supplied verified input. No broader claim of agreement or direct reading of either complete monograph is made.
edges.map_label: Hammer and Hoe influenced Defying Dixie

edges.relationship: In Defying Dixie: The Radical Roots of Civil Rights, 1919–1950 (2008), Gilmore connects southern struggles against racial segregation with Soviet communist networks and international antifascism, contributing a transnational account of the civil-rights movement’s radical precursors.
edges.evidence_note: O’Brien’s complete review was read. It identifies Soviet archives as an added resource and explains connections between southern activism and international movements. The global/connected-history classification is editorial, limited to these documented connections; the book itself remains unread.

edges.relationship: In “The Idea of Wartime” (2012), Dudziak extends Lynn Hunt’s example in Measuring Time, Making History (2008) of historical actors excusing their actions through their era to American justifications of wartime conduct.
edges.evidence_note: IAS essay, paragraph beginning 'The idea that wartime is exceptional': Hunt's phrase 'a new kind of determinism' introduces the Barère example that Dudziak then applies to war. Hunt's book not independently read.
edges.map_label: Hunt: time as an excuse for action

edges.relationship: In “Law, War, and the History of Time” (2010), Dudziak uses Durkheim’s account of socially produced temporal categories to question whether wartime is a natural division of history.
edges.evidence_note: Read search-indexed excerpts of the journal/library PDF, Law, War, and the History of Time (2010), pp. 1672 and 1675, especially the body paragraph beginning Emile Durkheim noted and nn. 24–27. Durkheim is an explicitly named premise for treating temporal categories as socially produced; the essay then uses this premise to question wartime’s supposedly essential character. Part of the explanation is mediated through Carol Greenhouse. This is a local argumentative use, not a general or career-wide intellectual debt. The cited Durkheim edition is the 1976 translation; original unread. Direct PDF retrieval returned 403; the present check is limited to the indexed page excerpts.

edges.relationship: In “Law, War, and the History of Time” (2010), Dudziak questions framing persistent American warfare as exceptional time, contrasting Agamben’s state-of-exception formulation with wartime law as ordinary practice.
edges.evidence_note: Published essay p. 1670, opening discussion and nn. 1–2, juxtaposes Agamben with 'the longstanding persistence of war'. A bounded objection to this framing, not a rejection of his entire project; Agamben's text unread independently.

edges.relationship: In “The Idea of Wartime” (2012), Dudziak uses Benedict Anderson’s concept of simultaneity to explain shared national feeling produced by watching the September 11 attacks unfold on television.
edges.evidence_note: IAS essay, paragraph beginning 'September 11, 2001': expressly calls the experience 'simultaneity' in Anderson's terms. Documents this application only; neither direct personal contact nor independent reading of Anderson's book is asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Nations United?” (2013), Dudziak praises Governing the World (2012) but argues that Mazower underexplains how contemporary international law can enable warfare as well as constrain it.
edges.evidence_note: Opening assessment and final section, especially paragraphs beginning 'At this point' and 'Following the path of lawfare': law becomes a 'technology of warfare'. Review read; Mazower's book not independently read.
edges.map_label: Mazower: law as a technology of warfare

edges.relationship: Cold War Civil Rights (2000) explains federal responses to Black freedom struggles through the international costs of American racism, while showing how anticommunism narrowed the scope of reform.
edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2025 excerpt, closing paragraphs beginning 'Yet the Cold War' and 'The narrow boundaries'; Arnesen (2002), pp. 243–245, identifies the contribution and questions evidence of overseas effects. Full book unread.
edges.map_label: Civil rights reform and its Cold War limits

edges.relationship: Exporting American Dreams (2008) follows Thurgood Marshall's work in Kenya to examine the limits of individual-rights-based law in inscribing equality; Farber's 2013 review places it where diplomatic and African American history meet.
edges.evidence_note: Named mediation: Farber (2013), publisher-displayed extract, paragraphs beginning 'Back in 1996' and 'Compared to her first book'; explicitly places the books between diplomatic and African American history. Full book and full review unread; a specific connected history, not world-scale synthesis.
edges.map_label: Marshall, Kenya and the limits of law

edges.relationship: War Time (2012) makes the presumed temporariness of war a historical problem, examining how it justifies exceptional powers despite continuing American military involvement.
edges.evidence_note: Book introduction pp. 3–9 read; Kohn (2013), publisher-displayed extract's opening paragraphs, places this intervention alongside military historians' understanding of persistent war. Full book and full review unread; contribution concerns war's legal and political framing.

edges.relationship: At the 2017 Grotius Lecture, David Armitage acknowledged that Mary L. Dudziak’s War Time: An Idea, Its History, Its Consequences (2012) inspired his Civil Wars: A History in Ideas (2017), according to Amy Flick’s contemporaneous conference report.
edges.evidence_note: Read the report’s opening three prose paragraphs and contextual discussion. This is an acknowledgment reported by a conference observer, not a quotation independently checked against the lecture recording or either book. The official professional-association publication carries Flick’s original report. The journal text remains unread beyond its displayed extract and references.
edges.map_label: Armitage acknowledges War Time as an inspiration

edges.relationship: In “High Modernism, Conflict, and the Nature of Change in Canada” (2016), Loo questions the opposition between local knowledge and state expertise in Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Publisher-indexed author abstract, final sentence: “takes issue with Scott’s contention”. Article body returned HTTP 403 and remains unread; this proposal covers only the stated objection.

edges.relationship: Reviewing The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) in 1998, Loo praises Harris’s account of land and power but criticizes its limited treatment of Indigenous agency and its weakening connections between settlement and colonization.
edges.evidence_note: Complete BC Studies 117 review, pp. 64–67; criticism at pp. 66–67, including “emerge as victims” and “fade away”. Harris’s book was not independently read; the claim is Loo’s assessment.

edges.relationship: In her 1992 review of The Age of Light, Soap and Water (1991), Loo asks Valverde for fuller treatment of Protestantism and stronger evidence connecting reform discourse to state practice.
edges.evidence_note: Labour/Le Travail 30, pp. 277–279, read in the national library’s journal archive; pp. 278–279: “religion and sectarian differences” and “more asserted than proved”. She also values the theoretical intervention. Book unread.

edges.relationship: In the introduction to States of Nature (2006), Loo draws on Cronon's argument in 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) that concepts of wilderness place it outside history, and extends the point from wilderness to wild animals.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 2 (PDF leaf 26), paragraph naming Cronon: “the trouble with wilderness”. This is an explicit conceptual resource, not evidence of supervision or personal contact; Cronon’s essay was not reread.

edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Loo explicitly uses Foucault’s distinctions between sovereign and disciplinary power to interpret relocation and the shaping of citizens.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 18 (PDF leaf 18): “to use Michel Foucault’s terms”. The adjoining governmentality discussion credits Timothy Mitchell and Tania Murray Li as well; no exclusive derivation is claimed.

edges.relationship: Loo and Carolyn Strange coauthored Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada, 1867–1939 (1997).
edges.evidence_note: Bacchi’s review, p. 247 heading, and Osgoode Society bibliography, Making Good entry, explicitly credit both authors. Book unread; the proposal asserts coauthorship only. Strange is another candidate in entries.json.

edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Loo compares her effort to historicize state officials with E. P. Thompson’s recovery of historical actors in The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 6 (PDF leaf 6): “my purpose is broadly similar”. This is Loo’s bounded comparison of historical empathy, not an identification of officials with Thompson’s working class or a shared political programme.
edges.map_label: Compares the recovery of historical actors

edges.relationship: States of Nature (2006) makes wildlife conservation a history of state authority, competing social values and the continuing importance of private and rural actors.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, introduction pp. 5–7, especially the three arguments on pp. 6–7: “three main arguments”. Selected opening passages read; later chapters unread. Existing environment roster row is retained.

edges.relationship: Strange and Loo's Making Good (1997), a survey for undergraduates, traces the changing scope and subjects of moral regulation in Canada from 1867 to 1939 and the often ineffective enforcement of moral laws.
edges.evidence_note: Carol Bacchi, Australian Journal of Legal History 4 (1998), pp. 247–249, complete review: “uneven, inconsistent and contradictory” (248); criticism of self-regulation (249). Mediated claim with joint authorship preserved; book unread.

edges.relationship: Moved by the State (2019) links forced relocation to postwar welfare and development policy, examining how the state’s pursuit of improvement also shaped political subjects.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, introduction pp. 6–8 and 18: “project of improvement” (8). Only these selected argument passages and the publisher description support the proposal; case-study chapters unread. Existing political-history roster retained.

edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Tina Loo examines forced relocation as an expression of the contradictions of extending Canada's liberal order, connecting individual development with coercive state intervention, as Caroline Desbiens explains in her review.
edges.evidence_note: Read Desbiens's complete review on the journal's website. This is a review-supported contribution to the framework's application, not evidence that McKay drew upon Loo. The book itself was not read for this edge. The review is printed in BC Studies 205 (Spring 2020), pp. 110–111; its webpage is dated 17 September 2019.

edges.relationship: Christopher Douglas Herbert identifies Tina Loo's Making Law, Order, and Authority in British Columbia, 1821–1871 (1994) as an innovative contribution to British Columbia's historiography that makes Cariboo gold-rush society central to understanding the province's development.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal's PDF, especially pp. 17–19. Herbert places Loo's argument within a substantive assessment of provincial historiography and explains the challenge to company authority. This supports a regional-history contribution; it does not establish influence on Barman or Perry, who are discussed separately. The book was not read for this edge.
edges.map_label: Makes the Cariboo central to provincial history

edges.relationship: In 'The View from Jacob Street: Reframing Urban Renewal in Postwar Halifax' (2019), Tina Loo contributes to urban history by examining municipal power alongside federal redevelopment policy and arguing that both race and class shaped vulnerability to displacement.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal-hosted HTML introduction, paragraphs 1–10, and conclusion, paragraphs 75–77. The edge records Loo's stated historiographical intervention, without treating her interpretation of municipal intentions as settled or asserting subsequent uptake by another historian. The journal identifies the article as a 2019 publication.
edges.map_label: Municipal power, race and class in urban renewal

edges.relationship: In “Against Interpretation,” collected in Against Interpretation and Other Essays (1966), Sontag criticizes Marx’s treatment of social events as concealing meanings that interpretation must uncover.
edges.evidence_note: Estate excerpt, section 3, paragraphs beginning “The modern style” and “This manifest content.” Marx and Freud are separately named. Read sections 1–4; this is Sontag’s characterization, not an independently checked account of Marx’s writings.

edges.relationship: In “Against Interpretation,” collected in Against Interpretation and Other Essays (1966), Sontag criticizes Freud’s search beneath observable events and artworks for latent meaning.
edges.evidence_note: Estate excerpt, section 3, same two paragraphs: “manifest content” and “latent content.” Freud’s symptoms, slips, dreams and art are specified. Claim concerns this interpretive procedure, not a rejection of everything in psychoanalysis. Later essay sections unread.

edges.relationship: Sontag edited Barthes’s writings and supplied the introduction to A Barthes Reader (1982).
edges.evidence_note: Publisher author-credit line explicitly names both roles; its paperback date is 1983. Maunsell, p. 192 n. 51, identifies the 1982 original and the introduction “Writing Itself.” Neither introduction nor anthology read; no particular theoretical debt or coauthorship inferred.

edges.relationship: In “Photography” (1973), Sontag disputes Benjamin’s account of photographic industrialization, arguing that it enabled photography’s emergence as an art.
edges.evidence_note: Original journal article, paragraphs beginning “This is as evident,” “The ‘industrialization’” and “Since there were then.” Explicit pivot: “Contrary to what Benjamin argues.” Sontag identifies his 1931 essay; Benjamin’s original was not read here. Do not date this intervention solely to the 1977 collection.

edges.relationship: In On Photography (1977), Sontag analyzes family albums as practices that preserve an image of kinship while industrial society disperses the extended family.
edges.evidence_note: Authorized “In Plato’s Cave” excerpt, successive paragraphs beginning “Memorializing the achievements,” “Through photographs, each family” and “As that claustrophobic unit.” The claim is this analysis of remembrance practices, not that Sontag founded memory studies. Full book unread.

edges.relationship: Illness as Metaphor (1978) made disease metaphors a contested resource for medical history; Barbara Clow’s “Who’s Afraid of Susan Sontag?” (2001) tests its claims against historical cancer experiences.
edges.evidence_note: Sontag’s 1978 article, opening and section I; Clow’s complete publisher SUMMARY, opening and concluding sentences, explicitly establishes scholarly uptake and challenges predictable silence or disgrace. Clow’s article body and Sontag’s full book unread. No universal reception asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Notes on ‘Camp’” (1964), Sontag analyzes the relation between camp taste and homosexuality while insisting that the two are not identical.
edges.evidence_note: Original journal p. 529, notes 51–53; p. 515 frames the inquiry as a history of sensibility. Publisher connects the essay with queer cultural codes. Selected pages only; this is a situated account of taste, not a universal description of queer people.

edges.relationship: In ‘Photography, War, Outrage’ (2005), Judith Butler challenges Susan Sontag’s account of photographic interpretation in Regarding the Pain of Others (2003), arguing that the photographic frame itself interprets rather than merely awaits interpretation, as Manisha Basu documents in her 2006 review.
edges.evidence_note: Read Basu’s complete review on the journal’s own site. She quotes Butler’s claim and explicitly disputes Butler’s reading of Sontag. This edge records the documented disagreement without endorsing Butler’s interpretation. Butler’s original essay was not read in full; its publisher opening extract and a limited book-preview search were also consulted.

edges.relationship: In Gout: The Patrician Malady (1998), Roy Porter and G. S. Rousseau challenge the separation of disease from cultural meaning advocated in Susan Sontag’s Illness as Metaphor (1978), arguing from the historical persistence of meanings attached to illness, as David E. Shuttleton reports in 2007.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction excerpt, including its substantive account and direct quotation of Porter and Rousseau’s objection. This is secondary evidence; the original epilogue was not read in full. The edge represents Porter’s explicitly co-authored criticism, not a claim that he alone formulated it. The licensed preview confirmed the passage’s location but did not expose the complete page.

edges.relationship: Mazower’s 2015 review credits The Guardians (2015) with transforming understanding of the League of Nations.
edges.evidence_note: Review, paragraphs beginning Susan Pedersen’s and Now Pedersen; “strikingly original”. Book unread.

edges.relationship: In I want to love it (2019), Pedersen argues that the marginalization of women, Africa and culture in Hobsbawm’s historical synthesis follows from its organizing assumptions.
edges.evidence_note: Final analytical paragraph beginning At the end of his book: “constitutive, not lapses”. She also praises his explanatory reach. Hobsbawm’s books unread here.

edges.relationship: In I want to love it (2019), Pedersen values Evans’s Eric Hobsbawm: A Life in History (2019) but questions its individual focus when explaining his institutional and publishing success.
edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning I am not criticising Hobsbawm: “isn’t really the right medium”; opening assessment praises the biography. Evans’s book unread here.

edges.relationship: In Settler Colonialism: A Concept and Its Uses (2005), Elkins and Pedersen use Wolfe’s structural account while distinguishing their twentieth-century cases.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 3: “Wolfe alerts us”; pp. 3–4 distinguish cases. Joint attribution retained; Wolfe’s book unread.
edges.map_label: Uses and differentiates Wolfe’s structural account

edges.relationship: Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993) explains how gender relations and family provision shaped welfare policies and citizenship in Britain and France.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge bibliography notice, p. 295: “gender relations and family maintenance”; Radcliffe profile, first paragraph. Summaries read; monograph unread.
edges.map_label: Gender relations in comparative welfare history

edges.relationship: Eleanor Rathbone and the Politics of Conscience (2004) connects Rathbone’s feminist thought and social reform to parliamentary and imperial politics.
edges.evidence_note: Yale description, three paragraphs; “public and private sides”. Displayed edition 2014; original 2004 checked in Pedersen’s report, p. 130. Book unread.
edges.map_label: Feminism, social reform and parliamentary action

edges.relationship: The Guardians (2015) explains how international scrutiny and petitioning within the mandates system reshaped imperial sovereignty and the possibilities of statehood.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). OUP abstract supports the claim on its own (online 18 June 2015). The second cited source (Goebel, H-Soz-Kult) was not accessible to me: the site served an Anubis bot check, the H-Net mirror returned 403 and the Wayback copy was bot-blocked. The coordinator may drop sp_w_goebel_review from this edge's source_ids. Phrase seen: “placed imperial rule under intense public scrutiny; exploited new rights of petition; brought normative statehood nearer but changed its nature; mattered not because it altered governance” Read at: https://academic.oup.com/book/6410

edges.relationship: With Elkins, Pedersen’s Settler Colonialism: A Concept and Its Uses (2005) proposes a comparative typology of settler power and privilege.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–4 and 17–18: “definition” and “typology”. Selected preview passages read; later chapters unread. Joint credit retained.

edges.relationship: In Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993), Susan Pedersen contributed to comparative social history by reconstructing the competing interests and processes that produced different welfare policies in Britain and France, as Maria Sophia Quine emphasizes in her 1999 review.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on pp. 149–150 in the publisher-hosted review section. Quine situates the book within empirically grounded social histories of welfare and identifies policy formation as its distinctive contribution. She also criticizes its limited attention to lived effects and its rationalistic account of reformers. The book itself was not read; this edge records the review’s assessment, not a claim that it founded a school.
edges.map_label: Comparative social history of welfare policy formation

edges.relationship: Susan Pedersen’s 2010 round-table review of Ross McKibbin’s Parties and People (2010) contributed to debate on interwar British political culture by stressing the electoral importance of international credibility and the Conservatives’ liberal-imperialist self-presentation, an argument Helen McCarthy uses in “Whose Democracy?” (2012).
edges.evidence_note: Read McCarthy’s substantive discussion and footnote 24 on Cambridge Core. The body expressly adopts Pedersen’s point to question the electoral marginality of foreign affairs. Pedersen’s original review was not read. This records a specific intervention received in political historiography; it is not an edge for participation in a round-table or for collective credit.
edges.map_label: International affairs in interwar electoral politics

edges.relationship: In the 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková, Abrams identifies Summerfield’s theoretically informed feminist oral history as an influence on her own approach.
edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 153, first answer to “Who influenced”: “I was influenced” and “I read all her work.” This is Abrams’s own attribution; no individual Summerfield title is specified there. Summerfield’s separate publisher endorsement of the first edition is also read, but does not date the original influence. Her works were not independently read for this packet.

edges.relationship: In the 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková, Abrams names reading Portelli among the influences on her understanding of oral history.
edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 153, answer to “Who influenced”, names Portelli alongside Summerfield, Frisch and Daniel James. The retrospective answer supports a limited reading debt; no particular Portelli work or sole theoretical derivation is specified. Portelli’s own texts and his 2011 review of Abrams remain unread.

edges.relationship: Abrams and Callum G. Brown co-edited A History of Everyday Life in Twentieth-Century Scotland (2010) and jointly wrote its introduction.
edges.evidence_note: EUP publisher record, editor byline, Contents chapter 1, and February 2010 publication dates; Glasgow publication list, 2010 entries, identifies “Introduction: conceiving the everyday in the twentieth century”, pp. 1–19. Verified collaboration only; neither equal division of intellectual labour nor an argument from the unread introduction is inferred.

edges.relationship: Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) links interview practice to analysis of how, why and with what meaning testimony is produced.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher companion Chapter 1, Chapter summary, paragraphs 1–3: interviews are a “communicative event”. The 2016 summary directly supplies this interpretation; the interview p. 151 and note 7 establish the original 2010 and second-edition 2016 dates. Full book unread.

edges.relationship: In Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016), Abrams treats remembering as an active process and asks historians to interpret relations between individual and collective memory.
edges.evidence_note: 2016 publisher companion Chapter 5, Chapter summary, paragraphs 1–3, and Discussion points 4–6. Exact phrase: “Memory is an active process”. This supports the second-edition formulation, not a claim that every passage appeared in 2010. Reliability questions are reweighted, not declared irrelevant to establishing events. Full chapter unread.

edges.relationship: Feminist Lives (2023) uses women’s testimony to explain how a postwar transition generation fashioned autonomous selves before and alongside the Women’s Liberation Movement.
edges.evidence_note: OUP book Abstract, both paragraphs, describes the transition generation and challenges its neglect as insufficiently feminist. Interview pp. 155 and 162–163 supplies authorial explanation and sample limits: her own interviewees were white and mostly middle class by interview time. The full book is unread; this is a scoped contribution, not a representative account of every British woman.

edges.relationship: In “Introduction: Gendering the Agenda” (2006), Abrams proposes using women’s history and the analysis of gender relations to reinterpret Scottish history.
edges.evidence_note: Public chapter Abstract, entire paragraph: “shift the agenda”. Original chapter dated 25 January 2006; book abstract lists politics, identity, work and religion as gendered subjects. Claim stays within the abstract; chapter body and named theoretical debts within it are unread. Four-editor collection credited separately.

edges.relationship: In Feminist Lives (2023), Abrams argues that expressing and acting on feelings helped postwar British women construct new selves.
edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 155, answer on the connection between feelings and self, and p. 161, answer on archival research. Abrams links emotion to feminist self formation and says organisational correspondence made that dimension visible. The OUP abstract confirms the work and date. Distinct from the women’s-history link: this claim concerns feelings as historical action and evidence. Full book unread; no derivation from Reddy or Rosenwein inferred.

edges.relationship: In her 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková discussing Feminist Lives (2023), Abrams reverses Sara Ahmed’s formulation of feminism as an emotional response to the world, describing emotion as a feminist response to the world.
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 155, answer to the question about feelings and the self in Feminist Lives. Abrams explicitly attributes the first formulation to Ahmed, reverses its terms, and then explains how postwar British women’s expression of feelings helped constitute a new self. This is named engagement with an argument in a published interview. The interview prints Ahmed’s first name as Sarah; the feminist theorist of emotion is identified here with the supplied run member Sara Ahmed. The supporting phrase preserves the printed spelling. The relationship is a comparison because the passage reformulates the proposition without asserting a broader disagreement. No specific Ahmed book is named in this passage, and neither Ahmed’s underlying text nor Feminist Lives was read for this backfill.
edges.map_label: Reverses the formulation of feminism and emotion

edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to labour history in Workers' Culture in Imperial Germany: Leisure and Recreation in the Rhineland and Westphalia (1992), interpreting workers' leisure in Bochum and Düsseldorf as an arena of assertiveness under bourgeois pressure to reform popular recreation.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete substantive annotation on printed p. 296 in the journal publisher's PDF. It identifies Abrams's book, its original 1992 publication and geographical scope, and describes her interpretation of workers' response to attempts to reform recreation. Labour-history classification is an editorial mapping of this stated argument to the existing field, whose scope includes workers' culture beyond formal labour organisations. The annotation is evidence of the book's argument and reception; the book itself remains unread. No claim of founding the field or subsequent personal influence is made.

edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to the history of everyday life through A History of Everyday Life in Twentieth-Century Scotland (2010), co-edited with Callum G. Brown, which examines mundane practices and daily spaces as sites of personal and national politics.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's complete description, editor credits, contents and original publication dates. The description explicitly treats apparently mundane activities and daily spaces as historical inquiries into politics. Abrams is both co-editor and a credited coauthor of the introduction and the chapter on the Scottish home. This field edge records her contribution through a substantive edited research collection, with credit retained for Brown and the other contributors. The target is the existing combined 'Microhistory / everyday life' node, specifically its everyday-life component; the evidence does not establish Italian microstoria affiliation or transmission from a particular school. Full chapters remain unread. The existing Abrams–Brown pair is not proposed again.

edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to urban history through Glasgow: High-Rise Homes, Estates and Communities in the Post-War Period (2020), coauthored with Ade Kearns, Barry Hazley and Valerie Wright, connecting architectural design and planning with residents' housing experiences through oral histories and archival materials.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete four-paragraph abstract and bibliographic record deposited by Abrams in her own institution's repository. The second paragraph specifies oral histories and archival materials, the third states the analytical connection, and the fourth explicitly names urban historians among the book's audience. This supports a contribution about housing, built environments and residents' experience, rather than mere shared subject matter. The record gives 2020 and first online publication on 7 July 2020. No book text is supplied there and the full book remains unread. The collective argument is attributed to all four authors; the other authors have no matching timeline endpoint in the supplied lists.

edges.relationship: As quoted and endorsed in Alan Taylor’s “The Old Frontiers” (2008), Limerick criticized Turner’s frontier account for centring English-speaking white men and marginalizing other historical participants.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Taylor, “The Old Frontiers,” 7 May 2008, paragraph beginning “Turner’s sharpest” (web line 60), with preceding paragraphs 57–59. Taylor quotes Limerick’s charge of being “ethnocentric and nationalist.” This is a named-reader route. The quoted Limerick work is unspecified in Taylor’s paragraph and no original page or publication attribution is supplied. The Legacy of Conquest is unread; no rejection of every Turner proposition is asserted.
edges.map_label: Criticizes exclusions in the frontier thesis

edges.relationship: Limerick and White each contributed an essay to The Frontier in American Culture (1994), the companion volume to the Newberry Library exhibition, edited by James R. Grossman.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh JSTOR publisher record: author and editor credits, copyright 1994, description of Newberry exhibition; contents assign separate essays. This is joint book authorship with separate essay responsibility. Full essays unread.
edges.map_label: Separate essays in one exhibition volume

edges.relationship: In “The Writer’s Studio with Philip J. Deloria” (2021), Deloria names Limerick among the scholars from whom he learned about writing and praises how her whimsical presence enters her prose.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh Cambridge HTML, question “Which scholars do you most admire as writers and why?”, answer first paragraph, web lines 506–508; issue pp. 305–313. Deloria says he “learned a lot” from Limerick, Cronon and White. The claim concerns prose, not supervision or the derivation of Playing Indian. No particular Limerick work is identified; none supplied. Selected professional-method passages read; later personal/family material is unused.

edges.relationship: In “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (1992), Cronon credits Limerick’s remark as the source of his epigram about the material constraints on environmental storytelling.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh author-hosted journal scan, printed p. 1372, ecological-constraints paragraph and note 45; also p. 1347 acknowledgment. Note 45 says “a remark of Patricia Limerick’s”; it credits the immediately preceding dust epigram. The surrounding claim that stories must make ecological sense is Cronon’s formulation. No sole authorship of his narrative theory is inferred. Read p. 1347 and selected pp. 1371–1374; remainder not closely read. Running heads establish March 1992 despite the PDF filename’s 1991.

edges.relationship: The Legacy of Conquest (1987) brought environmental history into Limerick’s reinterpretation of the American West, as the MacArthur Foundation’s account of her scholarship explicitly recognizes.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh MacArthur award biography, “About Patricia’s Work,” web line 54, explicitly lists “environmental history” and then discusses the book’s conquest framework. This mediated professional account supports inclusion in the field, not a fresh reading of the monograph or the claim that she founded environmental history.

edges.relationship: With White, Limerick contributed The Frontier in American Culture (1994) to the interpretation of frontier images through a Newberry Library exhibition and its companion book.
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR book description identifies the exhibition mounted in fall 1994 and its treatment of images, metaphors and reenactments, together with both author credits. “Public history” is the editorial field classification of this documented exhibition/book work. University biography corroborates her public-facing historical practice. Exhibition not visited and complete essays unread.
edges.map_label: Interpreting frontier images for exhibition audiences

edges.relationship: As Lauck documents (2011), Woodward’s The Burden of Southern History (1960) provided a model for Limerick’s project that became The Legacy of Conquest (1987).
edges.evidence_note: Lauck reconstructs the project from correspondence. This is a documented model, not inferred from seminar attendance. LSU Press supplies the corrected original year; neither book nor the letters were read directly.

edges.relationship: As Kearns reports (1998), Limerick criticized the frontier-process approach exemplified by Cronon, Miles and Gitlin’s “Becoming West” (1992) for privileging Anglo-American east-to-west movement over other populations’ movements.
edges.evidence_note: Mediated through Kearns’s substantive analysis; underlying chapter unread. He also reports Limerick’s later definitional truce (p. 398). This differs from the excluded epigram credit.

edges.relationship: In his opening contribution to ‘The Legacy of Conquest, by Patricia Nelson Limerick: A Panel of Appraisal’ (1989), Donald Worster assessed Limerick's The Legacy of Conquest (1987) as a candidate either to generate new research or to articulate an emerging trend in western history.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's linked Article PDF first page preview visually, including Worster's first two paragraphs, through the beginning of his summary at the bottom of p. 303. The quotation refers back to the two possible roles for a significant historical book set out in his first paragraph. The page also identifies the book's original publication as 1987. This records Worster's own evaluative prose. Only this first page of the 303–322 panel was read; later assessments and any criticisms remain unread. Accordingly this is an undirected review comparison, with no claim that Worster adopted Limerick's framework or that the book actually achieved the influence he considers possible.

edges.relationship: Dubinsky and Franca Iacovetta coauthored “Murder, Womanly Virtue, and Motherhood: The Case of Angelina Napolitano” (1991).
edges.evidence_note: Dubinsky’s own CV, printed p. 16, explicitly credits Iacovetta and gives Canadian Historical Review, December 1991, pp. 505–531; p. 3 records their joint article prize. Bibliographic collaboration only: the article body was not read and no joint argument or influence is inferred.

edges.relationship: Dubinsky, Adele Perry and Henry Yu coedited Within and Without the Nation: Canadian History as Transnational History (2015).
edges.evidence_note: Publisher/distributor page, title and Edited by line, publication date November 2015; author CV printed p. 11 corroborates joint credit. This is a co-editing relationship, not a claim that one editor influenced another. Collection and introduction unread.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity: A Response to Sangster” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks reject Sangster’s opposition between women’s and gender history and argue that gender analysis can strengthen feminist history without replacing women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh complete journal-archive PDF read, pp. 205–220; especially pp. 205–211 and 218–220. On p. 207 they say there is “no need to choose” between the approaches. Their qualification on pp. 218–219 acknowledges the risks of detached category analysis. Joint intervention, not Dubinsky alone; Sangster’s original 1995 essay not independently read.

edges.relationship: In “Reconsidering Dichotomies” (1996), Sangster criticizes Dubinsky and Lynne Marks for attributing to her a rejection of gender history and for reproducing oppositions in their response, while conceding that her own account had blurred separate theoretical questions.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh complete archived journal PDF read, pp. 239–248. P. 242 explicitly identifies the Dubinsky–Marks opening metaphor; pp. 243–244 reject the positions assigned to her and concede that the original essay “blurred two issues”; p. 248 rejects their description of her position as narrow. This incoming reply is distinct from the outgoing response and is not a criticism of every Dubinsky book.
edges.map_label: Sangster replies to Dubinsky and Marks

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Joy Parr’s The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) and “Gender History and Historical Practice” (1995) to support a contextual account of identity that gives no single category automatic priority.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 211 and n. 11 explicitly attribute the point to Parr, rejecting imposition of “one category”; p. 209 n. 6 also cites the 1990 book. This is documented conceptual use in the joint essay, not supervision or a career-wide lineage. Parr’s two originals not independently re-read.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Linda Gordon’s Pitied But Not Entitled (1994) to show how gender analysis can connect women’s lives to the social policies and competing visions of the welfare state.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; pp. 206–207 and n. 2 identify Gordon’s book and discuss social insurance and social work as differing gendered visions. The term “analytic” on p. 207 marks the methodological use. Gordon’s book remains unread here; this is the respondents’ uptake, not an independent judgment of her full argument.
edges.map_label: Uses Gordon on gender and welfare

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks draw on John Tosh’s work on masculinity to argue that treating men as an unmarked norm hides the operation of gendered power.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 214 n. 15 credits Michael Roper and Tosh’s coauthored introduction to Manful Assertions (1991); p. 217 and n. 20 explicitly use Tosh’s “What Should Historians Do with Masculinity?” (1994), p. 180, to explain the invisibility of masculinity. Short phrase: “relational concept” (p. 214). Credit to Roper retained; neither original newly read.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks praise Catherine Hall and Leonore Davidoff’s Family Fortunes (1987) for treating masculine power as socially made, but find it insufficiently attentive to consent and coercion.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 214 and n. 14 name both authors and the 1987 book, contrasting its historically constructed account with Rotundo’s before calling it “too quiet” on consent and coercion. Their further use of the book on p. 217 shows this is qualified criticism. Joint credit retained on both sides; Family Fortunes itself not newly read.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks praise Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall’s Family Fortunes (1987) for treating masculine power as socially made, but find it insufficiently attentive to consent and coercion.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 214 and n. 14 name both authors and the 1987 book, contrasting its historically constructed account with Rotundo’s before calling it “too quiet” on consent and coercion. Their further use of the book on p. 217 shows this is qualified criticism. Joint credit retained on both sides; Family Fortunes itself not newly read.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks quote Anna Clark’s 1993 Journal of Women’s History comment for the problem of how to link postmodernist attention to language with historical questions of power.
edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; pp. 218–219 and n. 22 explicitly attribute the problem of linking linguistic analysis to “questions of power” to Anna Clark’s 1993 Journal of Women’s History comment. Her 1995 book is also cited in n. 3 but does not by itself support this edge. The comment remains unread independently. Endpoint is another candidate in this run.
edges.map_label: Cites Clark on language and power

edges.relationship: In “A Haven from Racism? Canadians Imagine Interracial Adoption” (2010), Dubinsky invokes Veronica Strong-Boag’s warning against idealizing a uniform Indigenous family past.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, p. 24 and n. 52 on p. 32, explicitly attributes the caution “not to glamorize” to Strong-Boag’s Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006), p. 138. That book is unread here. Claim is limited to a scholarly caution; no family stories, narrator quotations or community knowledge are reproduced.

edges.relationship: Improper Advances (1993) contributes to Canadian women’s and gender history by analyzing sexual coercion and unequal power alongside women’s sexual agency in Ontario criminal case files.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, paragraphs 1–4, and 1993 copyright read; complete book unread. The claim follows the publisher’s account, not a fresh reading of its case studies. This field already has a Dubinsky roster row, which is preserved.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks defend gender history as an analysis of power that includes masculinity and connects categories of meaning with lived experience.
edges.evidence_note: Complete joint essay read, especially pp. 207–211 and 214–220. At p. 218 “gender is present” introduces their use of Ava Baron; the same page warns against an apolitical study of categories. This describes a methodological contribution rather than blanket adherence to poststructuralism.

edges.relationship: In “A Haven from Racism? Canadians Imagine Interracial Adoption” (2010), Dubinsky makes children’s symbolic power a problem for Canadian childhood history and questions explanations of adoption framed solely as rescue or kidnap.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, pp. 15–16, opening methodological statement; phrase “symbolic power” on p. 15. The entire book is unread, and the edge does not reproduce the chapter’s individual histories or generalize its limited archive into community-wide findings.

edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Anne McClintock’s Imperial Leather (1995) to argue that gender is integral to imperial power and that feminist historical inquiry can combine several theoretical approaches.
edges.evidence_note: Complete joint response read, especially p. 206 and n. 1. They explicitly discuss Imperial Leather, quote its argument about gender and imperial power, and praise its combination of historical materialism, poststructuralism and psychoanalytic approaches as “non-sectarian”. This is specific uptake in the response; McClintock’s book remains unread independently and no personal mentorship is inferred.
edges.map_label: Uses McClintock on gender and empire

edges.relationship: In her historiographical essay “The History of Us” (2000), Cynthia Comacchio discusses Karen Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) and The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) as Foucault-informed studies of the spatial, class and gender dimensions of sexuality.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s PDF discussion on pp. 191–195. Comacchio substantively uses both books to explain historical sexuality, rather than merely listing citations. This is uptake in a historiographical synthesis, not evidence that Dubinsky originated Comacchio’s research programme. The books themselves were not read for this task.

edges.relationship: Karen Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) contributed to the history of sexuality by examining heterosexual coercion and women’s agency through the interacting inequalities of gender, class and ethnicity, as Christina Simmons assessed in “A Proper Account of Improper Sex” (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Read Simmons’s ten-page review in the journal’s PDF. She explicitly evaluates the book’s contribution to sexuality history while also criticizing its presentation and limited account of change over time. The endpoint includes sexuality history; this claim does not make the book a study of queer identities. The monograph itself was not read.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg and Charles Rosenberg coauthored “The Female Animal: Medical and Biological Views of Woman and Her Role in Nineteenth-Century America” (1973).
edges.evidence_note: Fresh publisher byline, Journal of American History 60.2, pp. 332–356, read at the Oxford page listed in the reading log; both names appear. Smith-Rosenberg’s 1975 article, p. 2 n. 2, also identifies it as written “with Charles Rosenberg.” Coauthorship only; 1973 essay body unread in this dossier.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg and Linda K. Kerber contributed to the published forum “Beyond Roles, Beyond Spheres: Thinking about Gender in the Early Republic” (1989).
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR, William and Mary Quarterly 46.3 (July 1989), table of contents item 6, pp. 565–585, names both among six contributors. Short locator phrase: “Forum.” Metadata establishes a published exchange; text unread, so no shared thesis, direct response or agreement is claimed.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg and Nancy F. Cott contributed to the published forum “Beyond Roles, Beyond Spheres: Thinking about Gender in the Early Republic” (1989).
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR, William and Mary Quarterly 46.3 (July 1989), table of contents item 6, pp. 565–585, names both among six contributors. Short locator phrase: “Forum.” Metadata establishes a published exchange; text unread, so no shared thesis, direct response or agreement is claimed.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg and Lynn Hunt contributed to the published forum “Beyond Roles, Beyond Spheres: Thinking about Gender in the Early Republic” (1989).
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR, William and Mary Quarterly 46.3 (July 1989), table of contents item 6, pp. 565–585, names both among six contributors. Short locator phrase: “Forum.” Metadata establishes a published exchange; text unread, so no shared thesis, direct response or agreement is claimed.

edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel credits Smith-Rosenberg’s sustained manuscript reading and uses “The Body Politic” (1989) in explaining the social setting of textual meaning.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh official UC Press/CDL text: acknowledgments xiii, introduction 9–10 and introduction n. 7, p. 325. Spiegel says Smith-Rosenberg “read every chapter”; n. 7 identifies the 1989 essay, p. 101, and thanks her for the draft. Remaining chapters and the original essay unread. Direction records Spiegel’s expressed debt; does not transfer her medieval conclusions to Smith-Rosenberg.

edges.relationship: Hauptman’s 2021 interview report identifies Smith-Rosenberg as Hofstadter’s student at Columbia during the doctoral research completed in 1968.
edges.evidence_note: Interview report, paragraph beginning “One such opportunity” and the following dissertation paragraph: “was a student” of Hofstadter. Michigan education entry independently confirms the 1968 doctorate. The report discusses his reaction to a dissertation chapter; no formal supervisor designation or general theoretical inheritance is inferred.

edges.relationship: Hauptman’s 2021 interview report credits “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975), a close analysis of intimacy in nineteenth-century American women’s letters, as a pioneering article in the recovery of women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). Re-base on the OutHistory interview report (Hauptman 2021, csr_w_hauptman2021) and narrow the claim to what it says. Replace source_ids with ["csr_w_hauptman2021"].
