Phrase seen: “closely analyzed emotional (and, arguably, sexual) intimacy in the letters of nineteenth-century American women, changed women’s studies overnight ... a major, pioneering article in the recovery of women’s and LGBTQ history” Read at: https://outhistory.org/exhibits/show/csr/csr2
edges.map_label: Women’s intimate friendships as historical evidence

edges.relationship: “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975) treated women’s intimate relationships through a view of sexuality as fluid and shaped by cultural and social forces; Penn’s biography credits it with establishing the legitimacy of lesbian history.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). Penn GSWS biography (read via fetch) and the OutHistory report support a narrower claim. Replace source_ids with ["csr_w_pennbio", "csr_w_hauptman2021"]. Phrase seen: “established the legitimacy of lesbian history in the field (Penn); recognizes human sexuality as fluid and relativistic, susceptible to wide-ranging cultural and social forces (OutHistory)” Read at: https://gsws.sas.upenn.edu/people/carroll-smith-rosenberg

edges.relationship: In her 1986 review of Carroll Smith-Rosenberg’s Disorderly Conduct: Visions of Gender in Victorian America (1985), Linda Gordon criticized the treatment of sexual concerns as metaphors for other social conflicts and questioned the usefulness of its expansive application of liminality.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed first-page image preview, first by in-memory OCR and then visually checked against the image. The landing page identifies Gordon as reviewer and dates the review to September 1986. On p. 477 she questions reducing sexual issues to symbols of other concerns, then argues that an application of liminality broad enough to encompass most nineteenth-century experience limits its usefulness. Gordon also praises Smith-Rosenberg’s close reading and earlier work; the proposal concerns these specified criticisms, not blanket rejection. The review continues on p. 478, which remains unread. The web image fetch failed, but a normal direct request to the same publisher-supplied preview image returned HTTP 200. No full-review access is claimed.

edges.relationship: Cott's 1983 review of Good Wives (1982) credits Ulrich's reconstruction of women through contextual records and finds the deputy-husband role useful for explaining work across gender boundaries within patriarchal authority.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher's first-page preview, printed p. 173, right column, review's opening three paragraphs. Short anchors: 'eliminates the excuse' and 'particularly useful'. This is a documented published assessment, not a claim of personal mentorship or comprehensive agreement. Read only p. 173; continuation p. 174 and Good Wives itself unread.

edges.relationship: Good Wives (1982) explains how women could undertake men's work as deputy husbands while their authority remained contingent on household relationships.
edges.evidence_note: Cott, first-page review preview, printed p. 173, second paragraph distinguishes task from position and crossing gender boundaries from independence. The author's 2015 interview, answer beginning 'It's important to know that my first book', describes the relation between Good Wives and the later diary research. Cott is a named scholarly reader; the 1982 book body is unread. This contribution to the existing broad gender field does not subsume women's history into a single theory.

edges.relationship: Pearsall and Sword’s 2009 AHA biography credits A Midwife’s Tale (1990) with using one woman’s diary to reconstruct her community and reassess wider historical narratives.
edges.evidence_note: Sarah Pearsall and Kirsten Sword, AHA presidential biography (2009), Old Diary, paragraphs beginning A Midwife’s Tale showed scholars and Laurel’s painstaking reconstruction, read on the AHA’s site. These named scholars explain how reconstructing one woman’s life changes broader interpretations. The endpoint micro is labelled Microhistory / everyday life: this is a contribution to its broad everyday-life remit, not a claim that the biographers use the word microhistory or identify an Italian/German school affiliation. The library listing is removed as evidence; the monograph itself remains unread.

edges.relationship: The Age of Homespun (2001) interprets the making, use and preservation of textiles as evidence of social relationships and identity, contributing to material-culture history.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher's Book Description, final paragraph; Lees-Maffei's submitted review, PDF p. 1, opening and discussion of practical knowledge of spinning, and p. 2, closing assessment. Review anchors: 'analysis of its objects' and 'path well trodden'. Her criticism of novelty is retained in the node. Book body unread; no claim that Ulrich invented the study of objects. Only scholarly method is summarized.

edges.relationship: The Age of Homespun (2001) examines how household production became a nostalgic account of the American past and uses object histories to question that account.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher's Book Description, second paragraph; Lees-Maffei's submitted review, PDF p. 1, paragraph beginning 'The Introduction goes on', citing the book's p. 36 on a historical narrative becoming orthodoxy. This relationship concerns the construction of retrospective national memory, distinct from the material-evidence method in the consumption edge. Only description/review read; no debt to Halbwachs or Nora asserted.

edges.relationship: Ulrich collaborated in the documentary adaptation of A Midwife's Tale (book 1990; PBS broadcast 1998), making the process of reconstructing history from records part of its public presentation.
edges.evidence_note: PBS Film Description, paragraph beginning 'For five years', and Credits explicitly name Ulrich, Laurie Kahn-Leavitt and Richard P. Rogers and describe showing the historian's research. The CV, PDF pp. 4–5, PUBLIC HISTORY PROJECTS, identifies her as narrator and consultant and separately as DoHistory advisor. Claim is collaboration and interpretive presentation, not sole authorship or evidence from viewing the film. The displayed broadcast date is 19 January 1998.

edges.relationship: In her American Historical Review review (June 1991) of Merchant's Ecological Revolutions (1989), Ulrich notes its effort to connect ecology and feminism and praises its concrete accounts of farming, but finds its attempts to map long-term change 'often tenuous', points to 'a similar casualness about causality', and says Merchant is more comfortable contrasting fixed types than delineating causal and chronological sequences.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, AHR 96.3, June 1991, p. 945; the review begins in the lower left column and runs onto p. 946). Landing metadata: reviewer Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, University of New Hampshire. Phrases seen: 'Readers who know Carolyn Merchant's first book, The Death of Nature ... will find this new study both familiar and surprising—familiar in its effort to connect ecology and feminism'; 'Merchant has the gift of being able to make plain dirt interesting'; 'The chapters that follow are eclectic, even at some points eccentric, ranging from rich descriptions of objects, habitats, and processes to sometimes convincing, often tenuous, attempts to map long-term change'; 'Merchant is clearly more comfortable contrasting fixed types—corn mothers versus Puritan fathers, subsistence farmers versus market agriculturists—than in delineating causal and chronological sequences'; 'A similar casualness about causality makes it difficult to understand how the descendants of the witch-hunting Puritans ... became the benign subsistence farmers'; on Merchant's p. 86, 'Actually, the pathogens, borne by transient fishermen and traders, came first'; and, more favourably, 'The descriptions of subsistence farming are more convincing.' Limits: p. 946 (the end of the review and any final judgement) unread; the claim is limited to the criticisms and praise on p. 945. The review engages Merchant's argument directly; it is not a citation. Merchant's book itself not reread here.

edges.relationship: A Midwife's Tale (1990) reshaped women's history by challenging both accounts of an early golden age and narratives of a political void before feminism.
edges.evidence_note: Pearsall and Sword identify competing narratives displaced by the book; no claim about particular scholars.

edges.relationship: Ulrich's A Midwife's Tale (1990) inspired the documentary and DoHistory website, which Pearsall and Sword identify as an influential experiment in digital history.
edges.evidence_note: The authors describe a book–film–website sequence and participatory access to primary sources; credit remains collaborative.

edges.relationship: Heasim Sul's 2015 survey of microhistory in the history of medicine names A Midwife's Tale (1990), with works by Ruggiero and Cressy, as clearly demonstrating microhistory's methods and revealing the complexity of early modern medicine and personal relationships.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal-published English abstract, not the Korean article body. Sul explicitly includes Ulrich among three studies illustrating medical microhistory and the complexity of early modern medicine. This supports a bounded field contribution, not personal influence on Sul or a claim to have founded the field.

edges.relationship: In Colour-Coded (1999), Backhouse uses Higginbotham’s “African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race” (1992) to reject accounts that assume dominant and subordinated groups understood racial hierarchy alike.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11 (PDF p. 26), first two paragraphs, and printed note 13, p. 285 (PDF p. 300). Backhouse invokes Higginbotham on how racial meanings were “internalized”, in her argument that subordinate communities resisted claims of inferiority. Higginbotham’s original article was not independently read here; the edge records Backhouse’s own explicit use.

edges.relationship: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) made individual women’s encounters with marriage, fertility, family, work and criminal law a history of how Canadian law organized gender inequality, as Greg Marquis’s 1992 review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Marquis, p. 171 (PDF p. 10), the paragraph devoted to Petticoats calls its conclusion “patriarchal” and discusses both legal incapacity and the case method. Read the review and Osgoode’s contents/description, not the book. This is an attributed contribution to Canadian women’s history, not a claim that Backhouse founded the field.

edges.relationship: Colour-Coded (1999) argues that Canadian legislators and courts created and maintained racial hierarchy, making law an active agent in the history of racism rather than a neutral background.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 13–17, especially p. 15 (PDF p. 30), describes law as a “systemic instrument” of oppression and specifies racial classification, immigration and segregation. These pages were directly read in the author-posted original text; the whole book was not read. Contribution concerns the field’s legal construction of race strand, not immigration alone.

edges.relationship: Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) examines the legal regulation of marriage, courtship, sexual violence, fertility and prostitution, including labour laws that controlled working women’s sexuality, as Marquis’s 1992 review describes.
edges.evidence_note: Marquis, p. 171 (PDF p. 10), paragraph on Petticoats, characterizes protective labour law as “controlling the sexuality” of working-class women. Osgoode contents corroborate the selected domains. The book is unread; this scoped field contribution does not identify Backhouse with Corrigan’s or Valverde’s theoretical framework.
edges.map_label: Legal regulation of sexuality and family

edges.relationship: In Carnal Crimes (2008), Backhouse says her book builds on earlier Canadian research on sexual assault, crediting Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) with supporting a feminist analysis of the power dynamics of sexual violence and with showing that women were not silent victims but active in negotiating their own sexual encounters.
edges.evidence_note: Read the Introduction of Carnal Crimes: Sexual Assault Law in Canada, 1900–1975 (Irwin Law for the Osgoode Society, 2008; © 2008), pp. 3–14, in the author-deposited PDF of the paperback printing on the author’s own website. On p. 12 (PDF p. 24), in the paragraph beginning “This book builds upon the path-breaking research of other Canadian historians who have explored sexual assault”, the body text states: “Karen Dubinsky’s study of sexual crime in northern and rural Ontario supported a feminist analysis of the power dynamics of sexual violence, and it emphasized that women were not silent victims, but active in negotiating their own sexual encounters.” Note 28 (p. 302, PDF p. 314) identifies the work as Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (Chicago, 1993). The paragraph then says “This study expands upon the work of these earlier researchers with a specifically legal focus”. The same paragraph names other historians (Chapman, Erickson, Chunn, Phillips, Cliche, Olsen, Connor, Strange, Sangster, Ross, Adams, Chenier), but Dubinsky is the only one whose argument, rather than subject, is characterised. This body-text statement of debt and argument is not an acknowledgment list or a collective “see” note. Chapter 4 also quotes Dubinsky (p. 97, n. 51, Improper Advances pp. 132–33) on contemporary views of male sexuality, without naming her in the body; that is not relied on. Dubinsky’s book was not read.

edges.relationship: In Carnal Crimes (2008), Backhouse frames her nine twentieth-century Canadian sexual-assault cases as “a multi-dimensional examination of the forces of intersectionality” and argues that they bear out the premise that intersectional factors played a definitive role in women’s historical experiences of sexual assault.
edges.evidence_note: Carnal Crimes, Introduction, pp. 11–12 (PDF pp. 23–24). On p. 11 Backhouse summarises the critique by critical race scholars of the universality of “gender”: “not all women experienced sexual assault the same way” (n. 23 lists the scholars). On p. 12, in the paragraph beginning “The cases profiled here provide strong support”, she writes that “the cases in this study also amply bear out the premise that intersectional factors played a definitive role in women’s historical experiences of sexual assault”. In the next paragraph she says the book “contains a multi-dimensional examination of the forces of intersectionality”, which distinguishes it from earlier regional studies. This is the author’s own statement of her method and finding in her own book. The case chapters were not reread for this edge, and no claim is made about how the intersectional analysis works in each chapter. Some chapters concern cases with Indigenous complainants or accused; this edge relies only on the introduction, and nothing is said about those cases (OCAP care).
edges.map_label: Intersectional legal history of sexual assault

edges.relationship: Constance Backhouse and Adele Perry were two of the four co-editors, with Cynthia E. Milton and Margaret Kovach, of Royally Wronged: The Royal Society of Canada and Indigenous Peoples (2021), a twelve-essay scholarly collection examining the Royal Society of Canada's complicity in colonialism.
edges.evidence_note: Read Andrew Nurse’s review on the BC Studies journal website, especially the editorial attribution immediately below the title, the paragraph beginning “The result is a collection of twelve essays”, and Publication Information. The attribution explicitly identifies Backhouse and Perry as editors of the same book; Publication Information supplies the 2021 original publication year. The review describes a substantive scholarly essay collection, including an editorial introduction and afterword. Backhouse’s own Books page independently confirms the co-editorship in the Royally Wronged section. This edge asserts collaboration as co-editors, without assigning shared authorship of individual chapters or inferring intellectual influence. The underlying book is unread. OCAP scope: published editorial collaboration and scholarship only; no community knowledge, oral narratives, narrator quotations, ceremonies, genealogies or identity claims are included.
edges.map_label: Co-editors (with Milton and Kovach) of Royally Wronged (2021)

edges.relationship: In Manly Militants, Cohesive Communities, and Defiant Domestics (1995), Franca Iacovetta discusses Petticoats and Prejudice (1991) as an example of sophisticated legal history integrating racial-ethnic differences into gender analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Journal-hosted historiographical essay read at pp. 249–252, with its opening framing at pp. 217–219. The body names Backhouse and explains the book's treatment of differences among women. Recorded as a favorable published appraisal, without inferring a personal intellectual debt.

edges.relationship: Colour-Coded (1999) contributed to racial-formation history by analyzing racial categories' instability and racialization's continuing effects, as Tracey Lindberg's review (2001) explains.
edges.evidence_note: Review evidence only; pp. 199–200 read. No theoretical-school affiliation inferred.

edges.relationship: Tracey Lindberg's review (2001) judges that Colour-Coded (1999), by acknowledging First Nations systems of law alongside Canadian law, becomes 'in a sense, an anti-colonial' work, while calling it a largely successful but inconsistent attempt.
edges.evidence_note: Review pp. 197–198 read; Lindberg also qualifies its treatment of governance. Scholarship only.

edges.relationship: In 'Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science' (1986; cited in a 1996 reprint), Stepan likens the role of a metaphor in the logic of science to that of a Kuhnian paradigm, as Paul Bartha reports in By Parallel Reasoning (2010).
edges.evidence_note: Abridged reprint, reader p. 45 and p. 49 n. 37: ‘programme of research’. Names Structure and Kuhn’s metaphor essay. Selected primary passage; original Isis version and Kuhn texts uncollated. Not a claim of wholesale theoretical allegiance.
edges.map_label: Likens scientific metaphor to a Kuhnian paradigm

edges.relationship: In a 2016 interview, Levine credits The Hour of Eugenics (1991) as the first book to show a pro-natal 'other mode of eugenics' that sought better births through housing, medical care and antenatal care.
edges.evidence_note: Five Books interview, section 4, question naming the 1991 book and answer beginning I think it is important to ask: ‘this other way too’. Interview date not displayed. Published reception, not proof that Stepan supplied Levine’s entire framework. Book unread in full.
edges.map_label: Levine: first to show pro-natal eugenics

edges.relationship: In his 2002 review of Picturing Tropical Nature (2001), Arnold praises the book as a major advance in interpreting tropicality.
edges.evidence_note: Chicago publisher excerpt, description ending: ‘carries forward a field’. Excerpt credited only to Social History of Medicine; 15(1) contents name Arnold, pp. 175–176. Attribution joins these exact book/journal records; complete review unread. Evaluation only, not an established intellectual debt.

edges.relationship: “Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science” (1986) takes up the debated role of metaphor and analogy in scientific theory, against science’s traditional standing as the repository of nonmetaphorical, politically neutral knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary reprint, reader p. 42, Metaphoric interactions: ‘constituent elements of science’. Reader is abridged; original version uncollated.

edges.relationship: “Tropical Medicine and Public Health in Latin America” (1998) organizes medical history around political priorities, laboratory science, international agencies and race.
edges.evidence_note: English essay, pp. 104–106, especially the four-theme statement on p. 106 and question ‘who defines the public’. Selected review pages read; reviewed books unread. Contribution to a field, not evidence of a unified school.

edges.relationship: Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) studies tropical nature as a European and American imaginative construct, including anti-tropicalism's role in an emerging environmentalist sensibility and the imagery of tropical medicine.
edges.evidence_note: Davis excerpt in Cornell’s UTP distributor page, Reviews, web lines 71–75, explicitly identifies ‘environmental history’. Publisher description also discusses environmentalist sensibility. Named review excerpt only; book and complete Davis review unread.

edges.relationship: In 'Tropical Medicine and Public Health in Latin America' (1998), Stepan sets Latin American medical history beside postcolonial questions about colonies and science, arguing that the colonial framework developed in studies of India and Africa is of limited use for the region's independent countries.
edges.evidence_note: English essay p. 104: ‘uneasy fit’ and ‘limited use’. Opening acknowledges postcolonial questions but stresses political independence and changing centres of medical reference. Qualified regional criticism, not rejection of postcolonial history. Selected primary page; reviewed books unread.
edges.map_label: Colonial framework of limited use for Latin America

edges.relationship: In his 2003 review of Picturing Tropical Nature (2001), MacKenzie argues that Stepan does not follow her argument through to its logical conclusion: the tropics were never portrayed as a single entity opposed to temperate regions, as empathetic travellers and tropical plants in European winter gardens and greenhouses show.
edges.evidence_note: MacKenzie's complete review, AHR 108(1) (2003), pp. 150–151, read in the publisher's two publicly displayed first-page preview images. The first is linked from his own article; the second, containing the continuation and his signature on p. 151, is linked from the adjacent Harvey J. Kaye review of Ellen Fitzpatrick. On p. 151 MacKenzie praises Stepan's treatment of tropical medicine and medical photography, then argues that she leaves the complexity of tropical representations insufficiently developed. His examples include sympathetic travellers, tropical plants in European homes, and differences within tropical and temperate regions. The claim concerns this substantive criticism; it does not rest on his praise alone. Stepan's book itself remains unread. The checked URL is the publisher-supplied preview image of p. 151, linked at https://academic.oup.com/ahr/article/108/1/151/22648.
edges.map_label: Ambiguity in representations of the tropics

edges.relationship: Nancy Leys Stepan's ‘Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science’ (1986) contributed a historical analysis of race–gender analogies that Mary E. John engaged in Discrepant Dislocations (1996), in her discussion of gender and feminist theory.
edges.evidence_note: Read John's sustained discussion on pp. 87–90 and note 30 in the publisher's archive. John credits Stepan's historical account and considers its implications while criticizing Sandra Harding's analogies. This supports a bounded contribution to gender analysis, not founding the field. John cites the 1990 anthology version; the original 1986 publication was checked on the journal's own page. Stepan's full original article was not read. John has no eligible endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed.

edges.relationship: In “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991), Seed criticizes Orientalism (1978) for omitting non-Western texts and asserting rather than demonstrating how knowledge became power.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 189 and 192: “affirmed rather than demonstrated.” Qualified methodological criticism; Said’s book and reply unread.

edges.relationship: In “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991), Seed develops Bhabha’s account of an addressed colonial discourse by adding its enforcement through coercive institutions.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 184 n. 7: “To Bhabha’s proposition, I would add.” Specific conceptual use; Bhabha’s underlying text unidentified and unread.

edges.relationship: In “Failing to Marvel” (1991), Seed uses Derrida’s critique of Lévi-Strauss to question the cultural superiority attributed to alphabetic writing.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 8, text and n. 4, citing “The Violence of the Letter” in Of Grammatology (English translation 1976; French original 1967). Derrida’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Seed and C. A. Bayly were co-participants and credited coauthors of “AHR Conversation: On Transnational History” (2006).
edges.evidence_note: Read participant heading and pp. 1441–1443. Six-person published collaboration, not agreement or a separately documented two-person collaboration.

edges.relationship: Seed and Sven Beckert were co-participants and credited coauthors of “AHR Conversation: On Transnational History” (2006).
edges.evidence_note: Read participant heading and pp. 1441–1446. Six-person published collaboration; their individual positions remain distinct.

edges.relationship: “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991) synthesizes an interdisciplinary critique of colonial language, representation and authority.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 182–185 and 198–199: “interdisciplinary critique.” Contribution to debate, not a claim of founding the field.

edges.relationship: Crider’s 1996 review reads Ceremonies of Possession (1995) as connecting cultural interpretation with histories of colonial power.
edges.evidence_note: Review, opening and EVALUATION, especially paragraph beginning “What distinguishes.” Mediated reading; Crider also questions the book’s national comparisons.

edges.relationship: Gauderman’s review locates To Love, Honor, and Obey in Colonial Mexico (1988) within family-history debates about marriage choice and patriarchal authority.
edges.evidence_note: Review pp. 114–116: “Family history.” Supports a family-history contribution, not population reconstruction; primary book unread.

edges.relationship: In Law and Colonial Cultures: Legal Regimes in World History, 1400–1900 (2002), Lauren Benton criticized Patricia Seed’s Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995) for overstating differences between European possession practices through comparisons of different symbolic activities, while valuing its comparative approach.
edges.evidence_note: Read Cambridge University Press’s sample, including the discussion of jurisdictional and cultural boundaries. Note 17 directly evaluates Seed’s comparisons and warns against extrapolating from symbolic possession to mutual incomprehension of legal orders. The surrounding body develops the distinction between initial possession and subsequent legal relations; note 19 also discusses Seed’s argument about messages sent and received. This is substantive critical engagement, not a collective reference. The whole monograph was not read.

edges.relationship: In ‘Doing the Continental’ (1997), Gordon S. Wood drew on Patricia Seed’s Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995) to argue that inherited English practices of exclusion constrained later Anglo-American choices, using her comparative findings in his criticism of Lester D. Langley’s account of the American revolutions.
edges.evidence_note: The publisher’s review text explicitly uses Seed’s findings to challenge Langley on political choice. This records a specific use; Langley’s book is the work under review.

edges.relationship: Wood criticizes The Name of War (1998) for giving too little explanatory weight to political, social and economic forces, and The Whites of Their Eyes (2010) for insufficient sympathy toward popular memory of the Revolution.
edges.evidence_note: Wood, The Bloodiest War (1998), paragraphs beginning “In this sort of postmodern history” and “Instead of composing”; No Thanks for the Memories (2011), paragraphs beginning “The Tea Partiers are certainly not scholars” and final paragraph. The first review also praises her imaginative scholarship. Both reviews read in these passages; neither book independently read in full. These are Wood’s judgments, not established defects.

edges.relationship: Discussing New York Burning (2005) in her 2009 interview, Lepore explicitly relates the entanglement of liberty and enslavement to Morgan’s American paradox.
edges.evidence_note: NEH interview, answer beginning “I’m interested in our capacity,” ending with the explicit attribution “American paradox” to Edmund Morgan. A named conceptual resource, not a supervision claim. Neither Morgan’s original formulation nor New York Burning was read in full.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Book of Ages (2013), Edith B. Gelles places it in the historiographical line of Ulrich’s A Midwife’s Tale (1990) as a study of an obscure woman’s life.
edges.evidence_note: Book of Ages publisher page, Praise, Gelles excerpt: “descends historiographically.” This is Gelles’s interpretation, not Lepore’s self-attribution. Full review and both books unread; Ulrich is another person in this run. The 1990 date of A Midwife’s Tale is also checked in Lepore 2001, p. 132, note 5.
edges.map_label: Reviewer links Book of Ages to A Midwife’s Tale

edges.relationship: Book of Ages: The Life and Opinions of Jane Franklin (2013) reconstructs the life of Benjamin Franklin’s obscure youngest sister from little-studied documents, objects and portraits.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, paragraphs beginning “From one of our most accomplished” and “Making use”; Harvard biography, “absences and asymmetries.” This claim uses these summaries; the book was not read in full.

edges.relationship: The Name of War (1998) treats later remembrance of King Philip’s War as a force shaping American history, rather than merely a record of the conflict.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, final two paragraphs; NEH interview, answers to the questions about American identity and later removal, especially “what’s remembered and what’s forgotten.” Argument read through publisher summary and author testimony; book body unread.

edges.relationship: In her 2009 interview, Lepore explains Common-place and the coauthored novel Blindspot (2008) as ways of bringing archival scholarship to public audiences and offering another interpretation of Boston’s historic sites.
edges.evidence_note: NEH interview, Common-place answers and answer to “Where and when?” about Park Service consulting: explicitly “public history.” Blindspot publisher metadata confirms 2008 and joint authorship with Jane Kamensky. This is her account of purpose, not evidence of audience reception; novel unread.
edges.map_label: Archives, public audiences and historic sites

edges.relationship: The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014) locates the superhero’s creation within the history of women’s rights, linking early suffrage campaigns with later feminism.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, paragraph beginning “The Secret History of Wonder Woman is a tour de force,” and original 2014 ebook date. The displayed 2015 paperback includes a later afterword. Publisher-mediated statement of argument; full book and afterword unread.

edges.relationship: In These Truths: A History of the United States (2018), Jill Lepore attempted a national synthesis joining the country’s achievements and atrocities, which she explained in a 2019 interview as an alternative to opposed partisan histories.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s interview transcript. Lepore explains the intended synthesis and evidence-based civic purpose of her book. Claim concerns her stated intervention, not its success or other scholars’ adoption; the book itself was not read. The target is the national-narrative teaching umbrella, with no endorsement of imperial history implied.

edges.relationship: Hall and Massey coauthor the dialogue “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), examining the financial crisis through conjunctural analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF p. 57 credits both authors and labels their turns; selected pp. 57–67 read. Coauthorship only; Hall’s particular formulations are not assigned wholesale to Massey.

edges.relationship: In “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), Massey says rereading Althusser helps her understand the crisis as a conjunction of economic, political and philosophical processes.
edges.evidence_note: p. 59, Doreen’s turn: “looked at the Prison Notebooks, and Althusser”. Lee pp. 164, 167 corroborates an earlier debt to overdetermination. Althusser originals unread; no sole derivation asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), Massey uses her rereading of Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks to argue against an exclusively economic account of crisis.
edges.evidence_note: p. 59, same explicitly labelled Doreen turn: “don’t only ‘do the economy’”. Hall identifies Gramsci on pp. 58–59; no independent Notebooks reading claimed. Her use is distinct from Hall’s exposition.

edges.relationship: In “Flexible Sexism” (1991), Massey criticizes Harvey’s The Condition of Postmodernity (1989) for excluding feminist contributions from geography’s modernism–postmodernism debate.
edges.evidence_note: 2018 Reader reprint, introduction, last two displayed paragraphs: “denial” of feminism; Cambridge chapter 15, pp. 221–242, opening only. Original pp. 31–57 remainder unread. Joint criticism also names Soja. Distinct from existing edge_1518 about tradition and place in 1995.

edges.relationship: Massey uses Lefebvre’s warning about undefined spatial concepts to frame “Politics and Space/Time” (1992).
edges.evidence_note: Public opening, paragraph beginning Buried in these unacknowledged disagreements; names The Production of Space and endorses its demand to debate spatial meanings. For Space sample p. 17 repeats this starting point. Limited framing debt, not adoption of Lefebvre’s whole theory; originals and subscription remainder unread.

edges.relationship: For Space (2005) argues that de Certeau’s tactics–strategy distinction reinforces the space–time dualism his account seeks to escape.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample pp. 25–27, especially p. 26: “cements into place”; references de Certeau’s 1984 English edition. Original unread.

edges.relationship: For Space (2005) criticizes Giddens and Beck’s risk-society writing for opposing dynamic culture to stable nature.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample p. 160: “such dualisms”; joint attribution followed by Nigel Clark’s 2002 argument. Chapter 9 and Giddens originals unread; limited joint criticism.
edges.map_label: Questions stable nature in risk theory

edges.relationship: Space, Place and Gender (1994) develops a wider notion of spatiality as the product of intersecting social relations.
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR part I introduction, displayed p. 19 opening: “spatial fetishism”. Only opening read; theoretical contribution, not a claim about reception or the whole discipline.

edges.relationship: Space, Place and Gender (1994) relates the conceptualization of space and place to the social construction of gender relations.
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR part III introduction, displayed p. 177 opening: “construction of the other”. A theoretical resource for gender history; historical uptake by particular historians is not established. Full section unread.

edges.relationship: For Space (2005) treats places as encounters between trajectories with different histories, making belonging open to renegotiation.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample pp. 149–151, Hamburg boulder example: “constellation of trajectories”. Historical-geographical framework, not evidence of adoption by a historian.

edges.relationship: Massey’s For Space (2005) supplied an open-ended account of place that Alan Lester used in imperial-colonial history, as Indra Sengupta explains in her introduction to Memory, History, and Colonialism (2009).
edges.evidence_note: Read Sengupta’s discussion on printed pp. 7–8 and notes 19–22 in the institute’s own publication. The body explicitly attributes Lester’s account of places as intersections of trajectories to Massey, then explains its usefulness for understanding colonial and postcolonial sites of memory. This supports a bounded contribution to imperial-colonial historiography. Lester has no eligible endpoint in the supplied lists, so no person edge is proposed. Neither For Space nor Lester’s original article was read for this proposal.

edges.relationship: Massey’s Spatial Divisions of Labour (1984) supplies an account of domestic economic geography within the international division of labour that Lachlan MacKinnon and Steven High use to frame Canadian deindustrialization in “Deindustrialization in Canada: New Perspectives” (2023).
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s own open article, especially its discussion of uneven deindustrialization and international industrial restructuring, and note 19. The authors invoke Massey by name in the body, quote her argument, and immediately discuss its consequences for Canadian manufacturing workers. Note 19 identifies the 1984 book, although it renders Divisions in the singular. This is evidence of use within labour historiography, not a claim that Massey founded the field. MacKinnon and High have no eligible endpoints in the supplied lists. The underlying Massey book was not read for this proposal.
edges.map_label: International divisions of labour and industrial decline

edges.relationship: In When Species Meet (2008), Haraway faults Derrida’s failure to pursue curiosity about his cat, as Zurn (2018) reads her.
edges.evidence_note: Zurn p. 87, paragraph beginning In one sense and its continuation, reports Haraway’s admiration and specific objection; Berkowitz p. 8 n. 15 quotes When Species Meet p. 20 (discussion pp. 19–27). Haraway’s and Derrida’s originals unread. This concerns a particular encounter, not rejection of all deconstruction.

edges.relationship: As Marie Draz reports, When Species Meet (2008) criticizes Deleuze and Guattari’s becoming-animal within a challenge to wild/domestic boundaries.
edges.evidence_note: Signed review reproduced under Praise, paragraph beginning Of particular interest: “critiques of Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari”. Complete review read; original book passage unread and its print pages unverified. Joint authorship retained; Guattari has no eligible endpoint.

edges.relationship: Situated Knowledges (1988) develops embodied, accountable objectivity for feminist science studies.
edges.evidence_note: Carried forward from existing graph source haraway_situated. Its verification, checked 2026-09-10, records consultation of the journal text, pp. 575–577 and 582–585, for situated objectivity, accountability and rejection of relativism, without implying a universal feminist position. The edge uses the latter pages. This correction read the existing source record; it did not re-read the article. The DOI resolved to a journal landing page without readable article text. The individual contribution complements gender → sts edge_337.

edges.relationship: Primate Visions (1989) examines race and gender in primatology’s history, as Barrett (2017) describes it.
edges.evidence_note: Barrett’s publisher extract, p. 309, paragraph beginning That book: identifies a historical account of primatology. Foundation biography, paragraphs beginning She gained and For instance, independently describes race/gender analysis. Book unread; 1989 original year from UCSC bibliography, not foundation’s 1990.

edges.relationship: In Making Kin (2015), Haraway treats environmental change as the historically situated work of human and nonhuman assemblages.
edges.evidence_note: Primary HTML, opening two paragraphs and note 5: “assemblages of organic species and of abiotic actors make history”. Read argument linking historical differences, ecological change and plantation labour; this is an interdisciplinary contribution to environmental explanation, not a claim to found environmental history.

edges.relationship: In How to Talk About the Body? The Normative Dimension of Science Studies (2004), Bruno Latour takes up Haraway’s call to locate political struggles within the sciences rather than leave scientific authority untouched while restricting activism to subjective feelings.
edges.evidence_note: Read the author-posted journal article’s opening and concluding argument, especially pp. 226–227. Latour explicitly aligns his intervention with Haraway’s advocacy; he does not identify a particular Haraway publication here. This supports a specific conceptual uptake, not a claim that his entire account of bodies originated with her.

edges.relationship: The editors’ introduction to Men and Masculinities in Modern Britain (2024) traces Connell’s theory of hegemony to a broader turn to Gramscian models in the social sciences and New Left politics of the 1970s and 1980s.
edges.evidence_note: Read Houlbrook, Jones and Mechen’s introduction to Men and Masculinities in Modern Britain (publisher release 2024), printed p. 37 n. 30 (PDF page 46), in the publisher’s open-access edition deposited at UCL: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10190042/1/9781526174703_fullhl.pdf . The editors situate Connell’s theory within a wider Gramscian turn. This is their retrospective attribution, not a debt stated by Connell and not a reading of the 2005 joint article. Retain the mediated/thin qualification. Source rc_w_mup_intro_2024 already exists in the supplied input and is already cited by this edge; no duplicate source is needed.

edges.relationship: In her 2011 interview published in 2013, Connell recalls that her first book of social theory, Which Way Is Up?, set out to move Australian social theory away from Talcott Parsons and toward Freud and Sartre, feminism, education and equality.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Connell's own interview (permitted, SciELO) supports a narrower claim of engagement with Freud. The interview gives no year for Which Way Is Up? (it is usually dated 1983; the coordinator should confirm it before adding a year). Weak: flag as thin, or hold if the coordinator wants a stated debt. Phrase seen: “Which Way is Up? foi uma tentativa de trazer a teoria social da Austrália para o mundo real, parar de falar de Talcott Parsons e companhia, e começar a falar de Freud e Sartre”

edges.relationship: In Southern Theory (2007), as Connell recounts in her 2011 interview published in 2013, she follows a critique of Eurocentrism in social thought with criticisms of Bourdieu, Giddens and other modern metropolitan theorists.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Connell's interview supports a different, permitted claim: criticism of Bourdieu in Southern Theory (2007). Phrase seen: “Começo com uma espécie de crítica ao eurocentrismo no pensamento social. Critico isso - e prossigo com críticas a Bourdieu, a Giddens e a algumas teorias modernas”

edges.relationship: In The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), Parr aligns her questions about fixed categories of gender and class with those raised in Connell’s studies of social practice, gender and power, and adopts Connell’s suggestion that such meanings are multiple and mutable.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh selected primary reading: Parr, introduction pp.8–9, especially printed p.9 (PDF page 23), paragraph beginning These two ruminations. Parr names Connell alongside Poovey, Scott and Riley, and explicitly invokes meanings as “multiple and mutable”. Does not establish exclusive derivation, agreement on every issue, or a reading of the complete book. Checked against the existing Scott→Parr edge_1683: same passage, different named resource; no Connell→Parr edge exists. Publisher preview: https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781442681347_A35143482/preview-9781442681347_A35143482.pdf .

edges.relationship: In “Masculinities and history for the present” (2024), Tosh acknowledges Gender and Power (1987) as a theoretical resource for the volume Manful Assertions (1991), which he edited with Michael Roper.
edges.evidence_note: Tosh printed p.178, paragraph beginning The history of masculinities, and n.2 on p.185: “theoretical debts” to Segal and Connell; note identifies Gender and Power (1987). Fresh primary retrospective testimony by Tosh, not a fresh reading of the 1991 volume. Shared editorial credit with Roper retained; no separate Roper endpoint is created. Publisher release year is 2024 although deposited PDF imprint says 2023.

edges.relationship: In “Masculinities and history for the present” (2024), Tosh qualifies Connell’s call in “The Big Picture” (1993) for a long history of masculinities, defending contextual case studies as a way to preserve subjectivity and illuminate present problems.
edges.evidence_note: Tosh printed pp.184–185, paragraphs beginning Shortly after Manful Assertions and There are several reasons, through the conclusion; nn.26–28 on p.186 identify Connell’s 1993 essay and The Men and the Boys (2000). The concern is that extended linear history can privilege “power and precept” over interiority. A qualified methodological disagreement, not repudiation of hegemonic masculinity or of the theoretical debt on p.178. Connell’s 1993 essay was not independently read. Distinct claim and direction from rc_w_05.

edges.relationship: Masculinities (1995), developed and reconsidered with Messerschmidt in “Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept” (2005), supplies gender history with an account of plural, unequal and historically changing masculinities.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. It is supported by the Crossref/SAGE abstract, the Wiley description ('not one masculinity, but many different masculinities, each associated with different positions of power') and the open-access MUP volume (editors' introduction: 'the intellectual indebtedness of foundational histories of masculinity ... to ... Raewyn Connell'; Tosh p. 178). Phrase seen: “what has been confirmed from early formulations (the idea of multiple masculinities, the concept of hegemony, and the emphasis on change)”

edges.relationship: In Southern Theory (2007), as Connell explains in her 2011 interview published in 2013, she challenges Eurocentric social theory and argues for treating intellectual work from the global South as theory rather than merely material for metropolitan analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Primary interview, answer beginning Comecei a trabalhar na teoria sulista and continuing through Essa é a história do Southern Theory (SciELO HTML paragraphs at lines165–168), plus the earlier answer about theory dominated by the North. Connell describes her critique and proposed globally democratic social science. Book year confirmed by the interview’s reference list. Southern Theory itself remains unread; claim is explicitly based on her retrospective account. The post endpoint concerns Eurocentric universals and imperial knowledge, so this is an adjacent sociological contribution to that critique, not membership in a uniform school. No community knowledge is reproduced.

edges.relationship: In their introduction to Nine Centuries of Man (2017), Lynn Abrams and Elizabeth Ewan acknowledge Connell’s Masculinities (1995) as influential in framing their interpretations of relations among men, while emphasizing the contestability of hegemonic masculinity.
edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction’s discussion on printed pp. 2–3 and its identifying note in the licensed publisher preview. The statement is jointly authored by Abrams and Ewan and explicitly acknowledges influence on their interpretations. This supports a bounded theoretical debt by Abrams, rather than exclusive derivation of the collection’s approach. Ewan is not an eligible endpoint in the supplied lists.
edges.map_label: Framework for interpreting relations among men

edges.relationship: In her IHR interview (2008), Nelson names Peter Brown, whose work she says took medieval history into cultural and social history, as “the third great influence on me”, as a reader of his work rather than a student.
edges.evidence_note: IHR transcript, answer beginning “But neither of those two”, through “third great influence on me, Peter Brown” (web lines 95–101): she places herself among Brown’s readers, not his students, and discusses his questions about religious belief and saints. Brown’s books were not newly read; no supervision relationship asserted.

edges.relationship: As Stafford documents, Nelson invokes Marc Bloch’s injunction to seek people behind historical evidence in “Monks, Secular Men and Masculinity, c. 900” (1999).
edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 24, paragraph beginning “And it was here”, n. 55, identifies Nelson’s invocation of Bloch and locates the essay passage at p. 138. Her phrase “real men” expresses the methodological point. Mediated evidence: the 1999 essay and Bloch’s original were not read directly.
edges.map_label: Bloch and people behind the sources

edges.relationship: According to Stafford, Nelson applies James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) to Charlemagne’s unsuccessful canal project in King and Emperor (2019).
edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 28, second sentence and n. 74, explicitly names Scott and locates Nelson’s application at King and Emperor, pp. 295–296. This is a specific application documented by a named scholarly reader; those pages and Scott’s book are unread.

edges.relationship: As Stafford reports, Nelson uses a Weberian pointsman metaphor for Charlemagne’s capacity to redirect ideas in King and Emperor (2019).
edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 28, opening paragraph, n. 75, calls the figure “Weberian” and cites King and Emperor, pp. 292 and 285. Limited to this metaphor; no general Weberian affiliation. Those book pages and the originating Weber passage are unread.

edges.relationship: In Julia M. H. Smith’s reading, “Gendering Courts in the Early Medieval West” (2004) challenges Elias’s male-centred court model by placing women within early medieval courtliness.
edges.evidence_note: Smith, in Rio et al. (2025), printed p. 321, paragraph beginning “It takes something of an effort”, names Elias, quotes Nelson’s criticism of a world consisting “of men only”, and explains her earlier chronology and women’s agency. The 2004 chapter, pp. 185–197, remains unread directly. The claim follows Smith’s specific reading, not an independently established refutation of all Elias.

edges.relationship: As Julia M. H. Smith documents, Nelson criticizes Foucault’s neglect of women in “Gendering Courts in the Early Medieval West” (2004).
edges.evidence_note: Smith, Rio et al. (2025), printed p. 321, same court-studies paragraph: Foucault is explicitly one of the two writers criticized. Limited to omission of women; neither rejection of genealogy nor a debt to Foucault inferred. Nelson’s chapter and the relevant Foucault books remain unread directly.

edges.relationship: “Queens as Jezebels” (1978), as Stafford explains, makes royal women’s action part of the explanation of early medieval political power.
edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed pp. 20–23, especially p. 20 n. 38 (1978 original) and p. 22 on integrating women into political history. This concerns interpretation of queens and power, not a claim of equal status or unrestricted agency. Original essay unread; Politics and Ritual (1986) is the reprint collection, not the essay’s original date.

edges.relationship: As Stafford explains, “Monks, Secular Men and Masculinity, c. 900” (1999) examines tensions between aristocratic masculine duties and Christian demands.
edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed pp. 23–24, nn. 52–55, describes violence, reproduction and monastic masculinity as historically situated pressures. Original essay unread; its 2007 collection does not replace the original 1999 publication. This is a specific gender-history contribution, not a generic field-membership inference.

edges.relationship: In her IHR interview (2008), Nelson, author of Politics and Ritual in Early Medieval Europe (1986), describes the early medieval study of ritual as tied to cultural history, so that ritual and the activities of legislative assemblies are seen as “both real” and “constantly interacting”.
edges.evidence_note: IHR transcript, answers to the cultural-turn questions (web lines 169–176), particularly the interaction of ritual with legislative assemblies. Politics and Ritual (1986) is the earlier collection identified independently by KCL. This records her explicit methodological account, not membership in a single school; neither the collection nor her cited historiographical chapter was read in full.

edges.relationship: In her funeral address quoted in David d’Avray and John Hudson’s memoir of Susan Reynolds (2022), Janet Nelson credits discussions with Reynolds with helping her refine and develop historical ideas.
edges.evidence_note: British Academy memoir (2022), p. 164, quotes Nelson’s funeral address and explicitly identifies their repeated historical discussions. This is a stated intellectual debt, with Reynolds as source and Nelson as recipient; no particular Nelson book is identified. The KCL profile additionally confirms their coediting of Gender and Historiography (2012), retained as supplementary bibliographic evidence.
edges.map_label: Nelson credits Reynolds with developing ideas

edges.relationship: In “Dispute Settlement in Carolingian West Francia” (1986), Nelson challenged accounts of Carolingian government centred on top-down control by showing the importance of local power, custom and participation in judicial decisions, as Wendy Davies explains in her 2025 retrospective.
edges.evidence_note: Read Davies’s complete section in the journal’s open HTML. It identifies the 1986 essay and explains its challenge to state-centred justice. This is a political-history contribution, independently of the existing cultural-history pair; the underlying essay was not read.

edges.relationship: In “Writing Early Medieval Biography” (2000), Nelson argued that an early medieval life could be written when varied evidence illuminates the subject’s life stages and inner life and connects the individual to historical context, using Charlemagne as her case.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher abstract and publication details, not the paywalled article. The abstract specifies varied genres, first-hand material, different life phases, inner life and contextual links, and states that Charlemagne meets these conditions. The claim is limited to this stated methodological argument.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Nelson’s King and Emperor: A New Life of Charlemagne (2019), Patrick J. Geary praised its involvement of readers in the historical investigation, comparing the resulting suspense to detective work, in the passage quoted by his institution.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete notice on Geary’s institutional site and the accessible opening three paragraphs of the linked newspaper review. The notice quotes his appraisal of the book’s method and identifies the review. The review’s remaining text was unavailable; this comparison records only that quoted appraisal and does not infer influence or the absence of criticism elsewhere.

edges.relationship: Brown identifies Morgan’s American Slavery, American Freedom (1975) as an inspiration for Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) in “Americans on the James” (2001).
edges.evidence_note: Brown’s own 2001 retrospective, opening paragraph: “the copy that inspired my first book.” Full essay read; Morgan’s book unread. This explicit debt is distinct from Brown’s criticism of its explanation.

edges.relationship: In “Americans on the James” (2001), Brown argues that Morgan’s American Slavery, American Freedom (1975) leaves white women’s investment in reproducing racism insufficiently explained.
edges.evidence_note: 2001 essay, paragraphs beginning But Morgan’s ambitious effort and The stake of white women. Brown preserves Morgan’s explanatory ambition while supplementing his political-strategy account. Full essay read; original Morgan book unread.
edges.map_label: White women and the reproduction of racism

edges.relationship: Reflecting on Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) in the 2014 Junto interview, Brown recalls developing the project while enrolled in the Women’s History Program under Gerda Lerner’s guidance.
edges.evidence_note: First answer, paragraph 1: “under the guidance of Gerda Lerner.” Original interview read; no specific Lerner work or formal dissertation-supervisor relationship is asserted.
edges.map_label: Lerner’s guidance in the Women’s History Program

edges.relationship: Brown (series co-editor from 2002, as Brown's own CV records) and Daniel K. Richter co-edit the Early American Studies book series published by the University of Pennsylvania Press with the McNeil Center for Early American Studies.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher front-matter PDF p. 2 (unnumbered series page): “Series Editors”; p. 4 gives copyright 2004. A formal joint editorial credit, not shared employment; no claim of coauthorship or volume editing, founding date, or continuous tenure. Undirected collaboration uses comparison metadata.
edges.map_label: Joint editors of Early American Studies

edges.relationship: Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) makes changing gender relations and ideals of masculinity part of the explanation of racial slavery and colonial authority.
edges.evidence_note: UNC description, paragraphs 1–4; corroborated by Coryell pp. 1–2 and Brown’s 2014 answer on teaching. Publisher and complete review read; original book unread. This is a specific analytical contribution, not a claim to have founded gender history.
edges.map_label: Gender in the making of colonial power

edges.relationship: Brown retrospectively describes Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) as an effort to show race, gender and class becoming mutually constitutive through historical processes.
edges.evidence_note: 2014 interview, second answer: Brown describes race, gender and class as “socially constructed and mutually constitutive” and says she had yet to read history treating “intersectionality as a truly historical process.” Interview read; no claim that Brown coined the term or derived the book from a named intersectionality theorist.

edges.relationship: Foul Bodies: Cleanliness in Early America (2009) connects changing ideas of health and bodily care to domestic labor, gender and public standards of civilization, as Janet Moore Lindman explains in her 2010 review.
edges.evidence_note: Lindman’s publisher-displayed extract, first two paragraphs, citing Brown p. 3; Yale description also read. Rest of review and book body unread. The edge is mediated by this named scholarly reading and limited to health, bodily care and their social organization.

edges.relationship: In an American Historical Review review (June 1999) of Gordon-Reed's Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings: An American Controversy (1997), Brown calls the book a 'persuasive critique of the consensus view among Jefferson scholars' and writes that it strengthened Brown's own inclination to believe that the Jefferson-Hemings relationship occurred.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, AHR 104.3, June 1999, p. 900, right column). Reviewer metadata on the landing page: Kathleen M. Brown, University of Pennsylvania. Phrases seen: 'Annette Gordon-Reed's persuasive critique of the consensus view among Jefferson scholars that there was no sexual relationship has strengthened my inclination toward belief'; 'Through careful research and meticulous reasoning, the virtuosity of which cannot be fairly represented in a short review, she argues that the evidence dismissed as insufficient by dozens of historians amounts to a strong circumstantial case'; 'The case being tried by Gordon-Reed is concerned less with Jefferson's sexual behavior, however, than with the intellectual integrity of a group of prominent Jefferson scholars, including Dumas Malone and Merrill Peterson'. Limits: pp. 901-902 (the rest of the review, including any reservations) unread; the claim is limited to the first page. A favourable review that reports being persuaded on one question is recorded as comparison, not as a broader intellectual debt. The review is also listed in Brown's own CV (book reviews section). Gordon-Reed is a run member, so the endpoint is pending.
edges.map_label: Brown reviews Gordon-Reed on Jefferson and Hemings

edges.relationship: In Laboring Women (2004), Jennifer L. Morgan identifies Brown’s Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) as a precedent for subsequent early American histories and explicitly engages Brown’s argument about women’s role in naturalizing slave status through race.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed Google Books search-preview excerpts, not the complete introduction or chapter. The p. 5 excerpt names Brown’s 1996 book and assesses its importance for later histories. On p. 93 Morgan explicitly attributes to Kathleen Brown an argument about women naturalizing slave status through race. The latter is substantive engagement in the body of Morgan’s argument, not an acknowledgment or isolated bibliographic citation. The complete surrounding pages and endnotes remain unread; no exclusive intellectual derivation is claimed. Penn’s own record confirms the original 2004 publication, distinct from the 2011 ebook date.
edges.map_label: Morgan engages Brown on gender and slave status

edges.relationship: Brown’s “Changed ... into the Fashion of Man”: The Politics of Sexual Difference in a Seventeenth-Century Anglo-American Settlement (1995) contributes to histories of sex ambiguity by interpreting community sex classification and the colonial labor interests surrounding the Thomas/ine Hall case, arguments that Maayan Sudai examines in “Sex Ambiguity in Early Modern Common Law” (2021; journal issue 2022).
edges.evidence_note: Read the open publisher PDF’s introduction, pp. 478–481; the Hall discussion, pp. 486–487; and the Brown reference on p. 509. On p. 487 Sudai specifically attributes the labor explanation to Brown (1995, 188–190), then contrasts Brown’s account of unstable sex differences with Norton’s interpretation. This is sustained body-text engagement. The field edge concerns historical sex classification, matching the existing queer node’s scope of changing sexual categories; it does not assign a modern identity to Hall or claim Brown invented the field. Brown’s original article and the rest of Sudai’s article were not read. Sudai is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person node or personal edge is proposed.
edges.map_label: Sex ambiguity, community judgment and colonial labor

edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Ngai’s Impossible Subjects (2004) to explain racialized nationality.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 13: “As Mae Ngai has shown”; cites Ngai p. 27. Ngai’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Jacobson’s Whiteness of a Different Color (1998) on consolidated whiteness.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 13: “Jacobson further explains”; cites Jacobson p. 14. Jacobson’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Lee’s 2006 “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” uses Gabaccia’s From the Other Side (1994) on gendered exclusion.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 11: “As Donna Gabaccia explains”; cites Gabaccia p. 37. Gabaccia’s book unread.

edges.relationship: In “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” (2006), Lee sets the argument that Chinese exclusion made the United States a gatekeeping nation against earlier historians, citing Higham’s Strangers in the Land (1955; cited in the 1978 edition), who treated anti-Asian movements as “historically tangential” to American nativism and the 1920s as the decisive period of restriction.
edges.evidence_note: Manuscript p. 9, paragraph beginning “Some of our leading scholars,” and note 19, p. 28, explicitly identify Higham. Short phrase: “historically tangential.” Published text not read beyond extract; Higham unread. The critique concerns narrative placement, not his whole scholarship.

edges.relationship: According to its abstract, “The ‘Yellow Peril’ and Asian Exclusion in the Americas” (2007) examines Asian migration and exclusion across North and South America and the transnational nature of anti-Asian racism, as a contribution to the global history of race.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 537–538, 556–557: “hemispheric Orientalism.” Selected passages only; comparative national distinctions retained.

edges.relationship: In “A Nation of Immigrants and a Gatekeeping Nation” (2006), Lee uses Omi and Winant’s concept of racial formation to describe how late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century immigration debates and policies produced new understandings and definitions of race and racial categories.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 545 and conclusion p. 557: “I build upon Winant’s claim.” Winant’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Lee led the original #ImmigrationSyllabus (2017), a collaborative resource explaining immigration history for teachers, students and the public.
edges.evidence_note: 2017 Libraries article, opening description and organizers; current About page, original-project credits. Later 2026 revision has separate leadership.

edges.relationship: In ‘America First, Immigrants Last: American Xenophobia Then and Now’ (delivered 2018; published 2019–20), Erika Lee argued for a more expansive definition of xenophobia as a constant, adaptable force in U.S. history, against the view that it peaked in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era and receded after the 1965 Immigration Act.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete editorial on Cambridge Core. Genetin-Pilawa and Cothran identify Lee’s intervention in the periodization and definition of xenophobia, including her challenge to the interpretation of 1965 as a turning point away from exclusion. Also read Lee’s publisher abstract and publication metadata: the abstract explicitly connects xenophobia with progressive reform and the expansion of state capacity. Her article body remains unread. This is a field contribution supported by the editorial and abstract, not a claim that the editors adopted Lee’s framework in their own research. Mapping to political history is an editorial classification of the specified argument about policy and power.

edges.relationship: Through Immigrant Stories (launched in 2013), Erika Lee helped connect immigration history with digital humanities by developing a collaborative project that lets immigrants and refugees create digital accounts of migration for archival preservation.
edges.evidence_note: Read the Radcliffe institutional profile and the IHRC’s project account. The profile names Lee’s role in launching Immigrant Stories and describes its multilingual storytelling website. The project account supplies the original 2013 launch date, participant control over the form and content of stories, video creation, and preservation and discovery through library collections. Credit remains collaborative: the IHRC launched the project, and Lee is not represented as its sole creator or software developer. This edge records digital creation and preservation of historical evidence; the input already records her public-history contribution. No individual participant narrative was opened or quoted.

edges.relationship: The ANU synopsis of Strange’s 2024 remembrance identifies Davis’s Fiction in the Archives (originally 1987) as a major influence on Strange’s career.
edges.evidence_note: ANU event notice, 27 March 2024, Strange abstract, first paragraph: “the greater impact on Strange’s career.” This is the seminar synopsis, not a reading of the lecture. The notice gives 1990 without identifying an edition; 1987 is retained from existing source nzd_fiction_1987. No new interpretation of Davis’s book is asserted.
edges.map_label: Fiction in the Archives as a career influence

edges.relationship: Sangster’s 2011 introduction identifies Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) as a conscious use of Foucault to study the discourses regulating women.
edges.evidence_note: Sangster, Through Feminist Eyes (2011), introduction, printed 26 (PDF page 34), with note 104 at 46 (PDF page 54): “drew consciously on Foucault.” Named-reader attribution; Toronto’s introduction was available only as a short JSTOR opening. No particular Foucault text or sole intellectual origin established.

edges.relationship: In “Discovering Women’s History” (2011), Sangster credits Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) with reinterpreting the medical testimony she had used for the 1907 Bell Telephone strike.
edges.evidence_note: Sangster, printed 50 (PDF page 58), paragraph beginning At the time; note 3 at 52 identifies the 1995 book. She credits “new analytical tools” for explaining medical knowledge as social power. This is Sangster’s 2011 retrospective recognition, not a claim that Strange influenced Sangster’s earlier strike article. Original monograph unread in full.
edges.map_label: Sangster credits a revised reading of medical testimony

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio asks whether the spatial account in Strange’s Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995), discussed alongside Dubinsky, gives sufficient attention to sexual expression within the parental home.
edges.evidence_note: Comacchio, printed 193–194 (PDF pages 27–28), paragraph beginning Engaging this concept and its continuation before The Second Greatest Disappointment: “truly limited to public spaces.” A qualified question about both books, not rejection of Strange’s argument. Her text’s 1993 date for Strange is corrected using the publisher’s 1995 metadata; full essay and books unread.
edges.map_label: Questions the emphasis on public sexual spaces

edges.relationship: Making Good (1997), coauthored with Tina Loo, explains law and moral regulation as a struggle over Canadian citizenship, in Tom Mitchell’s review.
edges.evidence_note: Mitchell, Making Good discussion, opening three substantive paragraphs: “site of struggle.” Read as a named reviewer’s account; original book unread. Existing moral_regulation roster already lists Strange and is preserved. Existing field links edge_858, edge_862 and edge_964 do not supply this person’s endpoint relationship.

edges.relationship: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) shows young wage-earning women in Toronto becoming a focus of anxieties about industrialization and female sexuality, whom social agencies sought to protect and the city's Morality Department sought to control, a mixture of paternalism and suspicion.
edges.evidence_note: Rebased on Rebecca Murdock’s complete CBRA review, review opening paragraph, and Joan Sangster, Through Feminist Eyes (2011), introduction, paragraph beginning “Carolyn Strange’s positioning” and note 104. Murdock supports the industrialization, sexuality, social-agency and Morality Department claims; Sangster locates the book’s analysis of regulation in Canadian feminist historiography. Earlier publisher and book references remain bibliographic context; neither is claimed as freshly read in full.
edges.map_label: Working women and the urban girl problem

edges.relationship: Honour, Violence and Emotions in History (2014), coedited with Robert Cribb and Christopher E. Forth, brings historically specific emotions into the comparative study of honour and violence.
edges.evidence_note: Bloomsbury publisher description, first two paragraphs, editor byline and contents chapter 1/afterword; phrases “historically specific understandings” and “history of honour and violence.” Publisher-level statement of the collection’s program, with all editors credited. Chapters unread; this does not establish Strange’s adoption of any particular theorist of emotion.
edges.map_label: Honour, violence and historically specific feeling

edges.relationship: In Manly Militants, Cohesive Communities, and Defiant Domestics (1995), Franca Iacovetta praises Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) for integrating class, race and gender in its analysis of urban wage-earning women, presenting it as an example in her argument for more integrative historical scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Selected journal PDF text read, especially pp. 248–251. This is an evaluative literature survey, not a standalone book review or a stated intellectual debt. The body explicitly assesses Strange’s analytical method; the edge records positive reception as an undirected comparison.
edges.map_label: Commends integrated class, race and gender analysis

edges.relationship: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) contributes a feminist perspective to urban history by relating young women’s work, leisure and public presence to Toronto’s industrial transformation and the discourses that treated working women as a moral problem, as its 1996 Urban History review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher’s first-page image visually read. Only p. 270 was available; the continuation, signature and original book remain unread. Reviewer authorship is left unresolved because the landing-page byline combines multiple names. The field assessment is explicit on the page.
edges.map_label: Feminist interpretation of the industrial city

edges.relationship: Stories of Their Lives: The Historian and the Capital Case File (1998) contributes to interpreting archives as constructed records of power by examining how officials turned competing voices into authoritative case narratives, an approach Alison Frank Johnson and Robert Nemes apply in Beyond the Verdict (2025).
edges.evidence_note: Selected publisher article passages and notes 40, 82 and 91 read; original chapter unread. Field mapping is editorial, limited to document construction and official authority. Both later authors lack eligible person endpoints, so no person edges are proposed. The article first appeared online in 2025; its volume is dated 2026.
edges.map_label: Capital case files as constructions of authority

edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger draws on Shapin's A Social History of Truth (1994) to explain how women in seventeenth-century England lacked standing in the economy of civility that guaranteed experimental truth, with Boyle as the ideal 'modest witness'.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF of “The Philosopher’s Beard” (2003), printed p. 195 (PDF leaf 12), paragraph beginning Other scholars have located the gendering of science, and n. 25. The body summarizes and uses Shapin’s account of women’s lack of standing in the economy of civility that guaranteed experimental truth; the following sentence identifies Boyle as the ideal modest witness. Note 25 cites A Social History of Truth (1994). This replaces the stale locator for a different chapter. Shapin’s book remains unread.

edges.relationship: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) connected women’s institutional exclusion with the gendering of scientific knowledge, a programme Schiebinger described in her 2024 Cell interview.
edges.evidence_note: Interview, first answer, paragraphs beginning “When I began the project” and “Beginning with my doctoral dissertation.” Author’s retrospective; book unread.

edges.relationship: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) recovered women’s scientific activity that histories of the scientific revolution had overlooked.
edges.evidence_note: Interview, first answer, paragraph beginning “The deciding point came around 1981.” Claim limited to the research intervention described by the author.

edges.relationship: Nature’s Body (1993) examines how assumptions about gender, sex and race shaped scientific explanations of nature.
edges.evidence_note: Rutgers publisher description, final paragraph, and contents; “assumptions about gender, sex, and race.” Description only; 2004 reissue distinguished from 1993 original.
edges.map_label: Gender and race in explanations of nature

edges.relationship: “Feminist History of Colonial Science” (2004) brings gender analysis to selective collecting and unequal knowledge transfer between Europe and its colonies.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, first two sentences: “selective collecting practices.” Editorial contribution to the imperial-knowledge field; no claimed debt to Said or Spivak. Article body unread.

edges.relationship: “Medical Experimentation and Race in the Eighteenth-century Atlantic World” (2013) studies the tension between racial differentiation and assumptions of interchangeable bodies in medical trials.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences 3–6: “required that human bodies be fully interchangeable.” Abstract only; no generalization to all experiments or periods.

edges.relationship: In his H-Atlantic review (2006) of Plants and Empire (2004), McNeill found the book's central argument, that knowledge of the peacock flower's abortifacient use did not travel from the Caribbean to Europe, 'interesting if not ... altogether convincing', and judged its conclusion not fully consistent with its earlier denial that the knowledge was suppressed.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review (10 paragraphs), John R. McNeill, 'One Plant and Several Scientists', H-Atlantic, H-Net Reviews, February 2006, in an Internet Archive capture of the H-Net page (capture 20150920135053) held in the project's H-Net review corpus; the live H-Net page returned 403 to the fetch tool. Paragraph 5 ('Among those abortifacients...'): 'I hoped for more explanation of that fact than the chapter provided.' Paragraph 7 ('In the conclusion (chapter 6)...'): the hypotheses are 'interesting and plausible, but not fully consonant with this earlier position', citing Schiebinger pp. 153 and 238. Paragraph 8 ('Of course, there may have been other inhibitions...') offers an alternative explanation (cost of a tropical plant, other abortion methods) and labels it 'a mere hypothesis'. Paragraph 10 ('This is a work in the history of science...'): 'makes an interesting if not, to my mind, altogether convincing case'. The review also praises the book ('an entertaining book that raises some interesting questions', paragraph 1). Plants and Empire itself unread; the edge records McNeill's assessment only.

edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger describes the eighteenth-century revolution in sexual science as marked by what Laqueur, in Making Sex (1990), called a shift from a one-sex to a two-sex model of difference, and points readers to Park and Nye's critical evaluation of his work.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF of the chapter (Cambridge History of Science, vol. 4, pp. 184-210).
