Body text, section 'The Science of Woman', PDF p. 14 (printed p. 197, inferred from the file's page range because the PDF's numerals do not extract): 'The revolution in sexual science was also marked by what Thomas Laqueur has described as a shift from a one-sex to a two-sex model of difference.' The following paragraph sets out the two models in her own words. Note 34 (printed p. 198) cites Making Sex and adds 'See also the critical evaluation of Laqueur's work by Katharine Park and Robert Nye'. This is body-text adoption of Laqueur's framework, not a footnote citation. Independently, Michael Stolberg's author abstract (Isis 94, 2003, read at PubMed 12879558) treats the claim as 'Thomas Laqueur's and Londa Schiebinger's influential claim'; that pairing corroborates the shared position but is not used as the basis of this edge. Making Sex itself unread. The held ls_w_03 (Laqueur drew on Schiebinger, the opposite direction) remains unverified and is not restored.

edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger presents Merchant's The Death of Nature (1980) as a classic explanation of the gendering of science and holds that Merchant 'rightly called attention' to the gendering of nature as female, while noting the criticism that the book reinforced the association of women with nature.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF, section '"Learned Venuses," "Austere Minervas," and "Homosocial Brotherhoods"', PDF p. 10 (printed p. 193, inferred from the file's page range), paragraph beginning 'Scholars have explained the gendering of science in different ways': 'In her classic [1980] Death of Nature, Carolyn Merchant revealed how the rise of a mechanistic worldview entailed the "death of nature."' The paragraph summarises Merchant's argument about Bacon's rhetoric and closes: 'Although roundly criticized for reinforcing the traditional notion that women belong to nature in ways that men do not, Merchant rightly called attention to the adamant gendering of nature as female in both ancient and modern science traditions.' Note 22 cites The Death of Nature. The year numeral does not extract from the PDF text layer; 1980 is the book's known original date and matches the graph's Merchant node. This answers the earlier held lead (Signs 2003 introduction unread) with a different, read passage. The Death of Nature itself unread here.

edges.relationship: Schiebinger's Gendered Innovations project (begun 2009) extended sex and gender analysis in research design to intersectional analysis, crediting the term to Crenshaw (1989), as she explains in her 2024 Cell interview.
edges.evidence_note: Stanford History reprint of the Cell Q&A (14 March 2024), already the source of ls_w_04. Answer to 'What is "Gendered Innovations?"': 'In 2009, when we started, "Gendered Innovations" was the right term; we have now expanded to include intersectional innovations', and the project's goal is 'to provide scientists and engineers with practical methods for sex, gender, and intersectional analysis.' Answer to 'What about intersectional analyses?': 'The term was coined in 1989 by legal scholar Kimberle Crenshaw', followed by the Gender Shades example; 'It's the intersectional analysis that most interests me'. Answer on journals: 'A group of us are now working on producing a similar set of author and editor guidelines for intersectionality.' Retrospective self-account of a current project; Gendered Innovations publications not separately read. Applies intersectional analysis to science and engineering research; no claim that she shaped the concept itself.

edges.relationship: In Secret Cures of Slaves: People, Plants, and Medicine in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World (2017), Schiebinger contributes to Atlantic history by reconstructing medical knowledge’s circulation and obstruction within the Caribbean and between the Caribbean, Europe and West Africa, as Helen Bynum’s review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Read Bynum’s complete review on the journal publisher’s site. It describes an integrated account of Atlantic medical exchange and maps showing its direction and interruptions. The field contribution is supported through this review; the book itself remains unread. No claim about particular transmitted remedies is proposed.

edges.relationship: Burbank and Cooper coauthored Empires in World History (2010), comparing imperial strategies for ruling diverse populations.
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR authorship/copyright and book description; NYU bibliography corroborates. Coauthorship only: joint argument retained, full book unread.

edges.relationship: In A Search for Sovereignty (2010), Benton credits Burbank and Cooper jointly with sharing ideas about imperial political imagination.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher front matter, printed xiv, paragraph beginning The NYU History Department: “generously shared their ideas” about “imperial political imagination.” Specific intellectual exchange; no sole origin or full-book debt asserted. Later chapters unread.

edges.relationship: Tony Ballantyne’s 2014 review reads Burbank and Cooper’s Empires in World History (2010) as confirming Bayly’s Imperial Meridian on the connection between weakening Muslim empires and European maritime ascendancy.
edges.evidence_note: Empires in History section, paragraph beginning The growing ability of Europeans, and note 10: “confirm the outlines.” Reader-mediated agreement, not demonstrated influence or personal contact. Both monographs unread in full.

edges.relationship: Empires in World History (2010), coauthored with Cooper, explains political possibilities through comparisons and interactions among empires rather than an inevitable transition to nation-states.
edges.evidence_note: Everill review, opening, chapter-one discussion and concluding evaluation: “repertoires of power.” Her limited-Eurasian-coverage criticism remains explicit; full book unread.

edges.relationship: In the interview Paysans et intellectuels en Russie (1999), Burbank proposes studying rural people’s changing experiences instead of assuming an isolated, timeless peasantry.
edges.evidence_note: Burbank’s answers, pp. 173–176: “individualize the experience” (174). Contribution to social-history questions, not membership in a unified school. Complete interview read; cited studies unread.

edges.relationship: In Insult and Punishment in Rural Courts (1999), Burbank argues that rural litigation connected villagers to state authority and helped produce a civic ideal.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary pp. 165–166, especially final paragraph: “a civic ideal.” Institutional participation is not equated with loyalty to autocracy; middle case analyses unread.

edges.relationship: Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) combines close reading of cases with statistical evidence to reconstruct rural legal practice, as Gregory L. Freeze’s review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Freeze, displayed extract, first paragraph, p. 1284: “statistical data set.” A methodological contribution, not a claim of cliometric affiliation; full book unread.

edges.relationship: Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper's Empires in World History (2010) contributes to nationalism studies by challenging the inevitability of the nation-state, an argument Eric T. Jennings takes up in ‘The French Empire’ (2023) to reconsider how nations and empires developed together.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's displayed Summary and Further Reading, not the restricted chapter body. The Summary explicitly names both authors, explains their challenge to national inevitability, and uses it to frame the chapter's investigation of French imperial nationalism and federal alternatives. This supports a bounded contribution to nationalism studies; the mapping to that existing field node is editorial. Jennings has no endpoint in the supplied lists, so no personal edge is proposed. Cooper retains equal credit. Everill's complete review was also read and independently confirms the book's challenge to an automatic empire-to-nation transition, while criticizing its conceptual distinction between those forms.

edges.relationship: Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper's Post-Imperial Possibilities: Eurasia, Eurafrica, Afroasia (2023) contributes to intellectual history by examining Eurasia, Eurafrica and Afroasia as political projects for reorganizing the world beyond existing empires and nation-states.
edges.evidence_note: Read Puri's displayed publisher Extract only, not the full review or book. It explains each of the three projects and expressly distinguishes the history of ideas from their partial practical realization. Also read Sergey Glebov's displayed AHR review Extract, which describes alternatives beyond national sovereignty and identifies the original Princeton publication as 2023. Puri reviews a 2024 edition; the relationship retains the original year. The field classification is an editorial mapping of the explicitly described intellectual projects, not a claim that either reviewer uses the precise field label. Both coauthors are credited; neither reviewer has a supplied endpoint.

edges.relationship: In Learning the Scholar’s Craft (2021), MacMillan acknowledges Tuchman’s influence; note 1 identifies The Zimmermann Telegram (1958) and The Proud Tower (1966).
edges.evidence_note: Essay paragraph beginning Yet all the time: “a huge influence”; note 1 names both works. Neither Tuchman book read here; no specific doctrine or exclusive influence asserted.

edges.relationship: In War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020), MacMillan quotes Tilly’s formula that war made the state and the state made war, according to Anthony Wilson-Smith’s review.
edges.evidence_note: Wilson-Smith’s review reports a quotation of Tilly; it does not establish adoption of Tilly’s wider account. The publisher preview consulted here does not contain the Tilly passage. Retain counts_toward_floor=false.
edges.map_label: Reported quotation of Tilly on war and the state

edges.relationship: Reviewing Canada and NATO: Uneasy Past, Uncertain Future (1990), jointly edited by MacMillan and David S. Sorenson, Granatstein recommends the collection while finding some essays overtaken by events.
edges.evidence_note: Complete CBRA Review section and Contributor header: “a very good book”, qualified by intervening events. This is reception of a jointly edited volume, not praise of every MacMillan argument; the reviewer singles out Halstead, English and Bercuson. Book body unread; review date unspecified.

edges.relationship: Women of the Raj (1988) contributed a study of British women in colonial India to the expanding field of women’s history, as MacMillan explains in Learning the Scholar’s Craft (2021).
edges.evidence_note: Essay paragraph beginning Because Ryerson, with note 4: “women’s history” and the decision to write about British women in India. First-person field positioning; no claim about Indian women’s perspectives or a full gender theory. Monograph unread.

edges.relationship: Peacemakers (2001; US title Paris 1919, 2002) reconsiders diplomatic responsibility for the postwar settlement and contests treating the negotiators as scapegoats for subsequent failures.
edges.evidence_note: Hachette description, final paragraph: “unfairly been made scapegoats”; Oxford research statement, final paragraph, balances individuals and wider forces. Publisher-mediated account of the argument; full book unread. Original and reissue years separated.

edges.relationship: The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; US title Dangerous Games, 2009) examines how remembered pasts help construct identities and sustain political claims.
edges.evidence_note: Leonard interview, answer to Why is this so fraught: “history is a very important part of identity”. Publisher excerpt, The History Craze, paragraphs on heritage and collective attachments. Remembered identity is distinguished from the public-institution edge below; complete book unread.

edges.relationship: In The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; Dangerous Games, 2009), MacMillan examines how museums, heritage policy and popular media shape public encounters with the past.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, chapter 1, from Museums and art galleries through the heritage-policy examples: “Governments tend to assume”. Specific sites of public interpretation, rather than institutional membership or influence on every public historian. Displayed excerpt read; remaining book unread.

edges.relationship: In The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; Dangerous Games, 2009), MacMillan disputes the claim that experiencing an event gives someone superior historical understanding.
edges.evidence_note: Leonard interview, questions/answers from Being there through the Cuban Missile Crisis discussion: eyewitnesses “only know a small part of the picture”. She calls for wider evidence. This is a limited epistemological intervention, not an argument against using testimony; book read only in separate excerpt.

edges.relationship: War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020) argues that war and human society are so deeply intertwined that the capacity to make war and the evolution of society are part of the same story.
edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher PDF preview, introduction pp. 1–5: “War is not an aberration” (p. 2); reciprocal war/society argument pp. 4–5. Selected first-chapter publisher excerpt also read. Full book unread. Scheidel’s named criticism remains in entry prose; no community knowledge reproduced.

edges.relationship: In her review essay “Von Hötzendorff’s Desire” (2004), MacMillan challenges Ferguson’s suggestion that Britain might have been wiser to stay out of the First World War, questioning the consequences of a quick German victory in light of German expansionism and occupation practices.
edges.evidence_note: The complete publisher-hosted 2004 review of David Stevenson’s Cataclysm was read. The paragraph naming Ferguson asks what a quick German victory would have entailed, then discusses the character of imperial Germany and German atrocities, exploitation and destruction in occupied Belgium and France. This is direct engagement with a named argument, not an inference from shared subject matter. The review does not identify a Ferguson book title; no particular Ferguson monograph is attributed or claimed read. The critic points toward the position criticized.
edges.map_label: Challenges the case for British non-intervention

edges.relationship: In her 2016 review of History’s People: Personalities and the Past (2015), Joanna Bourke endorses MacMillan’s argument for individual choices and actions in historical explanation, interpreting its counterfactual questions as devices for understanding what actually happened.
edges.evidence_note: Full review read in the 21 March 2016 capture of the magazine’s own page. Bourke distinguishes her general dislike of counterfactual history from her favourable assessment of this book. This records substantive review reception, without inferring intellectual debt. The original book’s 2015 publication is checked separately with House of Anansi; the review discusses the British edition. Joanna Bourke is an existing person endpoint.

edges.relationship: History’s People: Personalities and the Past (2015) contributes to biography and life writing by using the lives of historical actors and observers to examine individual agency and the recording of everyday experience, as the Publishers Weekly review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Complete review read on the review journal’s own site. It discusses the book’s structure and its treatment of diarists, rather than merely listing subjects. House of Anansi separately dates the original publication to 2015 and explicitly identifies the relationship between biography and history as the book’s subject. The book itself was not read; no wider influence on biographers is asserted.

edges.relationship: Women of the Raj (1988) contributed an early account of British women’s gender disadvantage under empire; Indrani Sen’s Gendered Transactions (2017) places it in a phase that portrayed the memsahib as a victim of a male-dominated colonial enterprise, before later scholarship more fully examined women’s simultaneous colonial privileges.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction, especially pp. 1–3 and note 2. The sample is linked directly from Manchester University Press’s book page. Sen identifies MacMillan’s place in the historiography and qualifies the earlier victim-centred approach against later gender-and-empire studies. This edge retains that limitation and does not credit MacMillan with those later analyses. It adds the gender-history endpoint; the input’s separate women’s-history pair is retained without duplication. Sen is absent from the allowed person endpoints, so no Sen–MacMillan edge is proposed.

edges.relationship: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Vickery endorses key points of Kerber’s 1988 criticism while retaining a stronger focus on social and economic behaviour.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge displayed note 14: “My argument endorses Kerber’s at certain key points.” Note read; article body and Kerber original unread in this dossier.

edges.relationship: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Vickery criticizes Davidoff and Hall’s Family Fortunes (1987) for neglecting the gentry; Clark identifies that book as a target of The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Primary reading is restricted to the substantive authorial comment in Cambridge’s displayed note 53; the article body, including pp. 393–401, was not freshly read. This supports the narrower gentry criticism. Clark’s review, paragraphs beginning “Vickery’s chief target” and “By demonstrating”, supports the 1998 engagement. These parallel edges retain both authors of one jointly authored book; they do not establish two independent exchanges.
edges.map_label: Questions Family Fortunes on the gentry

edges.relationship: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Vickery criticizes Davidoff and Hall’s Family Fortunes (1987) for neglecting the gentry; Clark identifies that book as a target of The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Primary reading is restricted to the substantive authorial comment in Cambridge’s displayed note 53; the article body, including pp. 393–401, was not freshly read. This supports the narrower gentry criticism. Clark’s review, paragraphs beginning “Vickery’s chief target” and “By demonstrating”, supports the 1998 engagement. These parallel edges retain both authors of one jointly authored book; they do not establish two independent exchanges.
edges.map_label: Questions Family Fortunes on the gentry

edges.relationship: Reviewing The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), Anna Clark praises its archival interpretation but argues that it caricatures feminist historiography and fails to establish a replacement paradigm.
edges.evidence_note: Clark review, lines 40, 51–58 and 90: “does not succeed”. Full review read; book unread.

edges.relationship: Clark identifies Vickery’s use of E. P. Thompson’s insight about outward deference and concealed resistance in The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Clark review, line 45: “citing E.P. Thompson’s insight”. Particular Thompson text unidentified; original passages unread.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Behind Closed Doors (2009), Berry compares Vickery’s treatment of British women’s crafts with Ulrich’s earlier intervention in early American historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Berry review, paragraph on chapter nine, browser lines 76–78. Ulrich is printed as “Laura Thatcher Ulrich”; resolved to this run’s Laurel Thatcher Ulrich. No Ulrich title named, no debt or collaboration claimed.
edges.map_label: A reviewer’s comparison of craft histories

edges.relationship: In her response concerning Behind Closed Doors (2009), Vickery questions the elite focus of an architectural-privacy narrative associated with Stone, Ariès, Girouard and Heyl.
edges.evidence_note: Author response, browser lines 107–113, especially 109: “the houses and privileges of a tiny elite”. Stone is one of four named exponents. His particular text is unidentified; no sole attribution or fresh Stone reading. Response timestamp inconsistent.

edges.relationship: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993) reopens women’s-history categories and chronologies by comparing recurring narratives of declining power.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge abstract, browser lines 451–453. Abstract and selected substantive notes read; full article body unavailable here. Existing women roster already names Vickery; this adds a direct edge, not a duplicate roster row.

edges.relationship: Berry places Behind Closed Doors (2009) within the historical turn to consumer behaviour and material culture, crediting its study of interiors and wallpaper with showing that consumer priorities were as much about rank and fortune as about gender.
edges.evidence_note: Berry review, browser lines 43–55, with book locators 3, 125, 259 and 299–304 reported by Berry. Those book pages not independently read. Existing consumption roster preserved.

edges.relationship: Reviewing The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), Linda Colley praises Vickery’s archival achievement but argues that her account of Georgian women’s lives sometimes becomes static and needs fuller consideration of political and social change.
edges.evidence_note: Read the review’s substantive text on the periodical’s own site. Colley values the book’s close archival work and treatment of household management and possessions, while questioning the extent of change in its narrative and asking how revolutions, war and class conflict affected its subjects. This records a qualified published criticism, not a claim that Colley rejected the book overall or derived her own research programme from it. The page’s bibliographical subtitle is inconsistent with the book’s title; the relationship uses The Gentleman’s Daughter, its unambiguous main title, and its original 1998 year.

edges.relationship: Vickery’s ‘Golden Age to Separate Spheres?’ (1993) contributed a critical examination of public and private spheres to gender history, a contribution explicitly identified by Jane Whittle and colleagues in The Experience of Work in Early Modern England (2025).
edges.evidence_note: Read section 3.5 and note 93 in the publisher’s open chapter. The authors explicitly attribute this conceptual contribution to Vickery, rather than merely including her in a collective reference. Their following discussion uses the scholarship to question assumptions about women’s work, domestic space and observation. The edge records the named contribution to gender history; it does not claim that Vickery founded the field. The original article’s publisher metadata confirms June 1993, distinct from its later online publication. The chapter’s authors are not eligible person endpoints in the supplied endpoint and run-member lists, so no person edges to them are proposed. The existing Vickery–women’s-history pair is preserved; this proposal addresses the separately existing gender-history node.

edges.relationship: Gabaccia and Franca Iacovetta co-edited Women, Gender, and Transnational Lives (2002) and coauthored, with Fraser Ottanelli, “Laboring Across National Borders” (2004).
edges.evidence_note: UTP/JSTOR book author and joint-introduction credits, pp. 3–42; RSA Journal p. 89 explicitly identifies the edited collection. Cambridge 2004 article author list and abstract checked. Collaboration is undirected; Ottanelli’s equal article credit is retained. Complete book and article bodies unread.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Dirk Hoerder’s chapter in A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), edited by Rosenberg, Gabaccia asks whether the volume’s essays on states, empire, trade and cultural exchange absorbed migration history; Rosenberg’s 2013 response acknowledges these possible missed opportunities.
edges.evidence_note: Gabaccia pp. 20–21, especially the final two paragraphs; Rosenberg p. 29 expressly summarizes the objection as “missed opportunities” for essays to address one another. A qualified critique of editorial integration alongside praise for the collection; no claim that Rosenberg wrote the other contributors’ essays. Original chapters unread.

edges.relationship: Foreign Relations (2012) connects migrants’ continuing transnational ties with U.S. diplomacy and trade, treating immigration as an enduring relationship between the United States and the wider world.
edges.evidence_note: Princeton University Press description: immigrants 'were not isolationists who cut ties to their countries of origin', and the book 'takes a comprehensive look at the links between American immigration and U.S. foreign relations' as 'a brand-new global history'; the quoted Choice notice frames it as 'trade relations'. Publisher-level reading; book body unread.
edges.map_label: Immigration and diplomacy in global history

edges.relationship: In Gender and International Migration (2015), Donato and Gabaccia argue that female migration has a long history and interpret changes in migrant gender composition through gender relations and political and economic conditions.
edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 1–2, publisher PDF: “feminization is not a recent development”; publisher date and coauthors checked. The field contribution is joint, and its claim is about the historical variability of gender composition, not proof from the unread empirical chapters.

edges.relationship: We Are What We Eat (1998) is a history of immigrant and ethnic eating in the United States, showing Americans’ long-term readiness to cross boundaries of taste and identity through food.
edges.evidence_note: Harvard publisher description displayed on JSTOR, paragraphs 1–3, read in full: marketplace as an “arena for defining and expressing ethnic identities”. Description supports this bounded contribution; book unread beyond displayed chapter openings.

edges.relationship: In “Laboring Across National Borders” (2004), Gabaccia, Iacovetta and Ottanelli use Italian labour migration to examine class, ethnicity and gender in the formation of modern national states.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge abstract, both paragraphs, and issue metadata: “transnational analysis of class, ethnicity, and gender”. Original print date 2004; 2005 is the online date. Joint argument and abstract-only reading retained; article body unread.

edges.relationship: In her 2013 H-Diplo review of Dirk Hoerder’s chapter in A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), Gabaccia compares Hoerder’s account of nationalism with the state-formation dynamics of Maier’s “Leviathan 2.0” in the same volume and asks how Maier would assess the significance of mass labour migrations for the state-building he describes.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Roundtable XIV-40 (15 July 2013), read in full on the H-Diplo/ISSF copy. Gabaccia review p. 20, paragraph beginning “But states also matter”: Hoerder’s distinction between earlier national consciousness and later chauvinism “invites comparison to the dynamics of state formation that are outlined in Charles S. Maier’s “Leviathan 2.0.”” p. 21, paragraph beginning “By calling attention to how effectively Hoerder’s account”: awareness of mobility in the essays on state, empire, trade and culture “requires greater thought”, then “How, for example, would Maier assess the significance of the mass labor migrations on the state-building dynamics that are his focus?” A qualified, named question about Maier’s chapter inside a review of Hoerder’s; she calls the volume “this very worthwhile collection”. Maier’s chapter unread; no claim that it ignores migration altogether. The p. 21 paragraph also supports gab_w_04 (to Rosenberg as editor); this edge rests on the Maier-specific sentences only.

edges.relationship: Introducing the 2013 H-Diplo roundtable on A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), Iriye, co-editor of the History of the World series, quotes Gabaccia’s question whether culture travels differently when mediated rather than carried by people, calls it of key importance for the volume, and extends her call for dialogue between histories of trade and migration to histories of the state, imperialism and global cultures.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Roundtable XIV-40, Introduction by Akira Iriye, pp. 3–4, paragraph beginning “Fourth, at the end of the spectrum from power-holders”: “as Donna Gabaccia points out, there are many ways of mass absorption into global culture”; quotes her question (“does culture travel differently when it is mediated …?”) and says “This is a fascinating question, which is of key importance for a volume like this”; quotes her call to “bring increasingly rich historiographies on trade and migration into a livelier and more extensive dialogue” and adds “To which we may add the historiographies on the modern state, on imperialism, and on global cultures.” Iriye introduces himself on p. 2 as co-editor, with Osterhammel, of the six-volume History of the World. An engaged response to her review, not a statement of debt either way; undirected comparison. Thin (one paragraph) but individualized: Iriye discusses each reviewer’s point separately.

edges.relationship: With Franca Iacovetta, Gabaccia edited Borders, Conflict Zones, and Memory: Scholarly Engagements with Luisa Passerini (a Women’s History Review special issue, 2016; book edition 2018), a tribute to Passerini’s scholarship that closes with a conversation co-authored by Passerini, Gabaccia and Iacovetta.
edges.evidence_note: Routledge publisher page read: editors Gabaccia and Iacovetta; description opens “This volume pays tribute to Luisa Passerini, whose scholarship has had a major impact on feminist and other scholars around the world” and states the book “was originally published as a special issue of Women's History Review”; contents list the editors’ introduction, Passerini’s “Response on Borders, Conflict Zones, and Memory”, and the final chapter, “‘Bodies Across Borders. Oral And Visual Memory in Europe and Beyond’ (BABE): a conversation with Luisa Passerini, Donna Gabaccia, and Franca Iacovetta”. DOI registration metadata (Crossref) gives the journal versions: introduction, Women’s History Review 25.3 (2016), 345–364 (doi:10.1080/09612025.2015.1071567); Passerini response, 447–457; conversation, 458–469 (doi:10.1080/09612025.2015.1071564, online November 2015), authors Passerini, Gabaccia, Iacovetta. The Taylor & Francis article pages returned 403 and the EUI repository record returned 403: the introduction, response and conversation bodies are unread. The claim is limited to the editing and joint authorship; no claim that Passerini influenced Gabaccia’s own work. Dating: special issue 2016 (online from late 2015), Routledge hardcover 2018; the 2017 date in the original lead is not used.

edges.relationship: In ‘A Long Atlantic in a Wider World’ (2004), Gabaccia urged greater engagement with literary and cultural scholarship in Atlantic history’s interdisciplinary dialogue, as William Boelhower explains in his 2016 assessment of Atlantic studies.
edges.evidence_note: Read Boelhower’s substantive account and bibliography on the publisher’s page. The supporting phrase is his quotation from Gabaccia. Her original article remains unread after its publisher page returned 403; no individual scholar’s debt is inferred.
edges.map_label: An interdisciplinary agenda for Atlantic history

edges.relationship: Rosenberg and Gary Gerstle coauthored America Transformed: A History of the United States Since 1900 (1999), with Norman L. Rosenberg.
edges.evidence_note: Sidney Sussex profile, Book publications, entry beginning “America Transformed”; History Matters, “Forum on Immigration & Ethnicity,” confirms the three authors and 1999. Bibliographic collaboration only; no claim of shared authorship of every passage or intellectual dependence. Full textbook unread.

edges.relationship: Rosenberg and James M. McPherson were among the coauthors of Liberty, Equality, Power: A History of the American People (1996), alongside John Murrin, Paul Johnson, Gary Gerstle and Norman Rosenberg.
edges.evidence_note: History Matters, Gerstle’s November 1999 “Forum on Immigration & Ethnicity” biography, sentence listing “Liberty, Equality, Power” and its six coauthors; Rosenberg’s December 2000 biography corroborates her credit. Names refer to the historian James McPherson. Original textbook unread; no attribution of particular chapters.

edges.relationship: In her 2013 response about A World Connecting (2012), Rosenberg defends a global history of uneven interactions and argues that connection can generate exclusion and conflict.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo XIV.40, Rosenberg pp. 30–32, especially response to Foster and Manela; “relational, co-productive, and nonsynchronous change.” Her own response read; the book’s chapters remain unread. No universal theory of all globalization is claimed.

edges.relationship: Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) examines U.S. lending and financial advising to less powerful nations, justified as extending 'civilization', and treats gender and race among the terms of that justification.
edges.evidence_note: JSTOR’s displayed opening of chapter 2, “The Roosevelt Corollary and the Dominican Model of 1905,” p. 31, names “race and manhood” among the conditions of dollar diplomacy; chapter 8 opening p. 219 names “masculine rationality.” Read in later Duke edition, copyright 2003. Full chapters and original 1999 edition unread; original date corroborated by Contemporary Authors.

edges.relationship: A Date Which Will Live: Pearl Harbor in American Memory (2003) examines competing public meanings of Pearl Harbor and their use in interpreting later events, including September 11.
edges.evidence_note: Duke publisher description, three paragraphs beginning with the date of the attack; specifically names movies, memorials, public ceremonies and competing political uses. Description read; book and complete reviews unread. A contribution to historical memory research, not a claim to have originated the field.

edges.relationship: In Spreading the American Dream (1982), as Rosenberg describes it in “Doing History” (2020), she wrote an interpretive history of the ideology of ‘free flow’ that joined trade and investment to communications, movies and consumerism, organised the interpretation around ‘liberal developmentalism’, and widened ‘American diplomacy’ to foreign relations carried by private-sector actors.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, “The Ideology of Liberal-Developmentalism,” five-feature definition and concluding paragraphs on promotional, cooperative and regulatory states. Author expressly limits this account to expansion’s American promoters rather than a complete assessment of its effects on other societies. Excerpt read; rest of book unread.

edges.relationship: In her H-Diplo essay “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg says that in her SHAFR presidential address, given after her election as president in 1997, she presented dollar diplomacy as part of a turn-of-the-century discourse of masculinity, “using discourse in the Foucauldian sense”.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (19 February 2020), Rosenberg’s own reflective essay, read in full on issforum.org. (1) Paragraph beginning “The actors in the drama of dollar diplomacy”: “I used my presidential address to suggest how this dollar diplomacy emerged as part of a turn-of-the-century discourse of masculinity (using discourse in the Foucauldian sense).” (2) Paragraph beginning “I began attending SHAFR conventions”: her cohort wanted the field to consider “theories related to discourse (Michel Foucault)”, with n. 8 citing Foucault’s The Order of Things (English ed. 1970). This is a stated methodological debt in her own words, tied to a named piece of her work. Limits: the presidential address itself (published in Diplomatic History) was not read; no claim is made about which Foucault texts shaped it beyond n. 8, and the claim does not extend to Financial Missionaries (1999) as a whole.

edges.relationship: In “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg recalls that Akira Iriye, after reading Spreading the American Dream (1982), promoted and taught the book, later collaborated with her on Pearl Harbor memory and on A World Connecting (2012), and was “the most generous of mentors”.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (2020), paragraph beginning “Chance #5 emerged after Spreading was published”: “That would change after Akira Iriye read Spreading and, without ever having met me, began promoting the book in all kinds of ways. He assigned it for years to successive classes at Harvard”; “Iriye and I would collaborate on two projects— one on Pearl Harbor in historical memory (resulting in my book A Date Which Will Live, 2003) and one reconceptualizing World History”; “One of the most influential historians of his generation, he was also the most generous of mentors.” A stated mentorship and collaboration in her own words. Same pair as the verified esr_w_02 (Iriye as general editor of the History of the World series), but a distinct and stronger claim; the coordinator may keep both, or fold esr_w_02 into this edge. It adds no new distinct partner. Rosenberg also says they “worked on parallel tracks” on cultural themes; no transfer of a specific argument is claimed.
edges.map_label: Iriye as promoter, collaborator and mentor

edges.relationship: In “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg says she gravitated in graduate school toward the New Left’s Wisconsin School of diplomatic history, identified centrally with its open-door interpretation, and built the thesis of Spreading the American Dream (1982) heavily on William Appleman Williams’s The Tragedy of American Diplomacy.
edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (2020). Paragraph beginning “The field of U.S. diplomatic history was, at that time, polarized”: “the so-called Wisconsin School of New Left historians (Williams A Williams, Walter LaFeber, Lloyd Gardner, and others)”; “I gravitated toward the New Left”; her “true academic mentors” were Williams, LaFeber, Barnet, Kolko and Marilyn Young (n. 2: “Especially influential were” Williams, Tragedy; LaFeber, New Empire; Barnet; Young). Paragraph beginning “With small children at home”, on Spreading: “Based on my own research, I now identified centrally with that position” (the open door); “This thesis leaned heavily on William A. Williams’s Tragedy of American Diplomacy, but bringing in the dimension of America’s enormous cultural influence”. The graph node newleft covers radical diplomatic history. None of the named Wisconsin School historians is an endpoint, so the debt is recorded as a field relationship, not a person edge. Self-description; the book itself remains unread beyond the original packet’s publisher excerpt.
edges.map_label: Wisconsin School open door, extended to culture

edges.relationship: In ‘How to Remember Pearl Harbor’ (2010), Mary L. Dudziak draws on Emily S. Rosenberg’s A Date Which Will Live: Pearl Harbor in American Memory (2003) to explain how remembering Pearl Harbor as the war’s beginning framed American military action as defensive, within Dudziak’s argument about the boundaries of wartime.
edges.evidence_note: Read Dudziak’s complete signed post on the blog where she published it, dated 6 December 2010. Two successive body paragraphs explicitly attribute the interpretation to Rosenberg; the first links to her book. Dudziak connects that interpretation with her own argument about war powers and the temporal framing of World War II. The closing note identifies the post as drawn from an in-progress chapter; this edge concerns the published 2010 post, not an unread final book. Duke University Press’s book page confirms Rosenberg’s title and original August 2003 publication. No supervision or general career influence is claimed.
edges.map_label: Pearl Harbor memory in Dudziak’s wartime argument

edges.relationship: In her introduction to Haunted by Empire (2006), editor Ann Laura Stoler summarizes Emily S. Rosenberg’s chapter ‘Ordering Others: U.S. Financial Advisers in the Early Twentieth Century’ as showing that circuits of knowledge production are remade by the individuals who travel them.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed preview’s preface and introductory chapter, especially printed pp. 16–18. On p. 18 Stoler names Rosenberg, explains her examination of financial advisers and imperial practices, and uses it to develop the account of knowledge circuits. The contents identify Rosenberg’s essay at p. 405; its body is outside this preview and remains unread. This is a narrow claim about Stoler’s explicit editorial engagement, not evidence that Rosenberg originated Stoler’s broader framework. Conservatively excluded from the floor under the editor–contributor ruling. Duke’s publisher page confirms the volume’s 2006 publication and sole volume editor, Stoler.

edges.relationship: Rosenberg’s contribution to A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012) brought histories of science into an integrated account with technology and culture, an achievement singled out by Michael Goebel’s 2013 review.
edges.evidence_note: Read the original English review on H-Soz-Kult. Goebel identifies Rosenberg’s own contribution, rather than attributing every chapter of the edited volume to her, and expressly praises its integration of these histories. He also finds its conclusion banal; this proposal preserves that qualification and makes no claim of unqualified acclaim or disciplinary founding. The review identifies the book’s original year as 2012. The chapter itself remains unread. Only one field edge is proposed for this integrated achievement.
edges.map_label: Science linked with technology and culture

edges.relationship: Connor’s 1997 review reads Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) as extending Scott’s relational analysis of gender.
edges.evidence_note: Connor, PDF p. 1, opening paragraph, explicitly names Scott and cites Morgan p. 9. A named reader's attribution; Morgan's introduction and the particular Scott text remain unread.
edges.map_label: Scott’s gender analysis, as Connor reads Morgan

edges.relationship: Connor (1997) attributes Morgan’s imagined middle-class community in Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) partly to Anderson.
edges.evidence_note: Connor, PDF p. 4, first paragraph, citing Morgan pp. 19–20. He names Anderson and Habermas together; their separate shares and particular works are unspecified. Book unread.

edges.relationship: Connor (1997) also identifies Habermas as a resource for Public Men and Virtuous Women’s (1996) account of class community.
edges.evidence_note: Same explicit joint attribution, Connor PDF p. 4, first paragraph. This is a reported resource, with no particular Habermas title or independently verified direct debt asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Old Ontario” (2000), Morgan finds Careless’s “limited identities” insufficiently attentive to domination and resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Primary PDF p. 8, paragraph beginning If anything, with n. 16 identifying Careless's 1969 essay. She calls the concept ‘fairly benign’ and proposes an additional settler-colony frame. The cited Careless essay itself was not newly read; this is her qualified assessment, not wholesale rejection.
edges.map_label: Questions the power analysis in “limited identities”

edges.relationship: Morgan’s “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010) praises McKay and Bates’s In the Province of History (2010) while questioning its omission of school textbooks.
edges.evidence_note: Primary review, para. 21: ‘school textbooks and readers’; paras. 22–23 retain praise and contextual comparison. Robin Bates shares the book's argument but lacks an eligible endpoint; no sole McKay authorship implied. Book unread independently.
edges.map_label: McKay and Bates: school readers omitted

edges.relationship: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) interprets gendered public and domestic authority as unstable, interconnected constructions in Upper Canada.
edges.evidence_note: UTP description, final two paragraphs: gender meanings varied by context and boundaries repeatedly failed. Publisher synopsis only for this book claim; Morgan's 2000 essay provides a separately read historiographical intervention.

edges.relationship: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) treats Upper Canadian Methodism, attacked by the colonial elite, as a religious arena where ideas of gender, race and class interacted with politics.
edges.evidence_note: UTP description, paragraphs on evangelical discourse and religion/politics in the 1840s. Connor's review pp. 2–3 was also read. This concerns gender and religious authority, not an asserted position in the later secularization debate.
edges.map_label: Gender in religion and colonial politics

edges.relationship: In “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010), Morgan asks memory historians to connect reception, classroom transmission and individual choices about commemoration.
edges.evidence_note: Primary review, paras. 21–23. Her school-textbook objection and closing emphasis on choices about remembrance supply the claim. Reviewing two monographs does not establish a complete theory of collective memory or the founding of the field.
edges.map_label: Reception, schooling and individual choices in memory

edges.relationship: “Old Ontario” (2000) proposes studying Ontario as a white settler colony, connecting gendered power to national and imperial processes.
edges.evidence_note: Primary PDF pp. 8–9, concluding paragraphs after the Careless discussion. The proposal extends analysis beyond conventional colonial institutions while preserving differences among colonies. No adoption of Wolfe's theory or membership in a later school is inferred; no community knowledge is reproduced.
edges.map_label: A settler-colony frame for Ontario feminist history

edges.relationship: Reviewing Cecilia Morgan’s Travellers through Empire (2017), J. R. Miller (2018) argues that its emphasis on gender and racial identity underestimates the practical purposes of many of the people whose journeys it examines.
edges.evidence_note: Read Miller’s review on pp. 122–124, distinguishing its beginning from the preceding review on p. 122. Miller praises the research and analysis but disputes the relative emphasis placed on identity and practical purposes. This edge records his qualified criticism, not an unqualified rejection. Morgan’s book was not read. The claim concerns published historical interpretation only; no community knowledge or biographical details of the book’s subjects are reproduced.
edges.map_label: Questions the weighting of gender, identity and practical purposes

edges.relationship: In Heroines and History (2002), coauthored with Colin M. Coates, Cecilia Morgan contributes to Canadian cultural history through literary analysis of historical narratives about Laura Secord, a method Renée Hulan’s 2005 review essay identifies as productive cooperation between literary criticism and historical research.
edges.evidence_note: Read Hulan’s journal-hosted essay, particularly its sustained discussion of Heroines and History in paragraphs 16–19. Paragraph 16 distinguishes Morgan’s narrative analysis from Coates’s section; paragraph 19 discusses historical difference and the contextual interpretation of commemorative writing. The mapping to English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history is editorial and limited to this named methodological contribution. Hulan has no eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed. The coauthored book itself was not read.
edges.map_label: Literary analysis of Canadian historical narratives

edges.relationship: Cecilia Morgan’s Commemorating Canada (2016) provides an account of labour’s marginal place in public commemoration and a warning against celebratory simplification that Janis Thiessen applies in “Remembering 1919: The Winnipeg General Strike” (2020).
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s HTML research note, with particular attention to the introductory framing, concluding discussion and notes 17–19 and 56. Thiessen uses Morgan in the body to contextualize labour commemoration and to qualify celebratory accounts of the strike. Notes 18–19 identify Commemorating Canada, pp. 102 and 164; note 56 identifies p. 184. The edge records a specific resource used within Canadian working-class history. Thiessen has no eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed. Morgan’s book was not read. No interview quotations or family histories are reproduced.
edges.map_label: A resource for analysing labour commemoration

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Parr’s The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) to explain why women’s importance to family earnings did not necessarily give them equal household authority.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 199–200 and n. 59. Comacchio explains Parr’s challenge to ‘binary opposites’, follows the two Ontario towns, and develops the implications of the gap between women’s economic roles and their familial power. Named constructive reception within Comacchio’s argument; no supervision, collaboration, exclusive influence or reciprocal endorsement asserted. Parr’s book was not independently read.

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Sangster’s Earning Respect (1995) to connect remembered respectability with working-class women’s family identities and subordination.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 189, paragraph beginning But, as Joan Sangster, with n. 41; also p. 188 n. 39. The substantive discussion praises Sangster’s critical handling of memory and uses her Peterborough study to explain how support networks could reproduce dependency. The phrase ‘neither entirely’ marks a qualified account of memory, not acceptance of recollection as transparent fact. Earning Respect and the separate 1994 oral-history essay remain unread.
edges.map_label: Sangster’s oral histories as an analytical resource

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio draws on Strong-Boag’s The New Day Recalled (1988) to explain how interwar media tied women’s opportunities and identities to domestic roles.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 196–197, especially p. 197 and n. 55. Comacchio calls Strong-Boag’s and Andrée Lévesque’s books ‘path-breaking life-course studies’, then distinguishes Strong-Boag’s analysis of family magazines, homemaking and consumption. Credit is limited to the named book’s use in this synthesis; Lévesque retains her own credit. No shared institutional affiliation or broad personal influence is inferred. The 1988 book remains unread.
edges.map_label: Strong-Boag’s life-course history in the family synthesis

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Ariès’s childhood history (1960; English translation 1962) to frame age as historically variable alongside class, gender and race, while reporting criticism of its narrow social evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 184–185, section ii opening and n. 34. Comacchio credits the international stimulus of Ariès’s book and adopts historical specificity as the premise for discussing age, while retaining the criticism of generalization from upper-class materials. The note distinguishes 1960 original publication from the cited 1962 English edition. This is bounded intellectual reception, not agreement with every Ariès thesis. Neither edition was read independently.
edges.map_label: Ariès’s historical childhood, with evidential limits

edges.relationship: The Dominion of Youth (2006) explains modern adolescence in Canada as a historical formation shaped by scientific ideas, national projects, institutions and young people’s changing relations with adults.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher description and contents on WLU Press’s book page, with the 2006 original-year metadata retained in graph source cdnsrc_comacchio_2006 (also corroborated by an indexed journal bibliography whose PDF fetch failed); no full-book reading. Comacchio’s own 2000 essay, pp. 184–187 and 219, already argues for age as an analytical category. The publisher page lists 2008 paperback and electronic editions; these are not treated as the first publication. Existing field prose and roster already name Comacchio; this proposal adds a person-entry relationship, not a duplicate roster row.

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio argues that demographic studies clarify family structures and economic adaptation but cannot by themselves reveal power, choices and relationships inside households.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 184, concluding paragraph of section II.i, following the Katz, Gossage and Canadian Families Project discussions. She explicitly affirms demographic research before identifying what numerical data cannot establish about unequal family members. ‘very little’ refers specifically to internal power dynamics. The target is the quantitative approach within this umbrella, not every form of family history or a rejection of demographic evidence.
edges.map_label: Limits of demographic inference about household power

edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio presents Nations Are Built of Babies (1993) as an analysis of scientific motherhood linking medical and state regulation of maternity to class and gender relations.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 186–187, first-person account beginning My own work, and n. 37. Comacchio names ‘social reproduction theory’ and explains her study’s relation to medical/state intervention, material constraints and national efficiency. The adjacent comparison with Katherine Arnup is credited separately. This establishes a specific contribution to women’s and gender history through the argument, not field membership inferred from subject or employer. The 1993 book remains unread.
edges.map_label: Scientific motherhood, state policy and social reproduction

edges.relationship: In ‘Mechanomorphosis: Science, Management, and “Human Machinery” in Industrial Canada, 1900–45’ (1998), Comacchio contributed to Canadian working-class history by connecting scientific management and industrial health with attempts to regulate workers’ bodies; Eric Strikwerda subsequently uses this analysis in his study of industrial nutrition (2019).
edges.evidence_note: Read Strikwerda’s journal-hosted HTML, especially the body discussion at the beginning of ‘Nutrition Science and the Industrial Body’ and its notes 15–17. This is substantive use: the body quotes Comacchio’s account of bodies and machines as components of industrial capitalism, and note 17 identifies pp. 41–42 of her 1998 article. Also read the original article’s opening pp. 35–38 and conclusion pp. 65–67 on the journal’s own PDF route. These passages connect labour discipline, medicine and bodily regulation, while the conclusion recognizes the limits of attempts to make workers function like machines. The edge records this specific contribution, not foundation of the field. Strikwerda is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed.
edges.map_label: Scientific management, industrial health and workers’ bodies

edges.relationship: In Labours Lost (2009), Steedman challenges Thompson’s account of servants’ resignation in “The Crime of Anonymity” (1975), emphasizing short service careers and inventive expressions of resentment.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 8–9: “not at all fatalistic about their future.” The cited Thompson chapter itself remains unread; this is Steedman’s explicit objection.

edges.relationship: In A Crooked Line (2005), Eley identifies reading Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) as important to his own encounter with changes in historical thinking.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher chapter 4, printed p. 173: “key part in my own encounter.” Read selected pp. 172–175 and 178–180; no claim about every aspect of Eley’s work.

edges.relationship: In “Inventing the ‘Traditional Working Class’” (2016), Lawrence develops Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) criticism of Young and Willmott’s treatment of mother–daughter relations.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge repository manuscript, p. 16, paragraph beginning “But even if,” and note 70 on manuscript p. 37: “guilt and resentment.” Lawrence adds interview evidence unavailable to Steedman; selected passage, not whole article, read.

edges.relationship: The abstract of “Why Clio doesn’t Care” (1992) presents Steedman’s argument that British women’s history constituted a politics through shared cultural and educational assumptions.
edges.evidence_note: Journal abstract, first two sentences: “a politics rather than a theoretical construct.” Body unread.

edges.relationship: The abstract of “Why Clio doesn’t Care” (1992) uses Steedman’s Margaret McMillan biography (1990) to examine the differing narrative conventions of biography, autobiography and history.
edges.evidence_note: Journal abstract, final two sentences on genre and public political lives. Full article and McMillan book unread.

edges.relationship: In Labours Lost (2009), Steedman proposes restoring waged domestic workers’ feelings and self-representations to histories of English social structure.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, p. 9: “move out of the big house.” A stated research programme, not verification of all the book’s cases.

edges.relationship: In “On the Doorstep” (2024), Steedman makes paid archival research and ownership of its products a central question for understanding how history is made.
edges.evidence_note: Complete institutional article, especially pp. 24–26: “Who does the work in the archive?” Her interpretation of Thompson–Dodd correspondence; underlying archive unread. Dust (2001) not freshly read.
edges.map_label: Who does and owns archival work?

edges.relationship: Eley’s A Crooked Line (2005) reads Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) as challenging the gendered working-class narrative offered by Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
edges.evidence_note: Eley, printed p. 173, “counter-counternarrative”; he says the challenge also re-enables Thompson’s narrative. Mediated assessment; Landscape body unread.
edges.map_label: Gendered limits of the class narrative

edges.relationship: In his review “Desire” (1986), Raymond Williams questions the theoretical development and reading behind the treatment of Marxism in Carolyn Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986), while endorsing its broader challenge.
edges.evidence_note: The complete review was read on the magazine’s own site. This paragraph criticises the theoretical treatment of Marxism; the next endorses the challenge to production-centred accounts of consciousness. The edge records a qualified criticism, not wholesale rejection.

edges.relationship: In the acknowledgments to Speaking with Vampires (2000), White credits Frederick Cooper with encouraging her to preserve the ambiguity of vampire stories and examine colonial relations of power and uncertainty.
edges.evidence_note: Primary acknowledgment, paragraph beginning This book was written, sentence naming Cooper: he encouraged her to let stories “remain ambiguous.” This is White’s explicit report of methodological advice to this project; it establishes neither supervision nor sole derivation. Cooper’s 2021 AHR comment supplies a separate first-person account of his engagement with her work, without extending this influence claim.

edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White uses Hayden White’s analogy between historian and psychiatrist to explain how historians rearrange testimony and authorize interpretations.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1, Translating Vampires, paragraph beginning It is with these varieties of vocabularies, sentence beginning Here Hayden White’s analogy; she calls the analogy “useful.” Read surrounding discussion of testimony, recoding and unequal power. Chapter 6, Evidence: Vampire Accusations, paragraph beginning Finding the single and note 52 also engage emplotment. His underlying essays remain unread; this is a specific use, not agreement with every aspect of narrative theory.

edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White proposes reading Foucault’s History of Sexuality for its account of speech and the management of subjects when interpreting gossip in African history.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 2, Gossip and Respectability, paragraphs beginning In the Western world and According to Foucault, with note 15 citing the 1978 English translation, pp. 23–31. White explicitly proposes an “Africanist reading”; the following paragraph tests the approach against gossip performance. This is a selective methodological resource, not a claim that her book applies Foucault’s entire account of sexuality. Foucault’s original French work (1976) and translation were not independently read here.

edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White uses Ginzburg’s attention to clues but questions whether a history derived solely from them is too linear for the invention and recurrence of gossip and rumour.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 2, Voices and Subjects, paragraph beginning Historicizing rumor and gossip and following paragraph beginning The clues and details, with note 48. The criticism is that clue-derived history may be “more linear” than these forms require. Chapter 6, note 53 explicitly preserves her debt to Ginzburg despite this criticism. Chapter 1, Translating Vampires also examines shared vocabularies in his witchcraft histories. Ginzburg’s works remain unread independently; this is a qualified criticism made by White, not a neutral verdict on his scholarship.

edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White places her treatment of oral and written evidence alongside Portelli’s The Death of Luigi Trastulli (1991) and The Battle of Valle Giulia (1997), crediting European oral historians with reaching this insight earlier.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1, Sources, paragraph beginning This book attempts to treat oral and written material, and its note 139 beginning Europeanists writing on oral history. The note explicitly names Portelli’s two books in support of the equal yet distinct treatment of these sources. Comparative positioning is documented; no personal contact, supervision or exclusive derivation claimed. Portelli’s books remain unread in this dossier. The note misspells Giulia; the existing graph’s publisher-checked title supplies the standard spelling.

edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White argues for using rumour and gossip as historical evidence in their own right, reading oral accounts alongside written sources and treating the negotiation of testimony as part of the evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1 opening; Truth in Vampires, Truth in Oral History, paragraph beginning But how well can oral historians; Sources, final three paragraphs; How to Read this Book, final paragraph. Read her dispute with neutral-interview prescriptions and her explicit retention of accuracy and chronology. The oral and written are “equal but distinct.” This is a claim about historical method, not verification of the events narrated in rumours. Book beyond selected passages unread.

edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home (1990) makes Nairobi women’s sex work, household strategies and economic agency central to African women’s history, as Pamela Scully and Corrie Decker explain in the AHR’s 2021 reappraisal discussion.
edges.evidence_note: AHR discussion: Corrie Decker, 5 January 2021, 12:56 am, paragraphs on economic and political change and classroom reception; Pamela Scully, 5 January 2021, 8:07 am, on women as workers and their historical agency. These are named scholars’ accounts of the book’s argument and teaching reception. Decker also questions its usefulness for her own research ethics questions; praise is not unanimous. The 1990 book is unread in full; no content of individual women’s oral narratives is reproduced.

edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home (1990) connects prostitution to household reproduction and the colonial wage economy, an intervention Frederick Cooper appraises in the AHR’s 2021 reappraisal discussion.
edges.evidence_note: AHR discussion: complete Fred Cooper contribution, 5 January 2021, 6:31 pm, especially paragraphs beginning For all her engagement and Her book made a splash. Cooper identifies political economy, social reproduction and the changing colonial state as specific arguments, and recalls publishing a precursor in Struggle for the City (1983). This is an attributed substantive reading of White’s book, not an independent reading of the book or its 1983 precursor.

edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) contributed to gender history by situating sexuality within economic and political change, as Corrie Decker explains in the AHR's 2021 reception discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Decker explicitly names the field contribution and explains its argument. This is substantive retrospective reception, not a contributor credit. Original book unread in full.
edges.map_label: Sexuality within economic and political change

edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) contributed to African urban history by showing cities as places of enjoyment and social experimentation, as Paul Ocobock explains in the AHR's 2021 reception discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Ocobock identifies a specific change in urban interpretation. Maddox's publisher extract independently identifies White's pioneering place in East African urban history, without naming a particular White title.

edges.relationship: McAlister’s 2021 remembrance identifies Said as an influence on Kaplan’s cultural study of imperialism, while describing The Anarchy of Empire (2002) as partly departing from Orientalism’s account of imperial coherence.
edges.evidence_note: Melani McAlister, Passport (January 2021), printed pp. 65–66: identifies Said as an influence and then qualifies Kaplan’s later relation to his model of imperial coherence. Both passages read in the society’s PDF. This is McAlister’s interpretation, not a direct reading of Kaplan’s or Said’s books; retain the Said → Kaplan influence edge with the departure explicit in its sentence.

edges.relationship: Manifest Domesticity (1998) made domesticity part of the explanation of U.S. imperial expansion, reading the home through its relation to the foreign as well as to men’s public sphere.
edges.evidence_note: Hoganson, H-Diplo, printed p. 10, paragraphs beginning Her 1998 essay and Although my own research, with note 19; corroborated by McAlister, Passport, p. 66, opening two paragraphs. These named scholarly readers explain the argument and its use in gender history. The 1998 original, pp. 581–606, remains unread; no claim to have checked its complete sequence of examples.

edges.relationship: In Left Alone with America (1993), Kaplan criticized the omission of U.S. empire from postcolonial studies and urged reading national culture through internal and external colonization together.
edges.evidence_note: Hoganson, H-Diplo, printed p. 9, paragraph beginning The publication of Cultures, specifically its account of Kaplan’s introduction. This is an explicitly attributed reading of the 1993 essay, pp. 3–21, not a full primary reading.
edges.map_label: Challenges the exclusion of U.S. empire

edges.relationship: In Commentary: Domesticating Foreign Policy (1994), Kaplan used cultural studies’ examination of disciplinary boundaries to question the separation of domestic and foreign relations in historical analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher-displayed extract, opening two paragraphs of p. 97, read: disciplines are ‘social constructions or representations’, and the symposium questions domestic/foreign separation. This is a methodological contribution mapped to New cultural history, not membership in a single school. Remaining pp. 98–105 unread; no position assigned to an unnamed symposium participant.
edges.map_label: Cultural analysis across domestic and foreign

edges.relationship: Stoler’s acknowledgments to Haunted by Empire (2006) credit Kaplan with helping plan the collection in spring 2002, while recording that Kaplan withdrew before publication.
edges.evidence_note: Authorized publisher preview, acknowledgments pp. xv–xvi (PDF pages 16–17): Stoler names Kaplan among those meeting at NYU to plan contributors and an organic exchange; p. xvi lists ‘some departed (Amy Kaplan)’. Intellectual planning collaboration explicitly documented. No coeditorship, coauthorship or chapter in the published volume claimed. Undirected collaborative connection; later published chapters unread.

edges.relationship: In Tense and Tender Ties (2001; read in its 2006 reprint), Stoler treats Kaplan’s three absences in Left Alone with America (1993) as illuminating an earlier historiography but qualifies their continuing scope in light of newer research.
edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2006 preview, pp. 26–27 (PDF pages 47–48), crosscurrents section: the earlier diagnosis was ‘instructive and productively disquieting’, but its ‘timely assessment was of another moment’. The following paragraph identifies subsequent research bridging those divisions. Qualified historiographical criticism, not denial of Kaplan’s earlier importance. Copyright leaf confirms original Journal of American History publication in December 2001; that original version not independently read.
edges.map_label: Qualifies the reach of the three absences

edges.relationship: In Revisiting Dollar Diplomacy: Narratives of Money and Manliness (1998), Emily S. Rosenberg drew on Kaplan and Donald E. Pease's Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as the cultural-history strand of her effort to bring economic history and cultural analysis together in studying U.S. foreign relations.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's indexed article text, including the methodological paragraph and note 6. The direct page open failed. This is a stated methodological resource, not a claim that Kaplan originated Rosenberg's research or supplied its empirical findings.
edges.map_label: Cultural analysis in the study of dollar diplomacy

edges.relationship: According to Alex Lubin’s welcome to the 2025 ASA meeting, Matthew Frye Jacobson’s 2012 ASA presidential address re-articulated the case Amy Kaplan made in her own presidential address, “Violent Belongings and the Question of Empire Today” (2003; published 2004), for thinking of the United States as an empire, while recognizing that empire had entered a different, neoliberal phase.
edges.evidence_note: Lubin explicitly describes Jacobson's continuation and revision of Kaplan's argument. Evidence is the association's retrospective account; Jacobson's complete address remains unread. The publisher excerpt of Brickhouse and Gillman's introduction, pp. 7–8, corroborates his turn to neoliberal empire but labels the conference year 2013; use the ASA's 2012 delivery date.

edges.relationship: Michael J. Hogan's The Next Big Thing: The Future of Diplomatic History in a Global Age (2004) identifies Kaplan and Donald E. Pease's Cultures of United States Imperialism (1993) as an early landmark in American studies' turn toward transnational and international inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's indexed article text and note 19; the direct page open failed. The field mapping records a named contribution to transnational inquiry, not the founding of global history or influence on every participant in that field.
edges.map_label: Imperial culture in the transnational turn

edges.relationship: In Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022), Edwards credits Jacquelyn Dowd Hall with sustained guidance of the manuscript through their writing group and with inspiring her historical writing.
edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments pp. xii–xiii, licensed preview: Hall’s group “read and reread” the project from proposals to manuscript; the following paragraph singles out Hall as a model for writing history. These are explicit scholarly and manuscript debts. No doctoral-supervision claim is inferred; remaining book chapters unread.

edges.relationship: In her 2022 AHA interview, Edwards identifies E. P. Thompson’s Whigs and Hunters (1975) as a favorite book that she repeatedly reads.
edges.evidence_note: AHA interview, question asking for a recommended book: “One of my favorite books” names Whigs and Hunters and refers to rereading it. This is deliberately limited to her stated reading and admiration, not agreement with any particular thesis or proof of direct derivation. Original year checked in Peluso’s review, p. 309; Thompson’s book itself unread.

edges.relationship: In Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000), Edwards brings Black and yeoman women into the center of southern women’s history while synthesizing research for a wider readership.
edges.evidence_note: Frisby review, opening statement of the book’s aim (quoting p. 2) and final substantive paragraph. Frisby praises this recovery while also criticizing gaps in domestic and family life beyond labor and law. Book read through this named reviewer only.
edges.map_label: Black and yeoman women at the center

edges.relationship: Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) explains how ideas about women’s and men’s household roles shaped political conflict during Reconstruction across racial and class divisions.
edges.evidence_note: Illinois Press, About the Book, both paragraphs: links household roles with groups’ understandings of public politics and extends the process beyond 1877. A substantive named framework, not a link based on the author’s faculty field classification. Publisher description only; full book unread.

edges.relationship: Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) connects textiles’ material qualities and legal standing to their use as property and economic resources by people with weak claims to rights.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–3 and 6–9 in the licensed preview: possession, exchange and material evidence connect textiles to economic participation. Scope is the book’s explicit intervention in material-culture history; it is not a claim of unrestricted property rights. Rest of book unread.
edges.map_label: Textiles as legally protected material resources

edges.relationship: Edwards’s essay on marriage, households and the politics of Reconstruction in North Carolina appeared in Jumpin’ Jim Crow (2000), the collection Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore co-edited with Jane Dailey and Bryant Simon.
edges.evidence_note: Two permitted witnesses. (1) Edwards’s 2023 Princeton vita, p. 3–4, under her 1996 Law and History Review article: “republished as ‘Marriage, Households, and the Politics of Reconstruction in North Carolina,’ in Glenda Gilmore, Jane Dailey, and Bryant Simon, eds., Race, Gender, and Politics in the New South, 1865-1980 (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2000), 7-27”. (2) Yale Black Studies page for Jumpin’ Jim Crow (Princeton, 2000): editors “Jane Dailey, Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore, Bryant Simon”; “In addition to the editors, the contributors are … Laura F. Edwards …”. The vita’s title is evidently a working title: same press, year and three editors, and Edwards is listed among Jumpin’ Jim Crow’s contributors. This is an editor–contributor link, the kind the coordinator accepted for dgw_w_03 (White’s Telling Histories). It is thin: one of twelve contributors besides the three editors, and no text says Gilmore shaped Edwards’s argument. Flag to the outside reviewers. Hall is also among the contributors, which gives Hall nothing new (Gilmore is already her partner).
edges.map_label: Essay in Gilmore’s co-edited Jumpin’ Jim Crow

edges.relationship: Edwards published “At the Threshold of the Plantation Household: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Southern Women’s History” (Mississippi Quarterly, 2012), an essay on Fox-Genovese’s place in southern women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Title-level evidence only. Princeton University research portal record: title, author Laura F. Edwards, Mississippi Quarterly 65:4 (September 2012), pp. 577–589, DOI 10.1353/mss.2012.0008; no abstract and no attached file. The article body (Project MUSE) returned a verification challenge to both the web tool and a plain request; it was not pursued, so the essay is unread. The relationship sentence says only what the title states: a whole essay whose subject is Fox-Genovese and southern women’s history. No argument, praise or critique is attributed. Hence comparison, undirected, and no critique typing. This is not the held lfe_w_05, which rested on a reviewer’s list in Frisby’s review of Scarlett. Verifier: hold if title-level evidence is below the bar; restore with fuller wording if the MUSE text can be read from another network.
edges.map_label: Essay on Fox-Genovese and southern women’s history

edges.relationship: Reviewing Dylan Penningroth's Before the Movement in 2024, Eric Foner writes that Penningroth's work builds on that of Laura Edwards and Martha S. Jones, who have expanded legal history to include the role of law in everyday life and argued that law is made also by people with limited representation in legislatures and courts.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the magazine’s own site. The paragraph beginning Penningroth insists that the standard narrative explicitly names Edwards and Martha S. Jones, then describes their argument about ordinary people creating law despite limited representation. This is substantive engagement with a specified argument, rather than a list of scholars sharing a topic. The relationship records Foner’s assessment, not an independently established debt on Penningroth’s part; no separate edge to Penningroth is proposed. Foner does not identify a particular Edwards book in this paragraph. Elsewhere in the review he dates Roll, Jordan, Roll to 1974, supporting the original year used in bf3_02.
edges.map_label: Foner places Edwards's everyday legal history

edges.relationship: In The People and Their Peace (2009), Edwards discusses the argument in Eugene Genovese’s Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974) that exceptions favoring individual enslaved people affirmed the underlying logic of the system.
edges.evidence_note: Limited primary-text evidence: read the Google Books search-within-volume excerpt for Genovese, result PA251 (printed p. 251), not the full page or chapter. The excerpt expressly attributes an argument to Genovese’s named book in body text. It continues into a qualification beginning But that logic and then cuts off; therefore this edge asserts discussion of the stated argument only, not Edwards’s agreement, intellectual debt, or the scope of her criticism. The full-page preview reported a viewing limit, which was respected. This is not a footnote citation or an acknowledgment. Publication of Edwards’s book in 2009 was separately checked on the UNC Press page; Foner’s 2024 review confirms Genovese’s original 1974 date. The restricted reading scope must remain attached to this edge at review.

edges.relationship: Laura F. Edwards's Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) contributes to the political history of Reconstruction by explaining how household gender roles shaped elite and poor, Black and white southerners' understandings of public life and their places in it.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's complete two-paragraph description and publication metadata.
