The following sentence explains how household roles shaped different groups' views of the public arena; the second paragraph describes Reconstruction as conflict and negotiation extending beyond 1877. This is a bounded field contribution supported by a publisher synopsis, not evidence of a later scholar's adoption. The book itself was not read. Endorsements are not used. The political endpoint is distinct from the existing gender endpoint, although the contributions overlap.

edges.relationship: Laura F. Edwards's Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) contributes to economic history by reconstructing how legal practices made textiles property that marginalized people could use as currency, credit and capital in the early United States.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete four-paragraph publisher abstract and publication metadata. It explicitly connects textiles' legally protected value to participation in the economy and describes the book's revision of production and exchange. The field mapping concerns property and economic transactions, extending beyond the existing consumption/material-culture pair. Abstract only: the book's chapters remain unread, and no particular scholar's debt is inferred.
edges.map_label: Textiles as currency, credit and capital

edges.relationship: As Carole Turbin explains, The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) draws on E. P. Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963) in combining culture with institutions and tracing plebeian class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Turbin, review PDF p. 1, opening paragraph: “owes much to Thompson”; she specifies culture/institutions and plebeian traditions. This is a named scholarly reader’s attribution. Neither book freshly read; no supervisory or personal relationship inferred.

edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark explicitly follows Stedman Jones’s Languages of Class (1983) in treating Chartist rhetoric as political action rather than simply a reflection of economic distress.
edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed p. 63, opening paragraph and n. 6: “In this I am following”; the note identifies Languages of Class, pp. 90–95. Selected primary passage read. The essay’s earlier 1982 publication and the 1983 collection are distinct; this claim dates the collection she cites. Original Stedman Jones text unread; selective uptake, not blanket agreement.

edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark qualifies Joan Scott’s account of masculine citizenship by arguing that domestic rhetoric could initially bring women into Chartism, even though its later effects narrowed women’s political scope.
edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed p. 65, paragraph beginning Surprisingly enough, and n. 14; conclusion pp. 87–88. She names Scott alongside Deborah Valenze and counters a fixed opposition between citizenship and community with a “larger notion of politics”. Scott is cited through Gender and the Politics of History (1988), p. 53. Specific qualification of this account; no rejection of Scott’s whole project. Scott’s chapter and the Smith/Valenze article unread.

edges.relationship: Clark’s 1998 review of The Gentleman’s Daughter uses Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes (1987) to defend historically changing public/private boundaries and domesticity’s role in middle-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Clark review, paragraphs beginning Vickery’s chief target, They demonstrate, This ideology, and Similarly (web-reader lines 55–58). The argument belongs jointly to Davidoff and Hall. Full review read; Family Fortunes itself unread. A resource used in this review, without claiming sole derivation or assigning a jointly authored passage to one author.
edges.map_label: Family Fortunes as a conceptual resource

edges.relationship: Clark’s 1998 review of The Gentleman’s Daughter uses Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes (1987) to defend historically changing public/private boundaries and domesticity’s role in middle-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Clark review, paragraphs beginning Vickery’s chief target, They demonstrate, This ideology, and Similarly (web-reader lines 55–58). The argument belongs jointly to Davidoff and Hall. Full review read; Family Fortunes itself unread. A resource used in this review, without claiming sole derivation or assigning a jointly authored passage to one author.
edges.map_label: Family Fortunes as a conceptual resource

edges.relationship: In “Anne Lister’s Search for the Anatomy of Sex” (2023), Clark takes the chronology discussed in Laqueur’s Making Sex (1990) as one starting point, then asks how an individual reader understood anatomical texts.
edges.evidence_note: Clark, printed pp. 49–50 and 63 n. 3, with conclusion p. 63. Opening discusses Laqueur, other historians’ objections, and a gap in work on the early nineteenth century; p. 50 shifts from what experts wrote to women’s interpretations. This is a bounded problem-setting resource, not endorsement of the one-sex/two-sex thesis. Her note cites the 1992 edition; original 1990 retained from the existing Laqueur node. Laqueur’s book unread.

edges.relationship: The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) makes conflict over work, marriage and domestic authority part of the explanation of British class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the UC Press About the Book description and contents; original 1995 confirmed by Minnesota bibliography, rather than the displayed 1997 paperback. This is publisher-mediated characterization, corroborated by Turbin’s review; full book unread. Projects a named individual contribution from existing group-level routes without replacing them.

edges.relationship: The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) contrasts artisans and textile workers in Lancashire, Glasgow and London, showing how each created distinctively gendered communities and political strategies.
edges.evidence_note: UC Press About the Book, regional/occupational comparison and concluding domesticity argument. Publisher description read; full chapters and underlying evidence unread. Existing gender → labourhistory edge_741 names Clark collectively; this new person route preserves that group claim.

edges.relationship: In “The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity” (1992), Clark treats rhetoric as a set of persuasive strategies that linked political language with domestic experience and could produce contradictory outcomes.
edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 63–65, especially discussion of persuasion and different tactics, read with conclusion pp. 87–88. The claim concerns her contribution to the debate, not membership of a homogeneous school. Existing edge_1174 names Clark within the debate → gender route; this distinct person endpoint is new.

edges.relationship: In “Anne Lister’s Search for the Anatomy of Sex” (2023), Clark develops queer reading as a way to explain how readers could use hostile texts to understand their desires and bodies.
edges.evidence_note: Primary printed p. 50, paragraph beginning Because these texts, and conclusion p. 63; n. 9 on p. 64 points back to Alternative Histories of the Self (2017). Selected chapter passages read; original diaries and 2017 book unread. Concerns an interpretive method, not a claim that historical subjects shared modern identity categories.

edges.relationship: In Masculinities in an Industrializing Society: Britain, 1800–1914 (2005), John Tosh questions the explanation, attributed to Anna Clark’s The Struggle for the Breeches (1995), that shared manhood could bridge class divisions, arguing that its effectiveness required a working-class acceptance of polarized gender identities for which evidence was limited.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF read. Note 39 identifies Clark, p. 2; the body grants partial support before challenging working-class diffusion, citing dual-income households and popular representations of female sexuality. This is a qualified criticism of one explanation.
edges.map_label: Questions manhood as a bridge across class

edges.relationship: In Presidential Address: The 1890s Debate over the Democratic Control of Hospitals in Britain and New Zealand (2021), Anna Clark contributes to medical and health history by comparing hospital scandals and interpreting unsuccessful demands for democratic control, patients’ rights and nurses’ health as possible precursors of patient-centered care.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract read, not the article body. It distinguishes these campaigns from economy-driven reform and state-efficiency proposals and cautiously suggests a connection with patient-centered care. The edge records this specific historical intervention, without claiming a demonstrated influence on later medical practice. The journal article appeared in 2021; the abstract identifies an earlier conference plenary in 2018.

edges.relationship: In the acknowledgments to Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan credits Deborah Gray White’s pioneering scholarship and critical support as foundations for her own work.
edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments p. xi, last sentences of first paragraph: “trailblazing” work and critical support. This is Morgan’s explicit intellectual acknowledgment, not an inferred employer link; no particular White title is specified here and none is silently supplied. White’s books unread.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Hartman's work among the scholarship that shaped the book and that she strives to emulate, and notes that her use of 'political arithmetic' echoes Hartman's Lose Your Mother (2007).
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13 n. 28 explicitly discusses Hartman’s phrase “political arithmetic” and its earlier demographic meaning. Acknowledgments p. xiii and p. 11 n. 22 corroborate a broader debt. This claim concerns the specified use, not adoption of every element of critical fabulation. Hartman’s book unread; her 2007 original date is distinguished from the 2008 edition named in Morgan’s epigraph.
edges.map_label: Hartman's work as model; political arithmetic

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Johnson’s “To Remake the World” as a resource for understanding slavery and capitalism together.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 16 n. 33 calls Johnson’s formulation “generative”; pp. 15–16 place the book beside scholars developing Robinson’s work. Specific methodological resource, not a claim of coauthorship or sole derivation. Johnson’s essay itself unread; conflicting secondary dates were not promoted to an original publication date.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan places her account of gender, kinship and capitalism in dialogue with scholarship returning to Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery (1944).
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “starting point”; pp. 16–17 and n. 33 state dialogue with renewed Williams scholarship. Morgan extends a research programme through reproductive labor and cultural logic; she does not here endorse every Williams claim about abolition. Williams’s original book not freshly read; 1944 matches the inspected existing Williams node.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan criticizes The Order of Things for omitting African experiences from its account of early modern knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13 n. 29, following discussion of the shift from display to tables: “experienced by Africans”; p. 18 n. 37 adds the contrast with Trouillot. A specific criticism of this book’s analytic omission, not rejection of Foucault’s entire scholarship. Foucault’s original and translation unread.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Trouillot among the scholars whose work shaped the book, and sets his account of the unthinkable in Silencing the Past against Foucault.
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 17, final paragraph and n. 58 explicitly identify an “obvious debt” to Trouillot. The claim concerns this formulation about archival absence and strategic thought. Morgan’s note dates the cited book 1992; the existing graph records original 1995, so the note’s date is not repeated as publication fact. Trouillot’s book not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Morgan’s acknowledgments to Reckoning with Slavery (2021) identify Burton’s repeated manuscript readings and help in conceptualizing and completing the book.
edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments p. xii, paragraph on readers of multiple drafts: “conceptualizing” identifies substantive project help. Burton is singled out as reading each draft; this is specified intellectual work, not generic thanks or institutional proximity. No independent account by Burton of those readings consulted.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan uses Sontag’s Regarding the Pain of Others to ask how commercial records neutralize the suffering behind slave-trade numbers.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 20 and n. 40: Morgan introduces Sontag through “wrath” and applies the point to ledgers and inventories; p. 21 develops the application. Limited borrowing for a representational problem; Sontag’s book unread and no wholesale theoretical allegiance inferred.

edges.relationship: In “The Belly of the World” (2016), Hartman uses Morgan’s work on maternity and slave law to explain the reproductive foundations of racial slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2017 HTML reprint, paragraph beginning Kinship loses meaning: “Extending and revising”; notes 1 and 7. Note 1 explicitly discusses Laboring Women (2004); note 7 points to a 2014 Irvine workshop called Partus Sequitur Ventrem. The later published 2018 article was not Hartman’s 2016 source. Original journal facsimile and workshop unread; this distinct incoming debt is not the reverse projection of Morgan’s 2021 Hartman citation.
edges.map_label: Hartman draws on Morgan’s maternity argument

edges.relationship: Laboring Women (2004) makes enslaved women’s work and childbearing central to the history of colonial slavery.
edges.evidence_note: MacArthur Foundation, Jennifer L. Morgan (1 October 2024), About Jennifer’s Work, paragraph beginning Morgan wrote her groundbreaking first book, read on the Foundation’s own site. The paragraph identifies Laboring Women (2004) and explains its account of agricultural labor and childbearing under slavery. This is institutional reception of the book, not an independent reading of the monograph. The edge is now supported by this single read source.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan argues that Virginia's 1662 rule that a child's condition followed the mother's tethered enslaved women's reproduction to enslavement, making racial slavery heritable and denying enslaved people kinship.
edges.evidence_note: Jennifer L. Morgan, Reckoning with Slavery (Duke University Press, 2021), publisher preview, introduction Refusing Demography, printed pp. 3–5 (PDF leaves 19–21), read. Printed pp. 3–4 discuss the 1662 maternal-status rule; p. 5 links hereditary enslavement, reproduction, property rights and the denial of kinship. These are passages from the book’s introduction, not selected article pages. The full book and the underlying legal records were not independently read.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan connects women’s commodification across Iberia, West Africa, the Middle Passage, the Caribbean and mainland colonies.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 26–27, especially the explicit geographic arc and proposal to center enslaved women over “geographies”; pp. 3–5 explain kinship and commodification. This is a stated Atlantic research design and argument, not shared-topic membership. Chapter bodies unread.
edges.map_label: Women and kinship across the Atlantic

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan argues that reproductive dispossession, race and numerical valuations developed together in early Atlantic capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 15–17, especially p. 16 and n. 31, state the intervention through “reproduction”; pp. 10–11 explain relatedness. This concerns the constitutive logic of racial capitalism; not an estimate of slavery’s numerical contribution to industrial growth. Full monograph beyond introduction unread.
edges.map_label: Gender and kinship in racial capitalism

edges.relationship: Discussing the research behind Dispossessed Lives (2016), Marisa J. Fuentes says that reading Jennifer Morgan’s social histories of enslaved women shaped her expectation of finding fuller accounts of their lives in Barbados’s archives.
edges.evidence_note: Read Fuentes’s answers in Andrew Mitchell Davenport’s 8 March 2017 interview. She directly connects her reading of Morgan and Beckles to her initial research expectations, then explains how archival absences changed her project. This establishes a particular influence on research expectations, not adoption of Morgan’s entire argument. The interview does not identify the Morgan title; the dated work named in the relationship is Fuentes’s 2016 book. The interview’s spelling of Beckles’s name is retained only in the verbatim phrase. Source record gb162_fuentes_davenport_2017 already exists in the graph and was freshly checked.
edges.map_label: Social histories shaped Fuentes’s archival expectations

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan proposes reading surviving evidence of enslaved women together with the ideologies that produced their archival absence.
edges.evidence_note: Read selected introduction passages in Duke University Press’s licensed preview, reached through the publisher’s book page and its introduction link. On pp. 9–10 Morgan examines how records erase and enumerate; p. 24 explicitly states the proposed method. The edge records a contribution to studying archival production, not complete recovery of missing lives. The full book and the chapters summarized by the introduction remain unread.
edges.map_label: Explains the production of archival absence

edges.relationship: As Erika Denise Edwards explains in her 2022 review essay, Morgan’s Reckoning with Slavery (2021) examines how racial categories and numerical valuation developed through the commodification of African women in the Atlantic slave trade.
edges.evidence_note: Read the opening discussion and Morgan-specific paragraphs of Edwards’s open review essay on Cambridge Core. This edge concerns historical racial formation, without asserting membership in any particular theoretical school. Edwards is not an eligible person endpoint, so her review supplies evidence for a field contribution rather than a reviewer–author edge.
edges.map_label: Numeracy and the formation of racial categories

edges.relationship: Sinha and Hall co-edit Cambridge’s Critical Perspectives on Empire series from 2006, a collaboration corroborated in the frontmatter of Scandal of Colonial Rule (2012).
edges.evidence_note: Sinha CV p. 1, Editorial Positions, names Hall and Wilson and dates this co-editorship from 2006; authorized 2012 frontmatter, PDF p. 2, lists all three as Editors. No individual book coauthorship or uninterrupted collaboration beyond the dated witnesses is inferred.

edges.relationship: Sinha and Wilson co-edit Cambridge’s Critical Perspectives on Empire series from 2006, a collaboration corroborated in the frontmatter of Scandal of Colonial Rule (2012).
edges.evidence_note: Sinha CV p. 1, Editorial Positions; authorized 2012 frontmatter, PDF p. 2, lists Hall, Sinha and Wilson as Editors. Hall’s shared credit is retained. This supports editorial collaboration, not a common argument or coauthorship of Epstein’s book.

edges.relationship: In “Imperial Optics” (2011), Burton identifies Colonial Masculinity (1995) and Sinha’s imperial social formation as a feminist model supporting her challenge to separate domestic and imperial histories.
edges.evidence_note: Burton’s own introduction, printed pp. 10–11, especially p. 11 paragraph beginning “In spite of these limitations,” explicitly describes Sinha’s model as “crucial.” Re-read in licensed preview, physical PDF pp. 33–34. Credit to Stoler and Cooper in the following sentences remains shared; neither exclusive derivation nor personal supervision is claimed. Sinha’s full 1995 book and Burton’s unseen endnotes remain unread.
edges.map_label: imperial social formation as a feminist model

edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha distinguishes Indian feminism’s simultaneous disavowal and constitution of communities from the paradox of sexual difference in Scott’s account of French feminism.
edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 11–12, passage spanning the page break that explicitly names Scott. This is Sinha’s comparison of different historical configurations, not a claim that Scott’s French account is wrong in its own setting. Scott’s original work and Sinha’s endnote 35 were not read; its exact bibliographic identification is not asserted.

edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha accepts Chakrabarty’s problem of indispensable yet inadequate European categories but argues that fragmentary histories alone risk conceding an exclusively European origin to universal rights.
edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 15–16, from the paragraph naming Chakrabarty through her alternative of intersecting global histories. Her objection concerns an emphasis on fragments “alone,” and she retains the problem that motivates provincializing Europe. This is a qualified methodological disagreement, not a wholesale rejection. Chakrabarty’s originals and Sinha’s endnotes 45–48 remain unread.

edges.relationship: Colonial Masculinity (1995) treats gendered colonial identities as historically produced in British–Indian political struggles; “Giving Masculinity a History” (1999) examines what colonial Indian historiography contributes to histories of masculinity.
edges.evidence_note: Hall’s review pp. 378–379 identifies the relational, changing categories in the 1995 book. The 1999 publisher abstract explicitly frames the contribution to masculinity historiography and feminist concern with gendered power. Full book and full 1999 article unread; claim stays at the argument and abstract level.

edges.relationship: Specters of Mother India (2006) locates women’s collective political agency at the centre of a contingent reworking of citizenship during the Mayo controversy and its aftermath.
edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 9–14: especially pp. 10–11 on a possible citizen-subject and its subsequent neutralization. The reading preserves Sinha’s limits concerning privileged protagonists, communal distinctions and the temporary character of the opening; no universal emancipation claimed. Later chapters and epilogue unread.

edges.relationship: Specters of Mother India (2006) develops an imperial social formation approach that combines intersecting histories, multiple scales and contingent events across Britain, India and the United States.
edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 16–19, especially pp. 16–17 on widening and deepening analysis and pp. 17–18 on imperial ordering, uneven connections and cultural/material mediation. This is an explicit methodological proposal for global history, not an inference from the international subject matter. Remaining introduction pp. 21–22, chapters and notes unread.

edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha argues that postcolonial critiques of liberal rights have not attended sufficiently to the alternative trajectories of rights in women’s collective struggles.
edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 12–13, paragraph beginning “Postcolonial critiques” and its continuation. She recognizes those critiques’ achievements while identifying an opening for an alternative genealogy; this does not deny colonial exclusion or endorse every liberal universal. A field-level criticism distinct from the named fragmentary-history objection at pp. 15–16. Chapters and endnotes unread.
edges.map_label: questions limits of postcolonial rights critiques

edges.relationship: In the introduction to Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005), John Tosh cites Sinha's 'Giving Masculinity a History' (1999) as the sole reference for his statement that historians now study masculinity in specific historical conjunctures alongside other identities and structuring principles.
edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction’s discussion on printed p. 8 and its note 18 on printed p. 9 in the licensed publisher preview. The body argues for interpreting masculinity within specific conjunctures involving other identities and organizing principles; its directly attached note identifies Sinha’s 1999 essay alone, specifically p. 446. This is a citation supporting a substantive methodological claim in the body, rather than a collective reading recommendation. The proposal records that limited use of her argument; it does not assert a general intellectual debt or adoption of her entire imperial framework. The collection’s original year is 2005, also given by the publisher’s indexed first-edition listing and the preview copyright; the preview reproduces a 2016 Routledge issue. The preview’s inconsistent first-publication line is not used for dating. The original Sinha essay and Tosh’s later chapters were not read for this proposal.

edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese coauthored Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983) and The Mind of the Master Class (2005), the latter studying history and Christian faith in slaveholders’ thinking.
edges.evidence_note: Read the Cambridge publisher excerpt, Prologue p. 1 and joint running credits, for The Mind of the Master Class. Read Hahn’s Divine Rights (2006), paragraph beginning Neither Genovese’s subsequent book, for the joint Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983). The Oxford Academic bibliographic header for Rawley’s review independently confirms both authors and 1983. Coauthorship establishes joint work, with no division of authorship or influence between the authors inferred. Retain comparison and directed false: Task M explicitly requires directed false exactly for comparison, overriding the older contribution/undirected convention cited in the finding.
edges.map_label: Coauthors: merchant capital and master-class thought

edges.relationship: In “Tuchman and History” (1978), Fox-Genovese challenges Stone’s professional-status test and his assumptions about progress and fourteenth-century crisis.
edges.evidence_note: Complete letter, paragraphs beginning “It is saddening” and “Stone doubts,” web lines 85–99; A Distant Mirror (1978) unread. Criticism addresses his review.
edges.map_label: Challenges Stone on authority and crisis

edges.relationship: In his reply in “Tuchman and History” (1978), Stone rejects Fox-Genovese’s objections by distinguishing innovative research from scholarly popular synthesis.
edges.evidence_note: Complete reply, numbered point 1, web lines 109–122; “haute vulgarisation” names his distinction. No agreement or reconciliation inferred.

edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese’s “Tuchman and History” (1978) defends A Distant Mirror (1978) for connecting social groups, political choices and material dislocation.
edges.evidence_note: Letter’s final three paragraphs, web lines 97–99. Tuchman explicitly does not share the Marxist perspective used in her defence; her book unread. Person route specifies the speaker of existing group route edge_555.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Within the Plantation Household (1988), Woodward disputes Fox-Genovese’s treatment of Mary Chesnut’s criticism of slavery as an anomaly, arguing that a privileged beneficiary of slavery could still criticize it with integrity.
edges.evidence_note: “Slaves and Mistresses” (1988), paragraphs beginning “As for those whose response” through “It is even possible,” web lines 140–150. “respectful exceptions” qualifies disagreement; he also praises the book. Original unread.

edges.relationship: Hahn’s “Divine Rights” (2006) criticizes The Mind of the Master Class (2005), jointly by Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese, for asserting broader hegemony without demonstrating it and underanalysing gender and enslaved participants.
edges.evidence_note: Read review, paragraphs beginning “Is there, finally,” “Now it may well be,” “Perhaps more striking” and “Most troubling,” web lines 63–67. “we never see this happening” targets hegemony. Also praises the scholarship. Book read only in publisher excerpt; parallel edge_2355 already targets Eugene.
edges.map_label: Hahn: hegemony, gender and absent participants

edges.relationship: In “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982), Fox-Genovese uses Du Bois’s divided consciousness to frame women’s historical inclusion.
edges.evidence_note: Opening, lines 8–12: “twoness”; expressly refuses equating racial and female experience. Du Bois original unread here.

edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) credits Kelly’s account of feminist theory’s double perspective on social and sexual oppression.
edges.evidence_note: Opening, lines 12–13: “doubled vision.” Underlying Kelly essay unread.

edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) credits Davis with showing how cultural forms reveal implicit gender relations and their reversals.
edges.evidence_note: Opening, line 23: “taught us”; charivari specified. Davis originals unread here.

edges.relationship: Within the Plantation Household (1988) makes relations between enslaved and slaveholding women central to women’s history, arguing that race and class divide experiences that gender alone cannot explain.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, web lines 68–69, and Woodward’s review, lines 90–98: “class and race.” Mediated reading; book unread. Existing women roster retained.

edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) proposes analysing gender systems as historically changing relations of power.
edges.evidence_note: Opening, line 18, propositions 1–2: “historically, not biologically.” Remainder unread.

edges.relationship: As Fredrickson reads Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983), Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese criticize social history that separates subordinate groups from relations of political domination.
edges.evidence_note: “Class Act” (1984), web lines 121–129, especially “principal targets” and “politics of domination.” Named-reader mediation; 1983 collection and 1976 precursor unread. Shared credit retained.

edges.relationship: In “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (2014), Catherine Hall argued that Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Eugene D. Genovese’s account of Southern paternalism and its anti-capitalist politics had little correspondence with her team’s findings about British slave-owners’ brutality and commitment to industrial capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Read Hall’s open-access publisher text, especially the adjacent sentences naming both Genoveses and contrasting their interpretation with the British evidence. This is a challenge to the model’s applicability across settings, not a claim that Hall disproves their interpretation of the American South. Hall discusses their corpus without identifying one particular book here. Checked 2026-11-01.
edges.map_label: Hall questions the paternalism model’s applicability

edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese’s joint scholarship with Eugene D. Genovese, including Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983), helped shape Gramscian Marxist interpretations of slavery and capitalism, as Michael Kazin stated in his 1988 reply in The New York Review of Books.
edges.evidence_note: Read the published letter and Kazin’s reply. Kazin expressly attributes an effect on many scholars to the pair’s theoretical contributions; the subsequent discussion names their 1983 collection and also criticizes idealization of slaveholders. The impact belongs to their joint body of work, not demonstrably to this book alone. The collection itself remains unread. The field endpoint denotes Marxist historical interpretation, not party membership or agreement with every British Marxist historian.
edges.map_label: Gramscian interpretations of slavery and capitalism

edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw repeatedly cites hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981), in notes 33, 38, 41 and 47, in discussions of Sojourner Truth, feminist exclusion, sexist imagery in Black liberation politics and racialized sexual stereotypes.
edges.evidence_note: Read the archived journal PDF, pp. 153–157: n. 33 cites hooks on Sojourner Truth; n. 38 cites her on exclusion from feminism; n. 41 on sexist imagery in Black liberation politics; n. 47 on sexual stereotypes. Visually checked printed p. 157: the hooks citation is in n. 47, not n. 46 as the finding recommends. These remain explanatory footnote citations rather than a named engagement with hooks in the body; hooks’s book unread. Retain the footnote-level warning and exclude this edge from the floor.

edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw develops intersectionality to explain Black women’s exclusion from single-axis antidiscrimination, feminist and antiracist frameworks.
edges.evidence_note: Primary opening pp. 139–141 and conclusion p. 167 read; “single-axis framework.” Existing approach node and roster already recognize earlier Black feminist roots. This adds a direct person-to-approach route, not a new origin claim.

edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw argues that feminist theory evolves from a seldom-acknowledged white racial context, and shows through the separate-spheres literature how generalizations drawn from white women’s experience misdescribe the gender norms racism imposes on Black women and men.
edges.evidence_note: Read Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex (1989), section II, printed pp. 154–155, in the archived journal PDF. The paragraph beginning The value of feminist theory explains its seldom-acknowledged white context; the following separate-spheres discussion shows how generalizations from white women’s experience obscure the simultaneous effects of racism and sexism on Black women and men. This supports a contribution to gender analysis through adjacent legal theory. No reading of Mapping the Margins (1991), no violence-specific argument, and no claim of adoption by all gender historians is asserted.

edges.relationship: Speaking at UCLA in April 2026 about her memoir Backtalker (2026), Crenshaw placed it in the tradition of Black memoir and said she was “deeply influenced by Angela Davis and George Jackson”.
edges.evidence_note: UCLA Law news report (24 April 2026) of Crenshaw’s 16 April 2026 conversation with Cheryl Harris, section “On the narrative tradition in which Backtalker resides”, quoting Crenshaw: “I think it pulls from the tradition of Black memoirs – I was deeply influenced by Angela Davis and George Jackson, and the broad groups of folks who shaped our thinking.” This is a stated influence in Crenshaw’s own reported words, limited by its context to the Black memoir tradition. It makes no claim about Davis’s influence on Crenshaw’s legal theory. Neither Davis’s autobiography nor Backtalker was read. In “Demarginalizing” (1989), n. 42, Crenshaw also cites Davis’s Women, Race and Class (1981), but only as “See generally”, so that note is not used. The source is already in Crenshaw’s original packet as kc_w_backtalker_2026 (then used only for life status); it is reused here.
edges.map_label: Influenced by Davis’s Black memoir tradition

edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins uses Cho, Crenshaw and McCall’s “Toward a Field of Intersectionality Studies” (2013) as a starting point for identifying intersectional thinking tools and framing her own questions about thinking, difference and power.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, chapter 1, p. 23: Collins explicitly takes the coauthors’ definition as a resource and develops questions from it. This credits joint intellectual work, not coauthorship between Collins and Crenshaw. The 2013 article body is unread; its repository record confirms metadata. This differs from held kc_w_04 and phc_w_05.
edges.map_label: Starting point for intersectional thinking tools

edges.relationship: In her essay on protected beliefs and employment tribunals (2024), Sara Ahmed applies Crenshaw’s analysis in King was a critical race theorist before there was a name for it (2022) to attacks on antiracist work in Britain.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s essay read. Ahmed quotes Crenshaw within her US–UK comparison, then applies the argument to Britain. The claim concerns this particular uptake, not Ahmed’s entire theoretical development or an independent assessment of tribunal law.
edges.map_label: Applies Crenshaw’s account of anti-CRT attacks

edges.relationship: In Fiefs and Vassals (1994), Reynolds challenged the feudal framework associated with Bloch’s Feudal Society (1939–1940), according to d’Avray and Hudson’s 2022 memoir.
edges.evidence_note: Named-reader route: d’Avray and Hudson, printed p. 153, paragraph beginning “During this time,” explicitly identifies Bloch’s Feudal Society among her targets. Read the memoir passage and the 1994 publisher abstract; neither complete book was read. This is a bounded critique of the feudal interpretation, not a rejection of Bloch’s entire method.

edges.relationship: In “Social mentalities and the case of medieval scepticism” (1991), Reynolds questions Duby’s inference from religious art to a society’s shared faith in Le Temps des Cathédrales (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Primary passage read in the authorized 1995 reprint, essay I, p. 26, especially the question containing “pathetic fallacy,” with notes 19–20. She also faults Duby’s limited treatment of unbelief. At p. 31, note 37, she accepts his warning against imposing modern mental attitudes: this is selective criticism. Duby’s complete 1976 book and 1981 translation unread.
edges.map_label: Challenges an inference of universal belief

edges.relationship: In “The idea of the nation as a political community” (2005), Reynolds explicitly derives her working definition of the nation from Anthony D. Smith’s 1973 formulation.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core displayed Summary, third sentence: the definition “lit up the subject for me in a flash.” The displayed passage identifies a specific debt, not membership in an entire theoretical school. The rest of Reynolds’s chapter and Smith’s 1973 text were not read; no title is assigned to that unread Smith text.
edges.map_label: Credits Smith’s definition of the nation

edges.relationship: Janet Nelson’s funeral address, quoted in d’Avray and Hudson’s 2022 memoir of Reynolds, credits their discussions with helping Nelson refine and develop historical ideas.
edges.evidence_note: Memoir p. 164, quoted funeral address, final sentence: “helping me refine and develop many ideas.” The surrounding paragraph identifies repeated intellectual discussions at the IHR Early Medieval Seminar. This goes beyond attendance or friendship, but names no particular Nelson publication; no book-specific influence is inferred. Address delivered after Reynolds’s 2021 death, published here in 2022. Nelson is another candidate in this run.

edges.relationship: In “Medieval urban history and the history of political thought” (1982), Reynolds calls for urban historians to study political thought alongside the institutional and material history of towns.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core opening extract, p. 14: paragraph beginning “One of the problems of urban history,” through the proposal to add the history of political thought. Footnote 1 links the argument to collective action and dates its delivery to 1981. Only the displayed extract, metadata and notes were read; no claim about the complete article’s demonstration.
edges.map_label: Brings political thought into urban history

edges.relationship: In the preface to The Middle Ages without Feudalism (2012), Reynolds renews Kingdoms and Communities (1984)’s emphasis on collective values, consultation and judgement in medieval government.
edges.evidence_note: Primary 2012 preface xiv, paragraphs beginning “However many mistakes,” “To those,” and “I nevertheless think.” She expressly says collective government was not egalitarian or democratic and could protect higher-status interests. The 1984 book was not read in full; this is her later explicit restatement.

edges.relationship: In the preface to Ideas and Solidarities of the Medieval Laity (1995), Reynolds describes reconstructing lay political ideas from collective activities, a project developed in Kingdoms and Communities (1984).
edges.evidence_note: Primary 1995 preface vii–viii: opening paragraph explains the move from English towns to their inhabitants’ ideas about society and politics, then to people outside towns; the next paragraph stresses lay capacities for “rational and independent thought.” Read this preface, not the whole collection or 1984 book. Contribution to the field is an editorial mapping of that explicit programme, not a claim of Cambridge School affiliation.

edges.relationship: In “The idea of the nation as a political community” (2005), Reynolds argues that a conception of nations as natural political communities was widespread before the eighteenth century.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core displayed Summary, opening and closing sentences. Her claim concerns a conception of political community; she explicitly withholds the inference that earlier people shared modern nationalists’ aims and policies. Only the summary and publication metadata were read. Mapping to nationalism studies follows the named subject and argument, not shared chronology alone.

edges.relationship: According to Sarah B. Lynch, Barbara H. Rosenwein’s Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) extended Susan Reynolds’s account of overlapping communities in Kingdoms and Communities in Western Europe, 900–1300 (1984; second edition 1997).
edges.evidence_note: Read Lynch’s discussion of interlocking communities and note 93. This is an explicit secondary attribution of extension, attached to substantive body analysis. The cited Rosenwein page and Reynolds book were not directly read; no claim that Reynolds originated emotional communities.

edges.relationship: In “Society: hierarchy and solidarity” (2015), Susan Reynolds contributed to world history by comparing inequality and the relationship between social hierarchy and solidarity across societies of the Middle Millennium.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher summary and volume contents. Claim limited to the stated comparative argument; full chapter unread. The British Academy memoir independently discusses this chapter’s extension across world history (p. 158). This records a specific field contribution, without asserting subsequent uptake.
edges.map_label: Compares hierarchy and solidarity across societies

edges.relationship: Labrousse supervised Perrot’s strike-history thesis (1971), published as Les ouvriers en grève (1974); she combined his serial methods with attention to workers’ speech and gestures.
edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe (2015), L’histoire du monde ouvrier, paragraphs beginning L’approche méthodologique and Si Michelle Perrot: “sous sa direction”; distinguishes thesis from book. Thesis and book unread; retrospective formation evidence.

edges.relationship: Perrot and Duby co-directed the five-volume French Histoire des femmes en Occident (1991–1992).
edges.evidence_note: Institut de France (2009), opening presentation and bibliography: five volumes, co-direction, 1991–1992; written text read, audio unheard and volumes unread. BnF (2025), pp. 5–6, distinguishes series directors from volume editors. Existing edge_442 joins Duby to women, not these two people.

edges.relationship: Perrot organized discussion with Foucault of Surveiller et punir (1975) in the collective L’Impossible prison (1980).
edges.evidence_note: Fabre interview (1980), p. 6, first answer: “engager une discussion”; identifies Léonard’s paper, Foucault’s reply and the round table. Both interview pages read; collected papers unread. Exchange does not imply agreement on every argument.

edges.relationship: Perrot and Farge co-led the women’s-history reading seminar from 1978–1979 that helped assemble the team behind Histoire des femmes en Occident (1991–1992).
edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe, Dictionnaire des féministes (2017), paragraph beginning De même, à partir de 1978-1979: “co-anime”; APHG report (2026), paragraph beginning Dans la suite de sa carrière, independently names Farge in the reading group. Seminar papers and volumes unread; series and volume editorships are not conflated.

edges.relationship: According to Isabelle Lacoue-Labarthe (2017), Perrot adopted gender as an analytical tool theorised by Scott; Ripa’s review of Les femmes ou les silences de l’histoire (1998) likewise presents her examination of employers’, unions’ and political-economic discourse on women’s work as following Scott.
edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe’s signed dictionary entry (2017), paragraph beginning “Si elle adopte”, explicitly associates Perrot’s analytical use of gender with Scott’s theorisation, dated there to 1988. Ripa (1999), p. 147, opening paragraph, independently describes her analysis of three discourses as following Scott. Both are mediated witnesses; the Perrot and Scott originals remain unread. Preserve counts_toward_floor false pending coordinator review of the strengthened evidence.
edges.map_label: Scott’s analytical gender and labour discourse

edges.relationship: Perrot says that Beauvoir’s Le Deuxième Sexe (1949) shaped her life and first impulse to research feminism, in her 2023 interview with Florent Le Bot.
edges.evidence_note: L’OURS (2023), answers to 1949, Le deuxième sexe: initial extracts, fuller reading in 1954–1955, then “orienté mon premier élan de recherches”. Complete interview read; Beauvoir’s book unread here. Influence distinguished from Perrot’s later active feminism.

edges.relationship: Lacoue-Labarthe places Perrot’s turn toward history from below in the wake of Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe (2015), L’histoire du monde ouvrier, paragraph beginning Aux côtés de l’initiateur: “dans le sillage”. Scholarly biographer’s characterization; no direct Perrot testimony or date of first reading established. Thompson’s book unread here.
edges.map_label: Thompson as a retrospectively identified resource

edges.relationship: In his review of Histoire de chambres (2009), Corbin praises Perrot’s synthesis but suggests that the partitioning of rural houses into private rooms receives overly brief treatment.
edges.evidence_note: Corbin (2009), Espèces d’espaces, final paragraph beginning Le processus qui conduit: “un peu trop rapidement, peut-être”. Full review and notes read; Perrot’s book unread. A local reservation within an appreciative review, not wholesale rejection.
edges.map_label: Corbin’s qualified reservation on rural rooms

edges.relationship: Les femmes ou les silences de l’histoire (1998) investigates women’s uneven survival in historical records and recovers their work, private lives and political action, as Ripa’s review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Ripa (1999), pp. 145–147, especially p. 146 on archival selection, private papers and the collection’s organization. Review read, book unread; claim is mediated through this named reader. Existing women roster row records volume editorship, not a person-node edge.
edges.map_label: Recovering women and interrogating historical silences

edges.relationship: In Brécy’s reading, Les ouvriers en grève (1974) shifts labour history toward strike action and workers’ lives while combining statistical series with qualitative analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Brécy (1976), pp. 115–116: opening contrasts institutions with strikes; p. 115 discusses statistics and psychology; p. 116 details collective life and criticizes festive emphasis. Complete review read, book unread. Its 1974 dating differs from BnF’s 1973; see chronology.

edges.relationship: In Les femmes ou les silences de l’histoire (1998), Perrot uses relations between the sexes to re-examine women’s work and exclusion from citizenship, as Ripa’s review describes.
edges.evidence_note: Ripa (1999), end p. 146 and first half p. 147, moves from description of women’s activities to discourse and civic exclusion; dictionary (2017), paragraph beginning Si elle adopte, independently identifies gender as an analytical tool. Book unread; no replacement of women’s history asserted.

edges.relationship: In L’immigration en France, une histoire en friche (1986), Gérard Noiriel draws on Perrot’s Les rapports entre ouvriers français et étrangers (1871–1893) (1960) to explain how hostility toward immigrant workers helped crystallize nationalism among French workers.
edges.evidence_note: Read Persée’s page-specific article text on pp. 760–765 and the references on p. 767. Noiriel names Perrot in the body and quotes her explanation of nationalism, then develops the relationship between immigration and labour politics. This is substantive uptake, not an isolated bibliographic citation. Her 1960 article itself was not read; the claim concerns Noiriel’s use of it.
edges.map_label: Worker xenophobia and the crystallization of nationalism

edges.relationship: In Différences entre les sexes et domination symbolique (1993), Roger Chartier questions the conventional periodization retained in Perrot and Duby’s Histoire des femmes en Occident (1991–1992), while acknowledging its legitimacy for a project examining how broader historical changes affected relations between the sexes.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete six-page note through Persée’s page-specific HTML, pp. 1005–1010. Although its bibliographic heading identifies volume III (1991), the periodization passage expressly discusses all five volumes. The criticism concerns the co-directed enterprise, not solely Perrot’s individual writing. It includes Chartier’s qualification rather than presenting him as simply rejecting the project. The volumes themselves were not read.
edges.map_label: Questioning conventional periods in women’s history

edges.relationship: Perrot’s Les ouvriers en grève. France, 1871–1890 (1974) contributes to quantitative history by combining measurement of strike activity with close analysis of manuscript and printed evidence, a methodological combination emphasized by Gabriel Désert’s review (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Read the opening page directly in Persée’s HTML. Désert identifies the quantitative method and its combination with extensive documentary analysis, then discusses the regional distribution of strikes and strikers. This records a specific methodological contribution, without claiming that Perrot founded the approach. The remaining review pages and the monograph were not read. The year follows this contemporary review; the original packet notes bibliographic variation between 1973 and 1974.
edges.map_label: Combining strike statistics with documentary analysis

edges.relationship: In Histoire de chambres (2009), Perrot historicizes the bedroom as a distinct space within the dwelling, connecting the specialization of rooms with experiences of privacy and enclosure, as Alain Corbin’s review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Read Corbin’s substantive review on the journal’s own site. It distinguishes the room’s spatial organization from the experiences it permits and details the progressive specialization of rooms. Mapping this contribution to spatialhistory is an editorial classification, not a claim that Perrot founded a school. The monograph was not read. Reuses the packet’s source mp_w_corbin_2009; no additional Perrot–Corbin pair is proposed.

edges.relationship: As founding director of UNC's Southern Oral History Program, Hall built a programme to document the lives of ordinary people and insisted that it be fully integrated into the history department.
edges.evidence_note: OHA report, paragraphs beginning When Jacquelyn and Telling the stories, lines 90–92; UNC Press Description and author credits, lines 34–38 and 70–76. These are substantive institutional and publisher accounts; no interview corpus or full monograph was read.

edges.relationship: Revolt Against Chivalry (1979; revised 1993) connects white southern women’s antilynching activism with struggles over women’s authority and racial justice.
edges.evidence_note: Columbia publisher description, lines 62–65, especially its account of Ames linking opposition to violence with self-definition. Oxford biography supplies original 1979; Columbia dates the revised edition to 1993. Description only; the book is unread.

edges.relationship: Like a Family (1987), written collaboratively by Hall and five co-authors from Southern Oral History Program interviews, presents the culture and politics of Piedmont cotton-mill workers as a history of resistance and radicalism, as Stephanie McCurry’s 1992 review essay characterizes it.
edges.evidence_note: UNC Press Description and Praise, lines 70–87; all six author credits, line 36. Read publisher account and attributed review excerpts only, not the book. This is a contribution to labour history, not a claim based solely on Hall’s professional office.

edges.relationship: “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (2005) examines how public remembrance narrows the struggle’s chronology and economic goals.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed Oxford excerpt, lines 10–15, including “remembrance is always a form of forgetting”; primary pp. 1233–1235. Read the licensed passage and selected original pages; no museum or commemoration corpus independently examined.

edges.relationship: In “The Long Civil Rights Movement and the Political Uses of the Past” (2005), Hall traces the civil rights struggle back to the “liberal and radical milieu of the late 1930s” and carries it beyond the landmark legislation of the 1960s into the 1970s, as JSTOR Daily (2024) and the University of Mississippi’s 2014 Gilder-Jordan lecture record summarize it.
edges.evidence_note: (1) JSTOR Daily, Matthew Wills, “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (8 Sept. 2024, updated 3 Dec. 2025), opening paragraph: Hall’s “influential exploration of the ‘long civil rights movement’ that began not in the mid-1950s but earlier, in the ‘liberal and radical milieu of the late 1930s’”; later: “Hall describes six major threads braiding together during the long civil rights movement”. (2) eGrove (University of Mississippi) record of the 2014 Gilder-Jordan Lecture: Hall “advanced an understanding of a dynamic movement not bound by 1954’s Brown v. Board and the Civil Rights Act of 1965”. Distinct from jdh_w_09 (memory), which concerns how public remembrance narrows the struggle. This edge concerns the movement’s chronology and the field’s framework. Target ‘black’ is the closest existing field node; there is no separate civil-rights historiography node. The Cha-Jua and Lang critique (2007) remains the main reception; its authors have no endpoints.
edges.map_label: The long civil rights movement framework

edges.relationship: In “A Later Comment” (Journal of American History, 1997), her response to Joel Williamson’s “Wounds Not Scars”, Hall takes up Benedict Anderson’s argument, from the revised Imagined Communities (1991), that the modern nation-state depends on an oscillation between remembering and forgetting. She uses it to suggest that lynching has not been forgotten but is one of the evils “we are doomed both to remember and to forget.”
edges.evidence_note: Read on the publisher’s own landing page for JAH 83:4 (March 1997), 1268–1272, Round Table “What We See and Can’t See in the Past”. Oxford Academic shows a first-page preview image of p. 1268 there, and I read the whole of that page. In the second paragraph, beginning “The symbiosis between cultural amnesia and historiographical neglect is not, of course, unique to the American South”, Hall writes: “Benedict Anderson has argued that the modern nation-state depends on the oscillation between remembering and forgetting. But atrocities banished from official memory are not in fact forgotten; rather, he says, conflicting memories are buried near the surface of consciousness ... memories we are supposed to forget.” Note 1 cites Anderson, Imagined Communities (London, 1991), 187–206, the chapter added to the 1991 edition; the book first appeared in 1983. She continues: “Lynching, I would suggest, has not been forgotten ... But it is perhaps one of those evils that we are doomed both to remember and to forget.” Anderson’s argument is in the body text and frames her own claim, so this is not a citation-only use. It follows the graph’s precedent for using Anderson’s framework (edge_2078, Anderson -> Ngai; edge_2796, Anderson -> Higginbotham). An editorial footnote on p. 1268 says Hall wrote the comment after the Journal accepted Williamson’s article and with access to the referees’ reports. Pp. 1269–1272 are unread, including whatever she says about the referees, among them Robin D. G. Kelley. No claim is made about Anderson’s influence on Hall’s other work.
edges.map_label: Anderson’s remembering and forgetting applied to lynching

edges.relationship: In Haunted by Empire (2006), Ann Laura Stoler uses Hall’s account of lynching and white chivalry to compare imperial racial logics and acknowledges conceptual borrowing from Hall’s work in ‘Tense and Tender Ties’ (2001; reprinted 2006).
edges.evidence_note: Read the relevant preface and chapter passages in the licensed Duke University Press book preview. The preface places Hall’s account of lynching and white chivalry alongside colonial racial and sexual anxieties in Stoler’s discussion of her comparative research. On p. 31 Stoler includes herself through the first-person plural in an account of colonial scholars drawing on Hall, then qualifies this borrowing as often privileging conceptual form over historical content. This is substantive discussion in the body, not a collective bibliographic note. The copyright page identifies the chapter’s original publication in the Journal of American History in December 2001. The preview does not include the chapter’s endnotes or the complete volume; no particular Hall title or additional debt is inferred from unread notes.
edges.map_label: Hall’s racial-violence analysis informs Stoler’s comparisons

edges.relationship: Dianne Feeley’s review ‘Northern Freedom Chronicles’ (2013) identifies Hall’s long civil rights movement conception as an inspiration for Thomas J. Sugrue’s Sweet Land of Liberty (2008), his history of northern African American struggles for equality.
edges.evidence_note: Read Feeley’s review on Against the Current’s own site, issue 162, January/February 2013. The opening discussion explicitly attributes Sugrue’s northern synthesis to inspiration from Hall’s conception, rather than merely listing scholars with a shared topic. The relationship is deliberately attributed to Feeley’s review. Sugrue’s complete introduction and book were not read; the publisher’s text sample and the available introduction preview pages did not expose the relevant acknowledgment. The review’s bibliographic heading and the publisher’s ebook listing establish the book’s original 2008 publication. This is an influence reported by a reviewer, not a claim to have read Sugrue’s own statement of debt and not a review edge between Feeley and Hall.
edges.map_label: Long-movement framework informs Sugrue’s northern history

edges.relationship: In a filmed IHR interview with Hobsbawm (catalogued c. 1988, though the transcript calls The Age of Empire, published 1987, 'shortly to come'), Thane questions him about Marxist historical explanation, Labouring Men (1964) and the relationship between working-class culture and labour institutions.
edges.evidence_note: IHR catalogue, Video details: “Date of creation: c. 1988”; transcript PDF pp. 5–11, especially p. 10 at 00:17:47 and 00:19:15 and p. 11 at 00:20:01. This is a documented intellectual conversation, not evidence that Hobsbawm supervised Thane or that she adopted all his answers. Only the transcript portion was read; recording not viewed. Machine transcription warning retained. Original creation is approximate; 2025 is digitization/release. The distinct 1978–79 interview with Liz Lunbeck was found bibliographically but not read and is not used for its content.

edges.relationship: Kelly Boyd’s “The Women’s History Seminar” (2024) identifies Thane, Janet Nelson and Penelope Corfield as the scholars whose lobbying established the IHR Women’s History Seminar in 1986.
edges.evidence_note: Read Background and founding, paragraphs beginning The founding of the Seminar and They included, then first-term account and notes 18–19. Named collaboration: “Janet (Jinty) Nelson, Pat Thane and Penelope (Penny) Corfield”. Boyd explicitly says the exact negotiations are not remembered; the edge claims joint founding work, not a reconstructed division of labour or personal intellectual influence. Nelson’s 2008 IHR interview corroborates her co-founder role but does not itself name Thane.

edges.relationship: In her June 1996 review of Hufton’s The Prospect Before Her (1995), Thane invokes Linda Colley’s warning that insistent prescriptions may signal challenges to the norms they announce, supporting the need to test prescriptive writing against other evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Complete review, paragraph beginning One of the strengths of the book and following paragraph on separate spheres. Thane attributes the point to “others, such as Linda Colley” and explains that prescription can be especially insistent when norms are challenged. This is a limited, explicit methodological uptake in this review, not a claim of formative influence, priority, or a uniquely Colley-derived method. Thane does not identify Colley’s particular work; it remains unidentified and unread. Hufton’s 1995 book also unread.

edges.relationship: Old Age in English History (2000) makes older people’s varied work, resources and agency part of social history, challenging the assumption that they were uniformly dependent burdens.
edges.evidence_note: Read publisher abstract and contents, plus Blackie’s complete review, PDF pp. 1–2, especially paragraph beginning Another major achievement. Blackie stresses older people’s agency while criticizing thin pre-industrial treatment. This contribution is supported by publisher framing and a named scholarly reader; the book body remains unread. This route concerns social agency and inequality, distinct from the family-support question on the demography route.

edges.relationship: Boyd’s “The Women’s History Seminar” (2024) places Thane’s founding work for the IHR seminar in 1986 within the institutional expansion of women’s history and records her opening-term paper “Ideologies of Gender”.
edges.evidence_note: Read Background and founding and Establishing the Seminar: named lobbying, first full term beginning 6 June 1986 and Thane’s paper, then discussion of the seminar’s function as a forum for new research. “Ideologies of Gender” is identified by Boyd through Nelson’s diaries; the paper itself is unread and no argument is attributed to it. The edge concerns a documented contribution to the field, not membership or shared employment alone.

edges.relationship: In “Gendered Narratives of Ageing in Britain since 1900” (2023), Thane connects older women’s poverty to unequal earnings and caring work, and argues that accounts of ageing often overlook women’s numerical predominance and varied contributions.
edges.evidence_note: Read printed pp. 14–19 (Introduction, Incomes of Older Women, feminist neglect and pensions), pp. 23–29 (positive ageing, diversity, caring and paid/unpaid work). Opening diagnoses omission of the “predominantly female experience”; income section connects working lives and pensions. Later sections complicate uniform dependency narratives. Claims are restricted to the article’s historical argument; its statistical sources were not independently rechecked.

edges.relationship: In her Social Care memorandum (October 2009), Thane challenges romantic accounts of past family care, linking older people’s access to children’s support to mortality, non-marriage, infertility and emigration.
edges.evidence_note: Memorandum PDF p. 4, Before 1939: Voluntary and Family Care, continuing onto p. 5: “Family care ... should not be romanticized”; she explicitly says the evidence is not systematic before listing demographic limits on available children. These pages were read directly. The edge connects history of the family and population to the mixed provision of care, not a claim that Thane developed a demographic reconstruction technique. Remaining memorandum pp. 9–15 not closely read.
edges.map_label: Family support across the life course

edges.relationship: Thane’s Social Care memorandum (October 2009), submitted to the House of Commons Health Committee, uses the history of public, voluntary and family care to explain the continuing difficulty of separating health care from chargeable social care.
edges.evidence_note: Direct memorandum reading, PDF pp. 1–8: submission heading and author statement p. 1; summary pp. 1–2; care in the new welfare state pp. 6–7. Source says it was submitted to provide historical context to the committee. Landing posted December 2009, distinct from October submission. No claim about parliamentary adoption or policy impact is made; the separate REF impact-case fetch failed.

edges.relationship: Helen McCarthy credits Thane’s ‘What Difference Did the Vote Make?’ (2001) with showing how voluntary organisations encouraged female voters to recognise their collective political power and civic responsibilities, a contribution to the history of interwar political participation.
edges.evidence_note: Read the relevant body discussion and note 32 in McCarthy’s 2012 historiographical review on Cambridge Core. The attribution is shared with Beaumont and others; no exclusive priority is claimed. Thane’s original essay was not read. This records a specific contribution to political history; McCarthy has no eligible person endpoint.

edges.relationship: Thane’s ‘Women in the British Labour Party and the Construction of State Welfare, 1906–39’ (1993) contributed to maternal and infant welfare history through its account of philanthropy politicising women who pressed for state provision, an interpretation Linda Bryder explicitly draws upon.
edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction and associated notes on Cambridge Core. Bryder also disputes Thane’s explanation of how welfare became a political issue, stressing campaigning alongside demographic fears. The original chapter was not read. The contribution concerns infant-welfare historiography, not medical practice. Bryder has no eligible person endpoint.

edges.relationship: Thane co-edited The Power of the Past: Essays for Eric Hobsbawm (1984), a Festschrift, with Geoffrey Crossick and Roderick Floud.
edges.evidence_note: Crossref records for reviews of the book (e.g. Ira Katznelson, Journal of Modern History 60:2, 1988, DOI 10.1086/600347) give the editors as Thane, Crossick and Floud and the title 'The Power of the Past: Essays for Eric Hobsbawm'. Bibliographic evidence only; the volume was not read. Added from Fable's review (F07-019).

edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon credits Harris’s Making Native Space (2002) but criticizes its transfer of metropolitan rhetoric onto settler society without sufficiently distinguishing rhetoric from practice.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted chapter, p. 58 and note 74, pp. 84–85: “conflation of rhetoric and practice.” Qualified criticism; she credits Harris with implicating settlers. Harris’s book not freshly read; no general rejection of it asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon explicitly adopts Foucault’s genealogical method to trace contingent connections between settler practices and dispossession.
edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 58–59, 76 and notes 7–9, 71 (pp. 80, 84). Her term “genealogical” is developed through Foucault’s “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History,” cited in the 1984 Foucault Reader. That edition is the witness she used; Foucault’s essay not independently read in this research.

edges.relationship: In “Transformational Listening” (2019 review version), Raibmon draws explicitly on Cruikshank’s warning about comparing another person’s life account with one’s own to explain the limits of sympathetic listening.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher review version, section “Resisting False Equivalency,” paragraph beginning “Unless we resist this pull”: names Cruikshank and warns against “implicit comparisons.” Cruikshank’s underlying text not identified here or freshly read; final 2019 chapter not collated. No shared-employer inference.

edges.relationship: In “Provincializing Europe in Canadian History” (2018), Raibmon explicitly borrows the title and terminology of Chakrabarty’s Provincializing Europe (2000) to challenge supposedly universal European categories in history teaching.
edges.evidence_note: Opening definition of provincializing and note 1: “I borrow terminology here.” Editor’s note also identifies the reference. This establishes the stated conceptual debt; Chakrabarty’s book is not freshly read and no personal mentorship is inferred.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Authentic Indians (2005) in 2006, Michael E. Harkin compares it with Deloria’s Playing Indian (1998), distinguishing Indigenous negotiations of identity from Euro-American performances of Indianness.
edges.evidence_note: Journal of American History 93:1 (2006), p. 236, displayed extract, paragraph beginning “Rather, ethnicity”: Harkin calls it “in a sense” a response. Undirected, explicitly a reviewer’s comparison; neither direct debt nor exchange is established. Full review and both books unread in full.

edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon uses Perry’s On the Edge of Empire (2001) to argue that evidence of individual relationships must remain connected to colonial power and that consequential practices need not share intentions.
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 75, two paragraphs beginning “And what of” and “Such genealogical connections,” with notes 69–70 on p. 84 citing Perry pp. 62, 75. Short phrase “bound by chronology.” Methodological use only; no genealogy or account of individual families reproduced. Perry’s book not freshly read.
edges.map_label: Connects intimate practices and colonial power

edges.relationship: Authentic Indians (2005) explains how colonial definitions of authenticity constrained Indigenous claims to land, resources and sovereignty while Indigenous actors negotiated those definitions.
edges.evidence_note: Duke publisher description, paragraphs beginning “In this innovative history” and “They recognized.” Publisher summary only; book not read in full. Existing native_newcomer roster row and bodies_missions_authenticity strand already name the work; this person-to-field edge is additive, not a duplicate roster proposal. No existing edge incident on paige_raibmon.

edges.relationship: In “The Practice of Everyday Colonialism” (2006), Raibmon criticizes labour history’s separation of Indigenous culture from modern wage work and calls for rethinking its analytical categories.
edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 23, 25–26 and 56, author-posted article: rejects the binary of “traditional culture” and “modern labor.” Field-level historiographical criticism explicitly addressed to labour historians; claim does not reproduce community knowledge. Middle of article unread.

edges.relationship: In “Transformational Listening” (2019 review version), Raibmon argues that hearing testimony requires sustained self-questioning and does not by itself guarantee reconciliation or decolonization.
edges.evidence_note: Sections “Stories Are a Gift” and “Resisting False Equivalency,” plus final two paragraphs; term “transformational listening.” This is Raibmon’s methodological argument in the identified publisher review text, not a claim to authorship of collaborators’ knowledge. Final chapter not collated.

edges.relationship: Written as I Remember It (2014), by Elsie Paul with Raibmon and Harmony Johnson, and the separate digital As I Remember It (2019) make collaborative authorship and publication form part of historical practice.
edges.evidence_note: UBC Press authorship credits and collaborative-research description for the 2014 book; separate digital-book credits; Raibmon’s UBC Research section. Scholarship and production process only. Lead authorship remains Paul’s, and the two publications retain distinct collaborator credits. Full books unread.

edges.relationship: In ‘Unmaking Native Space’ (2008), Paige Raibmon contributes a genealogical approach to histories of settler colonialism that brings settlement and Indigenous dispossession into the same analysis, as Daniel Rück explains in The Laws and the Land (2021).
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction excerpt, especially p. 7. Rück attributes this approach to Raibmon by name and explicitly positions his own book within that discussion. This supplies a substantive later assessment of her contribution to studying settler colonies. The edge records that methodological contribution, not the detailed historical contents of Rück’s case study. Raibmon’s UBC bibliography confirms the chapter’s original publication in The Power of Promises (2008). No new reading of the 2008 chapter is claimed. Rück has no endpoint in either supplied roster, so no person-to-person edge to him is proposed.

edges.relationship: In ‘Obvious but Invisible: Ways of Knowing Health, Environment, and Colonialism in a West Coast Indigenous Community’ (2018), Paige Raibmon contributes to environmental history by examining how state standards of evidence and assessments of risk shape the recognition of pollution claims under settler colonialism.
edges.evidence_note: Read Raibmon’s analytical opening, pp. 241–245, in her own article posted by her university and linked from her research bibliography. The opening connects scientific authorization, state risk calculations, environmental justice and colonial recognition; pp. 242–243 specify why struggles on Indigenous lands require a distinct analysis. The environmental-history classification is editorial and rests on this explicit argument, not on a declared research interest. Only the scholarly framework is recorded: no narrator quotations, oral narratives, teachings, genealogies or community knowledge are reproduced. No claim to have read the entire article is made. The DOI request did not resolve through the reading tool; the author’s institutional copy supplied the passage.

edges.relationship: In “Roland Barthes, à contre-courant” (2015), Kristeva recalls introducing intertextuality to Barthes, who developed it in his reading of Balzac in S/Z.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s 2 December 2015 lecture, section 1, concluding paragraph beginning Nos recherches se sont une fois de plus croisées: “l’intertextualité que je lui avais apportée.” Direction records Kristeva’s retrospective attribution. Barthes’s S/Z and L’Étrangère are unread; no claim that their theories were identical.
edges.map_label: Intertextuality as a resource for S/Z

edges.relationship: In her 2011 interview “Lacan ou la portée historique de la psychanalyse,” Kristeva identifies Lacan’s Encore as a resource for her dialogue with his ideas about feminine enjoyment in Thérèse mon amour (2008).
edges.evidence_note: Complete 2011 author-posted interview, answer to Que reste-t-il de Lacan d’un point de vue théorique aujourd’hui, paragraph beginning Sans avoir systématisé: “Je dialogue avec ses positions dans mon livre Thérèse mon amour.” The next sentence names Encore. The book and seminar are unread. This is a declared textual debt; no analyst, supervisor or seminar-attendance relationship is asserted.
edges.map_label: Encore as a resource for Thérèse mon amour

edges.relationship: In Gender Trouble (1990), Butler challenges Kristeva’s treatment of maternal drives as prior to culture, asking whether those drives are themselves culturally constituted, as Kathleen Lennon recounts (2010).
edges.evidence_note: Lennon, archived Winter 2013 SEP entry, section 4, paragraph beginning Kristeva’s account of the maternal body has, however, come under attack. Cites Butler 1990, pp. 88, 92–93, and the need to examine “specific power relations.” Named-reader route; Gender Trouble unread. Does not imply rejection of every Kristevan concept.

edges.relationship: In Hannah Arendt (1999; English translation 2001), Kristeva interprets Arendt through the relation between life and thought and freedom as beginning, an interpretation she explains in her 2025 interview on the Female Genius trilogy.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted 30 March 2025 interview, Q3 and answer: her account of Arendt links freedom to “a new beginning.” Read alongside Columbia’s description and contents, especially Life as a Narrative, and the official bibliography’s 1999 French date. Full book unread. This is Kristeva’s reading of Arendt, not a claim of personal collaboration.
edges.map_label: Reads freedom as beginning and renewal

edges.relationship: In “French Feminism in an International Frame” (1981), Spivak criticizes the homogeneous China/West opposition in Kristeva’s Des Chinoises (1974), as Nicolás Pastor-Berdún reconstructs (2026).
edges.evidence_note: Pastor-Berdún, p. 8, section 5, paragraph beginning Como señalan autoras feministas decoloniales; cites Spivak 1981, pp. 157–158 and 164. Phrase: “retrato homogéneo y unitario.” Spivak’s essay and Kristeva’s book unread. His p. 2 n. 3 says Spivak does not use the term orientalism; that label is therefore not attributed directly to her.

edges.relationship: In Des Chinoises (1974), Kristeva draws on Lévi-Strauss’s kinship analysis for her account of early Chinese social organization, as Pastor-Berdún shows through a textual comparison (2026).
edges.evidence_note: Pastor-Berdún, p. 9, section 6, from Kristeva (2016, p. 57) reconoce to the paragraph ending Lévi-Strauss: “incorporando sin embargo la corrección dualista.” He separates Granet’s hypotheses from Lévi-Strauss’s revisions. Original texts unread. The resource is documented; the historical validity of Kristeva’s reconstruction is not endorsed.

edges.relationship: La Révolution du langage poétique (1974) distinguishes the bodily rhythms and drives of the semiotic from the symbolic organization of language, treating them as interacting parts of signification.
edges.evidence_note: Kristeva’s 2015 Barthes lecture, section 1 closing paragraph, contrasts “mode sémiotique” and “mode symbolique” and names the 1974 book; the Holberg committee citation describes their interaction. Leeb and Zakin’s section 4.2 supplies a scholarly reading. Book unread; this is a contribution to language and subject-formation debates, not a claim about adoption by all historians.

edges.relationship: In “Le Temps des femmes” (1979; “Women’s Time,” 1981), Kristeva distinguishes three generations of feminism and favours a third that neither fixes identity nor neutralizes sexual difference, as the Stanford Encyclopedia’s account of psychoanalytic feminism explains (2025).
