edges.evidence_note: Re-based at verification on the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry by Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin, section on 'Women's Time': three generations of feminism, the third following 'neither the path of fixing identity nor the path of neutralizing difference'. The 1981 article is recorded bibliographically (Signs 7:1, 13–35; French original 1979) and was not read on a permitted route.

edges.relationship: In Histoires d’amour (1983; Tales of Love, 1987), Kristeva reworks Freud’s account of primary paternal identification into an account of a loving imaginary father preceding symbolic law, as Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin explain (2025).
edges.evidence_note: Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin, “Psychoanalytic Feminism,” substantive revision 3 October 2025, section 4.2, paragraph beginning “Although symbolic violence is integral”: links Kristeva’s imaginary father to Freud’s account in The Ego and the Id. Histoires d’amour and Freud’s book remain unread. The endpoint freud denotes the existing Freudian psychoanalysis tradition.
edges.map_label: Reworks primary identification in Tales of Love

edges.relationship: In Justice Interruptus (1997), Nancy Fraser criticizes Kristeva's discourse theory for reducing varied forms of human communication to a symbolic language system, as Sullivan and Tarver explain.
edges.evidence_note: Read the substantive discussion in section 10.2 and its bibliography. This is Sullivan and Tarver's attributed account of Fraser's criticism; Justice Interruptus itself remains unread. The claim is limited to that account.
edges.map_label: Criticizes the reduction of communication to a symbolic system

edges.relationship: Kristeva's theory of abjection in Pouvoirs de l'horreur (1980; Powers of Horror, 1982) became a resource for analysing spatial exclusion and marginalised communities in critical geography, as Ben Campkin explains in 2013.
edges.evidence_note: Read manuscript pp. 14–15 and notes 53–59. The body develops the application; note 58 specifies its disciplinary scope. Target mapping is to the node's critical spatial studies strand. Original and translation years checked in Kristeva's bibliography; the book remains unread.
edges.map_label: Abjection as a resource for analysing spatial exclusion

edges.relationship: In "The Task of the Historian" (2009) Spiegel takes Derridean deconstruction as the key expression of the linguistic turn and reads it as a philosophy shaped by the Holocaust, while adopting its lesson of listening for silence.
edges.evidence_note: Spiegel's AHA presidential address (2009), historians.org: 'I will take Derridean deconstruction as the key expression of the impulses at work in generating the linguistic turn'; 'Derrida alchemized into philosophy a psychology deeply marked by the Holocaust'; n. 14 'Derrida does not, however, specify the "event" he calls a rupture'; and the adopted lesson of 'listening to silence'. Reversed and retyped from a journalist's profile on Fable's reading (F07-029).
edges.map_label: Deconstruction as the linguistic turn, read historically

edges.relationship: In The Task of the Historian (2009), Spiegel uses de Certeau’s separation of present and past to frame historical writing as an engagement with absence.
edges.evidence_note: Address, paragraphs beginning One of the most significant characteristics through The historian’s task, and note 7: The Writing of History, English translation (1988), p. 5. De Certeau’s book unread here. Quoted phrase: “engagement with absence”.
edges.map_label: De Certeau on the absent past

edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel uses Raymond Williams’s account of the continuing production of cultural orders to frame aristocratic historical writing.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 5 and p. 325 n. 2: Culture (1981), p. 201, explicitly cited through Alan Sinfield’s typescript. A mediated resource; neither original read here. Quoted phrase: “actively made”.

edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel uses Le Goff’s account of social change to connect material conditions with aristocratic imaginative worlds.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 5; p. 325 n. 3 names the essay on Jacques de Vitry in The Medieval Imagination, English translation (1988), p. 181. The quoted essay is unread here. Quoted phrase: “material and imaginary realities”.
edges.map_label: Le Goff on social and imaginary change

edges.relationship: In Hayden White’s Return to the Past as a Source of Human Practice (2018), Spiegel interprets White’s practical past as the culmination of his concern with ethical choice and freedom from inherited historical necessity.
edges.evidence_note: Complete journal PDF, pp. 127–135, especially pp. 129–130 and 133–134. An affirmative reception argument, not a critique or proof of personal collaboration. White’s underlying works remain unread in this dossier. Quoted phrase: “logical culmination”.

edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel joins formal analysis to the social setting of historical texts.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 9–10, “social logic”; existing language roster retained. New timeline edge; no existing person edge.

edges.relationship: Romancing the Past (1993) explains vernacular prose as an ideological resource of threatened Franco-Flemish patrons.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–4 and 9–10; selected patrons, not all nobles. Whole book unread. Quoted phrase: “small group of patrons”.

edges.relationship: In Memory and History: Liturgical Time and Historical Time (2002), Spiegel contests the collapse of history into memory by distinguishing their temporal structures.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final paragraph, explicitly contests conflation. Abstract only; no claim to reading the article body or to all forms of memory. Quoted phrase: “collapse history into memory”.

edges.relationship: In The Task of the Historian (2009), Spiegel presents practice as a way to connect discursive formation with individual initiative.
edges.evidence_note: Address, paragraphs beginning As William Sewell and Culture, thereby, notes 35–37; also note 49. Specific proposal; no assertion of a consensus replacing poststructuralism. Practicing History (2005) unread. Quoted phrase: “discursive constitution and individual initiative”.

edges.relationship: In ‘The Task of the Historian’ (2009), Spiegel argued that historians moving beyond the linguistic turn should retain poststructuralism’s insights into rupture, displacement and the mediation of historical knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA’s primary text, particularly the discussion following notes 38–41. Spiegel accepts that historical concerns are changing but questions discarding poststructuralist insights; the following paragraphs explain their continuing relevance. Robert A. Schneider’s February 2009 AHR introduction independently identifies this as an argument for preserving core features of poststructuralism. This records a substantive intervention in the debate, not evidence that a particular historian adopted it. The address was delivered in January and published in February 2009; 2008 identifies Spiegel’s presidential term, not the work’s publication year.
edges.map_label: What to retain after the linguistic turn

edges.relationship: In ‘The Task of the Historian’ (2009), Spiegel proposed that transnational and diaspora history examine losses of cultural identity accompanying migration, qualifying accounts that celebrate mobility and hybridity.
edges.evidence_note: Read the primary discussion of transnational history and diaspora studies, from the paragraph preceding note 42 through the discussion following note 46. Spiegel explicitly proposes investigating losses associated with migration, exile and diasporic movement, and identifies celebratory accounts of transnationalism as the position to qualify. The existing global endpoint is the umbrella for this transnational intervention. The claim concerns her methodological proposal, not demonstrated adoption by the field. Schneider’s February 2009 AHR introduction also connects her concluding argument to transnational experiences of migration and displacement. This target pair is absent from the input; the edge records a specific intervention in transnational historiography rather than another general memory or language contribution.

edges.relationship: In “On Historians’ Re-Use of Social-Science Archives” (2022), Lawrence explicitly acknowledges a debt to Summerfield’s “Dis/composing the Subject” (2000) for his treatment of intersubjectivity in “Social-Science Encounters” (2014).
edges.evidence_note: Lawrence, p. 439, paragraph beginning “My 2014 article” and n. 25: “My debt has been principally to oral historians,” immediately naming Summerfield’s chapter. Publisher HTML argument and note read. The 2000 chapter and complete 2014 article remain unread; no claim that all of Lawrence’s method derives from Summerfield.

edges.relationship: In “‘My Heart Is a Piece of Stone’” (2023), Summerfield applies Foucault’s “technologies of the self” (1988) to letter writing as a practice of managing identities and emotions during wartime separation.
edges.evidence_note: “Epistolarity, Love, and Marriage,” opening paragraph, callout n. 16; conclusion, opening two paragraphs. Summerfield explicitly names the concept and n. 16 identifies Foucault’s 1988 seminar text as its origin. Selected primary passages read; the Foucault text is unread here. This establishes a specific conceptual resource, without a general allegiance claim.
edges.map_label: Letters as technologies of the self

edges.relationship: Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998) investigates how public representations of wartime men and women interact with women’s retrospective accounts of their own lives.
edges.evidence_note: MUP publisher description and August 1998 metadata read; the monograph remains unread. Claim confined to the stated research question, corroborated by the author’s 1998 essay, pp. 222–224.

edges.relationship: In “Research on women in Britain in the Second World War” (1998), Summerfield interprets wartime employment change through occupational redistribution and gender segregation rather than a simple expulsion of women from paid work after the war.
edges.evidence_note: Section I, pp. 210–213: author’s synthesis of earlier findings, including the 1984 Women Workers book (1989 republication). Those originals unread. No general claim about all belligerent countries.

edges.relationship: In “Research on women in Britain in the Second World War” (1998), Summerfield treats wartime welfare as compromises between production needs and patriarchal expectations that left women reconciling paid work and domestic responsibilities.
edges.evidence_note: Section II, pp. 214–215, especially the paragraphs distinguishing her analysis from Riley’s. This is the author’s 1998 retrospective synthesis; the earlier 1983 article and book remain unread.

edges.relationship: In "Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice" (2016), Summerfield argues that oral history has become an autobiographical practice centred on the narrator's subjectivity, making it more urgent to understand how subjectivity is constituted in an interview, a shift she says challenges how history itself is conceptualized.
edges.evidence_note: Complete author abstract in the Manchester repository read. Full journal article not accessible; no detailed interview analysis attributed on this basis. The abstract preserves recovery history’s continuing value alongside the autobiographical approach.

edges.relationship: In “Histories of the Self” (2018), Summerfield explains how historians interpret evasions, silences and interactions between spoken memory and popular culture when using personal testimony.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s departmental essay, paragraph beginning “It reviews historians’ attempts,” with the preceding discussion of referentiality and subjectivity. Essay read in full; this claim concerns the 2018 methodological self-account, not an independently read monograph.

edges.relationship: In “‘My Heart Is a Piece of Stone’” (2023), Summerfield uses wartime correspondence to study gendered anxiety, maternal subjectivity and family separation, extending composure analysis from interviews to letter writing.
edges.evidence_note: Abstract; introduction’s final paragraph; conclusion, first four paragraphs and n. 146. These selected primary passages explicitly connect fluent writing and psychic ease, and analyze their breakdown. The case is not presented as statistically representative; complete middle case study and archival letters unread here.

edges.relationship: In “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016), Summerfield argues that recovery projects such as Thompson’s large-scale study of Edwardian working lives, which strove for representativeness, faced major difficulties of sample and questionnaire, since no statistically representative sample of a past population can be obtained and interviews are dialogic.
edges.evidence_note: Read on OpenEdition (Miranda 12, 2016, online 1 April 2016), section on recovery history. ¶7 names “oral historians such as Paul Thompson, who undertook a large-scale project on Edwardian working lives” (with Elizabeth Roberts on Lancashire women), says they “strove for representativeness”, then: “However well-intentioned, such endeavours faced major difficulties, relating to the sample and the questionnaire” and “It is not possible to obtain a statistically representative sample of any population in the past”; a standard questionnaire does not suit a dialogic interview. Bibliography: Thompson, The Edwardians (1975); The Voice of the Past (1978). ¶¶5–6 also report, without dispute, Thompson’s account of oral history’s origins and his defence of memory’s reliability (Thompson 1978). A qualified methodological critique of the recovery programme’s sampling aim, not a rejection of Thompson’s work. The Edwardians unread.
edges.map_label: Questions representative sampling in oral history

edges.relationship: In “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016), Summerfield uses Scott’s “The Evidence of Experience” (1991), the point that accounts of experience cannot give direct access to social reality, to frame her critique of recovery history and her case that subjectivity is constructed in the interview.
edges.evidence_note: Read on OpenEdition (Miranda 12, 2016). ¶10: the telling of experience is, “according to post-structural theorists Joan W Scott and Judith Butler, the means by which subjects constitute themselves”, followed by “Subjectivity is constructed through the language of the interchange in an oral history interview” (Scott 1991; Butler 1990). ¶11, on critiques of recovery history: “as Joan W. Scott has pointed out, accounts of experience cannot give direct access to social reality” (Scott 1991). Bibliography: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience,” Critical Inquiry 17.4 (1991): 773–797. Body-text use of Scott’s argument at two points, the second attributed to Scott alone. Butler is named only jointly with Scott and is not proposed. Limits: a named conceptual resource in a methodological essay, not a claim that Scott shaped Summerfield’s earlier work; the 1998 monograph and 2004 article remain unread.
edges.map_label: Scott’s ‘evidence of experience’ in oral history

edges.relationship: In Histories of the Self: Personal Narratives and Historical Practice (2018; 2019 imprint), Summerfield contributes to historical life writing by examining how historians interpret autobiographies and memoirs, particularly their selectivity and the influence of the present on accounts of the past.
edges.evidence_note: Read Evans's complete review on the journal publisher's site. Its chapter-four discussion identifies genre, selective recollection and the narrator's present as methodological problems in autobiography. This supports a scoped contribution to life-writing methods. Summerfield's book was not read in full; no claim of founding the field or of influence on a particular eligible historian is made.

edges.relationship: In New Directions in Social and Cultural History (2018), the editors cite Summerfield's chapter 'Subjectivity, the self and historical practice' as the volume's discussion of new cultural history's turn towards histories of selfhood and subjectivity.
edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction in the licensed publisher preview. The passage explicitly names Summerfield's chapter while explaining a methodological development within new cultural history. The preview establishes the chapter title and 2018 publication year. The chapter itself falls outside the preview and remains unread. The edge records this identified intervention, without inferring personal intellectual transmission to the editors.

edges.relationship: The Social Life of Stories (1998), as its publisher describes it, draws on Walter Benjamin’s insights on storytelling and dialogue.
edges.evidence_note: UBC Press description of The Social Life of Stories (1998), which names 'the insights of Walter Benjamin, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Harold Innis'. The 1997 American Anthropologist article was not read on a recorded permitted route, so no page locators are used. Benjamin's own work unread; no personal contact asserted.

edges.relationship: The Social Life of Stories (1998), as its publisher describes it, draws on Harold Innis’s insights in its account of dialogue and storytelling.
edges.evidence_note: UBC Press description of The Social Life of Stories (1998), which names 'the insights of Walter Benjamin, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Harold Innis'. The 1997 article was not read on a recorded permitted route, so no page locators are used. Innis's books unread; intellectual use, not supervision or contact.

edges.relationship: In “Glaciers and Climate Change” (2001), Cruikshank follows Latour’s proposal that scientific research should address uncertainty rather than promise to end controversy.
edges.evidence_note: Primary discussion pp. 389–390 and conclusion p. 391: “Following Latour’s advice”; reference p. 392 names From the World of Science to the World of Research (1998). Latour’s original unread.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Do Glaciers Listen? (2005) in 2005/06, Cole Harris praises its interdisciplinary achievement but challenges its treatment of scientific explanation and asks Cruikshank to address communication across knowledge systems more squarely.
edges.evidence_note: Harris review pp. 104–106 read: praise p. 104, scales/explanatory objection p. 105, final request p. 106, “address this problem of communication more squarely”. A qualified criticism; not a wholesale dismissal. Book read only in selected introduction passages.

edges.relationship: In “Oral History Methods in Native Studies” (1999–2000), Innes adopts Cruikshank’s flexible account of oral history and oral tradition, alongside Angela Cavender-Wilson’s, as useful for interpreting his interviews.
edges.evidence_note: Innes pp. 65–67, nn. 8–14, read in Saskatchewan institutional PDF. Calls the two scholars’ conception “operational” (p. 67); cites Cruikshank’s 1993 draft and Life Lived Like a Story (1990). Shared credit retained. Interview narratives excluded; books unread.

edges.relationship: In Claiming Legitimacy: Oral Tradition and Oral History (1993 draft), Cruikshank asks historians to examine how oral traditions are used in the present rather than treat them as fixed stores of recoverable facts.
edges.evidence_note: Primary draft pp. 1–3 and 7–9 read: “how oral tradition is used” (p. 2). A methodological proposal, not adopted Commission policy. Distinct from the collective Life Lived Like a Story routes (edges 2173–2175 and 750); no new authorship claim.

edges.relationship: In “Glaciers and Climate Change” (2001), Cruikshank brings historical interpretation to climate debates and argues that local knowledge must be understood within the political histories that shape it.
edges.evidence_note: Primary abstract p. 377 and discussion pp. 390–391 read: knowledge cannot be “ahistorical, timeless, abstract data” (p. 390). Method and policy argument only; no community knowledge reproduced.

edges.relationship: In Do Glaciers Listen? (2005), Cruikshank connects social memory with environmental history by asking how changing landscapes help people interpret changing historical circumstances.
edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction pp. 11–12: fourth theme names “memory, stability, and change”; distinguishes changing landscapes from static archives of remembrance. Other chapters unread. UBC research statement explicitly links memory and environmental anthropology.

edges.relationship: In her 1999 review essay, Franca Iacovetta favourably reviews Life Lived Like a Story (1990), made by Julie Cruikshank in collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned, preferring its restrained authorial presence to Ruth Behar’s in Translated Woman (1993).
edges.evidence_note: Read Iacovetta’s substantive comparison and surrounding methodological discussion. This records favourable reception, not a demonstrated influence on her earlier monograph. Cruikshank’s book was not read. Review comparisons are undirected under Task O.

edges.relationship: In Life Lived Like a Story (1990), Julie Cruikshank’s collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned offered a model of ethnography that foregrounded the collaborators’ voices, as Wendy Wickwire’s 1993 review explains.
edges.evidence_note: Read Wickwire’s evaluation of collaboration and authorial restraint as a change in ethnographic practice. This is a methodological contribution supported by a review; the book itself remains unread. The original year is confirmed in Iacovetta, p. 289, note 23.

edges.relationship: Foner’s 2022 review of C. Vann Woodward: America’s Historian identifies Fields among Woodward’s former graduate students; Columbia dates her Yale doctorate to 1978.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted review, lines 44–46: “former graduate students,” including Fields. Columbia education, line 92. Supports graduate training, without asserting agreement with every Woodward argument; Cobb’s book unread.

edges.relationship: Berlin and Fields coauthored Slaves No More (1992) with Steven F. Miller, Joseph P. Reidy and Leslie S. Rowland.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge author list and 1992 print date; description identifies “three essays.” Coauthorship only; individual essay allocation and whole-book reading are not claimed.

edges.relationship: In “Brute Ideology” (2014), Johnson uses Fields’s 1990 distinction between doctrine and ideology to question Davis’s interpretation of slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted PDF, p.131, paragraph beginning “In her classic 1990 essay”: “doctrine and ideology.” Fields’s original article beyond its publisher opening remains unread.

edges.relationship: Johnson’s “Brute Ideology” (2014) praises Racecraft (2012) but questions its textual remedy and limited account of resistant political cultures.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted PDF, pp.129–130 and 132: “corresponding narrowness” and “corrective.” Joint critique concerns Barbara and Karen Fields; book unread.

edges.relationship: With Berlin, Miller, Reidy and Rowland, Fields’s Slaves No More (1992) places enslaved people’s actions at the centre of Civil War emancipation.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge book description, first-essay paragraph: “place their liberty on the wartime agenda.” Read description, not essay body; collective argument and credit retained.

edges.relationship: In International Labor and Working-Class History's 2001 controversy 'Whiteness and the Historians' Imagination', Fields's 'Whiteness, Racism, and Identity' argues that whiteness as an organizing concept replaces racism with race and skirts the relations of power that placed African Americans in American society.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract: “replaces racism with race”; issue 60 controversy category. Abstract only; criticism addresses that approach within labour history, not the whole field or an inferred named opponent.

edges.relationship: In “Labor in White Skin: Race and Working-class History” (1988), David Roediger criticised Barbara J. Fields’s “Ideology and Race in American History” (1982) for privileging class over race and underplaying Black nation-building in the formation of racial categories.
edges.evidence_note: The body text addresses Fields’s argument over several paragraphs and supplies counterarguments about worker consciousness, African ethnic groups and nation-building. This is a substantive critique, not a claim of positive intellectual debt. The original year and essay identification are supplied by the publisher’s headnote and note 19 respectively.

edges.relationship: In “Liberating Lincoln” (1994), James M. McPherson challenged Barbara J. Fields’s “Who Freed the Slaves?” (1990), arguing that emancipation remained reversible and depended on Union victory, Lincoln’s leadership and constitutional abolition.
edges.evidence_note: McPherson directly quotes Fields’s claim about the momentum of emancipation, rejects it, and discusses re-enslavement and the constitutional abolition of slavery. The review principally concerns books by other authors, so this records his substantive critique of Fields’s argument rather than treating it as a review of her book.

edges.relationship: In “Slavery, Race and Ideology in the United States of America” (1990), Barbara J. Fields contributed to historical analysis of racial formation by arguing that legal and everyday practices continually reproduce American racial ideology.
edges.evidence_note: The excerpt argues that the Supreme Court participates in practices that reproduce race and that historians must distance themselves from racial assumptions. Mapping this argument to the existing racial_formation endpoint is an editorial contribution classification; it asserts neither membership in Omi and Winant’s programme nor a debt to their work. No claim depends on the article’s unread remainder.

edges.relationship: As Isenberg (1995) reports, Kerber’s “Separate Spheres, Female Worlds, Woman’s Place” (1988) praises Welter’s “The Cult of True Womanhood” (1966) for its wit and subtlety but understands Welter to regard women’s separate sphere as oppressive; Isenberg disputes that interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Isenberg (1995), p. 97, reports and disputes Kerber’s reading. Kerber’s essay remains unread; no stated debt is established.
edges.map_label: Kerber’s reading of Welter, disputed by Isenberg

edges.relationship: As Isenberg reports, Cott’s The Bonds of Womanhood (1977) challenges the opposition between feminism and domesticity in Welter’s “The Cult of True Womanhood” (1966).
edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Isenberg pp. 97–99, with p. 102/n. 19 citing Cott pp. 198–199, 203–204. Isenberg names the opposition and disputes Cott’s reduction of Welter to victimization. Cott’s original book unread; Isenberg’s reported disagreement, not our independent reconstruction.

edges.relationship: Lerner uses Welter’s “The Cult of True Womanhood” (1966) in “The Lady and the Mill Girl” (1969) to explain domestic ideals as a means of marking class distinctions among women.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh Lerner pp. 11–12 and p. 15/n. 18: Welter is credited alongside Emily Putnam; the argument connects domestic prescriptions to middle-class status aspirations. Not sole intellectual parentage. Kerber p. 12 independently identifies this reinterpretation.
edges.map_label: Lerner’s class interpretation of true womanhood

edges.relationship: 'The Cult of True Womanhood' (1966) gave women's historians a much-used account of the nineteenth-century prescriptive ideal built on 'four cardinal virtues' (piety, purity, submissiveness and domesticity), which later historians adapted and contested.
edges.evidence_note: Isenberg (1995), p. 98, gives the 'four cardinal virtues' and the essay's reception; Lerner (1969) shows early use. The framework concerns prescriptions, particularly those for white middle-class women, not a universal account of women's lives. The 1966 article itself is recorded bibliographically (DOI 10.2307/2711179).
edges.map_label: Domestic ideology as an object of women’s history

edges.relationship: Welter’s “The Cult of True Womanhood” (1966) became a framework reassessed in debates about gender and ideology, as Isenberg’s “Second Thoughts on Gender and Women’s History” (1995) shows.
edges.evidence_note: Isenberg pp. 93, 97–99 explicitly places Welter’s essay in the reassessment of separate spheres through gender analysis. This is a later reception route, not a claim that Welter invented the gender category.
edges.map_label: A framework debated in the turn to gender analysis

edges.relationship: In her American Historical Review review (December 1977) of Cott's The Bonds of Womanhood (1977), Welter called it 'a thoughtful, scholarly, and well-written study' that shows through diaries, letters and the mentor literature how women 'saw themselves and their roles'; she judged the section on 'sisterhood' its most original analysis and the work on education and religion the least developed.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, AHR 82.5, December 1977, p. 1327, right-hand column; the review fits on this one page and ends with Welter's signature, 'Barbara Welter, Hunter College, City University of New York'). Phrases seen: 'This is a thoughtful, scholarly, and well-written study of the early Republic'; 'Nancy Cott shows us how these women saw themselves and their roles'; 'The work on education is the least well documented and that on religion the least comprehensive'; 'The most original analysis is in the section on "sisterhood"'; 'This well-researched monograph is a needed addition to the social history of this critical period.' The closing sentence also places the book beside work 'done by Carroll Smith-Rosenberg, Gerda Lerner, Mary Ryan, and others'; that is a reviewer's list and is not used for any edge. Limits: this is a favourable review, so the kind is comparison, not influence. The review does not mention Cott's challenge to Welter's own 'cult of true womanhood' (existing usable edge welter_w_03 runs Cott -> Welter as critique); this edge records the reverse engagement only and claims no reply to that critique. Cott's book itself not reread here.
edges.map_label: Welter reviews Cott's Bonds of Womanhood

edges.relationship: In her Journal of American History review (September 1983) of Ryan's The Empire of the Mother (1982), Welter summarises Ryan's argument that mentor literature conscripted mothers to domesticity as 'the special agents of childhood socialization', converting domestic space into 'an extensive social territory', and comments wryly that it was 'an assignment from which even the bravest "special agents" might flinch'.
edges.evidence_note: Read the opening of the review on the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, JAH 70.2, September 1983, p. 410, lower half; the review runs to p. 411). Bibliographic head: 'The Empire of the Mother: American Writing about Domesticity, 1830-1860. By Mary P. Ryan. (New York: Institute for Research in History/Haworth, 1982.)' Phrases seen in the first paragraph: 'Mary P. Ryan sees mothers as conscripted to domesticity in order to function most effectively as "the special agents of childhood socialization"'; 'Domestic space is thus converted into "an extensive social territory," a veritable moral maternal empire'; 'This is an assignment from which even the bravest "special agents" might flinch.' Reviewer identified by the page metadata as Barbara Welter, Hunter College, CUNY. Limits: p. 411 (the rest of the review and Welter's overall judgement) is unread, so no praise or criticism is claimed beyond the summary and the remark quoted. This review engages Ryan's argument directly, so it is not citation-only.
edges.map_label: Welter reviews Ryan's Empire of the Mother

edges.relationship: In her review of The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949), Beauvoir praises Lévi-Strauss for renewing French sociology through an intelligible account of human institutions.
edges.evidence_note: Read publisher opening extract of Beauvoir’s review, translated in Feminist Writings (2015), chapter spanning pp. 58–66, first four displayed paragraphs. It calls the book a “spectacular awakening” and contrasts its method with earlier French and American approaches. SEP bibliography establishes original 1949 review and Beauvoir’s authorship despite the publisher author-field error. Full review and reviewed book unread; no further claim about agreement with his kinship conclusions.

edges.relationship: As Kristeva reads The Second Sex (1949), Beauvoir objects to Freud’s systematic rejection of choice and to the absence of an originating intentionality in his account of existence.
edges.evidence_note: Kristeva’s 2010 author-posted intervention, opening sequence before Tout compte fait, des rêves, paragraph beginning En définitive: quotes “refus systématique de l’idée de choix” and cites The Second Sex p. 88 in an unspecified edition. Read together with the preceding paragraphs acknowledging Beauvoir’s sympathy with psychosexuality. Mediated reading explicitly attributed to Kristeva; complete Beauvoir chapter and Freud originals unread. Criticism concerns this conception of agency, not a rejection of everything in psychoanalysis.

edges.relationship: In “Beauvoir et la psychanalyse : un défi réciproque” (2010), Kristeva criticizes The Second Sex (1949) for simplifying Freud, including its charge that he neglected the symbolic paternal function, while recognizing Beauvoir’s closeness to Freud on psychosexuality.
edges.evidence_note: Author-posted 2010 conference intervention, opening paragraphs beginning Il n’en reste pas moins and En définitive, before the dream section. Kristeva identifies “simplifications” while crediting Beauvoir’s kinship with Freud on psychosexuality and warning against an anachronistic prosecution. This is a qualified criticism, not wholesale repudiation. Beauvoir’s complete psychoanalysis chapter and Freud’s books unread; only Kristeva’s own argument was directly read.

edges.relationship: The Second Sex (1949) makes women’s historically produced position as Other an explanatory problem for women’s history, as developed in Navarro Antolínez’s historiographical reading (2015).
edges.evidence_note: Navarro Antolínez, section 3, paragraphs beginning Simone de Beauvoir, por su parte and Lo importante de este estudio histórico, notes 45–52: asks “cómo la mujer ha llegado a constituirse en la otra.” Navarro distinguishes biological conditions from social destiny and explains the historical problem. Perrot’s interview provides a specific historian’s uptake. This is a theoretical contribution and named later interpretation, not a claim Beauvoir founded the entire field or that all of her historical claims are accepted. Complete The Second Sex unread.

edges.relationship: Navarro Antolínez’s “De la history a la herstory” (2015) uses The Second Sex (1949), especially its relational account of woman as Other, as a resource for explaining gender as a historical category.
edges.evidence_note: Navarro Antolínez, section 3, paragraphs beginning ¿Qué se puede entender por la categoría género? through Simone de Beauvoir, por su parte and final discussion of historical method, notes 45–58. Article explicitly locates Beauvoir in gender historiography while retaining limits concerning Eurocentrism and binary categories. No assertion that Beauvoir used the later technical vocabulary of gender history or that Navarro’s comparison establishes a personal Scott–Beauvoir relationship. Original Beauvoir monograph unread beyond the publisher excerpt.

edges.relationship: In ‘Variations on Sex and Gender in Beauvoir, Wittig and Foucault’ (1985), Judith Butler draws on Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949) to examine gender as an embodied project within cultural constraints.
edges.evidence_note: Read Jules Gleeson’s substantive account and quoted excerpts on JSTOR Daily. The passage explains Butler’s use of Beauvoir to address choice and cultural construction. This is secondary evidence; the complete 1985 and 1986 essays were not read. No claim that Beauvoir supplied Butler’s entire later theory is proposed.
edges.map_label: Develops gender as an embodied project

edges.relationship: In ‘The Personal and the Political’ (1993), Dorothy Thompson criticizes Beauvoir’s model of independent intellectual lives as unavailable to people choosing children and family.
edges.evidence_note: Read Thompson’s response in the book publisher’s authorized interview excerpt. She explicitly relates her criticism to the independent households of intellectuals and the practical demands of raising children. The passage does not identify a particular Beauvoir book, so the relationship names Thompson’s 1993 interview rather than attributing the criticism to a reading of The Second Sex. The original journal page independently confirms the title and 1993 date; its displayed opening does not contain this exchange.
edges.map_label: Questions independence without provision for children

edges.relationship: In ‘True Philosophers: Beauvoir and bell’ (2012), bell hooks reflects on the influence of Beauvoir’s philosophy and life on her own work and career, according to the publisher’s description.
edges.evidence_note: Read the SUNY Press description and chapter opening displayed by JSTOR. The description expressly identifies hooks’s essay as autobiographical and about Beauvoir’s influence. The full chapter was inaccessible and remains unread. The edge records only this broad retrospective influence; no particular concept, agreement, or criticism is attributed to hooks.

edges.relationship: Looking back in 2015 on Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973), Sheila Rowbotham identifies Beauvoir’s writings as part of her intellectual formation in connecting material life with consciousness.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s first-person retrospective, including the account of the book’s composition and publication. This is an explicit statement about Rowbotham’s intellectual formation within a substantive explanation of the book’s problem, rather than an acknowledgment or an incidental citation. Beauvoir is one of several formative writers named; no exclusive debt or particular Beauvoir title is claimed. The original book was not read.
edges.map_label: Informs the study of material life and consciousness

edges.relationship: Latour’s “Visualisation and Cognition” (1986) uses Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) to develop his account of mobile, stable inscriptions.
edges.evidence_note: Author manuscript pp. 10–12, section C: “mobilization and immutability”; sustained discussion follows. Selected manuscript, not a collation of 1986/1990 versions; Eisenstein’s complete book unread.

edges.relationship: In “Visualisation and Cognition” (1986), Latour objects that Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) leaves the invention of printing itself unexplained.
edges.evidence_note: Author manuscript pp. 12–13: “does not account for the technical innovations themselves.” Distinct criticism within his positive uptake; same version limits as ee_w_01.

edges.relationship: Reviewing The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) in 1981, Chartier calls Eisenstein’s long-term synthesis powerful but questions its ambition to encompass Western society’s transformations since the fifteenth century.
edges.evidence_note: Review p. 192: “sa force” and “sa démesure.” Only pp. 191–192 read; no more specific later objection asserted.
edges.map_label: Power and excess of the synthesis

edges.relationship: Chartier’s 1981 review contrasts Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), which stresses the manuscript-to-print transition, with Goody’s emphasis on the oral-to-written transition.
edges.evidence_note: p. 192, paragraph beginning “La première, celle des anthropologues”: named comparison by Chartier. Goody’s particular title is not specified there; originals unread; no personal exchange or influence inferred.

edges.relationship: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) explains how the circulation and comparison of printed materials helped transform early modern science.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge description explicitly names the rise of modern science; full book unread. Latour’s selected discussion corroborates this reading, but does not independently verify the historical cases.

edges.relationship: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) is “still cited as the seminal work in the cultural history of the book,” as Margaret Eisenstein DeLacy wrote in 2016; a 2007 collection, Agent of Change: Print Culture Studies after Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, took stock of the work that followed it.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). The cited UMass Press page returned 403 to me (WebFetch and curl), so the 'catalytic role' description could not be read. DeLacy's AHA obituary (read) supports a narrower claim. Note that DeLacy writes as a family member (Margaret Eisenstein DeLacy); the claim is attributed to her. Add ee_w_delacy2016 to source_ids. Phrase seen: “"It is still cited as the seminal work in the cultural history of the book."; "Among the most meaningful was Agent of Change: Print Culture Studies after Elizabeth L. Eisenstein (2007)"” Read at: https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/elizabeth-eisenstein-april-2016/

edges.relationship: In “The Rise of the Writer” (1979), Robert Darnton drew upon Elizabeth L. Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) to explain how multiplying and standardizing texts changed literature as a mode of communication.
edges.evidence_note: Read Darnton’s discussion of literary communication on the magazine’s own site, especially the paragraph beginning “Narrative intended directly”. He explains the consequences of standardized, multiplied texts and explicitly attributes that analysis to Eisenstein’s articles and her 1979 book. This is an affirmative use of her argument within his review of John Lough’s Writer and Public in France, rather than a review of Eisenstein’s book. It supports this specific uptake, not a general claim that all of Darnton’s book history derives from Eisenstein.

edges.relationship: Bert Hogenkamp’s 2004 review reports that, in A Social History of the Media (2002), Peter Burke and Asa Briggs weigh Eisenstein’s print-revolution thesis in The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) against its critics, noting that defenders of the thesis too easily forget the survival of oral culture while declining to take sides.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete Hogenkamp review on the journal publisher’s PDF, pp. 143–145. Its sustained discussion names Eisenstein and her book, then explains how Burke and Briggs treat her revolution thesis alongside oral continuity and contextual approaches. The reviewer emphasizes that they see merits on both sides and preserve the long-term explanatory value of the revolution approach. This is a qualified critique reported by a reviewer, not wholesale rejection. The underlying book passage was not read: its licensed preview displayed a viewing restriction. Credit is shared with Asa Briggs; the endpoint is Burke alone because Briggs has no eligible timeline endpoint. This is substantive engagement with Eisenstein, not an edge inferred from textbook co-credits.

edges.relationship: Davin recalls that Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963), especially its primary sources, inspired her decision to study history.
edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, answers beginning “Always watching!” and “We went to Warwick” (HTML paragraphs at lines 249–250): “inspiring”. Retrospective testimony; no claim to a particular argument in Davin’s later books.
edges.map_label: The Making inspired her history studies

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm supervised Davin’s research leading to her childhood thesis (1992); she later recalled disagreement over his demand for more statistics.
edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, paragraph beginning “Being a graduate student” and following answers (lines 280–288): “you need more statistics”. Archive biography dates submission to 1992. Thesis and supervision records unread; this is Davin’s recollection.

edges.relationship: In “Labouring Women” (1979), Davin, Sally Alexander and Eve Hostettler challenged Hobsbawm’s exclusion of wage-earning wives and women’s class agency, as Sonya O. Rose explains.
edges.evidence_note: Rose (1993), printed p. 156, paragraph beginning “This analysis” and notes 53–54: “excluded wage-earning wives” and “participation in class struggle”; note 54 points to reply p. 175. All three coauthors credited. Publisher byline read; original reply body unread. Do not infer that Hobsbawm accepted their criticism.

edges.relationship: Davin and Gareth Stedman Jones were founding coeditors of History Workshop Journal (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Bishopsgate RS 9 finding aid, PDF p. 2, Administrative/Biographical History, lists both among “The first editors”; Taylor (2025), paragraph beginning “History Workshop Journal was started in 1976”, independently confirms. Collective editorship, not a coauthored article or agreement on every position.

edges.relationship: As a founding editor of History Workshop Journal (1976), Davin pursued collective, accessible historical writing, as she recalls in “Making Histories” (2025).
edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, answers to “Was that part of what you were trying to do” and “So the collective” (lines 324–328); “not about the individual but about the collective”. Founding date independently supported by Taylor and archive. Existing History Workshop roster row preserved; no duplicate Anna Davin edge exists.

edges.relationship: With Sally Alexander, Davin made feminist analysis central to the journal’s programme in “Feminist History” (1976), as Kelly Boyd recounts.
edges.evidence_note: Boyd, “Background and founding”, paragraph beginning “Scholars themselves often worked together”, sentence beginning “The first volume” and note 9: “central a feminist analysis”. A named historical reader supports this limited programme claim; original editorial body unread.

edges.relationship: “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978) connected infant welfare and maternal roles to imperial and eugenic politics, an intervention Muggeridge and Davidson identify as pathbreaking.
edges.evidence_note: Muggeridge and Davidson (2026), section I, paragraphs beginning “Anna Davin’s pathbreaking article” and “Davin identified”, notes 6–8: “imperialist and eugenicist discourses”. Substantive reception of the 1978 essay; original and 1997 reprint unread in this assignment. No general derivation of gender history asserted.

edges.relationship: “Labouring Women” (1979), coauthored with Sally Alexander and Eve Hostettler, challenged labour history’s exclusion of married women as workers and participants in class struggle, as Rose explains.
edges.evidence_note: Rose (1993), pp. 155–156, especially p. 156 paragraph beginning “This analysis” and note 54. Field-level methodological intervention distinguished from the personal Hobsbawm critique. The 1979 article is known through this named reader and checked byline; full original unread.
edges.map_label: Married women as workers and class actors

edges.relationship: Growing Up Poor (1996) used autobiographies and interviews from oral-history archives to reconstruct children’s everyday lives, as Dietrich Oberwittler’s review documents.
edges.evidence_note: Oberwittler (1999), p. 761 final paragraph: “Autobiographien und Interviews” and “Oral History-Archive”; p. 762 opening discusses what interview material adds to accounts of poverty. Read complete review in publisher OCR. Book unread; no claim that Davin conducted every interview she used.
edges.map_label: Oral testimony and poor children’s lives

edges.relationship: In his London Review of Books review of Growing Up Poor (1996), Porter praised Davin’s reconstruction of the makeshift family economies and changing role of poor London children, but wished she had been more speculative and had said more about fathers and about charities, churches, clubs and cheap commercial culture.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own site: Roy Porter, “I ain’t a child”, London Review of Books 18, no. 17 (5 September 1996), a single-book review of Growing Up Poor: Home, School and Street 1870–1914 (Rivers Oram, 1996). Paragraph 1 (beginning “Anna Davin has risen admirably to the challenges facing the historian of working-class life in London”) praises her handling of Booth, school records, autobiography and her own oral-history tapes. Paragraph 6 (“She has done so with a strong historical sympathy”) says she “carefully reconstructs old makeshift ways” and aims “to trace the changing role of children in the family economy”; paragraph 7 states “Davin’s point” that the new domestic order “took hold only slowly and after protracted conflict”. Paragraph 17 of 18 carries the criticism: “Davin sticks close to her sources, and sometimes one hankers after a more speculative style”, adding that more might have been said about the role of fathers and about “charities and churches, clubs and cheap commercial culture”, and regretting that Steedman’s Strange Dislocations (1995) appeared too late for her to use; the paragraph closes in praise (“intimate, intense and often poignant”). A mixed review that engages the book’s argument, so critique rather than comparison. Porter’s comparisons with Anna Clark, Carolyn Steedman and Stedman Jones are his own framing and are not proposed as Davin relationships. Davin’s book was not reread for this edge.

edges.relationship: Anna Davin’s ‘Imperialism and Motherhood’ (1978) helped establish historical study of maternity care by examining infant welfare, imperial and eugenic concerns, and class tensions between mothers and reformers, as assessed by Anna Muggeridge and Ruth Davidson (2026).
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open body text and relevant notes. The authors identify Davin’s analysis of early maternity provision and its subsequent uptake. This supports a contribution to medical and health history specifically through maternity and infant welfare. It does not establish influence on every later author mentioned. The pre-existing women’s and gender-history pairs are excluded.

edges.relationship: As Talia Bettcher explains, Butler’s Bodies That Matter (1993) responds to hooks’s “Is Paris Burning?” (1992) by stressing that performance can reproduce and subvert dominant norms together.
edges.evidence_note: Bettcher, section 5.2, paragraphs beginning “Butler also allows,” “Butler’s discussion,” and “Butler, by contrast”; adjacent 5.3 retains criticism of Butler. Mediated reading only: both original Paris essays unread. No claim that Butler considers every drag performance subversive.

edges.relationship: In Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984), hooks challenges feminist accounts, beginning with Friedan's, that treat the situation of college-educated, middle- and upper-class white women as universal and assume a common oppression of all women.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter-1 preview, opening Friedan discussion and paragraph beginning “A central tenet”; no stable pagination. “Common oppression” is contested; full book unread. Adjacent theory challenges historical generalization.

edges.relationship: Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) connects racial hierarchy and capitalist class relations in explaining differences among women.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter-1 preview, paragraphs beginning “Yet class structure” and “White women who dominate”; selected primary argument, not authorship of Crenshaw’s later term or full-book reading.

edges.relationship: In “Postmodern Blackness” (1990), hooks challenges postmodern theory’s exclusion of Black women while retaining antiessentialism as a resource for resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Complete official journal essay read; paragraphs beginning “As a discursive practice,” “The failure to recognize,” “Criticisms of directions,” and “Employing a critique.” “Multiple black identities” preserves her positive use of antiessentialism. This is a bounded theory intervention, not rejection of all poststructuralism or participation in a historians’ truth debate.

edges.relationship: In “Feminist Killjoys (And Other Willful Subjects)” (2010), Sara Ahmed draws on hooks’s Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) for her account of the angry Black woman as a figure who is felt to kill feminist joy.
edges.evidence_note: Read Ahmed’s complete essay on the journal’s own site (S&F Online 8.3, Summer 2010, Barnard Center for Research on Women), print version; the passage is on page 4 of 8 of the paged version, section “Feminist Tables”, paragraphs beginning “After all, feminist spaces are emotional spaces” and “It is not just that feelings are ‘in tension’”, notes 10–11. Ahmed places the feminist killjoy beside “the figure of the angry Black woman, explored so well by Black feminist writers such as Audre Lorde and bell hooks”, quotes hooks’s description of a meeting where “the atmosphere will noticeably change when a woman of color enters the room” (n. 11: hooks, p. 56, citing the 2000 Pluto edition of Feminist Theory) and builds her analysis of affective tension on it. The body text engages hooks’s account; it is not a citation-only note. Lorde is named alongside; no claim that hooks is Ahmed’s only resource. hooks’s book not reread here for this edge.
edges.map_label: Ahmed builds on hooks’s angry Black woman

edges.relationship: hooks and Hall co-authored Uncut Funk: A Contemplative Dialogue (2018), a book of conversations begun in 1996 on conversation and writing, feminism and Marxism, home and kinship, and the costs of Black intellectual life in the academy; in a 2024 review, Tzarina T. Prater reports that hooks’s preface calls Hall “the closer kin”.
edges.evidence_note: Read in full Tzarina T. Prater’s review “Conversations between the Closer Kin” (SX Salon, Small Axe, February 2024), the journal’s own open review page. Its bibliographic head gives “bell hooks and Stuart Hall, Uncut Funk: A Contemplative Dialogue (London: Routledge, 2018)”. The paragraph beginning “When I started reading Uncut Funk” dates the conversations to 1996 and names Paul Gilroy’s foreword. Paragraphs beginning “They begin their discourse” and “Their ‘conversation’ is wide ranging” describe the exchange, with page references to the book. The paragraph beginning “Despite her confession in her short preface” reports that hooks identifies Hall as “the closer kin”. The reviewer also notes asymmetries (“hooks functions more as interviewer than dialogue partner” at moments). The book itself is unread: claims of content are limited to the review. This is a co-authored substantive work (contribution, undirected), not an influence claim. It does not restore held bh_w_02 (Hall’s representation argument in “The Oppositional Gaze”), which remains unread on a permitted route.

edges.relationship: In Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the ‘Politics of Recognition’ in Canada (2009), Glen Sean Coulthard draws on hooks’s Yearning: Race, Gender and Cultural Politics (1990) to articulate a politics of self-recognition directed away from dependence on recognition by the settler state.
edges.evidence_note: Read Coulthard’s conclusion on pp. 71–72 and note 129 in his university-deposited dissertation. He incorporates hooks’s argument into his own proposed alternative to state-centred recognition. Yearning itself was not read; the claim concerns Coulthard’s explicit use. Scholarly argument only; no community knowledge is reproduced.

edges.relationship: White and Marisa J. Fuentes coedited Scarlet and Black, Volume 1: Slavery and Dispossession in Rutgers History (2016), a collective investigation of Rutgers’s institutional past.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher page: title/editor credits; publication details, 20 December 2016; description; complete contents. Credits say “Edited by” both scholars; White separately wrote the introduction. Chapter findings belong to their named authors. Chapters unread; neither sole authorship nor personal intellectual influence is claimed.

edges.relationship: White served on the board of senior editors for Black Women in America, second edition (2005), edited by Darlene Clark Hine alongside a larger editorial team.
edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s participant-authored page, final Black Women in America section: Hine is editor; White is listed on the “Board of Senior Editors.” The roles are distinct. Rutgers also names their collaboration but gives 2004; the participant’s edition date is 2005. Entries unread.

edges.relationship: Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985) made enslaved women’s productive and reproductive labor central to explaining slavery’s place in American history, an emphasis White restates in her Rutgers interview.
edges.evidence_note: Lamiell interview, first question and White’s first answer: slavery was sustained “through the wombs” of African American women as well as their labor. Intro identifies the 1985 book. The displayed 1969 date is invalid and unused. Full monograph unread; retrospective testimony supports this contribution.

edges.relationship: In “Female Slaves” (1983), White argued that women’s resources and cooperation created a partly autonomous female world and matrifocal family relations within plantation slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences on work/resources, female cooperation and conclusions; short phrase “slave families were matrifocal.” Abstract only, not a fresh reading of the article body. Its 1994 reprint is separately identified in Half Sisters of History; no universal account of all slave societies is claimed.

edges.relationship: White’s edited Telling Histories (2008) used Black women historians’ autobiographical essays to examine exclusion and the making of the profession, a contribution Linda Wynn identifies in her 2010 review.
edges.evidence_note: Wynn review: paragraph introducing seventeen contributors; paragraphs beginning “Engagingly written” and “Even though the essayists.” She explains the collection’s historiographical value and questions of researcher identification. Full collection unread; this is attributed review evidence, with White’s editorial role preserved.

edges.relationship: With Fuentes and a collective of researchers, White’s Scarlet and Black (2016) brought Rutgers’s involvement in slavery into public institutional history and framed that research as a resource for the university’s future.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description’s final paragraph calls the collective history “a usable one”; contents credit White’s reconciliation introduction. Coeditor and contributor credits read. Chapter bodies unread. This projects White’s documented role alongside the existing Fuentes-to-public-history route; it does not duplicate that edge or attribute all findings to either editor.

edges.relationship: In her introduction to Telling Histories (2008), Deborah Gray White extends Darlene Clark Hine's argument that twentieth-century Black women developed a culture of dissemblance as a defense against rape, suggesting that the same mindset was one of the factors that kept educated Black women from writing anything but celebratory history.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed introduction excerpt through its final, truncated paragraph. Immediately after note 19, White names Hine’s explanation of protective concealment and then writes, “I suggest that this same conscious and unconscious mindset”, applying it to historical writing. The proposed debt concerns that application alone. The continuation and Hine’s underlying essay were not read. This differs from the existing encyclopedia editorial credit.

edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2005), Lerner identifies reading Beard’s Woman as Force in History (1946) as a formative source for treating women as historical agents, including differences and conflicts among women.
edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 12–13 (PDF pages 20–21), paragraph beginning “I had first read Mary Beard’s”: calls Beard her “principal mentor” as a historian while explicitly saying they never met. She retains reservations about Beard and adapts rather than simply repeats the argument. Woman as Force in History was not freshly read; its original 1946 date is independently retained in the existing Beard node and source record.
edges.map_label: Beard’s agency argument and intellectual mentorship

edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2005), Lerner recalls developing the interdisciplinary foundation course for Sarah Lawrence’s women’s-history MA programme with Joan Kelly-Gadol, Sherry Ortner and Eva Kollisch after establishing the programme in 1972.
edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 14 (PDF page 22), paragraph beginning “In 1972 I established”: the course was “team-taught” by all four named teachers and combined lectures, seminars, tutorials and student research. Kerber and Kessler-Harris (2013), paragraph beginning “Working with Renaissance historian Joan Kelly,” independently identifies programme development with Kelly. Kelly-Gadol is the queued joan_kelly identity. This is collaboration, not intellectual descent or a claim that two people alone taught the course. Original course materials unread.
edges.map_label: Joint development and teaching of women’s history

edges.relationship: Hunter’s 1988 review identifies Lévi-Strauss’s account of the exchange of women as a theoretical resource that Lerner reworks, alongside Engels, in The Creation of Patriarchy (1986).
edges.evidence_note: Hunter, p. 240, paragraphs beginning “There is more” and “What role”: names Lévi-Strauss and describes the synthesis with Engels as “she has wed the two.” Mediated evidence from a substantive named reader. Neither Lerner’s monograph nor Lévi-Strauss’s relevant text was read here; Hunter does not identify a particular Lévi-Strauss edition. No unqualified adoption, exclusive influence or agreement with all structuralism is asserted.
edges.map_label: Exchange of women reworked in a historical explanation

edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2020), Kerber credits Lerner’s perspective and pioneering work with providing later professional mentorship after Hofstadter’s death.
edges.evidence_note: Kerber’s own lecture, printed 9 (PDF page 21), paragraph beginning “Many people find their professional mentors”: explicitly assigns Lerner that role and describes her work as “a lodestar.” Kerber says she did not send Lerner drafts; no manuscript supervision or doctoral supervision is claimed. The full corpus of either historian’s work remains unread. Separate from the existing Hofstadter-to-Kerber edge_2234, whose evidence already mentions this later relationship but does not represent it as a Lerner edge.

edges.relationship: In her undated memorial “Biography,” Gordon identifies herself as Lerner’s co-director of the University of Wisconsin women’s-history programme until Lerner retired, and recalls working with her daily.
edges.evidence_note: Gordon, paragraphs beginning “At Wisconsin she took the job” and “I had the privilege,” and the author identification immediately after her signature: explicit “co-director” credit until Lerner retired. The text dates Gordon’s recruitment to 1984, but its sixteen-year recollection is not used to construct a duration. No publication date is displayed. Co-direction and pedagogical work, not employment alone, support this undirected collaboration. Programme records and teaching materials unread.

edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner calls for challenging what she regards as ahistoricity in influential theories of Simone de Beauvoir.
edges.evidence_note: Final theoretical-priorities section, paragraph beginning “We could, to begin with”: explicitly names Beauvoir alongside broader theoretical currents and uses “ahistoricity.” It is Lerner’s programmatic criticism, not an independently demonstrated defect in Beauvoir. No particular Beauvoir work is named, so The Second Sex is not silently supplied; Beauvoir’s works remain unread. The endpoint is another person in this run.
edges.map_label: Calls for historically contextualizing Beauvoir’s theory

edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner treats Smith-Rosenberg’s insights into women’s homoerotic relationships as a resource for further research, while questioning whether she has said the last word and calling for tests against other primary sources.
edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA article, paragraph beginning “On the subject of differences.” Lerner asks whether Smith-Rosenberg has said the last word, then proposes testing her insights against other sources. Retain the incoming resource classification but make its questioning explicit; this is neither blanket acceptance nor an assertion that Lerner completed such a test. No particular Smith-Rosenberg title is identified in this passage.
edges.map_label: Insights questioned and proposed for testing

edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner proposes documentary recovery, interpretation from women’s perspectives, comparison among women and reconstruction of historical concepts as a programme for women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Paragraphs beginning “These fall into four categories,” “Please notice,” and “The third point”: first priority is “Restoring and documenting the female past”; she opposes premature incorporation into an unchanged general narrative and makes differences among women analytically central. The essay is a situated intervention based on a 1987 paper; its statistical tables were not audited. Existing women/identity roster contexts and group edge_090 are retained. The new personal edge identifies Lerner’s own contribution without making her the field’s sole founder.
edges.map_label: Recovery, differences and a revised historical framework

edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner proposes comparing women across class and race and relating changing gender definitions to changing economic and social conditions.
edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning “For example, a comparison” explicitly links comparative work to gender and class formation; paragraph beginning “We might ask some basic transforming questions” asks about “changing gender definitions” and economic and social conditions. This is an analytic programme, not evidence that Lerner accepted every later version of gender history. Gordon’s memorial separately records her misgivings about a turn that displaced women as collective subjects. Group edge_091 already connects women’s history to gender history; this proposal records the named author’s distinct intervention.
edges.map_label: Historically situated gender, class and race analysis

edges.relationship: Black Women in White America: A Documentary History (1972) assembled primary sources and a bibliographic guide for researching African American women; Lerner’s A Life of Learning (2005) describes its role in developing that scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 15–16 (PDF pages 23–24), paragraphs beginning “During my research on this book” and “I am happy to say”: describes the source collection and bibliographic essay. Gordon’s memorial, paragraphs beginning “She devoted the rest of her life” and “It was her second book,” corroborates its research use. The anthology itself is unread. This is a contribution within Black history, not the origin of Black history or a priority claim over earlier Black scholars. Existing black node and its independent roots inspected.
edges.map_label: Documentary resources for African American women’s history

edges.relationship: Discussing The Creation of Patriarchy (1986) and The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993) in her undated “Biography,” Gordon identifies tension between their Marxist and radical-feminist explanations, calling the account of exclusion from education and historical knowledge non-materialist.
edges.evidence_note: Gordon, paragraph beginning “To do this massive study”: says the “two theoretical strands argue with each other” and calls the education-and-knowledge explanation “a most non-materialist claim.” The following paragraph connects this to Lerner’s advocacy of women’s history. A sympathetic but specific critical reading, not wholesale rejection. Both monographs remain unread; no original date is supplied for the undated memorial. Separate argument from the co-direction relationship.
edges.map_label: Gordon on competing explanations of subordination

edges.relationship: In Women, Race & Class (1981), Angela Y. Davis drew upon the analysis of rape in Gerda Lerner’s Black Women in White America (1972), crediting Lerner with examining racism and sexism together in Black women’s experiences.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed Google Books search extract of Davis’s body paragraph on p. 174. Davis explicitly identifies Lerner as the author of the passage under discussion and singles out her combined analysis of racism and sexism in writing about rape. Also read the 1983 preview’s search extract of p. 266, note 4, identifying Lerner’s Black Women in White America, p. 193 (https://books.google.com/books?jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Lerner&vid=iCknYRPikTEC). The complete p. 174 was restricted and remains unread; this proposal rests on the displayed body extract and identifying note, not a full-chapter reading. It records a specific use, not a general intellectual debt or agreement with Lerner’s entire collection. Original publication in 1981 is confirmed by the Google Books record for the Random House edition (https://books.google.com/books/about/Women_Race_Class.html?id=lye5AAAAIAAJ); 2011 and 1983 are the consulted reprint dates.
edges.map_label: Davis draws on Lerner’s analysis of racism, sexism and rape

edges.relationship: In her 1995 review of Gerda Lerner’s The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993), Lynn Hunt contrasted Lerner’s broad historical synthesis with the small-scale social history and microhistory then prevalent among historians.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s metadata and visually read its first-page preview, printed p. 675. The top of that page concludes a different review; Hunt’s review begins below the bibliographical heading for Lerner’s book. Hunt contrasts contemporary historians’ narrowing scales with Lerner’s two-volume synthesis and asks whether the book signals renewed grand synthesis or calls for caution about generalization. Only p. 675 was available; pp. 676–677 remain unread. The comparison classification records the review and this specific discussion of scale; it does not attribute a final favorable or unfavorable verdict to Hunt. No directed influence or definite criticism is inferred from the opening questions.
edges.map_label: Hunt reviews Lerner’s return to broad historical synthesis

edges.relationship: In her published education interview (2024), Collins credits Du Bois’s historical and sociological scholarship with sharpening her approach to critical education.
edges.evidence_note: First response, Harvard-training paragraph: “sharpened my critical education toolkit.” Specific Du Bois work and date unidentified; original scholarship unread here. This is retrospective testimony, not a teacher–student relationship.

edges.relationship: Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) treats Black women's thought, developed outside elite institutions and in Black women's own communities and political work, as critical social theory, as Collins describes it in 2019 and in a 2024 interview.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). Duke University Press's own preview of the 2019 book (introduction p. 3) and the open SciELO interview (Collins: 'Black Feminist Thought presents numerous examples of how education constitutes a site of Black women's political engagement'; 'I examine how Black women have developed a series of safe spaces that enabled Black feminist thought to flourish') support a narrower contribution. Replace the source_ids with phcw_theory_2019 and phcw_interview_2024. Phrase seen: “in previous work, I examined Black feminist thought as an example of critical social theory that did not come from elites (Collins 1998a; 2000)” Read at: https://assets-us-01.kc-usercontent.com/f7ca9afb-82c2-002a-a423-84e111d5b498/f0698fc2-2ecb-46cb-8cc8-335f7535c0bb/978-1-4780-0646-6_601.pdf
edges.map_label: Black women's thought as social theory

edges.relationship: In a 2019 interview about Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), published in Tempo Social in 2021, Collins says that Smith’s framework for decolonizing methodology (Decolonizing Methodologies, 1999) develops the kind of intellectual and political praxis that intersectionality needs.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete English interview PDF on Tempo Social’s own site (Tempo Social 33:1, 2021, pp. 323–355; interview held at USP on 29 October 2019). On p. 333, ending her answer to Marcos Nobre on methodology and praxis, Collins says: “Linda Tuhiwai Smith’s framework for decolonizing methodology develops the kind of intellectual and political praxis needed for intersectionality (Smith, 1999)”. The reference list (p. 354) gives Decolonizing Methodologies (Zed, 1999). This is an explicit, named intellectual resource stated by Collins, not an acknowledgment list. Smith’s name also appears among people thanked in the 2019 acknowledgments (Duke preview, p. x), which is not counted. Unread: the corresponding passage in the 2019 book. OCAP: the edge concerns Smith’s published research methodology only; it states no community knowledge or identity.

edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins places Beauvoir’s analyses of oppression and freedom in dialogue with Pauli Murray’s, arguing that Beauvoir, though familiar with oppressions of race, gender, class and sexuality, never advanced an intersectional analysis; in a 2019 interview she describes this as engaging Beauvoir’s ideas rather than criticizing her.
edges.evidence_note: Two permitted readings. (1) Duke University Press’s own preview of the 2019 book, introduction pp. 13–14, chapter summary beginning “In Chapter 6, ‘Intersectionality and the Question of Freedom’”: “Placing the ideas of two feminist intellectuals in dialogue”, and “despite being familiar with oppressions of race, gender, class, and sexuality, Beauvoir never advanced an intersectional analysis of oppression or freedom”. (2) Tempo Social interview (2021), pp. 337–338: Collins says she gives “a close reading of the work of Simone de Beauvoir” (The Ethics of Ambiguity, 1947; The Second Sex, 1949), juxtaposes it with Pauli Murray, and that “My goal was not to criticize Beauvoir to make room for my own arguments, but rather to engage her ideas as a way of pushing my own.” The chapter body is unread, so the claim is limited to Collins’s own summaries. The chapter number differs: 6 in the book’s introduction, 5 in the interview; the edge follows the book. Typed as a comparison because Collins herself disclaims a critique. Same pair as held beauvoir_w_06 (Beauvoir packet: Collins’s 2017 chapter, publisher summary only): this edge rests on a different work and a different route.

edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins develops intersectionality as a critical social theory in the making, distinguishing its core concepts from its guiding principles and mapping the field through how people use it; the book follows her earlier mapping of the field with Margaret Andersen in Race, Class, and Gender.
edges.evidence_note: Duke University Press preview, introduction p. 9 (“As a critical social theory in the making, intersectionality has a stake in clarifying what being critical means for its own project”, read on pp. 8–9) and pp. 17–18 (through nine editions of Race, Class, and Gender, “Margaret Andersen and I … effectively mapping the field every three years”). Tempo Social interview (2021), p. 332: “I chose to map the field by examining how people used intersectionality” and “in chapter 1, I finally was able to distinguish intersectionality’s core concepts from its guiding principles”. Supplementary: Keisha Jefferies’s review of Collins and Bilge, Intersectionality (2nd ed., 2020), Atlantis 41.2 (2020), p. 100, praises its “informative and fulsome discussion of the genealogy of intersectionality”. Limits: book chapters unread beyond the introduction. The edge makes no claim that Collins originated the term; Crenshaw’s term and the earlier Black feminist roots stay as the existing node describes them.

edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins examines the critical theory of the Frankfurt school, with British cultural studies and Francophone social theory, as a site of critical social theory against which she clarifies intersectionality’s own critical project; in 2019 she said the Frankfurt School “rightfully claims the term ‘Critical Theory’”.
edges.evidence_note: Duke preview, introduction p. 9, summary of chapter 2, “What’s Critical about Critical Social Theory?”: “I examine three particular sites of critical social theory … critical theory of the Frankfurt school (1930s–1940s), British cultural studies (1970s–1980s), and strands of Francophone social theory (1950s–1960s)”. Tempo Social interview (2021), p. 331, answering Marcos Nobre’s question on the Frankfurt School: “the Frankfurt School rightfully claims the term ‘Critical Theory’ and does incorporate praxis into their framework … My selection of critical theories was deliberate.” Chapter 2 itself is unread; the claim is limited to Collins’s own summaries. No claim of membership in or debt to the School. British cultural studies is named in the same sentence but is not proposed as a separate edge (see edge_search_log).

edges.relationship: In “Theorising power and resistance under contemporary capitalism” (2024), Fraser describes Collins’s Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019) as a critical theoretical account and relates Collins’s aim of explaining how gender, race and class co-constitute one another to her own analysis of these divisions within capitalist society.
edges.evidence_note: Read the open interview on the journal publisher’s own site. In the answer to Charles Masquelier’s question about the post-intersectional subtitle of her first Benjamin Lecture, Fraser explicitly appraises Collins’s account as critical theoretical. In the seventh paragraph of that answer she connects her own effort to explain gender, race and class within capitalist society with Collins’s aim of explaining their co-constitution. The question and the following interviewer turn identify the 2019 book; the reference list abbreviates its title. This is substantive named engagement, not a shared-topic inference. Classified as an undirected comparison: Fraser’s subsequent reservation about the depth of explanation in existing intersectionality theory is general, so it is not represented as a criticism specifically of Collins.
