No claim about Collins’s response to Fraser or about influence in the other direction. Collins’s book and Fraser’s Benjamin Lectures were not read in this pass.

edges.relationship: In “A Feminist Army” (2016), Sara Ahmed draws on Collins’s Black Feminist Thought (1990; citing the revised 2000 edition) to examine how Sojourner Truth challenges racial exclusions in the category of woman, while acknowledging the mediation of the surviving speech account.
edges.evidence_note: Ahmed engages Collins’s interpretation in the essay’s body, with citations to pages 12–13. This supports a specific interpretive resource, not a general intellectual genealogy. Collins’s book was not read for this task.
edges.map_label: Uses Collins’s reading of Sojourner Truth

edges.relationship: For Slum Travelers (2007), Ross credits Walkowitz’s readings of the introduction and suggestion for its clothing discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments, opening paragraph: “wardrobes of the slummers.” Indexed publisher extract only; book unread.

edges.relationship: In Slum Travelers (2007), Ross identifies Davin’s engagement with working-class London as an inspiration.
edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments, opening paragraph: “constant inspiration.” Indexed extract only; no particular Davin text identified.

edges.relationship: In “Sex and Society” (1981), Ross and Rayna Rapp explicitly adopt Foucault’s historical account of what counts as sexual.
edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core, displayed note 2: “We agree with Foucault’s contention.” Explicit joint attribution, not a claim about Ross alone. The note cites the 1978 English translation of The History of Sexuality, volume 1 (French original 1976); opening and notes read, complete article and Foucault volume unread.

edges.relationship: Ross and Walkowitz coauthored “Raphael Samuel (1934–1996): An Appreciation” (1997).
edges.evidence_note: Walkowitz institutional CV, p. 3, publication beginning With Ellen Ross. Authorship and year only; appreciation unread. This undirected collaboration differs from Walkowitz’s contribution to the 2007 introduction.

edges.relationship: Love and Toil (1993) makes mothers’ household choices central to working-class survival and cultural continuity.
edges.evidence_note: Oxford publisher abstract read: “survival and cultural perpetuation.” Book unread; a bounded statement of its announced intervention, not evidence of universal uptake.

edges.relationship: Love and Toil (1993) reconstructs the distinctive experience of poor London mothers; Slum Travelers (2007) recovers women’s writings on urban poverty.
edges.evidence_note: 1993 publisher abstract and 2007 publisher description/contents read. Monograph and anthology unread in full; distinct research and editorial contributions, not a founding claim.
edges.map_label: Mothers’ lives and women’s urban writing

edges.relationship: In her 2020 review of Emma Griffin’s Bread Winner, Jane Humphries drew upon Ellen Ross’s Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993) as an earlier study using autobiography to explain working-class motherhood, in arguing that Griffin needed to engage with preceding research on families and deprivation.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s print version of Humphries’s review. Humphries identifies Ross’s method and substantive achievement in the body of her argument about insufficient engagement with earlier research; this is more than a bibliography entry or a list of names. The claim is limited to Humphries’s use of Ross as a historiographical precedent in this review. It does not establish formative influence on Humphries’s earlier books. Jane Humphries is present in the supplied run-members list and therefore carries pending_endpoint: true. Neither Ross’s book nor Griffin’s book was read in full for this task.
edges.map_label: Earlier study used to assess Bread Winner, 2020

edges.relationship: Ellen Ross’s Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993) contributed to the history of motherhood by analysing class tensions between working-class mothers and women working in infant welfare organizations, an argument identified by Anna Muggeridge and Ruth Davidson in their 2026 historiographical review.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s open article introduction and its discussion of maternalism, including the named argument and footnote 8. The authors attribute the argument jointly to Dyhouse, Lewis, and Ross; the edge does not claim Ross originated it alone. The demography endpoint explicitly includes the history of the family and intimate relations. This proposal concerns motherhood and maternal welfare within that scope, not demographic measurement or family reconstitution. The text substantively explains Ross’s argument in the body rather than merely listing a citation. No claim of having read Love and Toil in full is made.
edges.map_label: Class tensions in histories of motherhood, 1993

edges.relationship: In her 1994 Albion review, Steedman placed Love and Toil (1993) within research on women's reproduction of everyday life and noted its dependence on earlier women investigators' records.
edges.evidence_note: Albion 26:3 (1994), pp. 550–551, first page read on Cambridge Core at verification. A published review engaging the argument; added from Fable's review (F09-015).
edges.map_label: Steedman's review of Love and Toil

edges.relationship: In Shopping for Pleasure (2000), Rappaport uses Thompson’s account of customary protest to interpret retailers’ charivari against William Whiteley.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter-one opening, paragraph beginning The appearance of a charivari, note 2: “rough-shod over local custom”. Underlying Thompson text unidentified in the displayed notes and unread; specific use only.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport names Mintz’s sugar history among the resources on which her account builds.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “build upon”; Mintz named. Book body and endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport names de Vries’s industrious revolution among her resources for early modern commodity history.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “industrious revolution”. Book body and endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport applies Beckert’s war capitalism to colonial tea cultivation.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 12: “war capitalism”. Book body and endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport draws on Appleby’s contingent account of capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 12: “historical creation”. Book body and endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport identifies Appadurai’s commodity biographies as a resource for the inquiry she develops.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13: “global biographies”. Book body and endnotes unread; bounded conceptual resource.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport follows Cooper’s advice to distinguish long-distance connections from inevitable globalization.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 15–16: “I have followed his suggestions”. Book body and endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: Shopping for Pleasure (2000) explains the making of women’s urban public culture through commerce, law and contested femininity.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, paragraphs 1–3; licensed chapter-one opening. “female urban culture”. Full book unread; a substantive contribution, not a founding claim.

edges.relationship: In the jointly authored introduction to Consuming Behaviours (2015), Rappaport, Dawson and Crowley treat consumer identities as historical and connect consumption with political regulation and international exchange.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–4, especially p. 3, final two paragraphs: “historical category”. Joint authorship; remainder unread.

edges.relationship: In Buying and Becoming (2003), Deborah Cohen reviews Erika Rappaport’s Shopping for Pleasure (2000) alongside two other books, interpreting their shared emphasis on consumption as a source of British middle-class identities, particularly women’s identities.
edges.evidence_note: Only the publisher’s substantive opening extract was read. Its characterization applies collectively to three books. This records a published review, without inferring intellectual debt or a specific criticism of Rappaport from the unread remainder. Cohen is a run member.

edges.relationship: In A Thirst for Empire (2017), Rappaport contributes to world history by combining comparative and connective approaches to tea’s markets and consumer cultures, foregrounding distribution and publicity in accounts of globalization.
edges.evidence_note: Read selected publisher-sample passages, especially pp. 14–16; the full book remains unread. This records a stated methodological intervention. Nierstrasz’s complete 2018 review was also read: he praises the research but questions whether its British-imperial concentration realizes its global ambition. No claim of comprehensive worldwide coverage is made.

edges.relationship: Christensen and Ivarsson identify A Thirst for Empire (2017) as a contribution to histories of capitalism that connects local interactions in the tea industry to global networks, while questioning its explanation of capitalism at the macro level.
edges.evidence_note: Read the substantive discussion and surrounding argument. The authors praise the interactions she reconstructs but question capitalism’s structural specificity. Neither author has an eligible endpoint; only the field contribution is proposed.

edges.relationship: Tilly and Scott coauthored Women, Work, and Family (1978), challenging an account of women’s employment as the expression of growing individualism.
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s retrospective, publisher abstract, final sentence; AHA bibliography confirms original 1978 joint authorship. “exchange of hundreds of letters” describes their collaboration. Full retrospective, correspondence and book unread.

edges.relationship: Louise and Charles Tilly, with Richard Tilly, coauthored The Rebellious Century, 1830–1930 (1975).
edges.evidence_note: Hanagan and Maynes, opening extract, second sentence and 1975 bibliographic reference; AHA bibliography independently lists all three authors. “along with Charles and Richard Tilly” establishes the joint work. Book unread; no individual allocation of arguments asserted.

edges.relationship: In “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989), as Varikas reads it in 1995, Tilly disputes Scott’s deconstructionist approach for overstating constraint and diminishing explanations of changes in power.
edges.evidence_note: Varikas, publisher extract, final two displayed paragraphs: “overestimate the weight of social constraint.” Read as an attributed scholarly account; the full 1989 English essay and its Italian version remain unread. Both historians’ demand for analytical gender history is retained.

edges.relationship: In his response to Tilly’s “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985), Paul Thompson (1985) disputes her generalization about oral historians and her separation of social relationships from psychological understanding.
edges.evidence_note: Individually signed Thompson response, printed 19–21 (PDF 17–19), freshly read by OCR in the authorized scan: “gross simplifications.” He agrees with part of her programme but rejects a single prescribed method. Tilly’s reprinted conclusion, 16–17 (PDF 14–15), was also read; Thompson’s books unread.

edges.relationship: Responding to Tilly’s “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985), Luisa Passerini (1985) argues that actions and social networks themselves manifest subjectivity and that subjective processes can be historically analysed.
edges.evidence_note: Passerini’s signed response, printed 21–25 (PDF 19–23), especially 22–24: “manifestations of subjectivity.” Full response read by OCR; no oral testimony reproduced. Does not assert that Tilly rejects all oral evidence. Tilly’s complete rejoinder was not read.

edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly uses E. P. Thompson’s concern with ordinary people’s agency to frame her own social history.
edges.evidence_note: Primary opening, paragraphs 1–6; notes 1–3 identify The Making of the English Working Class (1963) and other works. “With his work in mind” is explicit. Named inspiration, not complete agreement; Thompson works unread here.

edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly identifies Hobsbawm’s Industry and Empire (1968) as an influence on her research on industrialization.
edges.evidence_note: Primary note 8: “strongly influenced”; note 4 also acknowledges Hobsbawm. Collective credit with Landes and Wolf, not sole derivation. Cited book unread.
edges.map_label: Industry and Empire as a resource

edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly names Natalie Zemon Davis among the teachers and colleagues to whom her approach to social history is indebted.
edges.evidence_note: Primary note 4: “owes much”; Davis appears in a list, without a particular work. This establishes an acknowledgment, not formal dissertation supervision or exclusive influence.

edges.relationship: In “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989), Tilly calls for problem-solving women’s history whose findings change the questions asked by historians generally.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher opening extract, two concluding sentences, printed opening at 439: “analytical problem-solving studies.” Full article unread. This is a methodological proposal, not mere addition of women to an unchanged narrative.

edges.relationship: With Scott, Tilly questions the opposition between unproductive domesticity and productive employment in “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975).
edges.evidence_note: Publisher extract, opening paragraph at 36; “women at home” are described as being wrongly assumed non-productive. Original issue January 1975. Joint argument; full article and its quantitative evidence unread. Existing labour roster retained; no individual Tilly edge already exists.

edges.relationship: As Cohen explains, the collection The European Experience of Declining Fertility (1992), coedited by Tilly, John Gillis and David Levine, links declining birthrates to changing childrearing attitudes and political, economic and cultural conditions.
edges.evidence_note: Cohen, main-text paragraph beginning “Tilly’s co-edited collection,” with note 5; Hanagan and Maynes bibliography confirms all three editors and 1992. “new attitudes” is the limited explanatory claim. Collection unread; contribution is editorial and collectively credited.

edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly links cotton workers’ family and gender relations in India, England and France through industrialization and imperial economic connections.
edges.evidence_note: Primary opening and synthesis, paragraphs beginning “The interaction of pre-factory” and “A web of connections”; note 7 defines the larger project. “ongoing interplay” distinguishes connection from parallel national cases. Selected passages, not the full address or its source books, read.

edges.relationship: In Working Families (1993), Bettina Bradbury challenges the claim in Louise Tilly and Joan Scott’s Women, Work, and Family (1978) that single women have few competing claims on their time, as Yukari Takai explicitly reports in 2001.
edges.evidence_note: Read Takai’s journal text, especially pp. 129–132. The body explicitly attributes the challenge to Bradbury and then tests it against Lowell evidence about single daughters’ domestic and caring duties. This is a documented criticism reported by another scholar, not an inference from a bibliography. Bradbury’s Working Families (1993), p. 142, and the cited edition of Tilly and Scott were not read directly. The 1978 original year is distinguished from the 1987 reprint identified on Takai’s p. 128. The claim is limited to this particular assertion about single women’s time.

edges.relationship: In A Crooked Line (2005), Geoff Eley welcomes Louise Tilly’s rethinking of work and politics but criticises its continued materialist basis, placing Women, Work, and Family (1978) within that methodological divide.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed chapter preview, printed pp. 116–123, especially p. 122. Eley approvingly discusses Tilly’s conceptual questions before stating his reservation and naming the 1978 coauthored book. The edge preserves that qualified assessment; it does not imply rejection of all her findings. The chapter’s numbered endnotes are outside this preview and were not read here. The book’s 2005 original publication is confirmed by its publisher page. The same substantive reservation was also read in the credited journal translation of Eley’s essay in Genèses 7 (1992), pp. 166–167, on Persée; the English publisher preview supplies this edge’s quotation.
edges.map_label: Questions the limits of Tilly’s materialist framework

edges.relationship: In ‘Connections’ (1994), Louise Tilly proposes a social history that joins structures, processes of change and human action, combining narrative with causal explanation.
edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA’s own text of the address, particularly its opening methodological argument. Tilly specifies reciprocal relations between agency and structure and explains why narrative and causal analysis are both needed. This records her stated methodological contribution to social history, not a claim about subsequent adoption. It is distinct from the input’s global-history edge, which concerns connections among textile-producing regions. Reuse the packet source lt_w_connections; no additional source record is needed.
edges.map_label: Connects structure, change and human action

edges.relationship: In L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014), Fontaine explicitly follows Marc Bloch in moving between present questions and past practices.
edges.evidence_note: English introduction p. 2: “manner of a Marc Bloch.” Explicit methodological acknowledgment; no particular Bloch title is identified and no comprehensive dependence is claimed. Full book unread.
edges.map_label: Bloch: dialogue between past and present

edges.relationship: In L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014), Fontaine uses Foucault to frame the diffuse power operating through credit relations.
edges.evidence_note: English introduction p. 5 and note 11 link diffuse social power to Sécurité, territoire, population (lectures 1977–1978; published 2004); p. 2 also invokes genealogical questioning. This is a specified analytical resource, not an assertion of wholesale adherence. Cited Foucault volume unread here.

edges.relationship: Explaining chapter 3 of Le Marché (2014) in her 2015 reply to Skornicki, Fontaine argues that migrant merchant networks cut across Braudel’s division between subsistence markets, small commerce and high capital.
edges.evidence_note: Author response, PDF p. 7, paragraph outlining chapters 1–4: “casse la tripartition braudélienne.” Specific objection to that division, not a rejection of all Braudel’s history; Le Marché and the relevant Braudel books unread.

edges.relationship: Fontaine and John Brewer coauthored “Homo creditus et construction de la confiance au XVIIIe siècle” (1997), in La Construction sociale de la confiance.
edges.evidence_note: EUI report on 1997, published 1998, printed/PDF p. 50: the chapter appears under each author and is credited “with” the other, pp. 161–176. Corrects the counted record’s Brouwers, John to John Brewer. Chapter body unread; no individual division of arguments inferred.

edges.relationship: In “Reconsidering the Moral Economy in France at the End of the Eighteenth Century” (2019), Fontaine takes up Thompson’s concept of the moral economy and, through essays of 1777 on eradicating mendicancy, places his thesis in a wider context of charity, religion, Enlightenment and aspirations to political equality (per the abstract).
edges.evidence_note: Displayed EBSCO abstract, final sentence, says the essays situate Thompson’s thesis within that wider intellectual and political context. Abstract only; no claim about the chapter’s detailed conclusions or a rejection of Thompson. Publisher preview confirms title/year but does not include chapter.

edges.relationship: L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014) explains early modern exchange through overlapping cultures of credit and the dependencies linking lenders and borrowers across social ranks.
edges.evidence_note: English introduction pp. 3–6 states the credit network and competing-cultures argument; Minard 2009, pp. 1–3, identifies its contribution to ordinary economic practices. This is a substantive contribution to economic history, not an employer or topic-only link. Later monograph chapters unread.

edges.relationship: In “Women’s Economic Spheres and Credit in Pre-industrial Europe” (2001), Fontaine argues that household provisioning and commerce could enlarge women’s economic room for action while legal and marital status constrained it.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter preview, pp. 15–22, especially p. 19 on provisioning and pp. 20–22 on widowhood, trading capacity and restrictions. Claim retains regional and status differences; no uniform European emancipation asserted. Chapter remainder unread.
edges.map_label: Women’s economic action and legal constraints

edges.relationship: In ‘Household Strategies for Survival: An Introduction’ (2000), coauthored with Jürgen Schlumbohm, Laurence Fontaine contributes to the history of the family by treating household composition and boundaries as negotiated and by connecting family change to economic survival.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF’s methodological discussion on pp. 3–7 and its discussion of uncertainty, family relations and political economies on pp. 10–17. Pages 4–5 explicitly identify limitations of household-and-family history and propose an integrated research approach; p. 15 examines how migration changes family membership, obligations and power. The authorial footnote on p. 1 attributes pp. 10–17 to Fontaine and pp. 1–10 to Schlumbohm. The relationship preserves joint authorship, with Fontaine’s own section supplying the family-change component; it does not credit her alone with the wording on p. 5. This is a contribution evidenced by substantive argument, not merely editorial co-credit or a claim that she originated family-strategy research.

edges.relationship: In ‘The Circulation of Luxury Goods in Eighteenth-Century Paris: Social Redistribution and an Alternative Currency’ (2003), Laurence Fontaine contributes to consumption and material-culture history by examining ordinary and lesser-known circuits distributing luxury and fashion goods in Paris.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s abstract, bibliographic information and displayed notes. The abstract explicitly distinguishes the study’s focus on distribution from earlier emphasis on production and consumption, then identifies the ordinary circuits investigated. The claim is limited to that stated research contribution. The complete chapter was not accessible and is not represented as read; no detailed findings about redistribution, pawn credit or consumer behaviour are inferred from its title or notes. The publisher’s chapter citation and copyright give 2003; the later electronic publication is not treated as the original year. No editor–contributor relationship with Maxine Berg is inferred.
edges.map_label: Ordinary circuits of luxury and fashion

edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987; Italian original 1984), Passerini retains Durkheim’s collective representations but criticizes their reification and insufficient attention to individual activity.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 1–2: “collective representations”; p. 2 distinguishes an entity from a process. Publisher excerpt read; Durkheim’s cited text and book endnotes unread. Qualified criticism, not wholesale rejection.

edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987; Italian original 1984), Passerini sets her study against Febvre's call for a history of sensibilities and collective psychology, describing it as only a preliminary outline by that standard.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 3, paragraphs beginning A notable example and It is not difficult: “following Febvre’s directions”. Primary publisher excerpt read; exact Febvre edition not established from the unread notes.

edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini invokes Raymond Williams’s call for a critical study of past and present culture in defining her historical approach.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 3, paragraph beginning It is perhaps: “Raymond Williams noted”. Primary passage read; no particular Williams title supplied by the excerpt, and no claim of sole derivation.

edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini follows Gramsci’s treatment of folklore as a conception of the world to justify serious historical study of ordinary life stories.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 4, opening paragraph: “Following what Gramsci wrote about folklore”. Primary publisher excerpt read; particular Gramsci edition and endnote unread. This is a stated methodological debt.

edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini questions the correspondence between individual interviewee and social stratum assumed in Thompson’s The Edwardians (1975), while recognizing their different research aims.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 10, section 3 The interviewees, paragraphs naming Essex and Thompson: “only partially compensated”. Page visually checked as well as OCR-read. Final paragraph distinguishes documenting social change from studying narrative forms; no total rejection of Thompson or general rejection of sampling claimed. The Edwardians itself unread.

edges.relationship: In a retrospective interview (1996, 2002), Thompson says that by the second edition of The Voice of the Past (1988) oral historians had been very strongly influenced by Passerini's ideas on subjectivity, silence and memory, and he connects this to that edition's new chapter, "Memory and the Self".
edges.evidence_note: Karen Worcman interview (1996, 2002), UK Data Archive thematic highlights (June 2017), section 15, printed p. 13/PDF p. 16: “very strongly influenced both by Luisa Passerini”. Section 14, p. 12, contrasts the first edition. The same paragraph credits Portelli even more strongly; this new individual route preserves that mixed attribution. Existing edge_2974 is Portelli→Thompson, not Passerini→Thompson. The 1988 chapter is unread.

edges.relationship: Scott wrote the foreword to the English Autobiography of a Generation (1996; Italian original 1988), commending its way of approaching lived history.
edges.evidence_note: Wesleyan publisher contents, Foreword by Joan Wallach Scott, and displayed foreword quotation: “closer to lived history”. This verifies an introduction and a bounded published appraisal; whole foreword unread. Scott is not asserted to have supervised Passerini.
edges.map_label: Scott’s foreword to the English memoir

edges.relationship: In "Discontinuity of History and Diaspora of Languages" (2000), Passerini names Hobsbawm as an inspiration and says his work was very important in her formation, while granting the gulf Bewes saw between her fragmentary exposition and his continuous narrative.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, final displayed paragraph beginning As it happens: “one historian I have taken as an inspiration is Eric Hobsbawm”. No particular Hobsbawm work is identified in the read passage; no claim about agreement on every question or a supervisory relationship.

edges.relationship: Fascism in Popular Memory (1987) develops an oral-history method that interprets narrative form and the interview encounter alongside other historical sources.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 8–9: “pre-existing story-lines”. Read publisher excerpt distinguishes inherited narrative forms from interview effects, then discusses checking testimony against other sources. Whole book unread. Existing oral→memory and oral→political group edges are not direct person→oral edges.
edges.map_label: Narrative form and the interview encounter

edges.relationship: In “A Passion for Memory” (2011), Passerini argues that a memory of Europe includes how Europe is remembered by others as well as what Europeans remember.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final two paragraphs: “Europe is the object”. Abstract only; full article unread. Claim is this stated extension of memory’s subject/object, not proof of reception or a founding role in memory studies.

edges.relationship: With Selma Leydesdorff and Paul Thompson, Passerini’s introduction to Gender and Memory (1996) asks how memory is gendered while warning against treating cultural distinctions as universal gender differences.
edges.evidence_note: Joint Introduction, pp. 1–3 (licensed preview PDF pp. 20–22), especially p. 1: “transcultural essential gender differences”. Joint authorship explicit. Preview ends mid-sentence on p. 3; remainder unread. The separately authored new introduction in the 2005 edition belongs to Leydesdorff.

edges.relationship: Fascism in Popular Memory (1987) challenges labour histories that identify working-class subjectivity either with its organizations or with an inherently oppositional class.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 4–7, especially p. 6: “traditional Marxists”. Read primary excerpt addresses an explicit historiographical problem, not just workers as a shared topic. Claim concerns the Italian historiography described there, not all Marxist or labour history.

edges.relationship: “A Memory for Women’s History” (1992) describes an oral-history project accompanying the creation of an archive of recent feminism in Emilia-Romagna.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher extract, p. 669, opening two paragraphs: “an oral history project”. Supports the concrete contribution to documenting women’s movements; later argument and full article unread. Does not claim Passerini founded or solely created the independent Bologna archive.

edges.relationship: In Oral History Theory (first published 2010; second edition, 2016), Lynn Abrams uses Passerini’s Work Ideology and Consensus under Italian Fascism (1979) to explain why oral historians must investigate the production and cultural settings of remembered narratives.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed second-edition preview. Abrams reconstructs Passerini’s interpretation of workers’ silences and discrepant recollections, then derives an interpretive obligation from it. The claim concerns this substantive methodological use; the 2010 edition was not separately read.
edges.map_label: Interpreting how memory narratives are produced

edges.relationship: In their introduction to Beyond Women’s Words (2018), Franca Iacovetta, Katrina Srigley and Stacey Zembrzycki draw on Passerini’s understanding of the interview as a social relationship and credit her argument that present circumstances help shape memories of the past.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed preview’s introduction through its available p. 11. At p. 1 the authors invoke Passerini’s ‘social relationship that is the interview’; at p. 8 they explicitly credit her account of memory’s dependence on the present. This is a jointly authored conceptual uptake, not an inference from editorial co-credits. The endnotes are outside the preview, so no particular earlier Passerini publication is assigned to these statements.
edges.map_label: Interview relationships and memory in the present

edges.relationship: In Love and the Idea of Europe (2009; revised as Women and Men in Love, 2012), Passerini connected European political identity with the history of courtly and romantic love while questioning claims that this form of love belonged exclusively to European civilization.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction, especially pp. 1–6. The opening explains her historical inquiry into political belonging and emotions and its critique of European exclusivity. This supports a specific contribution to the history of emotions. Edition years follow her institutional publication list, p. 2: 2009 for the earlier English title and 2012 for the revision. The publisher also lists a December 2008 hardback release. The rest of the book was not read.
edges.map_label: Love, political identity and European exclusivity

edges.relationship: Rowbotham recalls that Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963), which she read in proof, made “a profound impression” on her through its account of how economic transformation affected daily experience and gave rise to an emergent consciousness among people without power.
edges.evidence_note: LEHMT, English paragraphs beginning “He was in the process” and “His account”; “made a profound impression upon me”. Her retrospective testimony is read; Thompson’s complete book is unread here.

edges.relationship: In Remembering Dorothy and Edward (2012), Rowbotham credits Dorothy Thompson’s respect for local activists and insistence on examining original evidence as formative historical examples.
edges.evidence_note: Spanish translation, p. 142: “activistas locales”, “datos originales”; her 1964 adult-education research is explicitly recalled. Self-reported influence; Dorothy’s cited books and English lecture unread.
edges.map_label: Dorothy Thompson: evidence and ordinary activists

edges.relationship: In her 2025 Nueva Sociedad interview, Rowbotham identifies Hobsbawm as supervisor of the doctorate she began in 1964 on the University Extension movement.
edges.evidence_note: Supervision question and answer: “Mi supervisor de tesis fue Eric Hobsbawm”. She expressly distinguishes admiration from political influence. The 2014 retrospective records abandonment; no completed doctorate asserted.

edges.relationship: Looking back in 2015 on Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973), Rowbotham recalls working within Marx and Engels’ framework while finding Marxist texts “apt to wear somewhat thin” for tracing inner perceptions and material life, or women’s activities in the household and child rearing.
edges.evidence_note: 2015 retrospective, paragraphs beginning “If participating” and “But when”; “wear somewhat thin”. Marx and Engels receive joint credit. This retrospective supports qualified criticism, not rejection; original book unread.
edges.map_label: Marx: a resource with feminist limits

edges.relationship: As recalled in Remembering Dorothy and Edward (2012), Thompson challenged the early women’s liberation claim, initially shared by Rowbotham, that experiencing oppression confers superior authority to write about it.
edges.evidence_note: Spanish translation p. 152: “Edward criticó”; Rowbotham accepts a qualified warning about identity-based authority. Retrospectively reported criticism of her movement’s early position, not a review of a named Rowbotham book; English lecture unread.

edges.relationship: Reflecting in 2014 on Women, Resistance and Revolution (1972), Rowbotham describes rewriting history with women in mind as a collective endeavour and traces themes from that book into Hidden from History (1973).
edges.evidence_note: Read Rowbotham’s retrospective on the publisher’s site (18 February 2014), paragraphs beginning Indeed it was eerily evident, I carried on writing, and I could see how rewriting history. These establish the thematic continuity with Hidden from History (1973), the original 1972 publication of Women, Resistance and Revolution, and the collective character of rewriting history with women in mind. This retrospective supports the revised contribution claim; it does not independently establish every claim in the original relationship about exceptional heroines or continuous progress. Selected books remain unread. The separate labour-history edge sr_w_08 retains its existing, explicitly mediated review evidence.

edges.relationship: The Trouble with Patriarchy (1979) questioned whether an unchanging account of male domination could explain historical variation, women’s agency or cooperation between women and men.
edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, question naming the 1979 essay and following answers: “rigidez ahistórica”. Retrospective account; original essay unread. The interview identifies Alexander and Taylor’s replies without supplying their full arguments.

edges.relationship: Hidden from History (1973) made women’s overlooked labour and differences between working-class and privileged women part of the history of capitalism and resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Kirkus review, paragraphs on production and “hidden labour”. Selected reading supports this labour-history contribution, not a claim that Rowbotham originated all study of women’s work; book unread.

edges.relationship: At History Workshop 4, Rowbotham argued that women's history should be researched as a specific area of study; after the laughter that greeted this, she was among the women who convened Britain's first Women's Liberation Conference at Ruskin (1970), an episode she recounts in Daring to Hope (2021).
edges.evidence_note: Whitehead, “In turn” and “That mocking hostility” paragraphs, explicitly names the memoir. Mediated account; memoir unread. Direct person-to-movement projection complements existing group edge_375; no claim of sole organization or founding.

edges.relationship: In White, Male and Middle Class (1992), Catherine Hall draws on Sheila Rowbotham’s Hidden from History (1973) to explain early feminist history’s recovery of women’s labour and reproduction.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed chapter preview. Hall identifies Rowbotham’s book as crucial and quotes its question about production and reproduction while discussing the recovery agenda and her own early housewife research. This supports use of a framework, not supervision or a claim that Hall adopted every argument. The complete books were not read.
edges.map_label: Hall: recovering women’s labour and reproduction

edges.relationship: Julianne Nyhan, Andrew Flinn and Anne Welsh’s ‘Oral History and the Hidden Histories project’ (first published online in 2013) connects the recovery agenda of oral history to the historical exclusion named in Rowbotham’s Hidden from History (1973).
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open text, including the surrounding discussion of recovery, feminist approaches and methodological change. The attribution occurs in the body, not merely the references. Limit this edge to the recovery formulation: it does not establish that Rowbotham invented oral history or its interviewing methods, or a personal debt by a particular timeline oral historian.
edges.map_label: Hidden from History: oral history’s recovery agenda

edges.relationship: Barbara Taylor’s 2024 appraisal identifies Rowbotham’s Edward Carpenter: A Life of Liberty and Love (2008) as a major contribution to the pursuit of freely chosen sexuality.
edges.evidence_note: Read Taylor’s complete signed appraisal. The parenthesis explicitly links the biography to sexual freedom. Mapping that historical contribution to the existing Sexuality & queer history field is an editorial classification; Taylor does not name a school or assert an influence on a particular scholar. The biography itself was not read. This is a field edge, not a Taylor-to-Rowbotham review edge.
edges.map_label: Edward Carpenter: history and sexual freedom

edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb criticizes White’s treatment of historical writing through literary forms.
edges.evidence_note: Read paragraphs beginning ‘Hayden White’ and ‘For the postmodernist’; ‘Poetics of History’. White’s originals unread; records her interpretation.

edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb challenges Scott’s linkage of feminist history with poststructuralist epistemology.
edges.evidence_note: Read ‘The political potential’ through ‘If conventional history’; ‘radical epistemology’. Scott’s original passage unread; criticism remains Himmelfarb’s.

edges.relationship: In ‘Resisting the New’ (1987), Stone disputes Himmelfarb’s exaggerated account of new history’s dominance while accepting some objections.
edges.evidence_note: Read review paragraphs ‘All this granted’ through ‘Thus outside France’; ‘overstates a good case’. Reviewed book unread; qualified criticism.

edges.relationship: In ‘What is History Now?’ (2004), Cannadine rejects Himmelfarb’s diagnosis of disciplinary ruin, arguing that political history remains vigorous.
edges.evidence_note: Read official PDF, printed pp. 31–32, paragraph crossing the page break and note 10: ‘political history remains alive and well’. Lecture delivered 2002; published text 2004, not all wording backdated. Cited Himmelfarb books unread.

edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes Braudel’s account of individual freedom, as Stone reports.
edges.evidence_note: Read Stone’s paragraph ‘One of Himmelfarb’s beliefs’; ‘efficacy of individuals’. Both original book discussions unread; mediated criticism only.

edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb defends evidentiary checks against what she calls postmodern relativism.
edges.evidence_note: Read ‘Critical history put a premium’ and concluding methodological defense; ‘canon of evidence’. Her contested position, not a disciplinary verdict.

edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes quantitative history as deterministic and mechanistic and singles out cliometricians such as Robert Fogel, as Stone reports.
edges.evidence_note: Read ‘Again, however’ through ‘Here the historian’ and ‘To barzun’ through ‘But in these cases’; ‘for whom it is a method’. Fogel and Engerman are joint authors. Their book and Barzun’s book unread; objection concerns explanatory sufficiency, not all counting.

edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb dismisses psychohistories, including Erikson’s study of Luther, as unscholarly for lacking historical evidence, as Lawrence Stone reports.
edges.evidence_note: Lawrence Stone, “Resisting the New,” New York Review of Books, 17 December 1987, paragraph beginning She lists the types of new social history, and the following sentences naming Erikson’s Luther study and describing her dismissal as unscholarly for lack of evidence. Stone does not supply the book title. This is his account of the 1987 collection; the collection and the psychohistorical studies remain unread.

edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes social history’s fragmentation and displacement of political inquiry, as Stone reports.
edges.evidence_note: Read Stone’s ‘She also sees’ and following paragraph; ‘factional and parochial’. Collection unread; attribution preserves disagreement.

edges.relationship: The Idea of Poverty (1984) makes changing conceptions of poverty a historical problem, joining social and intellectual history in Nisbet’s reading.
edges.evidence_note: Read Nisbet’s opening, especially paragraphs ‘Style’ through ‘The important characters’: ‘social history’ and ‘intellectual history’. Book unread; contribution framed through this named reviewer, without treating his favorable assessment as consensus.
edges.map_label: Studies poverty as a historical idea

edges.relationship: In her review “Sire of the Poor” (1988), Linda Colley questioned the claim in Gertrude Himmelfarb’s Victorian Values and 20th-Century Condescension (1987) that Victorian England shared a consensual value system across social groups.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-hosted review, including its discussion of Himmelfarb and the contrasting studies by Read and Anderson. Colley accepts that some workers embraced the virtues under discussion, but questions generalizing that agreement across Victorian society. This records reception through criticism, not adoption. The pamphlet itself was not read.
edges.map_label: Questions a shared Victorian value system

edges.relationship: In “A Neo-Victorian Romance” (1987), Keith Thomas criticized Gertrude Himmelfarb’s Marriage and Morals Among the Victorians (1986) for selective portraits of Bentham, Bloomsbury and the Webbs and for judging past thinkers without sufficiently situating them in their own contexts.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-hosted review. Thomas praises the essays’ literary qualities while challenging their selection of evidence and historical contextualization. The claim is limited to this review; the collection was not read. Its 1986 publication year is corroborated by the publisher excerpt of T. G. Otte’s The Foreign Office Mind, introduction p. 10, note 44.
edges.map_label: Challenges selective portraits and missing context

edges.relationship: In “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976), Kelly draws on Rowbotham’s Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) to connect women’s work and family relations with the formation of consciousness.
edges.evidence_note: Read licensed abridged reprint in Just Methods, printed pp. 8, 12–13, especially the final substantive paragraph and n. 26, which explicitly attributes its point to Rowbotham’s 1973 book. Notes 6–7 and 23 also name Rowbotham. The argument does not make women a homogeneous economic class. The 1976 journal article is excerpted, and Rowbotham’s original book and Kelly’s separate review of it remain unread.

edges.relationship: In “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976), Kelly invokes Marx’s account of production as reproducing people and social relations to include procreation and child socialization in the productive work of society.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed abridged primary reprint, Just Methods, printed pp. 10–11, particularly the opening paragraph on p. 11, which expressly attributes the continuous process of reproduction to Marx. This supports Kelly’s stated use of a conception, not endorsement of all Marxist theory or identification of a particular Marx passage. No exact Marx work is supplied in that retained paragraph; original Marx text not collated.
edges.map_label: Marx: reproduction as a resource for Kelly (1976)

edges.relationship: In “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977), Kelly answered her question in the negative, arguing that the period saw a relative contraction of the powers of elite secular women, as Brian Richardson summarises (2020).
edges.evidence_note: Read course reprint printed pp. 176–177, which differentiates women’s social positions and cautions about prescriptive sources. Richardson’s preface p. x n. 4 confirms first publication in 1977; the 1994 AHA retrospective describes the intervention’s importance and the Lerner collaboration. Existing women roster row is retained, not duplicated; no person-to-women edge currently exists.
edges.map_label: Women’s history: no Renaissance for women (1977)

edges.relationship: “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976) treats relations between women and men as historical social relations and makes them part of explanations of social change.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed abridged primary reprint in Just Methods, printed pp. 6–12: introductory formulation; sex as a social category, pp. 8–9; theories of social change, pp. 9–12. The distinction is “social and not a natural one.” Mapping this methodological contribution to the existing gender-history field is editorial, not a claim that Kelly founded that entire field or anticipated every later gender theory. The complete 1976 article remains unread.

edges.relationship: In ‘Polarities, Hybridities: What Strategies for Decentring?’ (2001), Natalie Zemon Davis places Joan Kelly’s ‘Did Women Have a Renaissance?’ (1977) within the social historians’ questioning of the Renaissance as a period, alongside her own decision to restrict the term.
edges.evidence_note: Read the opening of Davis’s chapter in the licensed University of Toronto Press preview; visually checked printed p. 19. Davis includes herself among social historians who questioned the period’s applicability and explicitly names Kelly’s 1977 intervention. On p. 20 she explains her own more restricted use of Renaissance. The edge records this specific methodological engagement; the passage does not establish Kelly as the sole cause of Davis’s practice. The preview ends during the chapter, so the complete chapter was not read.

edges.relationship: In ‘Joan Kelly Memorial Prize Marks Its Tenth Year’ (1994), Alice Kessler-Harris and Amy Swerdlow invoke Kelly’s Women, History, and Theory (1984) and describe the prize as a way to continue working in her intellectual spirit.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete AHA article. Its two authors discuss Kelly’s reinterpretation of historical change, recall the intellectual example of her collected essays, and explicitly ask how to continue working in that spirit. This is a jointly stated debt to Kelly’s scholarly example and a specific account of its institutional continuation. It supports no claim that Kessler-Harris adopted a particular Kelly argument. Amy Swerdlow is retained as coauthor in the relationship; she has no permitted endpoint in the supplied lists. No influence on prize recipients is inferred. Reuses packet source jk_w_kessler_swerdlow_1994, freshly checked here.

edges.relationship: As Eduardo Manzano notes (2015), Crone’s essay “Weber, Islamic Law, and the Rise of Capitalism” (revised English version 1999) criticizes Weber’s concept of rationality.
edges.evidence_note: Manzano, Medieval Worlds 1 (2015), p. 123 n. 22 (PDF page 6), explicitly identifies “A critique of Weber’s concept of rationality” in Crone’s essay, p. 251. Bibliography p. 135 gives the 1999 essay, pp. 247–272. Crone’s institutional bibliography distinguishes the 1987 German original from the revised English version. This is a named scholarly reader’s attribution; neither version of Crone’s essay nor Weber’s relevant original passage was read here, and their detailed positions are not reconstructed.

edges.relationship: In Recovering Submerged Worlds (2013), Brown praises The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012) for bringing Iran into the history of late-antique religious and intellectual change.
edges.evidence_note: Brown’s review, paragraphs beginning For another side of the story and By doing this, followed by the final two paragraphs: praises bringing Iran into the “mainstream of late antique history” and commends following Crone’s and Bowersock’s example. Review body read; Crone’s book and the other reviewed books unread. Brown’s treatment is not presented as unqualified assent to every reconstruction.

edges.relationship: Pre-Industrial Societies (1989) takes a broad comparative approach to the common features of pre-industrial societies. It ranges from the Mongol Empire and the Ming dynasty to seventeenth-century France, draws parallels between imperial structures, and examines economic organization, politics, culture and religion, as the publisher’s description and Judith Herrin’s account (2015) state.
edges.evidence_note: Original Preface in licensed 2015 Oneworld preview, paragraphs 1–5, and opening of chapter 1: explains constraints, uniformities and the distinction between common preindustrial features and civilization-specific ones. The author calls it a “rough-and-ready guide,” not a stringent ideal type. Preface and opening only; the main comparative chapters remain unread.

edges.relationship: In Guillaume Dye’s reading, God’s Rule / Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004) explains competing political arguments through the changing social and political settings of Islamic texts.
edges.evidence_note: Dye review, paragraphs beginning One of the main strengths and This may give the impression, then the sections on rightly guided rule and communal solidarity: stresses the relation between texts and practices and the plurality of positions within Islam. Whole review read; 2004 book unread. This connects to the broad intellectual-history field and does not infer membership in the Cambridge School.

edges.relationship: In Sadowski’s account, Slaves on Horses (1980) explains unstable political authority through the tension between tribal religious ideals and settled imperial government.
edges.evidence_note: Sadowski, Strong Society, Weak State, first three paragraphs, and endnotes 35–38, explicitly discuss Crone and cite Slaves on Horses pp. 62–63 and 84. His subsequent slave-soldier and modern-democracy claims also discuss Daniel Pipes and John Hall; those claims are not all assigned to Crone. Strong Society or Strong State?, first two substantive paragraphs, criticizes Crone’s persistence of tribal bias as essentialism. Named reader route; the book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987) challenged the accepted picture of Mecca as a major trading centre. In Judith Herrin’s summary, Crone argued that the spice trade was an Orientalist invention and that the trade depicted in the Muslim sources could not account for the supposed wealth and power of Quraysh.
edges.evidence_note: Two institutional or memorial texts, both read in full. (1) Judith Herrin’s memoir, the introduction to the Festschrift Islamic Cultures, Islamic Contexts (Brill, 2015), pp. xiv–xx, republished on openDemocracy (12 July 2015, CC BY-NC). I read it in a 2017 Wayback capture of the openly published page; the live page now shows only the opening to readers who are not signed in. Paragraph beginning “In 1977 Patricia took up an appointment at Oxford”: “This was followed by Meccan Trade …”, “She argued that the spice trade was an Orientalist invention and that the trade depicted in the Muslim sources couldn’t account for the supposed wealth and power of Quraysh.” (2) The Institute for Advanced Study obituary (15 July 2015), read in a 2022 Wayback capture because ias.edu returned 403. Its paragraph beginning “This was followed by work that closely related to her doctoral thesis” says Meccan Trade “challenged the widely accepted understanding of Mecca as a major trade center”. Meccan Trade itself was not read. The claim is limited to these two characterisations of its argument. No claim is made about its reception among economic historians.

edges.relationship: In “Getting the Conceptual Handles” (Government and Opposition, 1989), her review of Gellner’s Plough, Sword and Book (1988), Crone summarises his three-stage account of human history (hunter-gathering, agricultural and industrial) and his thesis that modern thought separates normative from referential truth. She notes that he writes at a high level of abstraction with few concrete examples, adds that informed readers will enjoy his concision, and judges that the overall vision makes compelling reading.
edges.evidence_note: Read on the publisher’s own page (Cambridge Core), which shows a first-page preview image of p. 375 because the item has no abstract. Government and Opposition 24:3 (1989), 375–378. Under the heading “Patricia Crone: Getting the Conceptual Handles. E. Gellner: Plough, Sword and Book. The Structure of Human History, London, Collins Harvill, 1988”, the paragraph beginning “The aim of this ambitiously, but not inappropriately, named book” sets out the stages (“hunter-gathering, agricultural and industrial”) and the book’s triad of cognition, political organization and production. It continues: “the author writes on a high level of abstraction with little in the way of concrete illustrations or examples, so that novices are likely soon to lose sight of what he is talking about”, and “Many of the arguments are familiar from his earlier works, but some are new and the overall vision makes compelling reading.” The next paragraph begins “The thesis may be summarized as follows. There are two kinds of truth, normative and referential.” Pp. 376–378 are unread, including any substantive disagreement. The critique claim is therefore limited to her stated reservation about abstraction, set beside her praise. If the coordinator prefers the Brown -> Crone review precedent (crone_w_03), it may be reclassified as connection/contribution.

edges.relationship: In Understanding Early Civilizations (2003), Trigger challenges the claim in Crone’s Pre-Industrial Societies (1989) that preindustrial societies lacked classes: Roman orders based on personal wealth, he argues, were classes even under her narrow definition. He nevertheless accepts the significance of her terminological distinction and of farmers’ difficulty in organizing collective action.
edges.evidence_note: Read the primary text in the licensed Pageplace preview of Cambridge University Press’s Understanding Early Civilizations, chapter 3, printed pp. 45–46 (PDF pages 63–64 of 78). On p. 45 Trigger identifies Crone’s 1989 discussion at pp. 101–102, explains her distinction between strata and politically organized classes, and then uses Roman orders based on personal wealth as a counterexample. His concluding sentence on that page is the supporting_phrase below. The opening paragraph of p. 46 qualifies this disagreement by accepting the importance of her terminological concern and farmers’ organizational difficulties. The following paragraph explains his decision to retain class as a comparative category. Only this scholarly argument is used. Crone’s book itself was not read in this pass; its position is attributed to Trigger’s reading. The publisher’s chapter page confirms the original 2003 publication year and chapter range, pp. 40–52; its 2014 online date is not the work’s original year. The graph and supplied usable edges contain no Trigger–Crone relationship.
edges.map_label: Challenges restriction of class to industrial societies

edges.relationship: According to R. Stephen Humphreys, Crone and Michael Cook’s Hagarism: The Making of the Islamic World (1977) prompted historians of early Islam to re-examine their sources and methods, although very few accepted its reconstruction.
edges.evidence_note: Read the institutional research-event report’s Hagarism assessment. This is reception evidence; the book remains unread. The target denotes source criticism broadly, without asserting Ranke transmission. Cook’s joint credit and limited acceptance are retained. The passage gives 1977, despite an inconsistent later reference to 1976.

edges.relationship: Chris Hann’s The Anthropology of Eurasia in Eurasia (2003) uses Crone’s Pre-Industrial Societies (1989; citing the 2003 edition) to advocate restoring broad historical comparison to anthropology beyond detailed local case studies.
edges.evidence_note: Read the institutional working paper, pp. 7–9 and bibliography p. 17. The claim concerns Hann’s documented use, not general adoption. Crone’s complete book remains unread; Hann cites its 2003 edition.

edges.relationship: Simpson and Coulthard coauthored “Grounded Normativity / Place-Based Solidarity” (American Quarterly, 2016).
edges.evidence_note: Byline; pp. 249–250, 254–255, read. Joint voice: “we are calling”. Coulthard’s separately marked autobiographical argument is not Simpson’s.

edges.relationship: In “Land as Pedagogy” (2014), Leanne Betasamosake Simpson invokes Audra Simpson’s Mohawk Interruptus (2014) for the politics of refusal.
edges.evidence_note: P. 22, n. 41: “politics of refusal”; bibliography p. 25. Selected article passages read; Mohawk Interruptus unread here. Specific resource, not sole derivation.

edges.relationship: “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) cites Deloria’s “Traditional Technology” (2001) to support education grounded in Indigenous contexts and processes.
edges.evidence_note: P. 9 cites Deloria pp. 58–60; reference p. 24. “Indigenous context” is methodological framing; Deloria’s chapter itself remains unread.

edges.relationship: “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) develops resurgence as an Indigenous intellectual and political project exceeding inclusion in existing academic institutions.
edges.evidence_note: P. 22: “resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems”. Selected article passages read; earlier book unread. No account of community teachings proposed.

edges.relationship: As We Have Always Done (2017) advances Indigenous resurgence as refusal of dispossession and an alternative to the settler state’s organizing logics.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher Description and eBook metadata read; original date 17 October 2017, paperback 2020. Book body unread; no criticism of a particular settler-colonial scholar inferred.

edges.relationship: “Aboriginal Peoples and Knowledge” (2001) argues that research direction belongs to Elders and community experts, rather than being secured by participatory methods alone.
edges.evidence_note: Pp. 140–142, especially p. 142: “control and direction of the work”. Publisher PDF read selectively; methodological claim only, without community-knowledge content.

edges.relationship: According to Tiffany Lethabo King, As We Have Always Done (2017) historicizes colonial gender violence through missions, schooling and white women’s enforcement of the Indian Act.
edges.evidence_note: King 2023, p. 184, discussion of chapter 7, citing book p. 97: “gendered analysis”. Review read; book chapter unread. Contribution is mediated by this named reader.

edges.relationship: In her closing essay for ActiveHistory.ca's January 2016 Indigenous theme week, Mary Jane Logan McCallum cites Leanne Simpson's and Billy-Ray Belcourt's posts from that week as identifying work still to be done beyond curriculum reform such as Winnipeg's Indigenous Course Requirement.
edges.evidence_note: The concluding body paragraph explicitly uses their critiques in evaluating curriculum reform; the opening collective thanks is not the evidence. No wider intellectual debt is claimed.

edges.relationship: In As We Have Always Done (2017), Simpson challenges the treatment of queer life as new to Indigenous societies and argues for its normalization within Indigenous life, as Tiffany Lethabo King explains in her 2023 review.
edges.evidence_note: King’s substantive discussion of chapter 8 supports this contribution to sexuality and queer history. Evidence is the review; the book was not independently read. No narrative or ceremonial content is used.

edges.relationship: In her 2022 review essay on Chakrabarty's The Climate of History in a Planetary Age, Brooke Ackerly names Simpson's account of Nishnaabeg methodologies, citing Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), as a resource for understanding the planetary age without constructing binaries.
edges.evidence_note: Ackerly names Simpson in the body and identifies both books in note 5. This records her assessment of a methodological contribution to climate history; it does not establish Chakrabarty’s reception of Simpson.

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls that reading Lévi-Strauss’s The Elementary Structures of Kinship transformed her thinking and fed into “The Traffic in Women” (1975).
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. JSTOR chapter and the 1975 anthology on Internet Archive are access-restricted). The interview supports the debt half only: Lévi-Strauss's Elementary Structures fed 'The Traffic in Women'. Re-base as influence; restore the critique only if the essay can be read on a permitted route. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"Sahlins sugeriu que eu lesse Estruturas Elementares do Parentesco, de Lévi-Strauss. Para usar a linguagem da época, 'o livro fez minha cabeça'"; "'The Traffic in Women' foi o resultado da confluência desses estudos"”

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls concluding that Marxism, though useful, could not account for gender difference and women’s oppression, the problem “The Traffic in Women” (1975) set out to address.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview supports a critique of the explanatory limits of Marxism (not specifically Marx's labour-power account) as the problem the essay addressed. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"O marxismo ... parecia incapaz de entender os temas da diferença de gênero e da opressão das mulheres"; "[o paradigma marxista] era útil, mas ao mesmo tempo tinha limitações no que diz respeito a gênero e sexo"; "'Traffic in Women' foi parte desse esforço"”
edges.map_label: Marxism’s limits on gender and sex

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin describes Lacanian psychoanalysis as a tool that was “very useful” for analysing structures of gender and desire in her work, while objecting to its totalizing tendencies and non-social conception of the symbolic.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. In the interview (GR answer after Butler's Gender Trouble remark), Rubin describes Lacanian psychoanalysis as a useful tool with reservations. This supports a qualified influence. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"a psicanálise lacaniana constituía uma ferramenta para isso"; "muito útil para lidar com estruturas de gênero e desejo, mas tem seu preço. Eu me preocupava com as tendências totalizantes em Lacan"”

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin says that Foucault’s History of Sexuality (English 1978) clarified issues and inspired the work behind “Thinking Sex” (1984), which had begun before she read it; she adds that Jeffrey Weeks influenced her as much.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview gives Rubin's own stated debt to Foucault for the Thinking Sex work, with the caveat that the work predated her reading. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"o trabalho começou antes que eu começasse a ler Foucault, mas o livro dele esclareceu alguns temas e me inspirou"; History of Sexuality "Foi um livro muito importante"; "Fui influenciada por Weeks da mesma forma que por Foucault"”

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Butler credits Rubin’s “The Traffic in Women” (1975) as one reason for developing Gender Trouble (1990).
edges.evidence_note: Portuguese translation (2003), JB paragraph beginning E o que me interessou, ending developed “Gender Trouble” (HTML lines 118–119): “um dos motivos”. Explicit first-person debt concerning gender’s mobility; English interview and Gender Trouble unread.

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin credits Althusser’s “Freud and Lacan” (English 1969) in the formation of “The Traffic in Women” (1975).
edges.evidence_note: Portuguese translation, GR paragraph beginning Li o artigo de Althusser (HTML line 92): “confluência desses estudos”. English publication year from interview bibliography; does not date the French original. Althusser essay unread here.

edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls that Charles Tilly’s 1973 Michigan course on the urbanization of Europe changed her thinking and led her to ask how forms of sexual identity arose from the same large-scale social changes.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview independently supports a teaching debt to Tilly, located in Rubin's history of sexual identity rather than in the 1984 acknowledgment. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"Em 1973, fiz outro curso que mudou minha vida 'A urbanização da Europa, 1500-1900', ministrado por Charles Tilly"; from these questions "a pensar em como diferentes formas de identidade e de subjetividade sexual resultaram das mesmas mudanças sociais em larga escala, foi um passo"”

edges.relationship: “The Traffic in Women” (1975) supplied a sex/gender-system framework for explaining women’s subordination through social relations.
edges.evidence_note: Mikkola, section 1.2, paragraphs naming Rubin (1975), describes the framework and social production of gender; Duke describes feminist reception. A theoretical contribution to the gender-history field, not a claim that Rubin founded that field.

edges.relationship: “Thinking Sex” (1984) set out to treat oppression based on sexual behaviour as distinct from gender oppression and to make structures of sexual stratification visible, as Rubin explains in “Sexual Traffic” (1994); Duke University Press calls it one of queer theory’s foundational texts.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Rubin's own interview account and the Duke description support the claim; 'historical analysis' is not stated in either, so dropped. 1984 is confirmed by the interview bibliography (Vance, Pleasure and Danger, 1984). Phrase seen: “"eu queria ser capaz de pensar sobre a opressão com base no comportamento sexual ou no desejo ilícito como algo distinto da opressão de gênero"; "articular as estruturas da estratificação sexual e torná-las visíveis"; Duke: "That essay became one of queer theory's foundational texts"”

edges.relationship: As Clyde Plumauzille documents, Rubin’s The Traffic in Women (1975) was among the critical resources Joan Wallach Scott attended to in seeking an approach beyond the category of woman and economic or familial explanations of women’s subordination.
edges.evidence_note: Substantive intellectual history in the Institute’s own magazine. This is Plumauzille’s account, not Scott’s stated debt; it supports a specific resource, not sole causation. Scott’s 1986 article itself was not readable at the JSTOR page checked.
edges.map_label: A resource for Scott’s methodological shift

edges.relationship: In Changing Hands (2013), Sara Ahmed draws on Rubin’s account in Deviations (2011) of gender circulating through conversations to argue against treating concepts as isolated individual inventions.
edges.evidence_note: Read Ahmed’s own published presentation. Her response develops Rubin’s atmospheric account into an argument about collective conceptual production. Ahmed cites a 2012 edition; the publisher dates the original collection to November 2011. Full collection unread.

edges.relationship: In the English version of Gender for a Marxist Dictionary (1991), Donna Haraway argues that Rubin’s The Traffic in Women (1975), alongside Rich’s and Wittig’s formulations, made racialized gender relations and barriers to interracial feminist solidarity difficult for white feminists to grasp.
edges.evidence_note: Read Haraway’s substantive discussion in a licensed Routledge preview. The criticism encompasses three formulations; it is not exclusively directed at Rubin. English text dated 1991 in the reprint; no complete-book reading claimed.
edges.map_label: Racial limits of the sex/gender framework

edges.relationship: In their review of The Hemingses of Monticello (2008), Edmund S. Morgan and Marie Morgan praise Gordon-Reed’s reconstruction for bringing fresh perspectives to a Jefferson long scrutinized by biographers.
edges.evidence_note: Review opening, second substantive paragraph, beginning The Hemingses of Monticello: “fresh perspectives.” Joint reception, not Morgan alone; no claim of direct influence on the book. Monograph unread.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Gordon-Reed and Peter S. Onuf’s “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs” (2016), Wood praises its insights but criticizes its uneven joint voice and its treatment of the Jefferson–Hamilton conflict as too personal.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher review, paragraphs beginning Although the two authors and But this claim: “a single voice” and “great political and social interests.” Criticism concerns the coauthored book; does not establish which author wrote a passage. Book unread.

edges.relationship: In President Tom’s Cabin (2008), Lepore praises The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) while questioning its reliance on analogies and assumptions about human nature.
edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning Gordon-Reed rested her case: “could do with more mortar.” Specific caution about inference, alongside praise; not rejection of the paternity case. Books unread.

edges.relationship: The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) makes enslaved people historical subjects by reconstructing family and social relationships marginalized by accounts centred on Jefferson.
edges.evidence_note: 2017 interview, answer following Did you know after your first book: “tell their story” and “web of relationships.” Own retrospective explanation of the book’s purpose; complete book unread.

edges.relationship: Writing Early American Lives as Biography (2014) discusses how to write the biographies of obscure figures and answers criticism of biography as a form of history writing.
edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on agr_w_hls_biography; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The author's Harvard Law School bibliography abstract (permitted, author's institutional page) supports a narrower claim. Replace the source with this page; the 'context matters' quotation is unconfirmed on a permitted route. Phrase seen: “Gordon-Reed's essay discusses the mechanics of writing the biographies of obscure figures, gives a brief history of modern biography, and addresses criticism of biography as a form of history writing”

edges.relationship: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997) argues that evidence of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship had been denied a fair hearing, pointing to inconsistencies in noted scholars' evaluations of the evidence and their exclusion of evidence from the Hemings family.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher summary, paragraphs 1–3: “fair hearing”; 2017 interview, answer beginning Instead I thought about teaching: “not proof” but “certainly evidence.” Original book body unread. The claim concerns evaluating evidence, not laboratory proof.

edges.relationship: In Keeping Their Stories Alive (2026), Gordon-Reed explains how historical and legal scholarship guides her work on Harvard’s public account of its ties to slavery and the memory of enslaved people.
edges.evidence_note: Q&A, answers to Why is the work and Council expertise: “educational mission” and “support of the law.” Current advisory practice, not a claim that an institutional project is complete.
edges.map_label: Slavery, institutional history and public memory

edges.relationship: In his 2008 review of Annette Gordon-Reed’s The Hemingses of Monticello (2008), Eric Foner praised her research and reconstruction of the wider family but criticized her interpretation of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship as an enduring romance, arguing that other readings of the limited evidence were equally plausible.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on Foner’s own website. Its praise of research and family reconstruction does not remove its explicit criticism of the romance interpretation. This records Foner’s assessment, not an independent finding about the relationship. The book itself was not read for this task.

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici criticizes Marx’s account of primitive accumulation for omitting women’s reproductive labour and the witch-hunts, and disputes its emancipatory assessment of capitalist development.
edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction, Spanish 2010 translation, printed pp. 22–24 (PDF pp. 19–21): “ausentes en Marx”. Read as Federici’s criticism of Capital I (1867), not an adjudication of Marx’s whole corpus. English original and Capital not freshly read.
edges.map_label: Reproduction and violence in primitive accumulation

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici argues that Foucault’s histories of bodily discipline and sexuality neglect reproductive labour, sexual differentiation and witch-hunting, obscuring the connection between biopower and capital accumulation.
edges.evidence_note: Primary preface p. 17 and introduction pp. 29–31, Spanish 2010 translation (PDF pp. 14, 26–28): “omisión de la caza de brujas”. Her retrospective preface also attributes the earlier criticism to the coauthored Il Grande Calibano (1984); the proposed claim is the 2004 restatement. No Foucault reply asserted; his original texts not freshly read.
edges.map_label: Questions the asexual subject of bodily discipline

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici credits Joan Kelly’s “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977; cited in its 1984 collected form) with challenging conventional periodization and identifies it among the works on which her own study builds.
edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction, Spanish translation pp. 24–25 (PDF pp. 21–22), explicitly names Kelly and says the book “se basa en estos trabajos”. Existing source kelly_renaissance supplies the original 1977 date; Federici cites the 1984 collection. Kelly’s essay not freshly read. This is an acknowledged intellectual resource, not supervision or personal collaboration.

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici values Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980) but disputes making scientific rationalism or mechanism the immediate cause of the witch-hunts, emphasizing the imposition of capitalist social discipline.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish translation, pp. 279–281 (PDF pp. 276–278), read with the appreciative introduction p. 25: “Ni el racionalismo ni el mecanicismo”.
