Federici argues that organic cosmologies also accommodated domination. Critique is qualified by explicit praise; Merchant’s complete book and any reply unread. Existing Merchant source used for original 1980 metadata only.
edges.map_label: Qualifies Merchant’s explanation of the witch-hunts

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici cites Clark’s Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919; 1968 reprint) but argues that midwives’ exclusion must be explained through control of reproduction as well as women’s loss of professional training.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish translation p. 252 (PDF p. 249), Clark quotation followed immediately by Federici’s objection to “desprofesionalización femenina”. Bibliography identifies Clark’s 1968 [1919] edition; existing clark_working_primary confirms the original title/date. This narrowly concerns the quoted explanation, not a rejection of Clark’s complete work. Clark’s occupational chapter not freshly read.
edges.map_label: Beyond deprofessionalization in the history of midwifery

edges.relationship: Caliban and the Witch (2004) reinterprets women’s history through changes in reproductive labour, bodily coercion and resistance during the transition to capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish introduction pp. 21–26 and 29–30 read. Explicitly situates the intervention within women’s history while opposing a history separated from male workers. This is Federici’s historical framework; no field founding or consensus claim. Whole book unread.

edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici interprets femininity and masculinity through the historical construction of a sexual division of labour and connects gender hierarchy to class relations.
edges.evidence_note: Primary preface p. 17 and introduction pp. 26–27, Spanish translation, read in full. The passage explicitly addresses the gender/class division and the analytical category women. Contribution records a disputed materialist interpretation, not a definition binding on gender history. English original unread.
edges.map_label: Historically constructed gender and class relations

edges.relationship: In “Social reproduction theory” (2019), Federici argues that unpaid housework and other unwaged or unfree labour belong within the analysis of capitalist exploitation, and treats wages as instruments that organize labour hierarchies.
edges.evidence_note: Complete primary journal HTML, printed pp. 55–57; paragraphs beginning What made, It was discovering and It was unmasking: “other unpaid and un-free labourers”. The labour-history connection is editorial placement of an explicit argument about labour and exploitation, not a claim that the essay is an empirical labour history or that the field accepts her value theory.
edges.map_label: Unpaid work and the hierarchy of wages

edges.relationship: Caliban and the Witch (2004) intervenes in the transition-to-capitalism debate by treating the reorganization of reproduction and the witch-hunts as constitutive of primitive accumulation and by arguing that dispossessive violence recurs within capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish introduction pp. 21–24 and 31 read. The introduction explicitly places the book in the transition debate and sets out its differences from Marx; the formulation is Federici’s contested argument. This debate edge concerns her explanatory intervention, distinct from the person-directed Marx critique. Original English book and other participants’ texts unread.
edges.map_label: A feminist account of the transition to capitalism

edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges: Mushrooms as Companion Species” (2012), an essay dedicated to Haraway, Tsing says she is indebted to Haraway for the concept of companion species and for permission to refuse the boundary between nature and culture.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 141 (dedication “for Donna Haraway”; abstract: “Haraway’s concept of companion species takes us beyond familiar companions”; second paragraph: “This essay is indebted to Donna Haraway not only for the concept of ‘companion species’”) with n. 1 citing The Companion Species Manifesto (2003); p. 145 n. 12 (“Haraway’s work on dogs is a key interruption”); acknowledgements p. 153 (Haraway gave “a most generous critical reading”). A stated debt in Tsing’s own text. Haraway’s Manifesto not reread here.
edges.map_label: Mutual exchange: companion species, refugia and the Plantationocene

edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing’s account of plantation sugar draws on Mintz: she quotes Puerto Rican cane workers from Worker in the Cane (1974) and cites Sweetness and Power (1985) for sugar’s late arrival as an object of mass consumption and for the plantation as a proto-industrial labour model.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 148–149: body text on sugar cane, coerced plantation labour and rum before mass consumption (“Long before sugar became an object and symbol of mass consumption”). Note 27 quotes Puerto Rican cane workers from Worker in the Cane, p. 16; note 30: “Caribbean sugar plantations formed a proto-industrial labor model that shaped nascent industrialisation in Europe”. Body text engages Mintz’s argument; it is not a passing citation. Mintz’s books not read here.

edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing’s passage on white women as agents of racial hygiene in plantation colonies cites Stoler’s Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) for the argument that the transformation of gender was key to emerging ideologies of race and medicine, and for the importance of white women’s migration to the tropics to late-colonial eugenics.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 149 (“White women became agents of racial hygiene”) through p. 150; n. 31: “Ann Stoler shows how the transformation of gender was key to emergent ideologies of race and medicine”; n. 32: Stoler “shows the centrality of the importation of white women to the tropics to the new eugenics”. The body argument is built on the cited work. Stoler’s book not read here.

edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing follows Latour’s The Pasteurization of France (French original 1984; she cites the Sheridan and Law translation) in treating colonial spaces in the tropics as the first living laboratories of Pasteurian hygiene.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 150 body: “Pasteurian germ theory was tested and boosted in the tropics, where white-controlled spaces could be organised as laboratories”; n. 32: “As Bruno Latour explains … Latour suggests that colonial armies in the tropics … were the first living laboratories for Pasteurian medicine”. Tsing’s note and bibliography cite the Harvard translation by Sheridan and Law, dated 1986 in her bibliography (the publisher’s date is not checked here); the French original is 1984. A bounded borrowing; Latour’s book not read here.

edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing extends Marx’s primitive accumulation, arguing that capitalism never transcends it but keeps depending on it, and she follows Marx in defining the capitalist commodity by alienation.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 21: “Marx’s term ‘primitive accumulation’ is useful in extension: Capitalism does not transcend primitive accumulation, but continues to depend on it.” P. 22 n. 1: “I define commodities by the alienation that constitutes them. In doing so, I follow Marx ([1867] 1992)”. P. 24: factory discipline “created what Marx ([1844] 1959) called ‘alienation’”. An extension, not an orthodox application. Her 2015 essay names a related process “salvage accumulation” without citing Marx.

edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing sets her capitalism-specific definition of the commodity against Appadurai’s, which treats any good in exchange as a commodity and, she argues, sidesteps the specificity of capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Read p. 22 n. 1: “Appadurai (2012), for example, defines commodities as any goods in exchange. This allows him to sidestep the specificity of capitalism … Following Kopytoff (1986), Appadurai rejects a gift-commodity distinction”. The note frames the article’s central gift–commodity contrast (body, pp. 21–22). Tsing cites Appadurai’s 2012 essay “Commodities and the politics of value”, not The Social Life of Things (1986). A definitional contrast, not a general critique; Appadurai’s essay unread.

edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing criticises accounts that picture capitalism as a singular, enclosed and coherent system; a note places Harvey’s The Limits to Capital (1982; cited in the 2007 edition) beside Hardt and Negri’s Empire as such an account, and she argues that these analyses miss the open-ended, contingent processes through which capitalism is made.
edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 38–39: “it has become increasingly popular for critics to imagine capitalism as a singular, enclosed, and coherent system”; n. 24: “Similarly, David Harvey (2007) shows capitalism as a coherent whole; like Hardt and Negri (2000), he aims to inspire resistance against this whole”; p. 39: “such analyses miss the open-ended processes”. Tsing cites the 2007 Verso edition of a 1982 book. A short critique within the conclusion; Harvey’s book unread.
edges.map_label: Against capitalism as a closed whole

edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing proposes multispecies landscapes as protagonists of world history, and in 2021 she asked historians to treat nonhumans as fully historical actors in histories of the Anthropocene.
edges.evidence_note: Unruly Edges, p. 141 abstract: “This essay opens a door to multispecies landscapes as protagonists for histories of the world”; the essay follows fungi through “the last ten thousand years of human disturbance history”. OSU abstract (2021), question (3): “What happens when we recognize nonhumans as fully historical — and thus mutable actors in the making of more-than-human histories?” Programmatic statements by Tsing; uptake by environmental historians is not claimed. Edge Effects (2019) adds her stated reason for keeping the term Anthropocene: it “allows interdisciplinary conversation between natural scientists and humanists”.

edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing argues that describing the rough edges of capitalist supply chains is a job for ethnographers, and that multispecies ethnography meets political economy in an emerging field; the 2016 Bateson Prize citation calls her Mushroom book storytelling-as-ethnography.
edges.evidence_note: HAU 2013, p. 39: “Describing those rough edges is a job for ethnographers”; “Multispecies ethnography meets political economy in this emerging field.” SCA announcement (2016), jury paragraph: “an open-ended polyphonic assemblage that performs in writing the very concepts it generates”; “Through such storytelling-as-ethnography she traces …”. The prize citation is the society’s reading, not Tsing’s own claim; the book is unread.

edges.relationship: Friction (2005), as its publisher describes it, replaces the view that globalization means a clash of cultures with friction as a figure for the conflicting interactions of global connection, and offers methods for studying global interconnections.
edges.evidence_note: AES 2005 Senior Book Prize page, reproduced publisher’s description: “Challenging the widespread view that globalization invariably signifies a ‘clash’ of cultures, anthropologist Anna Tsing here develops friction in its place as a metaphor”; “Providing a portfolio of methods to study global interconnections … and how much is overlooked in contemporary theories of the global.” Publisher description only; the book is unread. AES dates it 2004; Tsing cites it as 2005 (Unruly Edges, n. 39).

edges.relationship: In Planetary Longings (2022), Mary Louise Pratt draws on Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing’s Friction (2005) to interpret encounters with global capitalism as generative, unpredictable world-making.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed introduction, especially pp. 5–9. Pratt explains Tsing’s concept in the body of her own argument. The preview’s p. 8 gives 2004, but p. 9 cites 2005; the original publication year is 2005. No claim about chapters outside the preview.
edges.map_label: Friction and world-making in Planetary Longings

edges.relationship: According to Sarah Bellows-Blakely’s “Empowering African Girls?” (2023), Antoinette Burton’s Africa in the Indian Imagination (2016) draws on Tsing’s Friction (2005) to analyze the uneasy, productive tensions underpinning transnational alliances.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-served article PDF, specifically this paragraph and note 12. The preceding clause explicitly attributes Burton’s framework to Tsing and another scholar; the note identifies both books. Burton’s original passage remains unread. This is a qualified, mediated application under the relationship protocol.

edges.relationship: Tsing’s “Inside the Economy of Appearances” (2000) and Friction (2005) contribute an account of capitalist investment through performance and imagined economic futures, substantively discussed by Christensen and Ivarsson in “Global Capitalist Assemblages” (first published 2025).
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open text around notes 48–52 and its references. This is a named conceptual contribution to historical analysis of capitalism, not a shared-topic inference. The original Tsing works were not newly read for this edge.
edges.map_label: Performance and imagined futures in capitalist investment

edges.relationship: In “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990), as she summarised it in 2007, Fraser criticised what she called, following Habermas, the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere, for discounting the effects of social inequality on public opinion and for its masculinist bias, while keeping the public sphere as a concept to be reconstructed; in “Transnationalizing the Public Sphere” (2007) she argued that Habermas’s account tacitly assumed a Westphalian, nation-state frame.
edges.evidence_note: Transversal text (2007), section “Classical Public Sphere Theory and Its Radical Critique”: Habermas’s Structural Transformation as “the locus classicus of all discussions”; her own earlier article “directed criticisms of both types against … the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere”; the legitimacy critique “focused on the effects on public opinion of inequality within civil society”, “Exposing, too, the bourgeois masculinist bias”; “Tacitly, however, Habermas's account of the public sphere rested on at least six social-theoretical presuppositions”. Introduction: public sphere theory is a resource that “should be reconstructed rather than jettisoned”. Mansbridge’s abstract (2017) independently describes the move “from Habermas's unitary conception to Fraser's plurality of contesting publics”. Limits: Fraser dates her earlier article 1991 in this text; the Social Text printing is 1990 (Crossref 10.2307/466240). The 1990 article itself was not read on a permitted route for this draft (JSTOR did not load). Distinct from existing edges gender → jurgen_habermas (edge_652, edge_1511), which describe Fraser’s critique but have no Fraser endpoint.

edges.relationship: In “Heterosexism, Misrecognition, and Capitalism: A Response to Judith Butler” (Social Text, 1997; New Left Review, 1998), Fraser welcomed Butler’s “Merely Cultural” but disputed its account of Marxism’s legacy, of poststructuralism and of contemporary capitalism, and rejected the suggestion that she treated heterosexist oppression as merely cultural.
edges.evidence_note: NLR I/228 page, visible opening: “Judith Butler's essay is welcome on several counts”; “Nevertheless, Butler and I disagree”; disagreement over the legacy of Marxism, the assessment of poststructuralism and the character of contemporary capitalism; objection that Butler’s use of the “neoconservative Marxist” critique to frame Justice Interruptus is “unfortunate” because it could suggest Fraser treats heterosexism as “merely cultural”. Remainder paywalled, unread. Original Social Text 52/53 (1997) printing from Crossref metadata only. The Tanner text (1996 lectures as published) cites “Merely Cultural” as “the counterargument” (p. 21 n. 21). Butler’s own visible preview names no target, so no reverse edge is drawn; the coordinator may make this one undirected as an exchange if a Butler passage naming Fraser is later read.

edges.relationship: Fraser and the historian Linda Gordon co-wrote “A Genealogy of Dependency: Tracing a Keyword of the U.S. Welfare State” (Signs, 1994) and “Civil Citizenship against Social Citizenship? On the Ideology of Contract-versus-Charity” (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Gordon’s own CV, publications list: “A Genealogy of ‘Dependency’: Tracing a Keyword of the US Welfare State,” with Nancy Fraser, Signs, winter 1994, “and in many anthologies”; “Civil Citizenship Against Social Citizenship? …,” with Nancy Fraser, in van Steenbergen, ed., The Condition of Citizenship (CV: “The Quality of Citizenship”), 1994. Crossref DOI 10.1086/494886: Fraser and Gordon, Signs 19, no. 2 (1994): 309–336. Co-authorship of substantive articles only; the article text and its argument are unread (publisher 403, JSTOR did not load), so no claim about content is made.

edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser presented Taylor as a leading proponent of the politics of recognition but rejected his treatment of recognition as a matter of self-realization grounded in a thick theory of the good, arguing instead that recognition is a matter of justice.
edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text: p. 10, “proponents of the politics of recognition, such as Charles Taylor, insist that” a difference-blind politics of redistribution can reinforce injustice (n. 10 cites “The Politics of Recognition”); p. 24, “two major theorists, Charles Taylor and Axel Honneth, understand recognition as a matter of self-realization”, and she rejects justifying claims “by reference to a thick theory of the good, as Taylor does” (n. 23 cites “The Politics of Recognition” and Sources of the Self); p. 34 with n. 36. Body-text engagement. Page numbers from partly garbled running headers. Honneth (also criticised, pp. 24, 27, 29) is not an endpoint.

edges.relationship: In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014), Fraser takes Marx’s move from exchange into the “hidden abode” of production as her starting point and proposes to look further behind it, to the conditions of possibility of production.
edges.evidence_note: NLR 86 page, visible opening: “While Marx looked behind the sphere of exchange, into the ‘hidden abode’ of production”; “I shall seek production's conditions of possibility behind that sphere, in realms that are more hidden still”; she describes reconstructing his insights through feminist, ecological and political perspectives. A stated building-on and extension of Marx, not adoption of all his claims. Rest of essay paywalled, unread. The Tanner text also cites Marx for the Marxian concept of class (p. 8 n. 7), not used here.

edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser models the collectivities of the politics of recognition on Weber’s status groups, defined by esteem and prestige rather than by relation to production, citing his “Class, Status, Party”.
edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text, p. 8: in the recognition paradigm “the victims of injustice are more like Weberian status groups than Marxian (or Weberian) classes”; n. 8: “For the Weberian definition of class, see Max Weber, ‘Class, Status, Party’”; p. 31 n. 31 notes that “Weber's own distinction was tripartite not bipartite”. A conceptual borrowing named in the body text; no broader debt to Weber claimed. Flag for reviewers as a moderate-strength edge.

edges.relationship: As Mascaretti reconstructs her critique, Fraser’s “Foucault on Modern Power: Empirical Insights and Normative Confusions” (1981; collected in Unruly Practices, 1989) questions the normative basis of Foucault’s analyses of power; “Michel Foucault: A ‘Young Conservative’?” (1985) asks why a fully panopticized society should be opposed.
edges.evidence_note: Read Giovanni Maria Mascaretti, “Foucault, Normativity, and Freedom: A Reappraisal” (2019), https://rauli.cbs.dk/index.php/foucault-studies/article/download/5890/6560/21348, section 1, pp. 25–26 and notes 7–12. Mediated interpretation explicitly attributed in the sentence; Fraser’s original essays remain unread. Her own bibliography at https://nancyfrasernet.wordpress.com/publications/, first and fourth entries, confirms the original years. The 1985 journal record is https://doi.org/10.1086/292729. Existing nf_n_umn_unruly remains bibliographic context; the substantive witness is Mascaretti, identified here by full citation and URL.

edges.relationship: Fraser reconstructs critical theory from a feminist standpoint: Unruly Practices (1989) proposes a socialist-feminist critical theory built on the politics of need interpretation, and “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) brought the term “subaltern counterpublics” into critical theoretical discourse.
edges.evidence_note: University of Minnesota Press page: “Nancy Fraser develops a new and original socialist-feminist critical theory”; “the politics of need interpretation” as its “linchpin”. Mansbridge abstract (2017): the essay “brought the term ‘subaltern counterpublics’ into critical theoretical discourse”. Transversal (2007): public sphere theory is “an important critical-conceptual resource that should be reconstructed rather than jettisoned”. Fraser already has a frankfurt roster row (role critic) resting on fraser_sphere_primary; this is the first edge.

edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser argued that gender is a “bivalent collectivity” with both a political-economic and a cultural face, so that gender injustice requires both redistribution and recognition; her public-sphere critique had earlier exposed the masculinist bias in liberal views of what counts as a public concern.
edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text: p. 15, “Gender, I contend, is a bivalent collectivity”, encompassing “both political-economic dimensions and cultural-valuational dimensions”; “Understanding and redressing gender injustice requires attending to both distribution and recognition”; p. 17, “Gender, in sum, is a bivalent mode of collectivity”; p. 18, “Gender, we can now see, explodes this whole series of false antitheses.” Transversal (2007), her own summary of the 1990/1991 critique: “Exposing, too, the bourgeois masculinist bias in standard liberal views of what counts as a public concern”. A theoretical contribution to the analysis of gender, not historical research of her own. Distinct from existing edges gender → jurgen_habermas.

edges.relationship: In Subjects of Empire? (2009), Glen Coulthard criticises Fraser’s status model in Redistribution or Recognition? (2003) for insufficiently addressing the psychological dimensions of misrecognition, arguing that removing structural obstacles to participatory parity may leave those dimensions of domination intact.
edges.evidence_note: Read the repository dissertation’s printed pp. 52–57. Coulthard acknowledges the institutional model’s advantages but argues, through Fanon, that psychological injuries can persist independently. Specific critique only; Fraser’s 2003 book was not independently read here. Only scholarly argument is represented.
edges.map_label: Critiques the status model of recognition

edges.relationship: In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014), Fraser contributes to political economy by proposing to reconstruct the analysis of capitalism around gender, ecology and political power as well as production.
edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s visible opening through its initial account of capital accumulation. Fraser explicitly asks how capitalism should be conceptualized and proposes reconstructing inherited theory through these additional dimensions. The claim records this stated intervention only; the remainder requires subscription and was not read. Political economy is the existing economictheory endpoint; this does not assert that Fraser founded a field.

edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan grounds her question about how enslaved women understood their own commodification in Davis’s “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971), which she calls important work.
edges.evidence_note: Duke sample, introduction (“Refusing Demography”), p. 6, paragraph beginning “How does the concept of value”: “As early as 1971, the scholar and activist Angela Davis asked historians to consider the trauma that enslaved women experienced when they ‘had to surrender child-bearing to alien and predatory economic interests’” (n. 14); later in the paragraph, “To return to Davis’s important work, enslaved women were positioned to ‘attain a practical awareness’” of the slave owner’s power and dependence (n. 16). Body-text engagement in Morgan’s own framing of the book. The Morgan packet placed this on p. 7; the passage is on p. 6. Morgan’s chapters unread.

edges.relationship: In a 2020 interview (published 2021), Davis recalls studying with Adorno in Frankfurt, loving his lectures and reading his works “voraciously”, while criticising his view that students should immerse themselves in theory rather than activism.
edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138, paragraphs beginning “That is basically how I got hooked on philosophy” (Marcuse “suggested that I study with Adorno, Horkheimer, and Habermas”), “I did learn a great deal about working within the context of contradictions” (“I loved his lectures, read his works voraciously”; “critical of him for his failure to recognize that it was possible at that moment”) and “Many of us felt that this stance did not reflect” (an “immanent critique of his stand with respect to activism”). A stated debt and a stated disagreement in Davis’s own spoken words. Formal supervision by Adorno is not stated here and is not claimed. Adorno’s texts unread.
edges.map_label: Studied with Adorno; critical of his stance on activism

edges.relationship: Davis says she came to philosophy through the critical theory of Herbert Marcuse and the Frankfurt School, and that she has “certainly been inspired by critical theory” (interviews published 2005 and 2021).
edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138 (interview of 7 December 2020), paragraph beginning “That is basically how I got hooked on philosophy”: she was drawn to “critical theory, which was the approach taken by Marcuse and the Frankfurt School of philosophy”, rather than analytical philosophy; paragraph beginning “This is one of the things I really appreciate about critical theory”. Abolition Democracy (2005) excerpt on the Seven Stories blog, answer beginning “Well, I’ve certainly been inspired by critical theory”, in which she credits Marcuse with crossing “the disciplinary borders that separate philosophy, sociology, and literature” and Adorno with bringing “music and philosophy into the conversation”. Stated debt in her own words. Her doctoral work and Marcuse’s supervision are not documented on a permitted text read here (Marcuse has no endpoint).

edges.relationship: Davis closes “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) by quoting Du Bois’s Darkwater on Black women’s “revolutionary ideals”, and in Abolition Democracy (2005) says she has always preferred to identify with Du Bois’s pan-Africanism.
edges.evidence_note: (1) Massachusetts Review reprint, p. 100 (the essay’s last page): “Du Bois put it this way:” followed by a block quotation on “the up-working of new revolutionary ideals” among Black women, n. 46 “Du Bois, Darkwater, p. 185”. (2) Abolition Democracy excerpt (publisher’s blog), answer to “Do you think that there is a role for Black nationalism in the United States?”: “I’ve always preferred to identify with the pan-Africanism of W. E. B. Du Bois”, valued for its political, not racial, identification and its “Afro-Asian solidarities”. (3) Corroboration only: Crenshaw (2012), n. 1, says Davis’s account of the prison–industrial complex drew links to Du Bois’s assessment of Black imprisonment after Reconstruction (citing Women, Race & Class p. 89 on Black Reconstruction); that page is unread. Darkwater and Black Reconstruction not reread.
edges.map_label: Du Bois on Black women; Du Bois’s pan-Africanism

edges.relationship: In her contribution to Stuart Hall: Conversations, Projects and Legacies (2018), Davis argues, according to the publisher, that the model of politics, ideology and race developed by Hall and his Birmingham colleagues continues to resonate when applied to racialized policing in the United States.
edges.evidence_note: Goldsmiths Press description, paragraph beginning “Throughout these pages, Hall’s colleagues and long-term collaborators”: “North American activist Angela Davis argues that the model of politics, ideology, and race initially developed by Hall and his colleagues in Birmingham continues to resonate when applied to America’s racialized policing.” Publisher description only; the chapter (listed among counted works as “Policing the Crisis Today”, 2018) is unread. The claim is limited to what the description states.
edges.map_label: Hall’s model applied to US policing

edges.relationship: Davis recalls seriously reading The Communist Manifesto at fifteen, in a class taught by a Marxist history teacher, and says that “embracing Marxism came rather naturally” (interview 2020, published 2021).
edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138, paragraph beginning “My history teacher was a Marxist”: “At the age of 15, I seriously read The Communist Manifesto as a document we were studying in our class”; “Embracing Marxism came rather naturally.” She adds that it was not a moment of awakening but came “organically” from her upbringing and youth activism. A stated intellectual commitment in her own words, not a reading of specific Marxian arguments; the Manifesto is joint work with Engels. Thin; the coordinator may hold it if a self-described formation is judged too general.

edges.relationship: In Ruth Thrush’s account (2025), Davis’s Women, Race and Class (1981) is the most prominent critique of Federici’s wages-for-housework analysis: Thrush reads Davis as judging it reformist, because waged domestic workers already knew what wages for housework meant, and as proposing the socialization of housework instead.
edges.evidence_note: Tribune, 20 October 2025, paragraph beginning “Since the publication of”: “Most prominently, Angela Davis, in her 1981 Women, Race and Class, argues that Federici’s analysis is markedly reformist”; Davis on domestic workers who “know better than anyone else what it means to receive wages for housework” and on a wage that would “further legitimize” women’s “domestic slavery”; paragraph beginning “In the place of wages” (socialization of housework). Thrush also argues the two are “closer than is often thought”. Mediated through Thrush’s account; Women, Race and Class is unread, and whether the chapter names Federici herself (or only the campaign) was not checked. Federici’s reply, if any, not found.

edges.relationship: Saidiya Hartman (2016) writes that feminist thinkers, following the path cleared by Davis’s “groundbreaking” 1971 essay on Black women in the community of slaves, have considered the significance of gender, sexuality and reproduction in the constitutive relations of slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Hartman, “The Belly of the World”, authorised Vera List Center reprint, paragraph beginning “Black women’s labors have not been easy to reckon with conceptually”: “Feminist thinkers, following the path cleared by Angela Davis’ groundbreaking essay … have considered the significance of gender, sexuality and reproduction in defining the constitutive relations of slavery and the modes of its violence”, with n. 3 (Davis 1971 and two Hine articles). A named contribution in the body text of a substantive essay. Hartman does not discuss Davis’s argument further.

edges.relationship: Díaz Polegre and Torrado Martín-Palomino (2018) credit Davis with joining class to antiracist and antisexist perspectives in the 1970s, Women, Race and Class (1981) among the results, and name her among authors who had treated the concern before Crenshaw introduced the term intersectionality in 1989.
edges.evidence_note: Investigaciones Feministas 9(2), p. 294, paragraph beginning “Angela Davis, figura emblemática”: “Durante la década de los años setenta Davis realizó aportaciones significativas a la perspectiva feminista al enlazar la clase social con la perspectiva antirracista y antisexista … siendo uno de los frutos de estas aportaciones su libro Mujeres, raza y clase (1981)” (attributed to Curiel 2009, p. 41); p. 297: the concern “había sido tratada por autoras como Angela Davis o Gloria Anzaldúa” (after Cruells 2015, p. 34). A substantive open-access article that names her contribution, but its claims are mediated through the authors it cites. Women, Race and Class unread.
edges.map_label: Class, race and sex joined before the term

edges.relationship: Johnnetta Cole’s 1972 response calls Davis’s “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) a refutation of the Black matriarchy thesis’s “falsely assumed basis in slavery” and credits it with documenting enslaved women’s resistance, though written in prison from secondary sources only.
edges.evidence_note: Cole, “Affirmation of Resistance”, journal’s own PDF, p. 101: “The prime significance of the article is that it strikes at the heart of the so-called Black matriarchy issue through a refutation of its falsely assumed basis in slavery” (the myth “perpetuated in its fullest form by the ‘Moynihan Report’”); “the conditions of her imprisonment forced her to draw on secondary sources exclusively”; p. 103 (“In the cell of a California prison”). Davis’s own closing page (p. 100) corroborates the matriarchy argument. A substantive published response. Cole has no endpoint, so the claim is carried as a field contribution.

edges.relationship: In The Belly of the World: A Note on Black Women’s Labors (2016), Saidiya Hartman identifies Angela Davis’s Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves (1971) as a groundbreaking starting point for feminist analysis of gender, sexuality and reproduction in slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Read Hartman’s argument on the Vera List Center’s own publication page, which identifies its 2017 conference publication, the original 2016 Souls article and permission to reprint. The Davis paragraph expressly credits the essay before considering the difficulty of incorporating enslaved women’s reproductive and domestic labor into narratives of Black radicalism. Note 3 supplies the 1971 year. This is a specific intellectual engagement and credit, not a claim that Davis supervised Hartman. Hartman’s wording varies the essay title; the relationship uses the title supplied in the Davis input. The journal’s full-text endpoint returned 403; no text was obtained there.
edges.map_label: Hartman credits Davis’s analysis of enslaved women

edges.relationship: In the 2020 panel transcript Where Do We Go From Here, Robin D. G. Kelley credits Angela Davis’s Abolition Democracy (2005) with proposing a vision of abolition democracy for a Third Reconstruction, as he develops his account of that project.
edges.evidence_note: Read the opening question and Kelley’s first answer on Boston Review’s own transcript page. Kelley names Abolition Democracy, associates Davis’s argument with Du Bois’s abolition democracy and credits it in explaining his Third Reconstruction framework. He also credits William Barber; this is not an exclusive-origin claim. The 2005 original publication date was checked on Seven Stories Press’s book page. The complete Davis book was not read for this proposal.
edges.map_label: Kelley credits Abolition Democracy for a Third Reconstruction

edges.relationship: In “The Effort to Transform” (2017), written on Hall’s intellectual legacies, Ahmed says that reading Hall’s “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” during her PhD “changed everything”, taught her to think about identity from her own experience, and showed her how cultural studies could be turned on the university; though she spoke to him only once, she calls Hall her teacher through his texts.
edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s own 2017 essay, paragraphs on her PhD reading and the two closing paragraphs before the notes. She distinguishes Hall’s teaching through his words from having been taught by him personally and records only one conversation. This is stated intellectual debt, not supervision.
edges.map_label: Hall’s diaspora essay as a lifelong companion text

edges.relationship: In “The Effort to Transform” (2017) Ahmed names Angela Davis among the Black feminist writers whose texts “changed everything” for her during her PhD, and says that Davis and Stuart Hall made her aware of what it means to take race seriously as an object of thought.
edges.evidence_note: Same complete post. Opening paragraph: Ahmed introduced Davis at a 2014 conference on Hall’s legacies. Paragraph beginning “But then in the second year of my PhD I read a series of texts by black feminists and feminists of colour (including Angela Davis, Audre Lorde and Gloria Anzaldúa)”; paragraph beginning “Both Angela Davis and Stuart Hall made me aware of what it means to take race seriously as an object of thought.” Corroboration of engagement with Davis’s argument: “A Feminist Army” (2016), paragraph beginning “A call of arms is thus a recall”, uses Women, Race and Class on Sojourner Truth’s speech. Davis is named with Lorde and Anzaldúa; no claim that she is Ahmed’s only source. Davis’s books not reread here.
edges.map_label: Black feminist texts that changed everything

edges.relationship: Introducing a 2023 public conversation with Butler, Ahmed says she reused Butler’s definition of performativity from Bodies That Matter (1993) to describe what she called non-performativity, words such as “diversity” that do not bring into effect what they name, and that Butler’s work “keeps teaching” her.
edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s written introduction, posted on her own site on 26 July 2023, to a conversation with Butler at Cambridge on 28 April 2023. Paragraph beginning “A conversation needs a space. A conversation is a space”: “I think of how I reused your definition of performativity from Bodies that Matter to describe what I called non-performativity: how words do not bring into effect what they name (words like diversity, for instance).” Paragraph beginning “To be in conversation with someone else’s work”: “You keep teaching me in your work”. Paragraph beginning “And yes we do laugh”: “Judith taught me that we need to be in trouble”. A stated conceptual debt. Ahmed’s non-performativity essays and Bodies That Matter not reread here; the recorded conversation was not heard.

edges.relationship: Queer Phenomenology (2006) reads Fanon with Husserl, Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty in building a queer model of orientation; in a 2014 essay revisiting that book Ahmed writes that from Fanon “we learn about the experience of disorientation” under the white gaze.
edges.evidence_note: Duke University Press description of Queer Phenomenology: “she combines readings of phenomenological texts—by Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Fanon—with insights drawn from queer studies, feminist theory, critical race theory, Marxism, and psychoanalysis.” Ahmed, “Queer Angles” (2014), paragraph beginning “From Frantz Fanon, we learn about the experience of disorientation, as the experience of being an object amongst other objects”, citing Black Skin, White Masks; the preceding paragraph refers to the conclusion of Queer Phenomenology. Corroboration: “Being in Question” (2014), paragraphs beginning “When we are in question we question” (“This was after all how Frantz Fanon proceeded”) and “For Fanon, ontology is impossible.” The book itself and “A Phenomenology of Whiteness” (2007) are unread; the 2006 claim rests on the publisher description, the debt on Ahmed’s own 2014 essays.

edges.relationship: In the chapter on love in The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004), reproduced in her 2015 essay “Melancholic Universalism”, Ahmed criticises Kristeva’s Nations without Nationalism (1993), arguing that Kristeva’s abstract French national ideal in fact takes the shape of particular bodies and requires the veiled Muslim woman to give up her difference.
edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s own 2015 post reproduces her 2004 passage. Paragraph beginning “I first offered reflections on this theme in my book, The Cultural Politics of Emotion published over 10 years ago in 2004. It was in the chapter on love. I referred specifically to the work of Julia Kristeva.” Quoted passage: “However, the argument that the national idea is abstract (and the difference of the Muslim woman is concrete) breaks down”; “In Kristeva’s text, moving towards the abstract promise of the nation requires moving away from the veiled woman”. She also partly follows Kristeva (“I would follow Kristeva by arguing that the nation is hence an effect of how bodies move towards it”), so this is a qualified critique. Kristeva’s book not reread; the 2004 book read only in Ahmed’s reproduction.
edges.map_label: Kristeva’s national ideal is not abstract

edges.relationship: According to Julie Wuthnow’s 2002 review, Strange Encounters (2000) deploys Marx’s notion of commodity fetishism to link the representation of strangers to broader relationships of production, framing its argument as a critique of “stranger fetishism”.
edges.evidence_note: Sociological Research Online review, complete. Paragraph beginning “The notion that the Self constructs itself”: Ahmed augments the self–other approach first “through her deployment of Marx’s notion of commodity fetishism, which motivates her to attempt to ‘demonstrate the links between representation and broader relationships of production’ (61).” Opening paragraph quotes Ahmed (p. 6) on avoiding “stranger fetishism”. A reviewer’s account of the book’s method, with a page reference; the book is unread here.

edges.relationship: In “Feminist Killjoys” (2010) Ahmed places her figure of the feminist killjoy in the context of feminist critiques of happiness and quotes Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949) on how easy it is to call happy a situation in which one wishes to place others; a 2014 essay reports Beauvoir’s reading of Mrs Dalloway’s parties.
edges.evidence_note: S&F Online 8.3 (2010), section “Killjoys”, paragraph beginning “The figure of the feminist killjoy makes sense if we place her in the context of feminist critiques of happiness”: “As Simone de Beauvoir described so astutely ‘it is always easy to describe as happy a situation in which one wishes to place [others]’” (n. 4, The Second Sex, p. 28). “Dated Feminists” (2014), paragraph beginning “Much of the book is about an event that will happen”: “For Simone de Beauvoir, Mrs. Dalloway’s enjoyment of parties is read as a sign that she is trying to turn her ‘prison into glory’” (p. 554). Supplementary: Wuthnow’s 2002 review places Strange Encounters in a self–other line of social theory running from The Second Sex and Orientalism, which Ahmed “augments”. THIN: two body-text uses of Beauvoir as a resource for one argument, not a stated debt; flag for the outside reviewers. The Promise of Happiness itself unread.

edges.relationship: Queer Phenomenology (2006) proposes a queer model of orientations, examining how bodies are directed toward some objects and away from others and how queerness reorders those spatial relations; Ahmed’s 2014 essay “Queer Angles” extends its account of bodies “out of line”.
edges.evidence_note: Duke description (a single paragraph beginning “In this groundbreaking work, Sara Ahmed demonstrates how queer studies can put phenomenology to productive use”): “A queer phenomenology, Ahmed contends, reveals how social relations are arranged spatially, how queerness disrupts and reorders these relations by not following the accepted paths”; “Queer Phenomenology points queer theory in bold new directions.” “Queer Angles” (2014), paragraph beginning “By implication, then”: “I observed in the conclusion to Queer Phenomenology, how we can become what disorientates the picture, a body out of line.” Publisher description plus the author’s own restatement; book unread. Contribution to queer theory, not a claim about historians’ use of it.

edges.relationship: In “Killing Joy: Feminism and the History of Happiness” (Signs, 2010) Ahmed suspends the belief that happiness is good, a belief she treats as central to the intellectual history of happiness, and proposes that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness; The Promise of Happiness (2010) works through that intellectual history.
edges.evidence_note: Goldsmiths repository abstract of the Signs article: “It proceeds by suspending belief that happiness is a good thing, or that happiness is what we want, as beliefs that are central to the intellectual history of happiness. The article suggests that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness.” Duke description of The Promise of Happiness: “Ahmed draws on the intellectual history of happiness, from classical accounts of ethics as the good life” through nineteenth-century utilitarianism. Abstract and publisher description only; article body unread (DOI page 403, JSTOR JavaScript wall). The atlas node already notes that Ahmed’s affect inquiry needs separate research; this edge claims only her proposal of a feminist history of happiness, not adoption by historians of emotion.

edges.relationship: Ahmed describes taking the tools of cultural studies, learned from Stuart Hall, into ethnographic research on diversity work in universities, treating the university as a place to work on as well as at; the publisher describes The Promise of Happiness (2010) as combining philosophy and feminist cultural studies.
edges.evidence_note: “The Effort to Transform” (2017), paragraph beginning “I take seriously Stuart Hall’s suggestion”: “I began to think of how cultural studies provides the tools to interrogate the university as a place to work on as well as work at”; paragraph beginning “Why practical phenomenology?”: “This is what I learnt from doing ethnographic research on diversity within universities.” Duke description of The Promise of Happiness: “Combining philosophy and feminist cultural studies”. Self-description plus publisher description; On Being Included (2012) not read.
edges.map_label: Cultural studies turned on the university

edges.relationship: Strange Encounters: Embodied Others in Post-Coloniality (2000) argues that the stranger is not simply whoever is unfamiliar but a figure produced by processes of inclusion and exclusion; Julie Wuthnow’s 2002 review called it an original contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory, while judging that its closing chapter on global feminism underplays the power and antagonism stressed earlier.
edges.evidence_note: Sociological Research Online review, complete. Opening paragraph: “makes an original and insightful contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory”; Ahmed quoted (p. 6): “we need to consider how the stranger is an effect of processes of inclusion and exclusion”. Fourth paragraph, beginning “Finally, I found that her most ‘visionary’ chapter”: the reviewer’s criticism of the global-feminism chapter. A reviewer’s assessment; book unread.

edges.relationship: In Witness to History: Conversation with Leading Scholars (2020; transcript posted in 2021), Adele Perry draws on Sara Ahmed’s politics of citation to propose changing whose perspectives historians read and elevate in their research and teaching.
edges.evidence_note: Read Perry’s answer and surrounding discussion in the organizer-publisher’s transcript. Perry explicitly attributes the idea to Ahmed and explains its use in choosing whose scholarship receives attention. This supports a specific methodological uptake, not a claim about Perry’s whole historical project. Perry names no particular Ahmed publication, so none is supplied. The accompanying event page dates the discussion to 26 November 2020 and its online posting to 9 February 2021.
edges.map_label: Politics of citation applied to historians’ practice

edges.relationship: In 'More-Than-Human Emotional Communities' (2020), Thomas Webb, Chris Pearson, Penny Summerfield and Mark Riley invoke Sara Ahmed's insight from 'Affective Economies' (2004) that 'emotions do things' to explain how soldier–mule bonds helped sustain British forces in Burma.
edges.evidence_note: Read the abstract and introductory methodological discussion, numbered pp. 1–5, in Summerfield’s institutional repository. The body explicitly uses Ahmed’s insight to explain the practical effects of soldier–mule bonds, and note 14 identifies the source. The claim belongs to the four authors collectively; it is not evidence of Summerfield’s individual contribution to the coauthored argument. The manuscript distinguishes this use from its central borrowing of Rosenwein’s emotional-community concept. The complete article and Ahmed’s cited article were not read for this edge.
edges.map_label: Affective economies applied to soldier–mule bonds

edges.relationship: In “The Uses and Abuses of ‘Neoliberalism’” (2018) Rodgers takes Brown’s Undoing the Demos (2015) as the exemplar of the most enveloping use of the term, neoliberalism as a governing rationality, and argues that its language of exhaustion and collapse, and categories stretched so wide, may make a workable politics harder to see.
edges.evidence_note: Complete essay read in a Wayback capture of Dissent’s own page. Paragraph beginning “Neoliberalism (4), the latest entry into this parade”: “In the terms Wendy Brown takes from Foucault in her witheringly critical Undoing the Demos (2015), neoliberalism is … the ‘governing rationality’ of our times.” Paragraph beginning “Many of those who have written most acutely”: Brown is quoted on neoliberalism as “inconstant” and “plastic”. Paragraph beginning “At its extreme, bundling the ills”: “There is grit in her Undoing the Demos. But a language of pessimism … runs through it … Or perhaps it is that the distended categories make a workable politics all the harder to perceive.” Rodgers also calls her “one of the leading public intellectual activists of our day”: a respectful but pointed critique. Brown did not respond in the Dissent forum that followed; her response, if any, was not sought.

edges.relationship: In a 2022 Dissent interview Brown says that Foucault, among others, taught her generation to think of neoliberalism not as a set of policies but as a form of governmental reason that shapes conduct across every dimension of life; Daniel T. Rodgers (2018) likewise describes Undoing the Demos (2015) as using terms Brown takes from Foucault.
edges.evidence_note: Interview, Brown’s first answer, paragraph beginning “Foucault, among others, taught us to think about neoliberalism as more than a set of policies, and rather as a form of governmental reason.” Rodgers (2018), paragraph beginning “Neoliberalism (4)”: “In the terms Wendy Brown takes from Foucault”. Brown’s own words (“taught us”) state the debt as shared, not as hers alone. Undoing the Demos and its chapter on Foucault’s lectures are unread.

edges.relationship: In her introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) Brown argues that Marx’s distinction between “mere criticism” of religion and critique of the conditions that produce it is the move that bound critique to secularism in Western critical theory, a heritage she says the volume’s question upends.
edges.evidence_note: Brown’s introduction, complete. P. 10, section “Uncritical Secularism”: “we must consider Marx’s own development of critique out of what he took to be the shortcomings of the Young Hegelians’ critical approach to religion … This is the move that really secures the conviction that critique is secular in the Western critical theory tradition.” Pp. 10–11 expound Marx (n. 5–6, Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right, Introduction). Pp. 11–12: “It is this particular heritage from Marx, and the way it threads through German critical theory right up through Habermas, that has so overdetermined the imbrication … of critique with secularism”; p. 12: the question “upends one of critical theory’s founding planks”. A genealogical critique of what critical theory inherited from Marx, not a rejection of Marx’s analysis as such.

edges.relationship: Brown’s introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) draws on Koselleck’s Critique and Crisis (1959; cited in the 1988 English translation) for its history of the word: critique emerging in ancient Athens as the jurisprudential krisis and narrowing as it passed into Latin and the European vernaculars.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 8, section “Critique . . .”: “From Reinhart Kosellek’s Critique and Crisis, we learn that critique emerges in ancient Athens as the jurisprudential term krisis” (name so spelled in the text), followed by a paraphrase of Koselleck’s account; n. 2 cites Critique and Crisis (1988 English edition) and notes that Asad offers a different etymology. A body-text use of Koselleck’s argument in one section of a short introduction; no broader debt claimed.
edges.map_label: Koselleck’s krisis in Brown’s genealogy of critique

edges.relationship: Brown’s work draws on Nietzsche from States of Injury (1995), which its publisher says weaves Nietzsche together with Marx, Weber and Foucault to analyse how woundedness became a basis for political identity, to the final chapter of In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019), which a reviewer describes as working on a Nietzschean basis to return to the politics of resentment.
edges.evidence_note: Princeton description of States of Injury (Wayback capture): “She also develops an original theoretical practice that weaves together Nietzsche, Marx, Weber, Foucault, and cultural theories of gender and race”. McManus, Radical Philosophy 208 (2020), paragraph beginning “The book’s last chapter returns Brown to the politics of resentment she has been probing since States of Injury decades ago”: “Chapter Five operates on a more Nietzschean basis”; paragraph beginning “Brown´s reading in this concluding chapter”: “crucial as Nietzsche is to her work”, with McManus’s criticism that she largely ignores religious concerns about transcendent meaning. Publisher description and a reviewer’s account; neither book read, and “Wounded Attachments” (1993) not reached.
edges.map_label: Nietzsche and the politics of ressentiment

edges.relationship: In her response in Is Critique Secular? (2009) Butler adopts the distinction between critique and criticism that Brown drew in the volume’s introduction, and credits Brown with showing that Marx’s formulation of critique has its own history in religious metaphor and structure.
edges.evidence_note: Butler, “The Sensibility of Critique: Response to Asad and Mahmood”, p. 107, section “Criticism, Critique, and Formations of the Subject”: “As Wendy Brown has pointed out in the introduction to this volume, the distinction between ‘critique’ and ‘criticism’ is an important one. I would gloss that distinction in the following way”. P. 125: “the formulation of critique in Marx is not, as Wendy Brown has shown, without its own history and legacy in religious metaphor and structure”, n. 20 citing Brown, “The Sacred, the Secular, and the Profane: Charles Taylor and Karl Marx” (2009, forthcoming). Body-text engagement in a co-authored volume; the four authors’ co-credit itself is not counted as the relationship. The cited Brown essay is unread.
edges.map_label: Butler takes up Brown’s critique/criticism distinction

edges.relationship: States of Injury (1995), in its publisher’s description, offers a sympathetic critique of identity politics, exploring how woundedness became a basis for contemporary political identity and how the conditions that formed such identities constrain emancipatory desire.
edges.evidence_note: Princeton description: “A sympathetic critique that attempts to free Left politics from its own snares, States of Injury explores how woundedness became a basis for contemporary political identity. Without condemning identity politics, Wendy Brown carefully probes the varied historical forces generating them today and the ways these formative conditions constrain emancipatory desire.” McManus (2020) confirms that she has been probing the politics of resentment “since States of Injury”. Publisher description only; the book is unread. The edge concerns identity politics as a political form, which the atlas node treats under Hunt’s “identity politics” grouping; it does not claim a critique of historians’ identity histories.

edges.relationship: Opening a Berkeley critical theory programme meant to bridge European and non-Western critical theory, Brown’s introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) argues that the identification of critique with secularism, inherited from Marx and threaded through German critical theory up to Habermas, is one of critical theory’s founding planks, and that the volume’s question upends it.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 7: the symposium was “the inaugural public event for a new research and teaching program in critical theory at Berkeley, a program that aims to bridge conventional divides between modern European critical theory and non-Western and post-Enlightenment critical theoretical projects”. Pp. 11–12: the Marx heritage “threads through German critical theory right up through Habermas”; p. 12: “this question upends one of critical theory’s founding planks”, while allowing “other formulations of critique”. Context: McManus (2020) notes her use of Marcuse’s “repressive desublimation” in In the Ruins of Neoliberalism; the 2022 interview defines critical theory broadly. A critique from within critical theory, not a rejection of it.

edges.relationship: Nihilistic Times: Thinking with Max Weber (2023) is, in Samuel Moyn’s review, a meditation on Weber’s lectures on scholarship and politics as vocations that argues for a critical retrieval of Weber’s insistence on separating scholarship from politics, while staying wary of his longing for charismatic leadership.
edges.evidence_note: Moyn, Critical Inquiry, 1 February 2024 (one-paragraph review): “Wendy Brown’s exquisite meditation on Max Weber’s classic lectures on knowledge and politics as vocations”; “Sensibly, Brown argues for a critical retrieval of Weber’s insistence on the isolation of scholarship from politics, though on different grounds”; “Brown insists on much more wariness of Weber’s inchoate longing for charismatic leadership”. Moyn doubts that the present is as close to Weber’s world as Brown suggests. A reviewer’s account; the book (published in the Tanner Lectures on Human Values series, per search listings) is unread.
edges.map_label: A critical retrieval of Weber’s vocation lectures

edges.relationship: In the abstract for his lecture ‘Seeing Red: Recognition, Reconciliation & Resentment in Indigenous Politics’ (2012), Glen Coulthard challenges the argument he attributes to Wendy Brown and Saul Newman that ressentiment risks reproducing emancipatory movements’ powerlessness, arguing instead that resentment can be legitimate and politically transformative under continuing colonial domination.
edges.evidence_note: Read the complete lecture abstract on Fernwood Publishing’s own event page. It explicitly attributes the powerlessness argument to Brown and Newman, announces an engagement with that argument, and presents Coulthard’s contrary claims about the legitimacy and transformative possibilities of resentment. This is an abstract-level critique, not evidence that the lecture recording or Red Skin, White Masks (2014) was read. The abstract does not identify a particular Brown publication, so none is supplied here. The event header and body differ over the January day; both give 2012, the only date used in the relationship. The claim concerns published political scholarship only; no community knowledge or personal identity information is reproduced.

edges.relationship: Regulating Aversion: Tolerance in the Age of Identity and Empire (2006), as described by its publisher, contributes to postcolonial critique by arguing that tolerance discourse can distinguish a civilized West from a barbaric Islam and thereby justify Western imperial violence.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher description and bibliographic information in Google Books’ record of the 2006 Princeton University Press edition; also checked the description in its 2009 edition record. The description specifically connects tolerance’s civilizational hierarchy to the Iraq war, the War on Terror, and imperialism. The book’s chapters were not read. Assignment to the existing Postcolonial history / critique endpoint is an editorial mapping of this specific argument, not a claim that the source calls Brown a member of a school or establishes reception by particular historians. This is distinct from the input’s existing identity-politics and critical-theory pairs.

edges.relationship: Jacob and Joyce Appleby coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Lynn Hunt.
edges.evidence_note: Substantive monograph coauthorship; author metadata only. The separate 1994 record establishes original year; Norton displays the 1995 paperback.

edges.relationship: Jacob and Lynn Hunt coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Joyce Appleby.
edges.evidence_note: Substantive monograph coauthorship; author metadata only. Same three-author book as mcj_n_01; no claim about division of chapters.

edges.relationship: Recalling The Radical Enlightenment (1981) in her 2014 retrospective, Jacob credits Hill’s account of religious and political radicalism within the English Revolution.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit intellectual debt in Jacob’s own retrospective. No particular Hill book is identified; the 1981 original is unread.

edges.relationship: In her 2014 retrospective on The Radical Enlightenment (1981), Jacob recalls developing its dialectical approach through conversations with Pocock.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit recollection of conceptual formation; no publication by Pocock or date of conversation is inferred.

edges.relationship: In “How Radical was the Enlightenment?” (2014), Jacob criticizes Israel’s Radical Enlightenment (2001) for centring Spinoza and effacing political context.
edges.evidence_note: Direct, named criticism. Jacob also acknowledges the need to revise her own earlier account; neither original monograph is newly read.

edges.relationship: In The First Knowledge Economy (2014), Jacob adopts Mokyr’s focus on a small community exchanging technical knowledge, citing The Gifts of Athena (2002).
edges.evidence_note: Body engagement, followed by explicit adoption; note 14 identifies Mokyr’s book and p. 66. Mokyr’s original book unread.

edges.relationship: In “The Left, Right and Science” (2013), Jacob criticizes Latour’s approach for failing to explain historically specific religious motives in seventeenth-century science.
edges.evidence_note: Primary criticism distinguishes religious commitments from money and power. The 1998 chapter and Latour’s originals remain unread.

edges.relationship: Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West (1997) connects scientific knowledge with European culture, entrepreneurs and engineers.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description only; it identifies a substantive approach to the history of science. No whole-book reading claimed.

edges.relationship: With Appleby and Hunt, Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) defends accountable historical inquiry while accepting some criticism of historical authority.
edges.evidence_note: Joint argument as described by the publisher. Existing roster membership retained; chapters and specific philosophical debts unread.

edges.relationship: In “The Left, Right and Science” (2013), Jacob advocates contextual explanations of anti-science positions that distinguish religious commitments from profit motives.
edges.evidence_note: An explicit intervention in the science wars, distinct from the specific Latour criticism. Existing roster membership retained.

edges.relationship: The First Knowledge Economy (2014) explains industrial development through mechanical knowledge and the institutions that circulated it.
edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction read; claim records Jacob’s explanation rather than treating it as a settled causal finding.

edges.relationship: In his ‘Author’s response’ (2016) to ‘The Enlightenment as Modernity: Jonathan Israel’s Interpretation Across Two Decades’, Jonathan Israel criticised Margaret C. Jacob’s emphasis on Toland’s republican originality, arguing that Toland adopted Spinoza’s philosophical system.
edges.evidence_note: Read Israel’s response on the review journal’s own page. This is Israel’s explicit criticism of Jacob, not an inference from their differing subjects or a review of Jacob’s book. The passage does not identify a particular Jacob title, so none is assigned to the criticism. The year refers to the response itself.

edges.relationship: Jacob’s The Radical Enlightenment: Pantheists, Freemasons, and Republicans (1981) helped shape Enlightenment historiography through its category of radical Enlightenment, which Diego Lucci describes as highly influential and subsequently reformulated by Jonathan Israel.
edges.evidence_note: Read Lucci’s review, especially its substantive discussion of the category and note 7 identifying Jacob’s 1981 book. The endpoint is the existing intellectual-history field; no new Enlightenment endpoint is created. This records reception of a category, without claiming Jacob was its first user in all languages. The reviewed collection and Jacob’s book remain unread.
edges.map_label: Radical Enlightenment as a historical category

edges.relationship: Hudson and Maxine Berg coauthored Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023).
edges.evidence_note: The authors introduce their substantive joint monograph. Publication and coauthorship only; no inference of influence between the coauthors. Book body unread.

edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s “Slavery, Atlantic trade and skills” (2021) challenges Mokyr’s supply-side skills explanation, arguing that slave-based Atlantic demand better explains industrialisation’s timing and regional concentration.
edges.evidence_note: Joint response read at pp. 260–261 and 275–276. The authors retain a role for skilled artisans. Their objection concerns causal stimulus, timing and geography; Mokyr’s original lecture is unread.
edges.map_label: Atlantic demand challenges a skills-first explanation

edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution (1990 working paper) questions causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s national demographic aggregates, emphasizing regional and social variation.
edges.evidence_note: Selected working-paper pages 30–33 read, including the acknowledgment of Schofield’s subsequent revision. This supports a qualified methodological criticism, not a rejection of population reconstruction. The preliminary paper is not substituted for the unread 1992 journal body.

edges.relationship: In “Slavery, the slave trade and economic growth” (2014), Hudson re-examines Williams’s account of slavery and British industrialisation through regional and sectoral analysis, as described in the publisher’s chapter summary.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher summary only. It establishes a named reassessment, not agreement with every Williams thesis. Full chapter and Williams’s book unread in this task. Original 2014 distinguished from the later platform date.
edges.map_label: Reassesses Williams on slavery and industrialisation

edges.relationship: In The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986), Hudson connects West Riding domestic industry and factory transition to agrarian structures and changing landholding, according to the publisher’s summary.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter summary read; empirical chapters unread. The claim concerns this regional explanation, not a national test or endorsement of the entire proto-industrialisation thesis.

edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution (1990 working paper) makes women’s and children’s work, wage differentials and work discipline central to explaining industrial change.
edges.evidence_note: Selected labour-force section pp. 20–23 read. A substantive intervention on gendered labour, not a claim that Hudson founded gender history. The 1992 journal body is unread.
edges.map_label: Women’s and children’s work in industrial change

edges.relationship: History by Numbers (2000) presents quantitative methods through historical problems and data, explaining their purposes and interpretive pitfalls, according to the publisher’s description.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description and first-edition metadata only. This is a bounded methodological contribution; examples and calculations in the book were not independently read or replicated. No co-credit relationship is proposed from this textbook.

edges.relationship: In Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023), Berg and Hudson argue that slavery shaped British production, consumption, investment and enduring inequalities.
edges.evidence_note: Authors’ full account of their book read. Joint attribution retained. No claim that slavery was a sufficient or necessary sole cause; the monograph is unread.
edges.map_label: Slavery and the structures of British capitalism

edges.relationship: In the 2011 working-paper version of ‘The Lure of Aggregates’, Humphries builds on Berg's The Age of Manufactures (1985; cited in the 1994 edition), quoting its finding that machines and processes were invented with female and child labour in mind, to explain innovation that bypassed artisan controls.
edges.evidence_note: Oxford institutional working paper, July 2011, pp. 24–26 and associated notes read. Body text explicitly deploys Berg’s finding in its alternative account of innovation; n. 73 identifies the quotation as Berg, 1994 edition, p. 147. That edition and Berg’s other works were not independently read. The 2011 draft is not represented as the final 2013 article.
edges.map_label: Uses Berg on machinery and family labour (2011)

edges.relationship: In her review of Emma Griffin’s Bread Winner (2020), Humphries uses de Vries’s The Industrious Revolution (2008) on the value of domestic comforts to question whether rising male wages necessarily devalued homemakers’ contributions.
edges.evidence_note: Open review’s argument and bibliography read. De Vries’s account is used to counter a specific household mechanism attributed to Griffin. The 2008 book is not independently read here; the relationship is this documented argumentative use in 2020.
edges.map_label: Uses de Vries on valued domestic labour (2020)

edges.relationship: In her review of Bread Winner (2020), Humphries uses Mokyr’s ‘More Work for Mother? Knowledge and Household Behavior, 1870–1945’ (2000) to explain how knowledge about infection increased the value of cleanliness and housework.
edges.evidence_note: Read in the body of Humphries’s open review immediately after the de Vries paragraph. This is a specific explanatory use within her objection to the devaluation hypothesis, not an inference from a reference list. Mokyr’s original article was not independently read for this packet.
edges.map_label: Uses Mokyr on knowledge and housework (2020)

edges.relationship: In ‘Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women’ (1990), Humphries argues that loss of common rights changed women’s position within families and increased families’ dependence on wages because women and children had been their principal users.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract and original issue metadata read: Journal of Economic History 50(1), March 1990, pp. 17–42. Full article not read. Claim stays within the abstract’s stated argument; the online posting date of 2009 is not the original publication year.
edges.map_label: Connects common rights to women’s dependence (1990)

edges.relationship: In ‘Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution’ (2013), Humphries links an upsurge in children’s work to mechanization, work organization and vulnerable family economies, using working men’s autobiographies.
edges.evidence_note: Abstract and issue metadata read: Economic History Review 66(2), May 2013, pp. 395–418; first online in 2012. This article is distinct from the 2010 monograph. Its body was not read; no independent audit of the autobiographical data is claimed.
edges.map_label: Explains the expansion of child labour (2013)

edges.relationship: In ‘The Lure of Aggregates and the Pitfalls of the Patriarchal Perspective’ (2013), Humphries criticizes the high-wage explanation of British industrialisation for treating male earnings as family welfare and proposes cheap female and child labour as an alternative stimulus to innovation.
edges.evidence_note: Final article’s abstract and metadata read. The existing graph source already supports this bounded claim; reuse cd_humphries_2013. Selected passages in the separate 2011 working paper were also read. Do not conflate its pagination with pp. 693–714 of the final article. The existing field roster row is retained; there is no existing edge to duplicate.

edges.relationship: In ‘“…The Most Free From Objection …” The Sexual Division of Labor and Women's Work in Nineteenth-Century England’ (1987), Humphries contributes to women's history by arguing that the control of sexuality helped shape employment segregation, supplementing explanations based on childbearing and changes in production.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher abstract and issue metadata. The abstract identifies sexual control as an additional explanation for occupational segregation and says the argument is tested through regional correlations. The article body and statistical results remain unread; this edge records the stated intervention, without endorsing its causal inference. Women's history is an editorial field mapping to the documented argument about women's work. This work and endpoint pair are absent from the supplied input and from the earlier Humphries entry draft consulted for an additional duplicate check.
edges.map_label: Explains women's employment segregation through sexual control (1987)

edges.relationship: In ‘Careworn: The Economic History of Caring Labor’ (2024), Humphries contributes to quantitative history by using historical maintenance costs and commodity living costs to estimate paid domestic services, then imputing and aggregating the value of unpaid household labour.
edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's open abstract, publication metadata and introduction through the paragraph beginning ‘In closing’. The introduction explains comparison of maintenance costs with a commodity basket, regression controls for heterogeneous evidence, and aggregation over households without domestic servants. Later empirical sections, tables and calculations were not audited. The claim concerns her stated estimation procedure, not the accuracy of its totals or adoption by other scholars. Quantitative history is an editorial mapping to this explicit historical estimation method; no claim that she founded the method or field is made.
edges.map_label: Estimates and aggregates unpaid domestic labour (2024)

edge_1804.relationship: As Hannah Tandy documents from Woodward’s 1938 letter, Black Reconstruction supplied an acknowledged scholarly debt.

edge_1886.relationship: As Buckner reconstructs the 1997 argument, Owram calls for studying how regional and local identities interact within a shared national experience while rejecting a return to a patriotic elite’s master narrative.

edge_1970.relationship: Wood objects that Turner’s 1895 account of American origins leaves Indigenous people outside its historical explanation.

edge_2275.relationship: Winter challenges Ferguson’s confident counterfactual account of British nonintervention in 1914 as exceeding the available evidence.

edge_2357.relationship: Questions the internalist/externalist division associated with Kuhn’s 1968 history-of-science essay, treating the boundary itself as a historical problem.

edge_2527.relationship: Foner credits Thompson’s social history with helping him integrate ideas and social conflict, and uses The Making of the English Working Class to link class formation with political exclusion and the struggle for the vote.

edge_2530.relationship: Foner criticizes the exaggerated elitism and distrust of mass politics in Hofstadter’s accounts of Populism and reform, while crediting their analytical innovations and distinguishing his critical consensus history from celebratory versions.

edge_2531.relationship: Foner questions whether White’s Greater Reconstruction framework homogenizes federal action in the South and West, and argues that its emphasis on defeat and violence gives too little attention to Black political leaders.

edge_2536.relationship: Furet disputes Marx’s account of the Terror as a plebeian way of completing the bourgeois revolution, arguing that its essential transformation was already achieved in 1789–1791.

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and, as AHA president (2012; presidential address January 2013), 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'

rationale: The timeline drew its person entries mainly by dissertation-citation counts, which left it 75% men and structurally under-ranked the founders of women's and gender history. This revision adds women historians and theorists with verified relationships in both directions, so they sit inside the network rather than at its edge.
